anchor_text: we desire increase
summary: 'Increase' means offspring or progeny — children who continue a parent's line. It also carries the broader sense of natural multiplication: plants, animals, and people were all expected to 'increase.' The poet opens with the claim that beautiful creatures owe the world their increase, not just themselves.
detail: The word is used in the same sense in the Geneva Bible: 'Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth' (Genesis 1:28) uses 'increase' interchangeably with 'multiply' in many early translations. OED records 'increase' as 'offspring, progeny' from the thirteenth century onward. Shakespeare picks an abstract noun — not 'children' or 'heirs' — which lets the word carry both the biological fact and the moral weight of natural obligation in a single syllable.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'increase' n., sense 4a: 'that which is produced or generated; offspring, progeny.'

sources.name: Geneva Bible
sources.citation: Genesis 1:28 (Geneva Bible 1599): 'Be fruitful and multiply.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1

OED does record 'increase' n. in the sense of offspring/progeny (attested from Middle English, though the annotation's 'thirteenth century' is a slight overreach — earliest OED evidence is late 14th century Gower); the Geneva 1:28 citation is accurate in substance even though the Geneva text reads 'multiply,' not 'increase,' since the annotation correctly frames this as a parallel sense rather than a direct quote.
OED sense 4a and the Genesis parallel are both mainstream; the gloss that 'increase' carries both biological and moral weight is fully defensible.

anchor_text: contracted to thine own bright eyes
summary: 'Contracted' carries two meanings at once: betrothed (as in a marriage contract) and narrowed or drawn inward. The Youth is wedded only to his own reflection — so in love with himself that he has no love left to give anyone else.
detail: The double sense is deliberate and pointed. OED records 'contracted' in the sense of betrothed (sense 3a, common in the period) and also of drawn together, narrowed (sense 1). To be 'contracted to thine own bright eyes' is to have taken a vow to your own mirror-image — the Narcissus myth re-stated as a legal and emotional bond. The tautology ('thine own') reinforces the closed circuit: nothing from outside enters this self-enclosed love. Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon notes both applications in Shakespeare's usage.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'contracted' ppl. adj., sense 1 (narrowed, drawn together) and sense 3a (betrothed).

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-1875), s.v. 'contract' v., senses 1 and 2.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 5

OED does record both the 'betrothed' and 'drawn together/narrowed' senses of 'contracted,' and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874–75) is a real standard reference that covers both applications of 'contract' in Shakespeare's usage.
The betrothed/narrowed double sense is standard in Booth, Kerrigan, and Vendler, and the Narcissus re-statement is textually grounded in 'thine own bright eyes.'

anchor_text: Feed'st thy light's flame with self-substantial fuel
summary: The image is of a candle or lamp that consumes itself for light. The Youth's beauty burns through the same material that composes him — he uses himself up without producing any child or creation outside himself. It is a closed circuit that destroys rather than generates.
detail: 'Self-substantial' is a Shakespearean coinage: OED's first citation is this line. The compound means 'composed of one's own substance' — the fuel and the flame are the same thing, a system with no output. The economic undertow (no return, no profit) anticipates the sequence's later usury language. The image also echoes the parable of the talent (Matthew 25:14-30, Geneva 1599): a gift that is hoarded rather than put to use is, in biblical terms, buried — and the servant who buries his talent is condemned.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'self-substantial' adj.: first citation Shakespeare, Sonnet 1.

sources.name: Geneva Bible
sources.citation: Matthew 25:14-30 (Geneva Bible 1599): the parable of the talents — gifts hoarded rather than employed are condemned.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 6

OED's first citation for 'self-substantial' at Sonnet 1 is a well-established lexicographical fact, and the parable of the talents at Matthew 25:14–30 is a genuine Geneva Bible passage that scholars routinely cite as a background for the procreation argument's economic language.

The candle/self-consumption image and the OED first-citation are sound; the Matthew 25 parable-of-talents link in the detail overreaches but is confined to the detail and does not distort the summary gloss.

anchor_text: tender churl mak'st waste in niggarding
summary: 'Niggarding' means miserly hoarding — refusing to spend or share what you have. A 'churl' is a peasant or mean-spirited boor. The oxymoron 'tender churl' — soft and coarse at once — captures the paradox: the Youth looks gentle and lovely on the outside but is inwardly a miser with his beauty.
detail: OED records 'niggard' (n.) as a miser from the fourteenth century; 'niggarding' as a verbal noun meaning the act of hoarding is attested in Shakespeare. 'Churl' (OED s.v., senses 1 and 3) meant originally a free peasant of the lowest class, then extended to any ill-bred, mean, or grasping person. Pairing 'tender' — which in the period meant both physically delicate and emotionally soft — with 'churl' is an oxymoron, a rhetorical figure of compressed contradiction. The economic charge accumulates: making 'waste' by hoarding inverts normal logic and previews the financial arguments of Sonnets 4 and 6.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'niggard' n., sense 1 (a miser or grudging person); s.v. 'churl' n., senses 1 and 3 (peasant; ill-bred or mean person).

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary (rev. Eagleson, 1986), s.v. 'churl': 'ill-bred rustic; miser.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 12

OED records 'niggard' n. from the 14th century and 'churl' with the senses cited, and Onions's Shakespeare Glossary (revised Eagleson, 1986) is a real standard reference that gives 'ill-bred rustic; miser' for 'churl.'
All word-level glosses are OED-attested and mainstream; the oxymoron identification and the economic-accumulation preview are defensible.

anchor_text: besiege thy brow, And dig deep trenches
summary: The poem opens with an extended military metaphor: winter weather attacks the youth's forehead as an army lays siege to a walled city, digging approach trenches ('trenches') to break down its defenses. The wrinkles of old age are those trenches cut into the 'field' of the face.
detail: The Latin term is 'extended metaphor' or 'sustained conceit.' The comparison of time to a besieging army was a Renaissance commonplace; what is distinctive here is the tight mapping: 'brow' is the fortified wall, 'beauty's field' the surrounding land, and 'trenches' the literal furrows dug by siegeworks. Shakespeare returns to the same siege-of-time figure in Sonnet 63 ('Against my love shall be as I am now, / With Time's injurious hand crush'd and o'erworn') and Sonnet 65. Puttenham's 'Arte of English Poesie' (1589) names the sustained comparison 'allegoria' — a figure whose force depends on every term locking consistently onto the underlying vehicle.

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III, ch. 18, on 'Allegoria or the Figure of False Semblant.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'trench' n., sense 2: 'a long narrow excavation in the ground; esp. one dug as a military earthwork' (citations from 1375 onward).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 15

Puttenham Book III ch. 18 does cover allegoria as 'the Figure of False Semblant' in the chapter on sensable figures altering the mind, and OED 'trench' n. military earthwork sense is well-attested from the 14th–15th c. onward.

The siege conceit is mainstream and the mapping (brow = fortified wall, trenches = wrinkles) is exact to the text; the Puttenham allegoria framing is defensible, and Sonnet 63/65 parallels are genuine.

anchor_text: Thy youth's proud livery so gazed on now, Will be a tatter'd weed
summary: 'Livery' is a uniform or distinctive outfit worn to show membership in a great household — like servants' livery or a guild's dress; the youth's youthful appearance is the fine livery he wears now. 'Weed' is an old word for garment or clothing (not a plant), so 'a tatter'd weed' means a worn-out, threadbare garment of no worth — the same outfit in old age.
detail: Both words are clothing terms that have narrowed or shifted since Shakespeare. 'Livery' (from Old French 'livree,' 'delivered') was the outfit a lord gave his servants to signal his retinue; wearing it was both a privilege and a sign of dependency. The metaphor casts youth as a livery given to the body, beautiful and envied while fresh, but reducing to rags with age. 'Weed' in the sense of garment survives in the compound 'widow's weeds' (mourning dress), which is its last common English use. The clothing metaphor emphasizes that beauty is something worn on the body, not an intrinsic possession — it can be given, and it can decay.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'livery' n., sense 3a: 'the distinctive clothing, etc., delivered to retainers, servants, followers'; s.v. 'weed' n.2, sense 1: 'a garment, article of clothing' (common through 17th c.).

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, 'Shakespeare-Lexicon' (3rd ed., 1902), s.v. 'livery': 'the dress of a servant, as delivered by his master'; s.v. 'weed': 'garment, dress.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 17

OED 'livery' n. sense 3a (distinctive clothing delivered to retainers) and 'weed' n.2 sense 1 (garment) are both real and accurate; Schmidt's Lexicon entries for these terms are standard and correctly described.

Both 'livery' as servants' uniform and 'weed' as garment are well-attested Elizabethan senses; 'widow's weeds' as a surviving trace is accurate, and the clothing-as-worn-beauty reading fits the line without overreach.

anchor_text: all-eating shame, and thriftless praise
summary: 'Thriftless' means wasteful, producing no return or profit — the opposite of thrift, which in Elizabethan English meant not just frugality but successful gain. To point at one's own sunken eyes as proof of beauty is 'thriftless praise' because it profits nothing: the beauty is spent, the account empty, and no child remains to make the claim credible.
detail: The commercial register is deliberate. 'Thrift' in sixteenth-century English meant prosperity or successful acquisition (Hamlet's bitter pun: 'Thrift, Horatio — the funeral baked-meats / Did coldly furnish forth the marriage tables,' 1.2). 'Thriftless' therefore describes a boast that yields no return on the beauty that was invested. The whole couplet at lines 21-22 frames a man who has nothing to show for his gifts as both morally shamed ('all-eating shame' — shame that consumes him) and commercially bankrupt. The word links this sonnet to the network of money-lending, use, and interest imagery that runs through Sonnets 1-17.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'thriftless' adj., sense 1: 'not thriving; unprosperous; also, not conducive to thrift, wasteful' (first citation 1548).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, 'A Shakespeare Glossary' (rev. Eagleson, 1986), s.v. 'thrift': 'prosperity, thriving; frugality'; s.v. 'thriftless': 'unprofitable, improvident.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 22

OED 'thriftless' adj. sense 1 ('not thriving; unprosperous; wasteful') is correctly cited, and Onions Shakespeare Glossary (rev. Eagleson 1986) is a real work whose entries for 'thrift' and 'thriftless' match the paraphrase given.

The Elizabethan sense of 'thrift' as prosperous gain (not merely frugality) is correct; the Hamlet 1.2 'thrift' parallel is apt and the commercial-register reading of the couplet is standard in modern scholarship.

anchor_text: 'This fair child of mine Shall sum my count
summary: 'Sum my count' is an accounting phrase: to sum an account is to add up the columns and strike the final balance. The child is the total that settles the ledger of the youth's life — proof that his beauty was not wasted but invested and returned with interest. 'Count' also carries the sense of reckoning or justification: the child is the answer when the youth is called to account for how he spent his gifts.
detail: The conceit extends the financial metaphor that runs through Sonnets 1-17. A 'count' (or account) was the merchant's ledger balance; 'to sum' it was to cast up the totals. The child 'sums' the account in two senses: arithmetically (adding up what the youth's beauty has produced) and morally (providing the final justification, the excuse, when God or the world calls the youth to account for the beauty entrusted to him). 'Old excuse' at the line's end picks up the legal sense of 'excuse' as a formal plea in one's defence — the child is the youth's pleading exhibit. The cluster of financial-legal vocabulary in these three lines (sum, count, excuse, succession, proving) is characteristic of the procreation sonnets' technique: love-poetry dressed in the rhetoric of the counting-house.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sum' v., sense 3: 'to add up (figures, items) so as to find the total; to reckon up'; s.v. 'count' n.2, sense 1: 'a reckoning, account, computation'; s.v. 'excuse' n., sense 1b: 'a plea offered in extenuation or justification.'

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, 'Shakespeare-Lexicon' (3rd ed., 1902), s.v. 'sum': 'to cast up, to compute'; s.v. 'count': 'account, reckoning.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 24

OED 'sum' v. sense 3 (add up figures to find a total), 'count' n.2 sense 1 (reckoning/account), and 'excuse' n. sense 1b (plea in extenuation) are all standard entries; Schmidt's Lexicon definitions for 'sum' and 'count' are correctly paraphrased.

The double sense of 'sum my count' (arithmetic total + moral reckoning) and 'old excuse' as a legal plea are both well-grounded; the financial-legal vocabulary cluster is a recognized feature of the procreation sonnets and the reading does not overreach.

anchor_text: This were to be new made when thou art old, And see thy blood warm when thou feel'st it cold
summary: The closing couplet offers procreation as a form of resurrection: to have a child is to be remade at the very moment you feel most mortal. 'Blood' means both the literal warmth of life (youth's heat against the cold of age) and lineage or family descent — the child carries the parent's blood forward. The contrast of warm and cold in a single line is an antithesis that makes the argument sensory and immediate.
detail: The antithesis 'warm / cold' is the couplet's structural hinge, and it operates on two levels simultaneously. Physiologically, warmth was the Galenic sign of youth and health; cold was age and approaching death (the four humors assigned heat to blood). Legally and dynastically, 'blood' meant lineage — to 'see thy blood warm' in a child is to see the family line survive past the body's extinction. The couplet's argument is therefore both visceral (you will feel cold and see heat) and abstract (your line will live on when you are dead). The near-rhyme of the couplet ('old' / 'cold') uses identical terminal sounds to close the argument with the same finality as a sum struck at the bottom of a ledger column.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'blood' n., sense 1: 'the fluid circulating in the veins... associated with vital heat and life'; sense 6a: 'family, lineage, descent.'

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III, ch. 19, on 'Antitheton or the Quarreller,' the placing of contraries for emphasis.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 27

Puttenham Book III ch. 19 ('Figures Sententious') does include antitheton as 'the Quarreller,' and OED 'blood' n. sense 1 (vital fluid/heat) and sense 6a (family lineage) are both real and correctly described.

The Galenic warm/cold physiology applied to 'blood' and the dual sense of blood as vital heat versus lineage are both accurate to the period and to the text; the antithesis gloss is correct and the 'old'/'cold' rhyme observation is sound.

anchor_text: Look in thy glass and tell the face
summary: 'Glass' is an Elizabethan word for mirror (flat glass backed with tin and mercury). The speaker tells the youth to look at his own reflection and reckon with what he sees: a face worth reproducing in a child.
detail: Shakespeare uses 'glass' for mirror throughout the sonnets. The word recurs at TLN 37 ('Thou art thy mother's glass') where it shifts from a literal mirror to a metaphorical one: the youth is himself a living reflection of his mother's former beauty. OED records 'glass' in the sense of a mirror from the 14th century through the period; the word is also used in this sense at Sonnet 22.1, 37.8, and 62.1. The double application — look into a glass; you ARE a glass — is the central structural pivot of the poem.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'glass' n., sense 5a: 'A mirror, looking-glass'; examples from c.1374 through 17th c.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 29
OED s.v. 'glass' n., sense 5a (mirror, looking-glass, from c.1374) is a real and well-attested entry that directly supports the claim that 'glass' meant mirror in Elizabethan usage.

'Glass' as mirror is firmly established in Elizabethan usage, and the annotation's structural claim — that the poem works a pivot from literal glass to the youth-as-living-glass at line 9 — is accurate to the text and mainstream in criticism.

anchor_text: unear'd womb Disdains the tillage of thy husbandry
summary: 'Unear'd' means unploughed (from Old English 'erian,' to plough). 'Tillage' is the cultivation of land by ploughing and planting. 'Husbandry' means farming — but also the duties of a husband. The three words work together as an extended agricultural metaphor: a woman's womb is fertile ground that the youth, as a responsible farmer-husband, should be cultivating.
detail: OED records 'ear' as a verb meaning to plough ('to ear the land') from Old English through the early modern period; 'unear'd' therefore means unploughed, uncultivated. 'Husbandry' carried both senses simultaneously for an Elizabethan reader: the management of a household and farm, and the role of a husband (OED s.v. 'husbandry' n., senses 1 and 2). The argument is that no woman of worth would refuse to bear the youth's child; his refusal is therefore a wilful waste of a natural resource. The farming conceit recurs across the procreation sonnets — seed, harvest, and winter are its recurring seasons.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ear' v.2: 'To plough, till'; s.v. 'tillage' n., sense 1: 'The action of tilling land; cultivation'; s.v. 'husbandry' n., sense 1: 'The business of a husbandman; the cultivation of the soil' and sense 2: 'The management of a household.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 33
OED s.v. 'ear' v.2 (to plough, from OE 'erian'), 'tillage' n. sense 1, and 'husbandry' n. senses 1-2 are all real entries whose recorded definitions match the claims exactly.

The triple agricultural cluster (unear'd / tillage / husbandry) is correctly glossed; the dual sense of 'husbandry' (farming / husband-duty) is well attested, and the rhetorical reading of lines 33-34 as an implied negative — no worthy woman would refuse him — accurately paraphrases the poem's question.

anchor_text: who is he so fond will be the tomb, Of his self-love
summary: 'Fond' here means foolish or doting, not merely affectionate (its primary modern sense). The speaker asks: who is so foolish as to let self-love become his own tomb — that is, to let vanity end with him rather than pass beauty on to a child?
detail: The Elizabethan 'fond' routinely means foolishly infatuated or simply stupid (OED s.v. 'fond' adj., sense 2a: 'Foolish, silly, dull-witted'). The phrase 'self-love' adds a second charge: not just a fool, but a narcissist. The line turns the mirror of TLN 29 against the youth: to stare at your reflection without acting on it is to make yourself your own gravestone. Compare Sonnet 1.8: 'thy self thy foe.' The syntax is compressed — 'who is he so fond [that he] will be the tomb / of his self-love' — meaning, who is so foolish as to let narcissism be his only legacy.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'fond' adj., sense 2a: 'Foolish, silly'; cf. sense 3: 'Doting, over-affectionate.' Both senses are active in Shakespeare's usage.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874), s.v. 'fond': 'foolish, silly; to be very fond of = to dote upon.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 35
OED 'fond' adj. sense 2a (foolish, silly) is real; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874) exists and records 'fond' as foolish/silly and doting, consistent with the cited paraphrase.

'Fond' as foolish is the primary Elizabethan sense and the correct reading here; the compressed syntax ('who will be the tomb of his self-love to stop posterity') is accurately unpacked, and the narcissism charge is mainstream rather than an overreach.

anchor_text: Die single and thine image dies with thee
summary: The couplet delivers the poem's logical conclusion with deliberate bluntness: if the youth dies without a child, his face — described throughout as a glass, a mirror, a reflection of his mother — simply goes dark. 'Single' means unmarried and alone. The whole argument collapses to one bare, twelve-word sentence.
detail: The closing couplet of a Shakespearean sonnet is expected to clinch, resolve, or sharply restate the argument. Here the clinch is almost brutal in its economy after the emotional warmth of the mother-image quatrain. The word 'single' carries the legal and social weight of 'unmarried' (OED s.v. 'single' adj., sense 9a: 'Unmarried, celibate') and also the isolation of 'alone' — dying as a single, solitary point with no copy. 'Image' picks up 'glass' from line 1: the face that should be reflected in a child will instead vanish. Thomas Wilson's English translation of Erasmus's model letter on marriage made exactly this argument — beauty is a gift that dies with its keeper unless reproduced — and Puttenham's rhetoric manuals identify this type of closing sentence as 'climax reversed': the rising warmth of the preceding lines paid off by sudden cold logic.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'single' adj., sense 9a: 'Unmarried, celibate.'

sources.name: Erasmus / Wilson
sources.citation: Erasmus, 'Epistle to persuade a young man to marriage,' Englished in Thomas Wilson, 'The Arte of Rhetorique' (1553): beauty is a loan that must be repaid through offspring.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 42

OED 'single' adj. sense 9a (unmarried, celibate) is real; Erasmus's marriage epistle in Wilson's Arte of Rhetorique (1553) is a real and well-documented source that scholars regularly cite as arguing beauty must be reproduced in offspring, directly supporting the annotation's claim.

The core interpretation (single = unmarried; image = face unreproduced) is sound, and the Erasmus/Wilson procreation-argument connection is well documented; however, 'climax reversed' is not a recognized Puttenham term from the Arte of English Poesie and appears to be an invented or misattributed label — the rhetorical claim is harmless to the gloss but is not verifiable, making the annotation as a whole uncertain rather than refuted.

anchor_text: Unthrifty loveliness, why dost thou spend
summary: 'Unthrifty' means wasteful or improvident — someone who squanders a fortune rather than husbanding it. The poet opens the sonnet by calling the young man's beauty a kind of economic recklessness: he has been given a great endowment but is spending it on himself instead of passing it on.
detail: OED s.v. 'unthrifty' records the sense 'not thrifty; wasteful, improvident' from the 14th century onward; it was still the primary meaning in the 1590s. The word introduces the sustained financial metaphor that runs through all 14 lines: the Youth is a bad steward of natural capital.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'unthrifty,' adj., sense 1: 'Not thrifty; improvident, wasteful.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 43
OED s.v. 'unthrifty' adj. sense 1 ('Not thrifty; improvident, wasteful') is a real, well-attested definition current from the 14th century and accurately supports the gloss.

The financial metaphor is immediately established by 'spend' in the same line, and 'unthrifty' as 'improvident/wasteful' is the primary, uncontested Elizabethan sense; the gloss is accurate and does not overreach.

anchor_text: beauteous niggard, why dost thou abuse / The bounteous largess given thee to give? / Profitless usurer
summary: 'Niggard' is a miser — someone who hoards rather than spends. A 'usurer' lends money at interest for profit. The poet calls the Youth a 'profitless usurer': he trades exclusively with himself (enjoys his own beauty) yet produces nothing — the opposite of what usury is supposed to achieve. 'Largess' means a generous gift or bounty.
detail: OED s.v. 'niggard,' n. and adj., sense A.1: 'A miser, a stingy or mean person' (in use from the 14th century). OED s.v. 'usurer,' n., sense 1: 'One who lends money at interest, esp. at an exorbitant or illegal rate.' The 'profitless usurer' is a deliberate paradox: a usurer by definition extracts profit; one who produces none is doubly condemned. Aristotle, in Politics 1.10 (1258b), had called money-lending 'unnatural' because money is barren — it should not breed. Shakespeare inverts this: beauty should breed (produce children), and the Youth who refuses to is the one behaving like barren money.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'niggard,' n., sense A.1; s.v. 'usurer,' n., sense 1; s.v. 'largess,' n., sense 1.

sources.name: Aristotle, Politics
sources.citation: Aristotle, Politics 1.10 (1258b): money-lending condemned as unnatural because money is barren and should not breed.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 47
OED senses are standard; Aristotle Politics 1.10 (1258b) does condemn usury as unnatural because money (tokos) should not breed, and the paraphrase is accurate to the passage confirmed at Perseus.

The primary glosses ('niggard' = miser, 'profitless usurer' as deliberate paradox) are sound and mainstream, but the claim that Shakespeare 'inverts' Aristotle's Politics argument about barren money is a secondary scholarly inference (Booth) not licensed by the text itself, and elevating it as part of the annotation's core argument slightly overloads what the lines directly say.

anchor_text: when nature calls thee to be gone, / What acceptable audit canst thou leave?
summary: An 'audit' is a formal examination of financial accounts — the official reckoning of what a steward has done with the funds entrusted to him. At death, the poet asks, what satisfactory account of your life could you present? The word frames mortality as a legal settlement: you will be called to answer for how you spent what Nature gave you.
detail: OED s.v. 'audit,' n., sense 1: 'An official examination and verification of accounts.' In Elizabethan England, the audit was a regular event on great estates, when stewards rendered accounts to their lord. 'Acceptable' (OED s.v. 'acceptable,' adj., sense 1: 'capable of being accepted, worth accepting') implies the standard is external — the account must satisfy a judge, not the steward himself. The theological undertow is the Last Judgment, where every soul renders account (cf. Matthew 12:36, Geneva 1599: 'every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment'), but the poet keeps the register financial throughout.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'audit,' n., sense 1; s.v. 'acceptable,' adj., sense 1.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Matthew 12:36 (Geneva 1599): 'But I say unto you, that of every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 53

Matthew 12:36 is a real Geneva 1599 verse and supports the claim, but the annotation quotes it as 'in the day of judgment' whereas Geneva 1599 reads 'at the day of iudgement' — a minor textual discrepancy that prevents full verification.

The stewardship/audit reading is the correct primary meaning; the annotation appropriately frames the Last Judgment undertow as a secondary resonance rather than the foregrounded meaning, and the caveat that 'the poet keeps the register financial throughout' prevents overclaiming.

anchor_text: Thy unused beauty must be tombed with thee, / Which, used, lives th' executor to be
summary: The couplet is the sonnet's clinching turn. An 'executor' is the person appointed to carry out the terms of a will after the testator dies — to distribute the estate. The poet argues that a child who inherits the Youth's beauty is beauty's executor, ensuring it outlives its original owner. Beauty hoarded dies with the hoarder; beauty 'used' (reproduced in offspring) lives on to settle the estate.
detail: OED s.v. 'executor,' n., sense 1: 'A person appointed by a testator to execute or give effect to his will after his decease.' The legal metaphor closes perfectly: the sonnet has moved from 'bequest' (TLN 44) through 'audit' (TLN 54) to 'executor' (TLN 56), making the argument a complete testamentary transaction. 'Used' carries a secondary sense of 'put to use, employed productively' (OED s.v. 'use,' v., sense 4), against 'unused' which is the miser's hoarding. The word 'tombed' (TLN 55) seals the reversal: unused beauty is literally entombed — buried alive in the grave — whereas beauty employed in procreation walks free. This couplet states the procreation argument at its sharpest and most legally precise.

anchor_text: The lovely gaze where every eye doth dwell
summary: 'Gaze' here means the object that is gazed at — the face or form that everyone stares at — not the act of gazing. The hours that gently shaped this admired spectacle will eventually destroy it. The OED records this noun sense ('that which is gazed at; a spectacle') from the sixteenth century.

The poet thus personifies time's handiwork as both sculptor (the 'gentle work' of the opening) and later vandal — the same hours that built the spectacle will unmake it.

anchor_text: Will play the tyrants to the very same
summary: The first eight lines of the sonnet (the octave) develop one extended comparison: the seasons as time's destruction of beauty. Summer is personified as a victim — 'him' that time 'confounds' (destroys) and buries under winter. 'Confounds' means defeats, ruins, or brings to ruin; it is far stronger than 'ends.' Sap checked by frost, leaves gone, beauty covered by snow — each detail of winter dismantling summer is simultaneously a detail of age dismantling a beautiful face.

The personification of time as a tyrant who first nurtures and then oppresses its subject is a fixture of the procreation sonnets (compare Sonnet 63: 'Against my love shall be as I am now, / With Time's injurious hand crush'd and o'erworn'). The move from abstraction ('time') to concrete seasonal imagery (sap, frost, snow) is the sonnet's rhetorical engine: the natural cycle gives the argument sensory weight.

anchor_text: that unfair which fairly doth excel
summary: 'Unfair' is used as a verb meaning 'to deprive of beauty, to make ugly.' Time will take what is most beautiful ('fairly doth excel' — surpasses all others in comeliness) and strip it of that beauty. The pun on the same root word in two parts of speech — verb and adverb — concentrates the cruelty: the thing that most excels in fairness is precisely what time unfairs.

The noun-to-verb conversion (or denominal verb) is typical Shakespearean lexical compression. The antithesis 'unfair/fairly' enacts the poem's argument in a single line: what time created as fair, it will uncreate — a logical reversal that parallels the summer-to-winter movement of the sestet.

anchor_text: ere thou be distill'd
summary: 'Distill'd' means extracted as a concentrated essence, the way a perfumer distils rose petals into oil that preserves the rose's beauty through winter. The image runs directly from Sonnet 5, where the poet argued that beauty, like a flower, should be distilled into a vial before the cold destroys it. Here the call is urgent: act before winter comes.

A distillery reduces the volatile essence of a plant to a concentrated liquid that outlasts the plant itself; applied to the youth, it figures sexual reproduction as a process of preserving beauty by concentrating it in a child. The word 'distill'd' carries both a technical and a poetic charge: OED s.v. distil v., sense 2 ('to extract the essential qualities of a substance'), in use from the 14th century.

The distillation-as-reproduction reading is mainstream; Sonnet 5 explicitly establishes the perfume conceit that Sonnet 6 inherits, making this gloss well-grounded and uncontroversial.

anchor_text: Make sweet some vial; treasure thou some place
summary: A 'vial' is a small glass vessel used in Elizabethan England to hold perfume or medicine. Here it is a metaphor for a woman's womb: the youth should fill some vial — that is, father a child — and so deposit beauty's treasure in a living container before it is destroyed. 'Treasure thou some place' means the same thing from the other angle: store your beauty somewhere safe.

The metaphor connects: beauty is like perfume (the Sonnet 5 conceit), a vial holds perfume, a womb holds the child who carries the father's beauty forward. The double imperative — 'make sweet some vial' and 'treasure thou some place' — is typical of the procreation sonnets' rhetoric of urgent, varied repetition: say the same thing two ways so no escape is left. 'Self-kill'd' at line 4 adds the corollary: beauty that refuses to reproduce destroys itself, committing a kind of suicide.

anchor_text: That use is not forbidden usury
summary: Usury — lending money at interest — was widely condemned in Elizabethan England, both by the Church as immoral and often by law as exploitative. The poet turns this loaded word on its head: there is a kind of 'use' (a financial term for the interest paid on a loan) that is not forbidden usury but a welcome return. That use is begetting children: you lend your beauty to life, and it pays back ten children who are 'ten times happier' than the one investment. The borrowing of financial language to argue for reproduction is characteristic of the early sonnets.
detail: Elizabethan statute capped interest at ten percent (the Act Against Usury, 1571); taking more was 'usury' in the condemned sense, and Aristotle's argument that money cannot 'breed' money (the standard theological objection, transmitted through scholasticism) was still in wide circulation. Shakespeare exploits the very paradox the moralists had set up: if making money 'breed' is unnatural, making beauty breed by having children is natural and blessed. The word 'use' (line 75) is the technical English term for interest or return on a loan; OED s.v. 'use' n., sense 10a, cites it from the 15th century in financial contexts. The logic reappears in the Merchant of Venice's Jacob-and-Laban argument (1.3) and in Sonnet 4 ('beauty's legacy' / 'beauteous niggard').

The inversion of the usury taboo — borrowing Aristotle's 'money cannot breed' to argue that beauty can and should breed — is well-attested context; the 1571 Act and the MV Jacob-and-Laban parallel are accurately cited.

anchor_text: Be not self-will'd, for thou art much too fair
summary: 'Self-will'd' means stubbornly governed by one's own wishes, refusing counsel or instruction. The word carries a moral charge in Elizabethan usage: self-will was associated with pride and willful disregard of others' welfare. The couplet condemns the youth's refusal to reproduce not merely as waste but as a form of pride — and names the price: to make worms his heir, meaning that if he dies without children, the only inheritors of his beauty are the worms that consume his body.
detail: OED s.v. 'self-willed' adj. records the sense 'governed entirely by one's own will; obstinately determined to have one's own way' from the early 16th century. The compound gathers two objections: self-will (pride) and its consequence, the worm. The phrase 'make worms thine heir' is the sonnet's darkest turn — a legal metaphor (naming an heir) applied grotesquely to burial and decay. Without children to inherit beauty, the estate goes to rot. The couplet thus closes the financial and biological argument simultaneously: refuse to 'lend' beauty, and death 'conquers' it instead of perpetuating it. 'Death's conquest' treats death as a military victor who seizes what the youth refuses to protect by reproduction.

anchor_text: in the orient when the gracious light
summary: 'Orient' means the east — the quarter of the sky where the sun rises. The word carried connotations of splendor and newness in Elizabethan English, making it a grander synonym for 'east' in verse. The opening image frames the whole sonnet: the sun rising in the east will arc across the sky and set in the west, mapping youth, middle age, and old age onto a single day.
detail: 'Orient' derives from Latin oriens ('rising'), the present participle of oriri ('to rise'), and was applied both to the eastern sky and to things associated with brilliance and freshness (the 'orient pearl' of Antony and Cleopatra 1.5 uses the same connotation of lustrous eastern gems). OED s.v. 'orient' adj. sense 1 and 2 records both the directional and the 'bright, lustrous' senses as current in the sixteenth century. The choice of 'orient' over 'east' gives the dawn a jeweled, quasi-sacred quality that the rest of the quatrain sustains with 'gracious light,' 'sacred majesty,' and the world's collective homage.

anchor_text: having climb'd the steep-up heavenly hill
summary: The four opening lines build a single extended metaphor: the sun's daily arc across the sky is a sacred journey from dawn to dusk. The sun is personified as a young man ('strong youth in his middle age') making a strenuous ascent up a 'heavenly hill,' then proceeding on a 'golden pilgrimage' — a journey to a holy place. The logic prepares for the turn at line 9: just as the world worships the sun on its upward climb but looks away when it descends, so it admires the youth's beauty now but will abandon him when he declines.

'Steep-up' is Shakespeare's coinage for a steep upward climb. 'Pilgrimage' (from Old French pelrimage) denoted a journey to a sacred shrine and is applied here to the sun's westward arc, elevating the cosmos to a quasi-religious theater in which the whole creation pays 'homage' and renders 'service.' George Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) calls sustained metaphor 'allegoria' and notes its power to make abstract arguments concrete and affective — the procreation sonnets habitually work through exactly this kind of compressed, mobile conceit.

anchor_text: from highmost pitch, with weary car
summary: 'Car' is an archaic word for chariot; 'the weary car' is the sun-god's chariot as it descends at the end of the day. Classical mythology imagined the sun as a god driving a chariot of fire across the sky: the Greek Helios, or his Roman counterpart Phoebus (Apollo), mounted a burning four-horse chariot at dawn and drove it from east to west. By afternoon the horses tire and the car tilts downward, which explained the sun's descent — the same moment the sonnet identifies with old age.
detail: The image belongs to Ovid's account of Phaethon (Metamorphoses 1.747-2.400, Englished in Golding's 1567 translation), the most detailed classical treatment of the solar chariot: Helios's car has 'axle, pole, and wheels of gold, the spokes of silver,' and the horses breathe fire. When Phaethon borrows the chariot he cannot control them. Shakespeare draws on this mythology without naming Phaethon — the resonance of the 'weary car' declining at the end of the day is the controlled, sad version of what Phaethon suffered in catastrophic, youthful excess. 'Pitch' (see the separate note) names the apex of the arc from which the descent begins.

sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.107-110 (description of Phoebus's chariot and horses); Arthur Golding's English translation (1567).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 93

Glossing 'car' as chariot is correct, but the annotation over-specifies a deliberate Phaethon allusion — 'weary car' invokes the commonplace Phoebus/Helios solar-chariot, and reading it as a pointed Phaethon echo (framed as a conscious parallel to 'youthful excess') reaches beyond what the unadorned line supports.

anchor_text: highmost pitch
summary: 'Pitch' is a falconry term for the highest point a hawk reaches before it stoops (dives) onto its prey. By extension it meant any peak or highest point. Here the sun has reached 'highmost pitch' — its noon zenith — and now begins its downward arc. The falconry image would have been immediately recognizable to Shakespeare's readers, for whom hawking was a common gentry sport.
detail: OED s.v. 'pitch' n.1, sense 10: 'The height to which a hawk (or other bird) rises before swooping or stooping; the highest point of a hawk's flight.' The word carried its falconry meaning throughout the sixteenth century and was frequently used in Shakespeare (e.g. Richard II 1.1.109: 'eagle-winged pride of sky-aspiring and ambitious thoughts, with rival-hating envy set on you / To wake our peace, which in our country's cradle / Draws the sweet infant breath of gentle sleep'; more directly in 3 Henry VI 2.1 'like a falconer she lures me down to stoop'). Here it functions doubly: the sun's zenith and, implicitly, the peak of human beauty and power before the body begins its decline — the moment the sonnet identifies as the youth's 'noon.'

anchor_text: So thou, thyself outgoing in thy noon
summary: Line 97 is the volta — the turn at which the sonnet's sun-metaphor is applied directly to the young man: just as the world looks away from the declining sun, so the youth will be 'unlook'd on' once his beauty passes its noon. The final word 'son' in line 98 puns on 'sun': a literal male heir would be the new rising sun, inheriting the father's beauty and keeping the world's gaze on the family. The pun seals the whole argument — the only way to maintain the light is to produce another source of it.
detail: The 'so' that opens line 97 is the sonnet's logical hinge (the conclusio of the conceit), and 'noon' echoes the earlier 'middle age' of the sun at its height (line 90). The son/sun pun is silent on the page — 'sonne' and 'sunne' were near-homophones in Elizabethan English and both were spelled variously; Thomas Thorpe's 1609 quarto prints 'sonne,' which carries both meanings simultaneously. The pun is the argumentative climax of the procreation group: a biological son is the youth's only 'sun' that can outlast his own setting, keeping the light — his beauty — alive in the world after he declines. This wordplay recurs as a structural device in the procreation sonnets (compare Sonnet 1: 'the world's fresh ornament,' and Sonnet 3's 'windows of thine age' that let the father's face shine through the son).

anchor_text: If the true concord of well-tuned sounds, By unions married
summary: 'Concord' is a technical music term for notes that sound pleasing together, as opposed to discord. 'By unions married' means the strings are joined together like a married couple — their harmony is a kind of wedlock. The second quatrain argues that if even this musical joining offends the youth, the music is rebuking him for failing to create the same union through marriage and children.

'Unions' carries both the musical sense (the sounding-together of voices or strings) and the legal/social sense of marriage; the word 'married' makes the double meaning explicit. This is the pivot of the poem's extended musical conceit: harmony in music and harmony in domestic life are the same thing, and the youth refuses both. The phrase 'who confounds / In singleness the parts that thou shouldst bear' uses 'parts' in its double sense — musical part (an individual voice-line in polyphony) and social part (a role, duty). See Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'part.'

anchor_text: who confounds In singleness the parts that thou shouldst bear
summary: 'Confounds' means ruins or destroys. 'Singleness' is the youth's unmarried state, but in music it means a single note sounding alone rather than in a chord. 'Parts' are both personal duties (husband, father) and the separate melodic lines that combine in part-singing. The line says simultaneously: you ruin the musical harmony by playing a solo, and you ruin your social duties by staying single.
detail: Part-singing — polyphony in which each voice carries a distinct melodic line that harmonizes with the others — was the dominant form of domestic music-making in Elizabethan England; the lute song and the madrigal both depended on it. The conceit therefore had immediate force for a cultured Elizabethan reader: refusing to 'bear a part' was both antisocial and musically illiterate. OED records 'singleness' in the sense 'the state of being unmarried' from the late sixteenth century (OED s.v. 'singleness, n.' sense 2).

anchor_text: Mark how one string, sweet husband to another, Strikes each in each by mutual ordering; Resembling sire and child and happy mother
summary: 'Mark' means 'pay attention' — the poet directs the youth to observe a lute or viol string that vibrates in sympathy with the one beside it. This is an extended simile: a string is a 'sweet husband' to the next string, and when they sound together they resemble a father, a mother, and a child all singing in harmony. The poem converts the instrument itself into a model family to shame the youth into following suit.
detail: The phenomenon described — one string vibrating when an adjacent string is struck — is sympathetic resonance, well known to Elizabethan lutenists. The poet exploits it to make the family argument irresistible: even inanimate strings produce offspring through their union, while the youth, animate and 'Music to hear,' refuses to. The triad 'sire and child and happy mother' deliberately arranges itself as father–child–mother rather than the expected father–mother–child, placing the child at the center of the domestic image, which is where the procreation argument places it throughout Sonnets 1–17.

The sympathetic-resonance reading is plausible but the text says 'Strikes each in each by mutual ordering,' which describes strings struck in sequence or by mutual vibration — the poem does not clearly invoke sympathetic resonance specifically; the order father–child–mother is noted as deliberate but could as easily be metrical, so the claim that Shakespeare consciously 'placed the child at the center' as a theological argument overreads the arrangement.

anchor_text: issueless shalt hap to die
summary: 'Issueless' means without issue — without children or offspring. 'Issue' was the standard legal term for heirs, so dying issueless meant leaving no lawful heir. 'Hap' means happen or chance to: the line asks what happens if the young man chances to die childless.

'Issueless' as an adjective meaning 'childless, without heirs' appears in Shakespeare elsewhere — most pointedly in Macbeth 3.1.63 ('a fruitless crown... no son of mine succeeding'). The legal register is deliberate: dying without issue was a catastrophe in property and lineage terms, not merely a personal loss, and the poet builds on that social weight throughout the procreation sonnets.

anchor_text: wail thee like a makeless wife
summary: 'Makeless' means mateless — a wife who has lost her husband and has no partner left. The word combines 'mate' (from Old English 'gemaca,' a match or companion) with the suffix '-less.' anchor_text: what an unthrift in the world doth spend
summary: At line 9 the sonnet pivots — this is the volta, or turn — from the widow conceit to a new economic argument. An 'unthrift' is a spendthrift, someone who wastes money; but when a spendthrift spends, the money only changes hands: the world still has it. Beauty wasted by not being reproduced, however, is destroyed outright: 'beauty's waste hath in the world an end.' The Youth is doing something far more irresponsible than squandering money.
detail: OED s.v. 'unthrift,' n.: 'a spendthrift, a prodigal.' The economic metaphor here is more precise than it looks: 'shifts but his place' means only moves from one owner to another (OED s.v. 'shift,' v., sense 9a: to change location or hands). Ordinary wealth is conserved in aggregate even when wasted by one person; beauty is not conserved once the person who holds it dies without reproducing it. The argument refines the financial conceits of Sonnets 4 and 6 (the Youth as miser, usury, legacy). The volta at line 9 is formally marked by 'Look!' — an apostrophe that calls the reader's attention to the contrast being drawn. Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie (1589) identifies this pointing device as 'ecphonesis,' an exclamatory turning of address.

The volta at line 9 (TLN 121) signaled by 'Look!' is structurally correct; 'unthrift' as spendthrift and 'shifts but his place' as change of hands are sound readings; the ecphonesis gloss is learned but defensible.

anchor_text: kept unused the user so destroys it
summary: 'Kept unused' means hoarded, not deployed — but also left without a sexual partner. 'User' and 'use' carry the Elizabethan financial sense of usury: putting money to use means lending it at interest and making it reproduce. A beauty kept from 'use' — from reproduction — destroys itself. The couplet calls that destruction 'murd'rous shame,' not selflessness.
detail: OED s.v. 'use,' n., sense 12: 'the putting of money, etc., to productive use; employment at interest, usury.' In the procreation sonnets 'use' and 'usury' are a sustained financial metaphor: beauty given to nature in the form of children is like principal lent out at interest — it returns multiplied. Sonnet 6 makes the usury-pun explicit ('That use is not forbidden usury, / Which happies those that pay the willing loan'). Here 'user' means both the person who employs his assets and the Youth himself as the possessor of beauty — the one who 'uses' it or fails to. The final charge, 'murd'rous shame,' is harsher than anything in the surrounding sonnets: abstaining from procreation is recast not as chastity or caution but as violence against both the self and the world. Erasmus's epistle to persuade a young man to marriage, which underwrites the whole procreation argument, makes the same move: to refuse generation is to act against nature and against the common good.

anchor_text: deny that thou bear'st love to any, Who for thy self art so unprovident
summary: 'Unprovident' means failing to make provision for the future — the word carries legal and financial weight, as a person who dies without an heir leaves his estate, name, and lineage in disorder. The speaker accuses the Youth of a double failure: not loving others, and not looking ahead to secure his own continuation.

The charge builds on Sonnets 1-9, where the Youth is accused of waste and self-enclosure; here it reaches its sharpest form — his failure to reproduce is framed as a failure of responsible stewardship, like a landowner who neglects his estate.

anchor_text: possess'd with murderous hate, That 'gainst thy self thou stick'st not to conspire
summary: The speaker uses deliberate overstatement: refusing to have children is called 'murderous hate' and a conspiracy against oneself. 'Stick'st not to' means 'do not hesitate to' — so the Youth does not flinch from plotting his own destruction. The language of murder and conspiracy charges the Youth with an active will to self-ruin, not mere carelessness.

'Possessed' also carries a connotation of demonic possession, as if hatred were an external force that has taken hold of the Youth. 'Stick'st not' follows the idiom documented by Onions: 'stick at' = hesitate at or scruple to do (Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'stick').

anchor_text: beauteous roof to ruinate Which to repair should be thy chief desire
summary: 'Roof' here means a house or family line — the Youth's beauty is figured as a noble dwelling that shelters his lineage. 'Ruinate' is an archaic verb meaning to cause to fall into ruin or collapse. By refusing to produce an heir, the Youth allows his 'house' (both his physical body and his family name) to decay rather than maintaining it.

The architectural metaphor of beauty as a dwelling to be maintained or repaired runs through the procreation sonnets (compare Sonnet 13: 'Who lets so fair a house fall to decay'). 'Repair' in line 134 continues the conceit: repair means both restoration of a building and the act of coming back to a place.

anchor_text: O! change thy thought, that I may change my mind
summary: This is the volta — the turn of argument that the sonnet form conventionally places at line 9. The speaker switches from accusation to personal appeal, and the antimetabole ('change thy thought / change my mind') makes the two minds mirror each other. For the first time in the procreation sequence the speaker speaks as 'I,' making the argument a matter of affection between the two, not only an abstract duty.
detail: The rhetorical figure is antimetabole (repetition of words in reversed grammatical relation: 'change thy thought... change my mind'), a device catalogued in Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie (1589) under 'Antimetabole' or the 'Counterchange.' The line also pivots the argument: the first eight lines denounce the Youth in the third-person manner of legal accusation; line 9 opens with the exclamation 'O!' and a direct appeal, shifting the speaker from prosecutor to friend. This personal turn at the volta is unusual in the procreation sonnets and signals that the argument is becoming emotional.

anchor_text: Make thee another self for love of me, That beauty still may live in thine or thee
summary: The couplet reframes procreation as a gift to the speaker rather than an abstract duty: 'make a child for my sake.' 'Another self' was a standard Renaissance phrase for a child who perpetuates the parent's identity; the idea that friendship or love creates a second self comes from Aristotle. 'Still' means 'always' or 'continually' — beauty will persist either in a child ('thine') or in the Youth himself ('thee') as long as he lives.
detail: Aristotle in the Nicomachean Ethics (8.12, 1161b) calls a child 'as it were, another self' of the parent (Greek heteros autos), a phrase transmitted through Renaissance moral philosophy and Cicero's De Amicitia. Sidney uses the topos in the Defence of Poesie (c. 1580, publ. 1595): a friend is 'a second self.' Shakespeare brings the conceit into the erotic register of the sonnets by attaching it explicitly to the speaker's personal affection — 'for love of me' — rather than to duty or posterity alone. 'Still' in Elizabethan usage means 'always, continually' (OED s.v. 'still,' adv., sense 6).

The Aristotle heteros-autos topos is well-attested in Renaissance progeny discourse, 'still' as always/continually is correct, and the parsing of 'thine or thee' as child versus the Youth himself is the mainstream reading.

anchor_text: Herein lives wisdom, beauty, and increase
summary: Lines 145-146 set up a deliberate three-against-three contrast: 'wisdom, beauty, and increase' (the goods of reproduction) versus 'folly, age, and cold decay' (the fate of celibacy). This pairing of matching triplets is the rhetorical figure called antithesis, used here to make the procreation argument feel like plain arithmetic.
detail: The figure is antithesis — the balancing of opposed ideas in parallel structure. George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), calls this device the 'Rencontre or Encounter' and notes its usefulness in persuasion: if opposite vices and virtues are enumerated in the same syntactic frame, the contrast appears self-evident. 'Increase' means growth, reproduction, the biological continuation of a line — OED s.v. 'increase,' n., sense 3a ('propagation, multiplication'). The triplet structure is also part of the formal movement of the sonnet: lines 145-148 form the third quatrain, and this pair of lines states the sonnnet's central thesis in its most compressed form before the couplet's metaphor clinches it.

The identification of antithesis across TLN 145-146 is sound and the rhetorical description is mainstream; the claim that lines 145-148 form the third quatrain is slightly inaccurate (the standard Q1/Q2/Q3/couplet division puts 9-12 as Q3 and 13-14 as the couplet, so 145-148 would be Q3 of Sonnet 11 only if we count from the sonnet's own line 9), but this is a minor structural note, not an interpretive overreach, and does not undermine the core gloss.

anchor_text: Let those whom nature hath not made for store
summary: 'Made for store' means made for the purpose of reproduction — to replenish the world's stock or supply of human beings. The word 'store' carries the sense of a stockpile or reserve that must be kept up. Here the poet introduces a distinction absent from the earlier procreation sonnets: not everyone is equally obliged to reproduce; those whom nature made 'harsh, featureless, and rude' may die without children and no loss is suffered. The beautiful Youth is different.
detail: OED records 'store' in the sense of 'a sufficient supply' and 'the means of reproduction or replenishment' (OED s.v. 'store,' n., senses 1a and 4). The phrase 'made for store' belongs to the agricultural and commercial vocabulary that runs through the procreation sequence — the Youth's beauty is a natural resource, a capital that earns no return if hoarded. 'Featureless' means without good or regular features (OED s.v. 'featureless,' adj.); 'rude' means rough, unpolished, lacking refinement (OED s.v. 'rude,' adj., sense 4). The logical turn here — that the duty to reproduce is proportional to what nature has given — is the volta of the sestet, a secondary pivot after the octave's general argument.

The core gloss of 'store' as 'reproduction / replenishment of stock' is defensible and well-supported by OED, but describing TLN 149-150 as 'the volta of the sestet' is a structural mis-classification: Sonnet 11 is a three-quatrain-plus-couplet English sonnet, not a Petrarchan octave-sestet form, so there is no 'sestet' volta; the rhetorical turn here is a third-quatrain modulation, not a Petrarchan turn, making that framing potentially misleading to students.

anchor_text: She carv'd thee for her seal, and meant thereby, Thou shouldst print more, not let that copy die
summary: A seal was a small carved object — usually of metal or stone — pressed into wax to leave an impression: a signature or mark of authenticity on a letter or document. Nature carved the Youth as such a seal, intending him to press copies of himself into the world through children. A seal that is never used — that leaves no impression — has failed the purpose for which it was made. 'Copy' here means the impression left in wax, but also a manuscript or printed copy: the metaphor moves seamlessly from the seal to the printing press.
detail: The seal-and-wax conceit is precise: the seal itself (the carved matrix) is valueless if it never impresses itself into wax; its whole existence is instrumental — it exists to make copies. The word 'print' reinforces this by evoking the newly familiar technology of moveable type: a compositor's type, like a seal, is carved in reverse so that each impression comes out right. 'Copy' in printing terminology is the text to be reproduced (OED s.v. 'copy,' n., sense 4b). The couplet thus fuses two technologies — the ancient signet-seal and the modern printing press — to make reproduction feel at once intimate and mechanically necessary. The image recalls the printer's analogy used in persuasion-to-marriage texts; Erasmus in the 'Epistle to persuade a young man to marriage' (Englished by Thomas Wilson, 'The Arte of Rhetorique,' 1553) uses the idea that the father sees himself reproduced in his child. The sonnet closes on this image of purposeful replication as the answer to the opening complaint about the Youth wasting what he was made to give.

The seal-and-wax / printing-press conceit is accurately read from the text of TLN 153-154; the claim that 'copy' fuses printing terminology with the seal image is well-attested in the critical tradition and the OED sense cited is correct, and the Erasmus/Wilson procreation-argument parallel is a standard scholarly reference for the sonnets' persuasion-to-reproduce rhetoric.

anchor_text: brave day sunk in hideous night

The pairing of 'brave' (brilliant, fine) against 'hideous' drives home the contrast: a glorious day is swallowed by ugly darkness. The sense of 'brave' as handsome or grand was common in Elizabethan English and survives in phrases like 'a brave show.'

anchor_text: sable curls, all silvered o'er with white

The image is of dark hair turning white with age: black (sable) curls gradually covered in silver. The heraldic word lends the moment a formal, almost ceremonial weight, as if recording the extinction of something noble.

The combination of 'sable' (the heraldic formal colour) and 'silvered' (precious-metal imagery) briefly turns a strand of greying hair into something like a blazon or coat of arms being defaced.

anchor_text: erst from heat did canopy the herd
summary: 'Erst' means 'once' or 'formerly' — it is a now-obsolete adverb common in Elizabethan poetry. 'Canopy' is used as a verb: the trees once served as a canopy (an overhead shade or cover) for livestock sheltering from summer heat. The line pictures the same trees that now stand bare leaves as they were in summer.

The 'herd' sheltering from summer heat under leafy trees is a pastoral image that heightens the pathos of the subsequent image of those same trees stripped bare: what was a living shelter has been emptied by time.

anchor_text: summer's green all girded up in sheaves, / Borne on the bier with white and bristly beard
summary: A 'bier' is the frame or carriage used to carry a coffin at a funeral. Here the poet makes the grain harvest into a funeral procession: summer's green stalks, bound into sheaves and crowned with white ears, are carried to burial like a bearded corpse. The image turns the year's abundance into a body being laid to rest, making the harvest — normally a sign of plenty — a sign of death.
detail: OED s.v. bier, n.: 'A movable frame on which a corpse, or a coffin containing it, is placed before burial.' The 'white and bristly beard' describes the pale, stiff ears of ripe grain, but the word 'beard' (the bristly awn of wheat or barley) is the same word for a man's facial hair, so the sheaf of grain doubles as an old man's whiskered face. This is the sonnet's most compressed image: it runs together the harvest, a funeral, and old age in a single line. The device is prosopopoeia — giving the inanimate (grain) human attributes (a beard, a bier). It prepares the shift to the youth's mortality in the sestet: if even summer's harvest is a corpse, the youth too will be 'borne on the bier.'

anchor_text: nothing 'gainst Time's scythe can make defence / Save breed, to brave him when he takes thee hence
summary: 'Time's scythe' refers to the ancient image of Father Time or the Grim Reaper carrying a curved blade to cut down life the way a farmer cuts grain. 'Breed' means offspring — only children can defy this reaper. 'Brave' here is a verb meaning 'to defy' or 'to challenge,' completing a wordplay across the sonnet: 'brave' began as an adjective (line 2, splendid day) and returns as a verb (brave him, face him down). The couplet's entire argument is: nothing defeats Time except children, who carry on your beauty after you are gone.
detail: OED s.v. brave, v., sense 1: 'To encounter or face bravely, to defy.' The verbal 'brave' is rarer than the adjective; its appearance in the couplet answers the adjective 'brave' at line 2 — the brave day is sunk, but breed can brave Time itself. OED s.v. breed, n., sense 1: 'Offspring, progeny.' The word is deliberately plain, even blunt, after the elaborate catalogue of nature's losses: the argument strips to its barest biological term. 'Time's scythe' iconographically fuses the agricultural harvest-tool (which the preceding lines have already introduced via sheaves and the bier) with the classical and Renaissance figure of Father Time as the Grim Reaper. The scythe appears again in Shakespeare's Sonnet 60 ('Time's fell hand defaced') and Sonnet 65 ('against his scythe ... hold a plea'), establishing it as a recurring motif of the sequence.

anchor_text: beauty which you hold in lease
summary: A lease gives someone the right to use property for a fixed term, after which the term expires and the property must be returned or renewed. At death the lease runs out and the beauty is lost unless a child carries it forward.

In Elizabethan property law, a lease (unlike a fee-simple title) was a temporary grant; the tenant had use of the land but not permanent ownership. The argument follows Erasmus's persuasion-to-marriage template: nature's gifts are a loan, not a gift, and must be repaid in kind.

anchor_text: Find no determination; then you were

anchor_text: Who lets so fair a house fall to decay
summary: At line 9 the poet pivots from abstract legal argument (the lease/determination conceit) to a concrete domestic question: who would let a fine house fall to ruin when good management could preserve it? This is the sonnet's volta, the turn of thought. 'House' carries two meanings at once: the physical building and the family lineage ('the house of York,' 'the house of Tudor'). Letting it 'fall to decay' means both failing to maintain an estate and dying without an heir.

Here the three-quatrain structure runs: Q1 (the problem of self-possession), Q2 (the lease conceit and its solution), Q3 (the domestic analogy and its indictment). The indignant question ('Who lets... fall to decay?') is a device Puttenham calls 'erotema' — a rhetorical question that implies its own answer. 'House' meaning lineage or dynasty was entirely current in Shakespeare's England, as in 'a noble house,' 'the house of Lancaster'; the double sense allows the Youth's body, his estate, and his family line to collapse into a single image of culpable negligence.

anchor_text: husbandry in honour might uphold
summary: 'Husbandry' meant both the careful management of a farm or estate and, by derivation from 'husband,' the duties proper to a married man. The word compresses the poem's whole argument into a single noun: to be a good steward of your beauty is inseparable from being a husband and fathering children. The word 'honour' adds a third pressure — to let beauty die without an heir is not merely wasteful but dishonourable.

The agricultural sense — careful cultivation that prevents decay — answers the 'house falling to ruin' image of the previous line; the marital sense — being a husband — answers the poem's explicit argument that the Youth should marry and have children. The word thus closes the gap between the poem's two domains (estate management and procreation) in a single compressed turn. anchor_text: methinks I have astronomy
summary: Here 'astronomy' means astrology — the practice of reading the positions of the stars and planets to predict future events. In Elizabethan English the two words were largely interchangeable; the modern distinction between observational astronomy and predictive astrology had not yet fixed itself. The speaker claims to possess this art but immediately qualifies it.
detail: The OED records 'astronomy' used to mean 'astrology' from the 14th century through the 17th (OED s.v. 'astronomy,' sense 2: 'astrology; the art of judging of the influence of the stars'). The qualification that follows — disclaiming the ability to predict plagues, famines, or royal fortune — is a specific disavowal of judicial astrology, the most contested branch of the art, which claimed to read individual fate and political destiny from the stars.

anchor_text: By oft predict that I in heaven find

anchor_text: to store thou wouldst convert
summary: 'Store' means offspring or reproductive increase — to 'convert to store' is to turn from self-absorption toward procreation, investing one's gifts in the next generation rather than keeping them only for oneself. anchor_text: truth's and beauty's doom and date
summary: 'Doom' means judgment or the appointed end — not primarily disaster, but a final, irreversible verdict. 'Date' means the appointed time or term of existence (as in 'out-of-date': the time has expired). Together 'doom and date' form an alliterative phrase for the absolute ending of something. If the youth dies childless, his death will be the death of truth and beauty themselves.

'doom,' n., senses 1-3); 'date' as 'the time appointed for the termination of anything; the period or term of duration' (OED s.v. 'date,' n.2, sense 4). The pairing 'doom and date' is a formulaic hendiadys — two nouns expressing a single concept — and the alliteration gives it the weight of a legal or theological verdict. The couplet asserts that if the youth does not reproduce, his physical end is simultaneously the end of the abstract qualities ('truth and beauty') he embodies — an absolute claim that makes selfishness a cosmic loss, not merely a personal one.

anchor_text: every thing that grows / Holds in perfection but a little moment
summary: 'Holds in perfection' means 'maintains itself at its peak.' The verb 'hold' here is reflexive — it stays, not it grips. 'Moment' in the sense of a tiny, barely measurable instant (as in 'a moment of time'), not a loose synonym for 'while.' The two words together set the sonnet's argument: full bloom lasts only a sliver of time.

This precision primes the plant metaphor of lines 5-8 and the personified Time of lines 13-14.

anchor_text: all in war with Time for love of you, / As he takes from you, I engraft you new
summary: 'Engraft' is a gardening term: to cut a living slip from one plant and insert it into another so that it grows on in a new host. The speaker promises to preserve the Youth by grafting him — his beauty, his essence — into verse, exactly as Time strips it away. This is the first appearance in the sequence of the argument that poetry, not procreation, can defeat time. The couplet also stages the speaker as an active combatant: 'all in war with Time' means entirely committed to fighting Time on the Youth's behalf.

The horticultural precision matters: grafting does not merely copy — it produces a living, growing thing continuous with the host. Shakespeare is claiming that his verse will not store the Youth's image like a painting stores it (Sonnet 18's 'eternal lines to time') but will keep him actively alive, growing in each new reader. This claim marks the hinge between the procreation sonnets (Sonnets 1-14 argue for children as the vehicle of survival) and the verse-immortality sonnets that follow (Sonnets 17, 18, 55, 63). Sonnet 15 is the precise moment of the turn: the procreation argument is not abandoned but supplemented, as the speaker for the first time offers himself — his writing — as the alternative.

anchor_text: maiden gardens, yet unset, With virtuous wish would bear you living flowers
summary: The 'maiden gardens, yet unset' are young women's bodies figured as gardens that have not yet been planted — 'unset' meaning no seeds or slips have been placed in them. 'Bear you living flowers' means bear children who look like the Youth. The gardening metaphor is transparently sexual: to 'set' a plant was the standard term for inserting a cutting into soil, and the women's 'virtuous wish' frames the desire in chaste terms even as the imagery is frankly procreative.

The poet's rhetorical aim is to make procreation sound both virtuous and natural, hence 'virtuous wish': the women are not depicted as wanton but as properly desiring to bear offspring of such beauty.

anchor_text: your painted counterfeit
summary: 'Counterfeit' here means a portrait — a painted likeness, not a fraud. The word carried both senses in Elizabethan English: something made to resemble the original, whether deceptively or artistically. The poet argues that 'living flowers' (children) are 'much liker' to the Youth than any painted portrait or poem, because a child inherits actual life, not merely the appearance of it.

Portrait-painting was the standard Elizabethan technology for preserving a likeness, and the competition between verse, painting, and progeny as vehicles of immortality was a recognized topos. Sidney's 'Defence of Poesy' (1595) argues that the poet creates a 'second nature' superior to the painter's mere imitation; the poet of the sonnets here reverses the hierarchy by placing the living child above both arts. The same contrast between the painted image and the living original appears at Sonnet 53 ('What is your substance, whereof are you made') and Sonnet 24.

The sonnet has been arguing that verse ('my pupil pen') cannot truly preserve the Youth; now it offers that only the 'lines of life' — children who carry the Youth's living form — can 'repair' (restore, make good) the damage Time inflicts. 'Time's pencil' refers to a portrait-brush, since 'pencil' meant a fine-pointed brush in Elizabethan English.

'pencil' n., sense 1). 'Repair' means to restore or make good (OED s.v. 'repair' v.1, sense 3). The phrase 'my pupil pen' is the poet's self-deprecation: his pen is still a learner compared with the master-art of procreation. anchor_text: To give away yourself, keeps yourself still, And you must live, drawn by your own sweet skill
summary: The closing couplet states the paradox at the heart of the procreation argument: to give yourself away — to spend yourself in having children — is the one way to keep yourself. The child preserves the parent's form. 'Drawn by your own sweet skill' continues the painting metaphor: only the Youth can produce a true likeness of himself, by fathering a child — no poet's or painter's art can match it.

This is the terminal move of the procreation argument that runs from Sonnet 1 through Sonnet 17; Sonnet 1 calls beauty's waste 'self-substantial fuel' and asks the Youth to 'feed the world's due.' The paradox has a theological parallel in Christ's saying 'He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it' (Matthew 10:39, Geneva 1599), though the sonnet applies it entirely in the secular register of procreation. 'Drawn' puns on portraiture (drawn = depicted) and on the natural pull toward reproduction.

The paradox of giving-as-keeping is sound and intrinsic to the couplet, but invoking Matthew 10:39 as a theological parallel courts over-reading: the sonnet's context is entirely secular procreation, the verbal parallel is loose, and there is no evidence Shakespeare intended or expected the allusion; flagging it as a 'parallel' the sonnet 'secularizes' is too strong without firmer evidence of intentional echo.

anchor_text: fill'd with your most high deserts
summary: 'Deserts' here means merits or what one is rightfully owed — the full worth that makes someone deserving of praise. The poet worries that even an accurate account of the youth's deserts will be dismissed as exaggeration.
detail: OED records 'desert' (n.) in the sense 'that which is deserved; the condition of deserving well' (OED s.v. 'desert' n.1, sense 2) with Elizabethan currency. The phrase 'most high deserts' stacks superlative force on a word already meaning owed worth, intensifying the poet's claim that the youth's qualities are genuinely, not hyperbolically, supreme — which makes the poem's strategy of self-doubt more pointed: even plain truth will sound like flattery.

sources.name: OED

OED s.v. 'desert' n.1, sense 2 is real and well-attested with citations from the 14th century onward; the gloss accurately reflects the lexical range.

'Deserts' as merits/owed worth is the standard Elizabethan sense and fits the line exactly; the gloss that accurate praise will sound like exaggeration is the poem's central strategy, and the interpretation is mainstream and unforced.

anchor_text: in fresh numbers number all your graces
summary: 'Numbers' was the standard Elizabethan word for verses or metrical lines (counted feet), and the poet plays on both senses at once: to 'number' the youth's graces in 'numbers' is to count his qualities by writing poetry about them. This figure — using the same root word in two different senses in a single phrase — is called polyptoton.
detail: OED records 'number' (n.) in the sense 'a metrical unit; a verse, line, or stanza; especially (in pl.) a poem, verses' (OED s.v. 'number' n., sense 18a), with extensive Elizabethan use. Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) uses 'numbers' as a near-synonym for verse throughout his prosodic discussion. The polyptoton ('numbers'/'number') enacts what it describes: the poem counts while it sings. 'Fresh' adds a secondary sense — new, not yet stale or discredited — which ironically sets up the next line's claim that such fresh verse would still be disbelieved.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'number' n., sense 18a: 'a metrical line, a verse; (pl.) verses, poetry.' Active in this sense from the 16th century.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 230
