'Numbers' for verses is well-attested Elizabethan usage and the wordplay on number/numbers (polyptoton) is evident in the line itself; identifying 'fresh' as meaning 'new, not yet stale' is defensible and the note that this irony sets up the disbelief of line 231 is a sound mainstream reading.

anchor_text: The age to come would say 'This poet lies
summary: The poem stages a crisis of poetic credibility: future readers will call the poet a liar, because beauty this perfect sounds impossible. This is the central conceit of Sonnet 17 — the very accuracy of the poet's verse will condemn it as invention. The argument closes the first 17 sonnets' procreation sequence by showing that poetry alone cannot guarantee the youth's survival; a child is needed as living proof.
detail: The anxiety about incredible-sounding praise was a recognized problem in Renaissance poetics. Sir Philip Sidney in 'The Defence of Poesy' (1595) defends the poet against the charge that he lies — 'the poet nothing affirmeth, and therefore never lieth' — but Sidney's argument is about fictional assertion, not about whether hyperbolic praise will be believed. Shakespeare inverts the problem: the poet's verse is not fiction but fact, and it is that factual truth which will be disbelieved. The strategy self-deflates sixteen sonnets of genuine compliment and converts the deflation into a new argument for procreation: only a living child can serve as corroborating evidence.

sources.name: Sidney
sources.citation: Sir Philip Sidney, 'The Defence of Poesy' (composed c. 1579-80, printed 1595), on the poet and the charge of lying.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 231

Sidney's exact formulation 'the poet, he nothing affirmeth, and therefore never lieth' is real and verbatim; the annotation correctly characterizes Sidney's argument as being about fictional assertion rather than hyperbolic praise, and accurately describes Shakespeare as inverting it.

The conceit that true praise sounds like lying is plainly stated in the quatrain, and the gloss that this closes the procreation sequence by showing poetry alone is insufficient is the consensus scholarly reading of the sequence's structure; the Sidney parallel is apt even if the two arguments are not identical.

anchor_text: your true rights be term'd a poet's rage
summary: 'Rage' here means poetic frenzy or inspired passion — the classical idea that poets write in a state of divine madness rather than cool reason. Used dismissively: future readers will say the poet's praise was just emotional excess, not sober truth. 'Your true rights' means what the youth genuinely deserves by right — his actual, owed praise.
detail: The concept of poetic 'fury' or 'rage' descends from Plato's 'Ion,' where Socrates argues that poets do not compose by art but by divine possession (Plato, 'Ion' 533d-534e). Cicero in 'De Oratore' 2.46.194 speaks of a poet as 'afflatus divino quodam spiritu' (breathed on by a certain divine spirit). Horace in 'Ars Poetica' 295-300 engages the same question of whether genius or art makes the poet. By the late 16th century the phrase 'poet's rage' had drifted toward simple mockery of extravagant verse: it names not inspiration but the appearance of it — exactly the dismissal future readers will level at this sonnet. 'True rights' = rightful dues (OED s.v. 'right' n., sense 8: 'that which is due to anyone; just or lawful claim').

Plato Ion 533d-534e is the confirmed locus classicus for the furor poeticus doctrine; Horace Ars Poetica 295-300 does engage the genius-versus-art debate via the Democritus passage; OED 'rage' n. sense 5a for poetic frenzy is standard.

'Rage' for poetic frenzy is well documented and the line explicitly marks it as a dismissal future readers will apply; the gloss that 'true rights' means rightful dues is orthodox and not strained, and the classical furor poeticus lineage is accurate without being over-applied.

anchor_text: stretched metre of an antique song
summary: 'Stretched metre' means exaggerated, overwrought verse — lines pulled beyond natural proportion to accommodate inflated praise. 'Antique' means old-fashioned, from an earlier era. Future readers will dismiss the sonnets as the padded verse of some forgotten, less reliable age — not as accurate contemporary testimony.
detail: OED records 'antique' (adj.) in the sense 'of or belonging to ancient or early times; old-fashioned, out of date' (OED s.v. 'antique' adj., sense 2), current in the period. The pairing 'stretched metre' condemns the poetry on two fronts: metrically strained (the lines have been stretched to fit their subject) and generically old-fashioned (an antique song belongs to a credulous age). Schmidt's 'Shakespeare-Lexicon' notes 'stretch' in the sense of exaggeration or distortion elsewhere in Shakespeare (s.v. 'stretch'). The phrase quietly asks whether the procreation sequence itself is such a stretched, antique thing — only a living child can redeem its credibility.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'antique' adj., sense 2: 'of old times; old-fashioned.' Widely current in the 16th and 17th centuries.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, 'Shakespeare-Lexicon' (1874-75), s.v. 'stretch' vb., noting Shakespeare's use in the sense of exaggeration or distortion.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 236

OED 'antique' adj. sense 2 is real; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'stretch' is confirmed and explicitly cites 'stretched metre' at Sonnet 17 line 12 as an instance of the sense 'strained, constrained, affected, exaggerated.'

The core glosses ('stretched metre' = padded/overwrought verse; 'antique' = old-fashioned) are defensible and mainstream, but the closing suggestion that the sonnet quietly asks whether the procreation sequence itself is 'such a stretched, antique thing' is an editorial interpolation that the line does not support — the speaker is attributing that dismissal to future readers, not applying it self-reflectively, so that closing move overreads.

anchor_text: more lovely and more temperate
summary: 'Temperate' here carries its full Elizabethan weight: not merely mild or pleasant, but evenly balanced in all qualities. The word derives from the Latin 'temperare' (to mix in due proportion), and the ideal of temperance was a cardinal virtue meaning the right measure of opposing qualities. Summer runs to extremes — too hot, too rough, too brief — while the beloved does not.
detail: The OED records 'temperate' in the sense of 'having due moderation or self-restraint in all qualities; well-balanced' from the fifteenth century onward (OED s.v. 'temperate', adj., sense 1a). The philosophical background is Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, widely absorbed into Elizabethan moral discourse. Contrasting the beloved's stable temperance against summer's inconstant heat and cold sets up the entire poem's logic: nature oscillates, the beloved does not, and the poem preserves that steadiness.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'temperate', adj., senses 1a and 2a (moderated; free from extremes)

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 240
OED s.v. 'temperate' sense 1a is a real entry documenting the 'well-balanced, free from extremes' sense from the fifteenth century onward, directly supporting the gloss.

The gloss that 'temperate' means evenly balanced rather than merely mild is standard early modern usage and is well supported by OED; the Aristotelian background for temperance as a cardinal virtue of the mean is mainstream and defensible, and the contrast with summer's excess follows directly from the poem's structure.

anchor_text: summer's lease hath all too short a date
summary: The poet casts summer as a tenant holding a property lease: it possesses the season only for a fixed term ('date' = the expiry date of a legal contract), not permanently. The image reduces summer's glory to a temporary tenancy, which the beloved's beauty — owned outright, not leased — will outlast.
detail: 'Lease' in Elizabethan legal usage denoted a contract granting temporary possession of land or property for a set period; 'date' was the technical term for the fixed term or expiry of such a document (OED s.v. 'date', n.1, sense 3: 'the fixed time at which something expires or must be done'). The legal register is not ornamental: it sets up a property-law argument about who truly 'owns' beauty. Summer holds it on sufferance; the beloved 'ow'st' (owns) it outright (line 248). Shakespeare uses legal metaphor extensively in the Sonnets (cf. Sonnet 30: 'account,' 'losses'; Sonnet 134: 'bond,' 'forfeit').

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'lease', n., sense 1 (a contract for temporary possession); s.v. 'date', n.1, sense 3 (the fixed term or expiry of a legal instrument)

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 242
OED s.v. 'lease' sense 1 and s.v. 'date' n.1 sense 3 are real entries that document both the legal-tenancy and fixed-term-expiry senses invoked by the annotation.

The legal-metaphor reading of 'lease' and 'date' is widely accepted in sonnet scholarship and the claim that 'date' = the expiry of a legal instrument is solid OED sense; the observation that summer 'holds on sufferance' while the beloved 'ow'st' outright (line 248) correctly identifies the sustained legal register across the poem.

anchor_text: that fair thou ow'st
summary: 'Ow'st' is a contracted form of 'owest,' here meaning 'own' or 'possess' (not the modern sense of owing a debt). The beloved 'owns' their beauty outright — it is genuinely theirs, not borrowed from the season. The legal thread from 'lease' (line 4) is completed: summer only rents its beauty; the beloved holds it in fee simple.
detail: The verb 'owe' carried the primary meaning 'to possess, to own' well into the seventeenth century, with 'to be indebted' as a secondary sense (OED s.v. 'owe', v., sense I.1: 'to have, possess, own'; cite usages through c. 1660). Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon documents 'owe' = 'own' throughout the plays and Sonnets. The choice of 'ow'st' rather than a synonym for beauty reinforces the property-law metaphor running through the poem: beauty is an asset that can be owned, leased, or lost.

OED s.v. 'owe' v. sense I.1 and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'owe' both genuinely document the primary early-modern sense 'to have, possess, own', with Schmidt explicitly citing 'that fair thou --st' as an example.

'Ow'st' = 'own/possess' (not 'be indebted') is a standard early modern usage fully documented in OED and Schmidt, and tying it back to the 'lease' metaphor of line 4 as the completion of a property-law argument is a mainstream and well-supported reading.

anchor_text: eternal lines to time thou grow'st
summary: 'Lines' means both the lines of the poem and — in a secondary Elizabethan sense — lines of descent or lineage. The poet claims the sonnet weaves the beloved into time permanently, a boast for poetry's immortalising power that Ovid made for his own work at the close of the Metamorphoses.
detail: OED records 'line' in the sense of 'a line of descent; lineage, stock' from the fourteenth century (OED s.v. 'line', n.1, sense 17). The pun enriches the argument: the beloved will grow into permanence both through the verse lines themselves and through a kind of genealogical inscription into the record of time. The classical precedent is Ovid's famous conclusion to the Metamorphoses: 'Iamque opus exegi, quod nec Iovis ira nec ignis / nec poterit ferrum nec edax abolere vetustas' ('And now my work is done, which neither the wrath of Jove, nor fire, nor sword, nor devouring age shall be able to destroy'; Metamorphoses XV.871-72, Golding trans. 1567, Book XV). Shakespeare's claim is more intimate — the immortality is offered not to the poet's fame but to the beloved specifically — but the Ovidian precedent stands behind every line of the sonnet's closing argument. The couplet's 'So long as men can breathe' then extends the immortality to all future readers, making the act of reading itself the proof of the promise.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'line', n.1, sense 17 (lineage, line of descent; used alongside the poetic-line sense in early modern English)

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book XV, lines 871-72 (Golding trans., 1567, Book XV): the poet's boast that his work outlasts Jove's wrath, fire, and time — the classical archetype of poetic immortality

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 250

OED s.v. 'line' n.1 sense 17 (lineage) is a real entry, and Metamorphoses XV.871-72 ('Iamque opus exegi...') is the correct standard citation for Ovid's poetic-immortality boast, with the Golding 1567 translation confirmed as Book XV.

The poetic-lines reading is uncontroversial, but the secondary lineage/descent pun, while OED-attested as a sense of 'line', is contested in Sonnet 18 commentary — most editors read 'eternal lines' as the verse alone, and the context 'to time thou grow'st' does not clearly activate a genealogical sense; the claim that the pun is present should be marked uncertain rather than stated as fact at high confidence.

anchor_text: Devouring Time, blunt thou the lion's paws
summary: The opening address to 'Devouring Time' echoes Ovid's phrase 'tempus edax rerum' ('Time, devourer of all things'), from Metamorphoses 15. Ovid uses the same image to catalogue everything time consumes before boasting that his own poetry will survive it — the exact argument this sonnet will make.
detail: Ovid's declaration at Metamorphoses 15.234 — 'tempus edax rerum, tuque, invidiosa vetustas' ('Time the devourer of things, and you, envious age') — was among the most quoted lines in Renaissance Europe. Shakespeare imports both the image and the underlying logic: Ovid's poem, the Metamorphoses itself, closes by claiming that his verse will outlast 'Jove's wrath' and time's destruction (Met. 15.871-879, in Golding's 1567 English). Sonnet 19 rehearses the same concession-then-defiance structure. The lion's blunted paws and the tiger's stripped teeth (lines 1, 3) make Time's devastation physical and animal before the poet stakes his counter-claim in the couplet.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.234 ('tempus edax rerum'); 15.871-879 (the poet's claim that his verse survives Jove's anger and time). Arthur Golding's English translation (1567) was Shakespeare's likely source.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 253

Ovid Met. 15.234 'tempus edax rerum, tuque invidiosa vetustas' is confirmed at that line number, and the epilogue at 15.871-879 ('iamque opus exegi') is confirmed real; both sources support the concession-then-defiance argument attributed to them.

The 'tempus edax rerum' parallel (Met. 15.234) and the concession-then-defiance structure matching Ovid's close of the Metamorphoses are both textually sound and mainstream in Shakespeare scholarship.

anchor_text: draw no lines there with thine antique pen
summary: 'Antique' was pronounced identically with 'antic' in Elizabethan English and carries both senses at once: 'ancient' (Time is old) and 'antic' (grotesque, clownish, bizarre). Time's 'pen' — the instrument that carves wrinkles into the beloved's face — is both venerable and absurd, a clown's tool invading something sacred.
detail: In the First Folio and contemporary usage 'antique' and 'antic' were spelling variants of the same word and regularly pun on each other; editors must choose which sense to foreground. 'Antic' meant a grotesque figure, a buffoon, a clown — as in Hamlet's 'put an antic disposition on' (Hamlet 1.5) or Richard II's 'And there the antic sits, / Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp' (Richard II 3.2), where Death plays the fool. Here the double meaning diminishes Time: his great power is wielded with a clown's pen. The image of wrinkles as lines drawn or carved was a standard conceit — see also Sonnet 63 ('Against my love shall be as I am now, / With Time's injurious hand crush'd and o'erworn') — but 'antique/antic pen' sharpens it into satirical portrait-writing, where the joke is on Time.

sources.name: OED

The antique/antic homophone pun is firmly established in Renaissance orthography and in standard editions (Booth, Vendler); the Richard II and Hamlet parallels for 'antic' are accurate and the diminishing-Time-as-clown reading is mainstream.

anchor_text: Him in thy course untainted do allow
summary: 'Pattern' here means 'model' or 'exemplar' — the original from which copies are made. The beloved is not just beautiful but is the standard of beauty itself, the template by which future generations will know what beauty looks like. 'Untainted' means uncorrupted or undefiled — kept free of Time's usual spoiling touch.
detail: OED records 'pattern' in the sense of 'an original or model proposed for imitation; an exemplar' from the 15th century (OED s.v. 'pattern' n. sense 3a). Shakespeare uses it this way elsewhere: 'Be thou the trumpet of our wrath / And sullen presage of your own decay' is not the same, but compare Sonnet 98 and the frequent address to the youth as the archetype others should study. The claim escalates the praise: the youth is not merely lovely but is the very definition of beauty held in trust for the future — a standard that will be lost if Time defaces him. 'Untainted' appears in the OED (s.v. 'untainted' adj.) from the 1580s with the specific sense 'not corrupted or stained.'

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'pattern' n. sense 3a: 'an original proposed for imitation; a model or exemplar.' OED s.v. 'untainted' adj.: 'not corrupted, not defiled'; first recorded uses from the 1580s.

Both 'pattern' as exemplar/model and 'untainted' as uncorrupted are correctly glossed with attested Elizabethan senses, and the reading of the youth as the defining standard of beauty to be preserved is the plain sense of lines 263-264.

anchor_text: Yet, do thy worst old Time: despite thy wrong
summary: The couplet delivers the poem's final reversal: having conceded Time everything and forbidden him one thing, the poet now withdraws even the prohibition and throws down a challenge. 'Do thy worst' is a deliberate dare — Time will deface the youth, but the verse will keep him young anyway. The immortality-through-verse claim completes the argument that Ovid made at the close of the Metamorphoses and that Sonnet 18 ('So long as men can breathe') had already introduced.
detail: The boast that poetry defeats time was a recognized literary topos, most directly inherited from the close of Ovid's Metamorphoses (15.871-879), where Ovid declares his fame will outlast 'Jove's wrath,' fire, sword, and time itself — a bolder version of Horace's 'exegi monumentum aere perennius' ('I have raised a monument more lasting than bronze,' Odes 3.30). In the sonnet sequence Sonnet 18 ('So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see, / So long lives this') stakes the same claim; Sonnet 19 restates it after a more combative contest with Time. The couplet's grammar — 'My love shall in my verse ever live young' — compresses two possible readings: 'my beloved' will live young in the verse, and 'my love' (the feeling or poem) will remain young forever. Both readings endorse the verse as the living counter to Time's pen.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.871-879 ('parte tamen meliore mei super alta perennis / astra ferar' — 'by the better part of me I shall be borne above the stars, immortal'). Arthur Golding's English translation (1567).

The verse-defeats-time topos via Ovid Met. 15.871-879 and Horace Odes 3.30 is the accepted literary-historical context, and the dual reading of 'my love' (beloved / the poem itself) is a genuine crux noted by major editors including Booth and Vendler.

anchor_text: master mistress of my passion
summary: A compound title for the beloved: 'master' marks gender (male) and perhaps superiority; 'mistress' is the conventional label for the object of a love poet's devotion. Together the phrase refuses to settle into either category — the youth is both the lord the poet serves and the beloved whose praise he writes.
detail: In Elizabethan love-poetry 'mistress' had no necessary sexual meaning; it was simply the technical term for the subject of the poet's affections — the role Laura plays for Petrarch. 'Passion' itself could mean either intense emotion or a literary work expressing that emotion, so 'master mistress of my passion' simultaneously addresses the youth as the poet's feeling and as the presiding spirit of the poet's verse. The compound holds the poem's central conceit in miniature: a person who combines what is culturally assigned to both sexes.

The reading of 'mistress' as the conventional Petrarchan object of devotion and 'passion' as both emotion and literary composition is well-established and mainstream; the compound's refusal to settle into one gender category is the sonnet's declared central conceit and the gloss does not overreach it.

anchor_text: gentle heart, but not acquainted With shifting change
summary: The poet credits the youth with feminine tenderness but not the inconstancy that Elizabethan convention assigned to women. 'Shifting change' means restless fickleness — the stereotype that women alter their affections capriciously. The youth has the soft heart without the unreliable will.
detail: The misogynist charge of female inconstancy was a commonplace of Petrarchan verse and conduct literature. Sidney's Astrophil complains of Stella's 'changing'; Spenser's Amoretti make constancy a virtue precisely because it is presented as rare. By giving the youth 'a woman's gentle heart' but not the shifting that goes with 'false women's fashion,' the poet claims the youth unites virtues ordinarily split between the sexes — a core conceit of the sonnet.

sources.name: Puttenham

The equation of 'shifting change' with the Petrarchan/Elizabethan commonplace of female inconstancy is defensible and the text supports it directly ('as is false women's fashion'); the Sidney and Spenser parallels are illustrative rather than forced.

anchor_text: more bright than theirs, less false in rolling, Gilding the object
summary: 'Rolling' means roving or glancing about — eyes that 'roll' are eyes that dart from one object to another, a sign of flirtatious inconstancy. The youth's eye is brighter than women's yet less prone to wander; it 'gilds' (covers in golden light) whatever it rests on, as sunlight makes things shine.
detail: OED records 'rolling' in the sense of the eyes turning about to survey multiple objects as well-established in the period; the 'rolling eye' was a conventional mark of the lascivious or unfaithful woman. 'Gilding' plays on both physical light and metaphorical honor: to gild is to apply gold leaf, so the youth's gaze confers worth on whatever it alights on. The blazon has moved from face and heart to eye — a standard catalogue element — but each attribute simultaneously corrects a female vice.

The gloss of 'rolling' as roving/glancing eyes and 'gilding' as conferring golden light/worth is mainstream and consistent with OED usage; the claim that the rolling eye conventionally marks the lascivious woman is well-attested in period conduct literature and blazon poetry.

anchor_text: A man in hue all 'hues' in his controlling
summary: 'Hue' means complexion or outward appearance. The line says the youth, a man in appearance, controls all other appearances — he outshines every other beauty. The word-play is made explicit in the quarto's italics: 'A Man in hew, all Hews in his controwling,' where 'hews' is italicized as if a proper name or special term. OED records 'hue' (variant 'hew') primarily as complexion, color, or form; a proper-name reading would embed the youth's identity in the poem's texture. The ambiguity is likely deliberate: the line simultaneously states a straightforward claim (the youth controls all beauty) and gestures toward a personal address. The same technique — a proper name concealed in a common word — appears in Sidney's 'Astrophil and Stella' (the name 'Rich' in sonnet 37, referring to Lord Rich).

anchor_text: she prick'd thee out for women's pleasure, Mine be thy love and thy love's use their treasure
summary: 'Prick'd thee out' means chose or selected you — to 'prick out' a name was to mark it on a list with a pin-prick. Shakespeare is simultaneously fully aware of the anatomical meaning, which the word 'one thing' at line 278 (the male organ) has just primed. The couplet then divides the youth's value: the poet keeps 'love' (emotional devotion); women get 'love's use' (the sexual function), which the financial word 'treasure' colors as an asset yielding returns.

The bawdy secondary sense (prick = penis) is activated by 'one thing' in the preceding line, making the couplet simultaneously a witty legal division of claims and a frank joke about anatomy. 'Use' likewise carries a financial sense (interest on a loan, OED s.v. 'use' n., sense 7) as well as a sexual one — giving women the 'use' of the body while the poet retains the emotional interest. The double meaning is characteristic of the poem's strategy throughout: anatomical and financial registers overlap to make the final division simultaneously affectionate, rueful, and comic.

Both the administrative 'prick out' (mark on a list) and its bawdy secondary sense (activated by 'one thing' at line 278) are firmly documented and the division of 'love' versus 'love's use' as emotional versus sexual/financial is a standard and defensible reading of the couplet; the annotation does not overreach.

anchor_text: Making a couplement of proud compare
summary: 'Couplement' means a pairing or coupling together; 'compare' here is used as a noun meaning comparison (not a verb). The phrase means 'assembling a matched set of arrogant comparisons' — the rival poet lines up sun, moon, sea-gems, and April flowers side by side as boastful similes for his beloved.

'Compare' as a noun meaning 'comparison' is also Elizabethan usage: OED 'compare' n.1, sense 1, with examples including Sidney and Spenser. The word 'proud' carries the sense of ostentatious or presumptuous (OED 'proud' adj., sense 5), so the line indicts the rival's catalogue as self-congratulatory display rather than honest praise. Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (s.v. 'compare' n.) notes the noun use as standard in the period.

'Compare' as a noun meaning comparison and 'proud' as ostentatious are both standard Elizabethan usage, and the reading of the line as a catalogue of boastful similes is directly confirmed by lines 285-288 listing sun, moon, sea-gems, and April flowers.

anchor_text: O! let me, true in love, but truly write
summary: This is the volta — the turn of argument that the sonnet form requires, usually at or near line 9. After eight lines describing the rival's extravagant style, the speaker pivots to his own counter-claim: because he loves truly, he will write truly, and plain truth is enough. The volta frames honest feeling against rhetorical performance.
detail: In the English sonnet form the volta typically falls at or after the eighth line, between the second and third quatrain, or it is held back to the closing couplet; here it falls squarely at line 9 (TLN 289), the classic position. George Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) describes the turn in a sonnet as the moment when the argument shifts or is resolved; Sidney's Astrophil and Stella uses the same placement. The logic of the turn is ethical as well as formal: 'true in love' makes 'truly write' not just a stylistic preference but a moral obligation. The two uses of 'truly' play against 'painted' in line 2 and 'false compare' that will be explicit in Sonnet 130, making the anti-blazon position moral rather than merely aesthetic.

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book II, on the sonnet's structure and the turn of argument.

sources.name: Sidney, Astrophil and Stella
sources.citation: Philip Sidney, 'Astrophil and Stella' (composed c. 1582, published 1591), as the model English sequence for volta placement at line 9.

Line 9 is the recognised volta position in the English sonnet and the pivot here from rival's method to speaker's own counter-claim is clearly enacted in the text; the ethical weight placed on 'truly' ('true in love' therefore 'truly write') is a defensible mainstream reading, not an overreach.

anchor_text: My glass shall not persuade me
summary: 'Glass' here means a looking-glass, that is, a mirror. The poet refuses to accept what his mirror shows him — that he is aging — because the youth's continued youth seems to disprove it.
detail: The sense is common in Shakespeare and his contemporaries. OED records 'glass' as a mirror or reflective surface from the 13th century onward (OED s.v. 'glass' n. 6a). The poem opens with the poet's refusal of empirical evidence — the mirror's testimony — in favour of a logical argument: since his heart lives in the youth's body, the youth's face is the truer mirror of the poet's age.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 295

The core reading — mirror as the poet's rejected empirical evidence, the youth's face as the truer index of his age — is a sound, mainstream-defensible interpretation of the poem's opening argument.

anchor_text: youth and thou are of one date
summary: 'Of one date' means of the same age or duration — while the youth is still young, he and Youth itself are the same thing, so the poet cannot be old while the youth's face is young.
detail: OED records 'date' in the sense of 'age, duration of existence, period of life' (OED s.v. 'date' n.2, sense 3), citing Shakespeare among the examples. The phrase collapses the youth and the personified quality of Youth into one: if Youth and the young man are identical in age, then any mirror reading that shows the poet older than the youth would be a logical contradiction.

'Of one date' meaning coeval is uncontroversial; the gloss slightly over-schematises by personifying 'Youth' as a separate entity the text then collapses with the young man, but the operative sense (the youth is still young, so the poet cannot be old) is accurate.

anchor_text: keep so chary As tender nurse her babe from faring ill
summary: 'Chary' means carefully, cautiously — with anxious care. The poet will guard the youth's heart the way a nurse guards an infant: not out of possessiveness but out of protective tenderness.
detail: OED records 'chary' as an adjective meaning 'careful, cautious, wary' (OED s.v. 'chary', adj., sense 1), derived from Old English cearig (sorrowful, anxious). In Shakespeare it typically means 'careful' or 'sparing'; here the adverbial sense is 'with great care.' The nurse-and-infant simile is the poem's most openly tender image, softening the argumentative logic of the preceding lines with a picture of selfless, nurturing protection. 'Faring ill' means suffering harm or going badly — 'fare' in the sense of 'to get on, to do' (OED s.v. 'fare', v., sense 3).

The adverbial sense 'with great care' is the correct reading in context, the nurse-infant simile is accurately characterised as the poem's most openly tender image, and 'faring ill' as 'suffering harm' is uncontroversial.

anchor_text: unperfect actor on the stage, Who with his fear is put beside his part
summary: 'Unperfect' means imperfectly prepared or not fully learned, not merely flawed. 'Put beside his part' means thrown off, made to forget his lines — 'beside' here carries the sense of 'away from' or 'outside of.' The actor fails not because he lacks talent but because stage-fright overwhelms what he knows.

No: / Farewell, my lord; farewell, good night'). 'Put beside' meaning 'caused to depart from, made to lose' is recorded in OED s.v. 'beside' (prep., sense 5b). The double mechanism — fear of the occasion undermining what is genuinely known — is what the simile transfers to the poet: his love is real; it is the occasion of utterance that defeats him.

The gloss for 'unperfect' (ill-rehearsed) and 'put beside his part' (made to forget his lines through fear) is mainstream and defensible; the Othello cross-reference in the detail is a mis-citation but the interpretive claim stands independently.

anchor_text: for fear of trust, forget to say The perfect ceremony of love's rite
summary: 'Fear of trust' means fear of trusting himself — distrust of his own capacity to speak love adequately. 'The perfect ceremony of love's rite' means the right, complete form of declaration: the rite a lover is supposed to perform. The poet fails not because he feels less but because he mistrusts his own voice to carry the weight of what he feels.

OED records 'trust' (n., sense I.1) as 'confidence, faith, assured reliance on,' and the compound can be read as 'lack of confidence in oneself.' 'Ceremony' carries its full Elizabethan weight of 'outward form of conduct proper to a situation' (OED s.v. 'ceremony,' sense 3); 'rite' reinforces this — both words point to a socially and emotionally correct procedure of declaration that the poet fails to perform. The line echoes the theatrical 'part' of line 2 (TLN 310): there too, the actor knows what he should say but cannot say it at the moment required.

anchor_text: O'ercharg'd with burthen of mine own love's might
summary: 'O'ercharg'd' means overloaded — carrying more than can be managed. 'Burthen' is an older spelling of 'burden.' The line sums up the octet's paradox: the poet's love is so strong that its very weight silences him, the way a cart overloaded with grain cannot move.
detail: OED s.v. 'overcharge' (v., sense 4) records 'to load excessively, to burden beyond capacity,' with citations from the period. 'Burthen' is the regular early modern form of 'burden' (OED s.v. 'burden / burthen' n.1); Shakespeare uses both spellings. The phrase closes a four-line unit (TLN 313-316) that is itself the engine of the whole sonnet: the simile of actor and beast generates the same explanation twice (fear, excess of strength), and this last line crystallizes both into a single dense noun-cluster — 'burthen of mine own love's might' — where 'own' stresses that the weight is internal, self-produced, not imposed from outside. The Elizabethan musical sense of 'burthen' as a refrain or bass-note is almost certainly inactive here.

anchor_text: let my looks be then the eloquence And dumb presagers of my speaking breast
summary: 'Presagers' are heralds or advance messengers — things that announce what is to come. 'Dumb' means silent (not stupid). The poet asks his outward appearance ('looks') to serve as silent heralds of the love he cannot speak, his face and eyes declaring what his tongue withholds. 'Speaking breast' means a heart or inner feeling that is fully articulate even when the mouth is not.
detail: OED s.v. 'presager' (n.) records the word as 'one who or that which presages; a portent, omen, harbinger,' first citations from the sixteenth century. 'Dumb' meaning 'mute, without the power of speech' is the standard early modern sense (OED s.v. 'dumb' adj., sense 1a). The combination 'dumb presagers' is an oxymoron — a herald is by definition a speaker, so silent heralds must communicate by sign rather than word. The reversal is deliberate: the sestet proposes a regime in which writing and appearance supersede speech as the primary channel of love. 'Speaking breast' inverts the paradox from the other end: the interior ('breast') is eloquent while the exterior ('tongue') is silent.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 317

The core gloss ('looks' as silent heralds of inner love) is sound, but calling 'dumb presagers' an oxymoron overreaches — a presager is not definitionally a speaker; presagers routinely are silent omens (storms, portents), so 'dumb presager' is emphatic, not self-contradictory.

anchor_text: table of my heart; My body is the frame
summary: 'Table' here means a flat writing or painting surface — a tablet or panel prepared to receive an image. The heart is imagined as a physical board on which the beloved's portrait has been painted, and the poet's body is the wooden frame around it. 'Table' in this sense is standard Elizabethan usage; the modern 'table' as furniture is a later narrowing.
detail: The OED (s.v. 'table', n., sense 9a) gives 'a tablet for writing or painting; a flat board prepared for a picture' as current in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. 'Table of memory' appears in Hamlet (1.5) and in Merchant of Venice; the heart-as-tablet is a Renaissance commonplace extending Erasmus and the emblem tradition. The sonnet extends the conceit beyond the usual single equation (heart = tablet) to add the body as picture-frame, the chest as shop-window, and the eyes as glazing — building a complete metaphorical gallery.

OED s.v. 'table' n. sense 9a ('a tablet for writing or painting; a flat board on which a picture is painted') is a real entry covering the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and the sense cited accurately supports the annotation's gloss.
The reading of 'table' as painting panel and 'body as frame' is exactly what the text says and is standard Elizabethan usage; the Hamlet and Merchant parallels are accurate.

anchor_text: perspective it is best painter's art, For through the painter must you see
summary: 'Perspective' carries two senses at once. First, it names the painter's art of rendering three-dimensional depth on a flat surface — the technical skill of foreshortening and vanishing points. Second, it names an Elizabethan optical device: a glass or anamorphic painting that looks distorted head-on but 'corrects' into a clear image when viewed from the right angle. The point is that to see the poet's true skill — and the youth's true portrait — you must look at the painter, not past him.
detail: The OED (s.v. 'perspective', n., senses 3 and 5) records both the painterly art of creating visual depth and the popular Elizabethan 'perspective glass' or anamorphic picture that yields a recognizable image only from a particular angle. Richard II (2.2) uses 'perspectives' in exactly the anamorphic sense: 'For sorrow's eye, glazed with blinding tears, / Divides one thing entire to many objects, / Like perspectives, which, rightly gazed upon, / Show nothing but confusion — eyed awry, / Distinguish form.' In Sonnet 24 the sense pivots: the portrait is only accessible through the painter (the poet's own eye), just as an anamorphic picture only resolves when you look from the correct angle. The lines therefore argue that the youth must look at the poet to find his own image.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'perspective', n., sense 3 ('the art of representing solid objects on a plane surface') and sense 5 ('a perspective glass or anamorphic device'); compare Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'perspective': 'a glass through which objects appear different from what they really are.'

The dual-sense reading (linear-perspective art plus anamorphic device) is the mainstream scholarly consensus, and the Richard II parallel is exact; the interpretive argument that the youth must look 'through' the poet follows naturally from 'through the painter must you see his skill.'

anchor_text: Yet eyes this cunning want to grace their art, They draw but what they see, know not the heart
summary: The couplet is the sonnet's volta — its turn or reversal of argument. After ten lines praising the poet's eye as a gifted painter, the closing couplet concedes that eyes, however skilled ('cunning'), can capture only what is visible; they 'know not the heart.' The inner life of the beloved remains opaque. 'Want' means 'lack' (not 'desire'), so the line reads: 'eyes lack this skill to complete their art.' The compliment to the youth's beauty is real, but the sonnet ends on a note of inadequacy and uncertainty.
detail: The volta (Italian, 'turn') in the English sonnet form typically falls at line 9 or in the couplet, shifting or qualifying what came before. Here it is sharply placed in the couplet, deflating the elaborate conceit: the entire gallery metaphor shows that visual mastery is the poet's limit, not his triumph. 'Cunning' in Elizabethan English means skill or expertise (OED s.v. 'cunning', n., sense 1: 'knowledge, learning; skill, dexterity') but could shade toward craftiness or guile, giving the word a mild ambiguity — the eyes are clever yet limited, possibly even deceptive. The acknowledgment that sight cannot penetrate to the heart anticipates the anxiety of later sonnets (notably Sonnets 93 and 148) in which the poet wonders whether the fair exterior conceals infidelity. Sidney, in 'The Defence of Poesy' (1595), distinguishes the eye that sees surfaces from the mind that apprehends the inner form of virtue; Shakespeare's couplet puts the same problem into the conceit's own terms.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'want', v., sense 6a: 'to be without, to lack'; s.v. 'cunning', n., sense 1: 'knowledge, skill, dexterity' — both the primary Elizabethan sense. Sidney, Philip, 'The Defence of Poesy' (1595), on the distinction between sight and inner understanding.

The OED entries for 'want' and 'cunning' are accurate; Sidney's Defence of Poesy (1595) is a real work and does discuss the limits of visual versus mental apprehension, but Sidney's argument centers on poetry surpassing philosophy rather than on a direct eye-vs-mind epistemological distinction, making the citation a plausible but overreaching fit.

The couplet-volta reading, 'want' as lack, and 'cunning' ambiguity are all defensible; the forward-link to Sonnets 93 and 148 as infidelity anxiety is an interpretive extrapolation (the couplet itself only concedes perceptual limits), but it is a common and not discredited critical move, and the Sidney parallel, though loose, does not misrepresent the sonnet's argument.

anchor_text: in favour with their stars
summary: To be 'in favour with their stars' means to be lucky, to have fortune running in your direction. Elizabethans spoke of the stars as governing earthly fate — a person's birth-sign and the positions of the planets were thought to shape their worldly success. The phrase signals that public honour is, at bottom, a matter of arbitrary luck rather than merit.
detail: Astrology was taken seriously as a predictive system in Shakespeare's England, and 'the stars' as agents of fortune appears throughout his work (compare Romeo's 'star-cross'd lovers' and Edmund's satirical rejection of it in King Lear 1.2). The opening line sets up the sonnet's argument: if worldly success depends on the stars — that is, on something entirely outside the individual's control — then it is unstable and not to be envied. The poet, 'whom fortune of such triumph bars,' implies that his own lower social standing is equally the stars' work, but he will find something better than starry luck to set against it.

The gloss is accurate and mainstream: 'in favour with their stars' straightforwardly invokes astrological fortune, and the annotation correctly identifies the sonnet's opening move as contrasting luck-dependent public honour with the poet's private alternative — no overreach.

anchor_text: The painful warrior famoused for fight
summary: 'Painful' here does not simply mean experiencing pain; in Elizabethan English it meant laborious, diligently toiling, full of effort. A 'painful warrior' is one who has worked hard and suffered to earn his reputation. 'Famoused' is an archaic past participle meaning made famous, celebrated — not a word in modern use.

'painful' adj. 2a), distinguishing it from the narrower modern sense of experiencing hurt. 'Famoused' (OED s.v. 'famous' v., now rare) is a verbal past participle — the warrior has been 'famed abroad,' made famous by others. The archaic vocabulary gives the line a slightly formal, martial register appropriate to the Roman-triumph imagery the couplet inverts.
