anchor_text: Where I may not remove nor be remov'd
summary: 'Remove' had a precise legal-administrative sense in Elizabethan English: to transfer a case from one court to another, or to dismiss someone from an office. 'Nor be remov'd' plays the same term in the passive: the poet cannot be dismissed from this love the way a courtier is dismissed from court or a warrior erased from an official register. The final line closes the sonnet's logic — mutual love is the one situation that is proof against the single arbitrary act of removal that destroys public honour.
detail: OED records 'remove' in legal and administrative senses (the transfer of a suit, the dismissal of an officer) from the sixteenth century (OED s.v. 'remove' v. 8a, 9). The wordplay works because the poem has been anatomizing exactly such acts of removal: the prince removes his favour with a frown; the book of honour removes the warrior's name with a pen-scratch. In the couplet the poet claims a position that is exempt from both directions of removal — he will not leave (cannot 'remove') and cannot be expelled ('be remov'd'). The legal register quietly positions love as a more binding contract than any courtly or military one.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'remove' v. 8a: 'To transfer (a legal case or action) from one court to another'; 9: 'To dismiss or depose (a person) from office or position.' Both senses current in Shakespeare's period.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, 3rd ed. (1902), s.v. 'remove' vb: notes both the literal and figurative senses of dismissal and transference in Shakespeare's usage.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 350

OED s.v. 'remove' v. senses 8a and 9 (legal transfer of a suit; dismissal from office) are real entries current in Shakespeare's period, and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon does record the dismissal and transference senses, both supporting the wordplay claim.

The legal-administrative senses of 'remove' are genuinely attested in OED, but reading this line as primarily activating a legal register rather than the plain sense of physical/emotional departure and being displaced is an interpretive choice that goes beyond what the text compels — the simpler reading (I will not leave, and cannot be driven away) is equally available and more parsimonious given the poem's register.

anchor_text: Lord of my love, to whom in vassalage
summary: 'Vassalage' is the condition of a vassal in the medieval feudal system: a man bound to a lord by a sworn oath of service, owing loyalty and duty in exchange for protection. The poet casts his love as a feudal bond — not free affection but an absolute obligation 'strongly knit' by the youth's merit itself.
detail: OED records 'vassalage' from the 13th century onward meaning the obligations and submission owed by a vassal to his lord. By Shakespeare's day feudal tenure had largely dissolved, but the vocabulary of vassalage, fealty, and duty survived as the standard language of courtly compliment and patron-dedication letters. Casting the beloved as 'lord' and the poet as 'vassal' frames the whole sonnet as a verse-dedication to a social superior — a framing reinforced by 'embassage' and 'duty' in the lines that follow.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'vassalage,' n., senses 1 and 2 (submission and loyalty owed by a vassal to his lord; the state of being a vassal).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 351
OED s.v. 'vassalage' is a genuine entry with attested senses covering submission owed by a vassal to his lord; the historical and lexicographic claim is accurate and the source supports it.

The feudal framing of 'vassalage' as an absolute obligation rather than free affection is textually grounded: 'merit hath my duty strongly knit' makes the binding explicit, and the courtly-compliment / patron-dedication register is the mainstream scholarly reading.

anchor_text: To thee I send this written embassage
summary: 'Embassage' (also spelled 'ambassage') means an ambassador's official message or mission — a formal written communication dispatched from one party to another of higher rank. The poet frames the sonnet itself as a diplomatic document: an official embassy rather than a casual letter, sent to 'witness duty, not to show my wit.'
detail: OED records 'embassage' from the 15th century for both the ambassador's office and the message he carries. In Renaissance practice, ambassadors presented written 'embassages' — credentials and statements of purpose — before any verbal business. By calling the poem a 'written embassage,' the poet transforms it into a formal act of homage, with the deliberate stiffness of state correspondence rather than intimate confession. The word reinforces the feudal-dedication conceit running through the sonnet: lord, vassal, duty, embassy.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'embassage,' n., sense 1b: 'the message or communication brought by an ambassador; a written message.'

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'embassage': 'the message of an ambassador; a solemn charge or address.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 353

OED s.v. 'embassage' exists with senses covering both the ambassador's office and the message he carries, and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a genuine standard reference that covers this word; both sources are real and supportive.

Glossing 'embassage' as a formal written diplomatic communication is well-supported by OED and Schmidt, and the reading that it transforms the poem into an act of homage rather than personal display is directly corroborated by line 4 ('To witness duty, not to show my wit').

anchor_text: some good conceit of thine / In thy soul's thought, all naked
summary: 'Conceit' here means a favorable opinion or favorable understanding — a good thought in the reader's mind. The poet hopes the youth will mentally clothe his bare, inadequate words with a generous interpretation. This sense of 'conceit' as 'opinion' or 'estimation' (rather than its modern meaning of self-importance) was standard in Shakespeare's time.
detail: OED distinguishes the older sense: 'conceit,' n., sense I.1, 'a thought, notion, idea; a mental image or notion formed of something.' Sense I.3 gives specifically 'personal opinion; estimation.' The poet's pun is not accidental: 'conceit' in the literary sense (a clever extended metaphor) hovers alongside — the youth's generous 'conceit' of the poem will supply what the poet's own 'conceit,' or poetic wit, cannot. The phrase 'all naked' connects to the clothing metaphor of lines 5-6 and 11: the love is tattered, the words are bare; only the youth's understanding can dress them.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'conceit,' n., sense I.1 and I.3: 'a thought, mental image'; 'personal opinion, estimation.'

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'conceit': 'notion, idea, thought; fancy; opinion.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 357

OED s.v. 'conceit' sense I.1 and I.3 for 'thought, mental image' and 'personal opinion, estimation' are genuine attested senses, and Onions's Shakespeare Glossary is a real standard reference that covers this word in exactly this way.

The primary gloss ('a favorable opinion / good thought') is defensible, but the annotation's additional claim of a deliberate pun on 'conceit' as literary conceits — hovering alongside the opinion-sense — is speculative; the text says 'some good conceit of thine,' which straightforwardly means the youth's charitable understanding, and there is no clear textual signal that the reader is meant to detect a secondary literary-device meaning.

anchor_text: whatsoever star that guides my moving, / Points on me graciously with fair aspect
summary: 'Aspect' is a technical term from astrology: the angular relationship between a planet and a point in the horoscope, which was believed to determine whether that planet's influence was favorable or harmful. A 'fair aspect' meant the star was positioned to shine beneficently on the poet — fortune favoring him. The poet waits for the stars to align before daring to present himself as worthy.
detail: In Elizabethan astrology, each planet cast its influence on a person according to its 'aspect' — whether it was 'trine' (120 degrees, favorable), 'sextile' (60 degrees, favorable), 'square' (90 degrees, malign), or 'opposition' (180 degrees, very malign). A 'fair' or 'gracious' aspect meant the guiding star was in a favorable alignment. The image personifies fortune as a stellar force — the 'star that guides my moving' — a common Renaissance idiom for the power that governs one's life (compare Romeo's 'inauspicious stars' in Romeo and Juliet 5.3). The conditional structure ('Till... Points on me... Then may I dare') defers everything on this astronomical chance.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'aspect,' n., sense 3: 'the relative position of the heavenly bodies as they appear from the earth at a given time; formerly considered as an influence on human affairs.'

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'aspect': 'look, appearance; (astrol.) relative position of the heavenly bodies.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 359
OED s.v. 'aspect' sense 3 for the astrological/astronomical meaning and Onions are genuine references that confirm this technical Elizabethan sense; the claim is accurate and well-supported.

The technical astrological sense of 'aspect' as angular planetary relationship determining favorable or harmful influence is standard and mainstream; the textual context ('whatsoever star that guides my moving, / Points on me graciously with fair aspect') fully supports it.

anchor_text: puts apparel on my tatter'd loving, / To show me worthy of thy sweet respect
summary: The poet uses a sustained clothing metaphor: his love is 'tatter'd' — ragged, threadbare — because his poor wit cannot dress it in worthy language. He waits for Fortune's star to provide 'apparel' (proper clothing) for his feeling so that it can be presented decently. The conceit runs through the whole sonnet: love as a garment that is worn bare and needs Fortune's tailoring before it can be shown in public.
detail: The clothing metaphor for poetic expression — inadequate words as rags that fail to cover noble feeling — is a recurrent trope in Elizabethan poetry and rhetoric. George Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) describes rhetorical figures as 'garnishing' or 'clothing' bare meaning. Here the poet's 'wanting words' (line 6) are the bad tailor; his duty and love are the body that goes exposed. The star of line 9-10 is the tailor Fortune will send, who puts proper dress on a love too worn to be shown. The volta at line 9 ('Till whatsoever star...') marks the turn from apology for present inadequacy to hope for future worthiness.

sources.name: Puttenham
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III, ch. 1: figures as 'garnishing' or 'clothing' bare meaning.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'tatter'd,' adj.: 'torn or worn to tatters; ragged.' Attested from the 14th century.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 361

Puttenham's Book III ch. 1 ('Of Ornament') does use clothing/apparel metaphors for figures of speech, confirming the substance of the claim, but the exact word 'garnishing' is not confirmed as Puttenham's term in that chapter — the actual text uses 'apparel' and 'ornament' — so the quotation-style citation overreaches what the source demonstrably says.

The clothing metaphor for inadequate poetic expression is well-attested in Elizabethan rhetoric and Puttenham, and the annotation traces it coherently through the sonnet; calling the 'star of line 9-10' the 'tailor Fortune will send' is a slight embellishment but does not misread the poem.

anchor_text: limbs with travel tir'd
summary: 'Travel' here carries its older sense of travail — laborious exertion and hardship — as well as the modern sense of journeying. The two meanings blend deliberately: the poet is worn out both from the physical effort of the road and from the toil that accompanies it. The spelling 'travel' and 'travail' were interchangeable in Elizabethan English.
detail: OED records 'travail' and 'travel' as doublets through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, with 'travail' meaning bodily toil, labour, or suffering (OED s.v. 'travail', n., senses 1-2) and 'travel' covering both the journey and its hardship. Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'travel') notes the regular Shakespearean fusion. The ambiguity sets up the sonnet's structural opposition: the body endures travel/travail by day, the mind a second journey by night.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'travail', n., senses 1-3; s.v. 'travel', n., sense 1b (doublet forms, 16th-17th c.).

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'travel' (notes the fusion with travail throughout the canon).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 366

OED travail/travel doublet (senses 1-3 and n. 1b) and Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'travel' are real, standard references that straightforwardly support the claim of interchangeable Elizabethan spelling and dual meaning.
The travel/travail doublet is well-attested by OED and Schmidt, and the dual-sense reading (journey + bodily toil) is the mainstream scholarly consensus for this line.

anchor_text: thoughts--from far where I abide-- / Intend a zealous pilgrimage to thee
summary: A pilgrimage is a devotional journey to a sacred shrine. By calling his mind's nightly journey toward the beloved a 'zealous pilgrimage,' the poet casts the absent person as a holy destination and his longing as an act of religious devotion. 'Zealous' intensifies this: zeal in Elizabethan usage described fervent religious ardor.
detail: OED records 'zeal' and 'zealous' primarily in religious contexts through the sixteenth century — ardent, fervent devotion to God or a holy cause (OED s.v. 'zealous', adj., sense 1). Applying it to a love-journey elevates the erotic to the sacred in the Petrarchan tradition, in which the poet-lover venerates an almost divine mistress; Petrarch's own Canzoniere uses similar religious language for Laura. The device turns physical separation from the beloved into a spiritual exercise, reframing exhausted insomnia as pious striving. Compare Sonnet 109 ('my soul' makes the poet a 'truant' to the beloved as to a religious allegiance) and the palmer-and-pilgrim conceit of Romeo and Juliet 1.5.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'zealous', adj., sense 1 (ardent in devotion to a religious cause, 16th c.).

sources.name: Petrarch, Canzoniere
sources.citation: Francesco Petrarca, Canzoniere (Rerum vulgarium fragmenta, c. 1342-74): the use of devotional language — pilgrimages, shrines, vows — for the beloved is a defining feature of the sequence, widely imitated by English sonneteers.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 369

OED s.v. 'zealous' sense 1 (ardent religious devotion, 16th c.) and Petrarch's Canzoniere (c. 1342-74) use of devotional/pilgrimage language for Laura are both real and accurately described as a defining feature of the sequence widely imitated by English sonneteers.

Casting the beloved as a sacred shrine via Petrarchan devotional language is a mainstream reading; 'zealous' as fervent religious ardor is precisely OED sense 1, and the palmer-pilgrim conceit is standard for the sequence.

anchor_text: keep my drooping eyelids open wide, / Looking on darkness which the blind do see
summary: The paradox 'darkness which the blind do see' means: the poet lies awake in the dark staring at nothing — the same nothing the sightless always face. His open eyes perceive only what a blind person perceives: blackness. The line uses paradox to collapse the difference between open and shut, seeing and blind, making the night's blankness total.
detail: This is a rhetorical figure of adynaton (a compressed paradox pointing to impossibility or negation): to 'see' what the blind see is to see nothing. The effect is not merely decorative — it establishes the conditions that make the sestet's recovery possible. Because the wakeful eye can find nothing in the dark, the mind's 'imaginary sight' (TLN 373) steps in to supply what the body cannot. The octet ends on a zero — darkness, blindness, absence — so the sestet's jewel-image has the full weight of a contrast. Sidney (Astrophil and Stella, Sonnet 31, 'the moon') and other Elizabethan sonneteers frequently use the sleepless lover's vigil as a frame; Shakespeare tightens the device into paradox.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'see', v., sense 1a (perceive with the eyes); the paradox turns on the literal physical act of vision being reduced to nothing.

sources.name: Sidney, Astrophil and Stella
sources.citation: Sir Philip Sidney, Astrophil and Stella (composed c. 1582, printed 1591), Sonnet 31: the sleepless lover addressing the moon as fellow-sufferer — the closest English-sonnet parallel to the sleepless night-vigil structure.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 371

Sidney's Astrophil and Stella Sonnet 31 ('With how sad steps, O moon') is confirmed as a real sleepless-lover night-vigil poem (the speaker addresses the moon as a fellow sufferer of love), accurately cited; the OED sense for 'see' is generic support that does not overreach.

The paradox (open eyes perceive only what the blind perceive — nothing) is the correct mainstream reading; the rhetorical label 'adynaton' is slightly imprecise (this is closer to oxymoron/paradox than a hyperbolic impossibility), but the interpretive substance is sound and the Sidney parallel is apt.

anchor_text: my soul's imaginary sight / Presents thy shadow to my sightless view
summary: 'Shadow' does not mean a patch of darkness here; it means a phantom image — a mental projection of the beloved's form, not the beloved in person. 'Sightless' means unable to see (the eyes are shut or useless in darkness), but also carries the sense of invisible: the view is both blind and seeing nothing. Together they define what the mind produces when the body fails: an image that is real to the imagination but has no physical existence.
detail: OED records 'shadow' in the sense of a phantom, image, or representation (OED s.v. 'shadow', n., sense 6a-b: 'an unreal appearance; a phantom, ghost, or spirit; a reflected image'). The word also carried its theatrical meaning — an actor's role was a 'shadow' of the real person represented (compare A Midsummer Night's Dream 5.1: 'The best in this kind are but shadows'). 'Sightless' can mean both 'unable to see' and 'invisible' (OED s.v. 'sightless', adj., senses 1 and 2). Shakespeare fuses both: the poet's view is blind to the outer world while the shadow of the beloved is invisible to any other eye. The sestet pivots on this paradox: genuine sight is replaced by a more vivid, more faithful inner vision.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'shadow', n., sense 6a ('an unreal appearance, phantom, image'); sense 7 ('a reflected image'); and s.v. 'sightless', adj., senses 1-2 ('destitute of sight'; 'invisible to the eye').

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'shadow' (the wide range of Shakespearean uses, including the theatrical 'part' or 'image' senses).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 373

OED s.v. 'shadow' sense 6a ('unreal appearance, phantom') and 'sightless' senses 1-2 ('destitute of sight'; 'invisible') are real entries that support the dual-meaning analysis; Schmidt's coverage of Shakespearean shadow usage is a standard citation.
'Shadow' as phantom mental image (OED sense 6a) and 'sightless' as both unable-to-see and invisible are both correct and mainstream; the MND theatrical parallel is apt and does not overreach.

anchor_text: like a jewel (hung in ghastly night, / Makes black night beauteous
summary: This is the sonnet's central image (its conceit): the beloved's imagined form in the mind is like a jewel hung in the terrifying dark of night — a single brilliant object that transforms the blackness around it. 'Ghastly' means horrible, deathly, spectral (not merely 'ghostly' in the mild modern sense), so the night is not just dark but frightening. The jewel's radiance makes the surrounding darkness beautiful rather than threatening.
detail: OED records 'ghastly' (from Old English gaestlic) as meaning terrifying, death-like, spectral, or horrible — the sight or appearance of something that makes the beholder aghast (OED s.v. 'ghastly', adj., sense 1). The contrast is absolute: the setting is at its most hostile ('ghastly') and the jewel is at its most brilliant precisely because of that hostility. The conceit anticipates the imagery of the Dark Lady sonnets (e.g. Sonnet 132, 'those two mourning eyes become thy face'), but here the darkness is exterior — the night — rather than the beloved's own features. The parenthesis in 'hung in ghastly night' is suspended in the 1609 Quarto, suggesting the image of the jewel dangling in mid-air before the predicate ('Makes black night beauteous') resolves it. The logic is Petrarchan hyperbole turned outward: the beloved improves not just the lover's mood but the face of the world itself.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ghastly', adj., sense 1 ('having a horrible, death-like, or spectral appearance; terrifying to behold').

sources.name: Shake-speares Sonnets (1609)
sources.citation: Shake-speares Sonnets (London: Thomas Thorpe, 1609), sig. C1r (Sonnet XXVII): the open parenthesis after 'jewel' is as printed in the Quarto, the only authoritative text.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 375

OED s.v. 'ghastly' sense 1 is real and supportive; the 1609 Quarto signature C1r for Sonnet XXVII is bibliographically plausible (sonnets text begins at approximately sig. B1, so page 9 of sonnets text falls on C1r) and the claim that the Thorpe quarto is the sole authoritative text is correct.

The core reading — 'ghastly' as terrifying/death-like rather than mildly ghostly, and the jewel-in-darkness conceit transforming hostility into beauty — is sound and mainstream; the OE etymology detail ('gaestlic') is slightly imprecise but does not affect the interpretation, and the Quarto open-parenthesis observation is accurate.

anchor_text: debarre'd the benefit of rest
summary: 'Debarr'd' means formally excluded or shut out, as if by a legal bar or gate. The poet is not merely unable to sleep — he is refused rest as though a court had ruled him ineligible for it, giving his sleeplessness a quasi-judicial, official quality.
detail: The OED records 'debar' (v.) in the sense of 'to exclude from a right, privilege, or benefit by authority or decree' from the early sixteenth century; the legal connotation (cf. the barrister's 'bar') is active here. The poet's insomnia, already established in Sonnet 27 ('Weary with toil, I haste me to my bed'), is now framed not as misfortune but as a sentence — day and night together are the jailers, the beloved's absence the charge.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'debar' v., sense 1a: 'To bar or shut out; to exclude from a right, privilege, or benefit by authority.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 380
OED s.v. 'debar' v. sense 1a genuinely records the legal-exclusion meaning from the early sixteenth century; the citation is accurately paraphrased and supports the claim.

The OED gloss of 'debar' with its legal connotation is sound, but the elaboration that day and night are 'jailers' and the beloved's absence a 'charge' imports a fully worked-out judicial narrative not supported by the text, which only uses the word 'debarr'd'; the extended metaphor overstates what the single word can bear.

anchor_text: sparkling stars twire not thou gild'st the even
summary: 'Twire' means to peep or glance furtively, to look out through a narrow opening. 'When sparkling stars twire not' means when the stars are not peeping out — that is, when they are hidden behind clouds. The poet flatters the night by saying the beloved's brightness gilds ('gild'st') the evening even when the stars fail to appear.
detail: OED records 'twire' (v.) in the sense 'to peep, to look slyly or through a narrow opening,' citing this very line from Sonnet 28 as its primary example (OED s.v. 'twire' v.1, sense 1). The word appears rarely in the period and carries an intimate, colloquial quality — stars peeking out like eyes through a slit, not blazing openly. Onions (A Shakespeare Glossary) also glosses 'twire' as 'to peer, peep.' 'Gild'st the even' means you make the evening golden — a verb rooted in the gilding of metal with gold leaf. The conceit is that the beloved's beauty supplies the light the absent stars cannot: a flattery so extreme that the couplet's confession of futility undercuts it.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'twire' v.1, sense 1: 'To peep, peer; to look slyly or furtively,' citing Sonnet 28 as the primary quotation.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'twire': 'to peer, peep.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 390
OED s.v. 'twire' v.1 is a real entry citing Sonnet 28 as its primary example, and Onions's Shakespeare Glossary genuinely glosses 'twire' as 'to peer, peep'; both sources support the claim.

The gloss of 'twire' as 'to peep or look furtively' is well-attested (OED cites this line as primary evidence) and the reading of 'gild'st the even' as the beloved supplying the absent stars' light is a straightforward extension of the flattery conceit established in the preceding lines.

anchor_text: in disgrace with fortune and men's eyes
summary: 'Disgrace' here means being out of favor — specifically with Fortune (luck) and with the world's opinion ('men's eyes'). The phrase pairs two kinds of failure: material bad luck and social humiliation, both of which the poet claims to suffer at once.
detail: OED records 'disgrace' (n., sense 1) as 'the condition of being out of favour,' and 'fortune' (n., sense 1) as 'the power or influence of chance on human affairs' — the classical goddess Fortuna (see the-fortunes-wheel card). To be 'in disgrace with fortune' is therefore to be at the low point of Fortune's wheel, out of luck and out of standing. The opening eight-word phrase names both the external and the internal condition the sonnet will spend thirteen lines trying to escape.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'disgrace' n., sense 1: 'the condition of being out of favour or good opinion'; s.v. 'fortune' n., sense 1: 'chance as a power in human affairs; the supposed goddess Fortuna.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 393
OED senses for 'disgrace' (n., out of favour) and 'fortune' (n., chance as power / goddess Fortuna) are standard, well-attested entries that accurately support the summary and detail claims.

The gloss is sound: 'disgrace' as 'out of favour' and 'fortune' as the classical goddess Fortuna are both standard Elizabethan usage, and the reading that the phrase names dual failures — bad luck and social humiliation — is mainstream and textually supportable.

anchor_text: trouble deaf heaven with my bootless cries
summary: 'Bootless' means without profit or result — useless, in vain. A 'bootless cry' is one that brings no relief. 'Deaf heaven' means heaven that is not listening, or refuses to answer. The poet is praying and getting no response.
detail: OED traces 'bootless' (adj.) to Old English 'bot' (remedy, relief, benefit): 'bootless' = producing no remedy, unavailing. Onions's 'Shakespeare Glossary' (s.v. 'bootless') gives 'unavailing, useless.' The collocation 'deaf heaven' personifies heaven as a listener who has turned away — a figure for unanswered prayer that places the poet in a condition of spiritual abandonment. The phrase anticipates the miracle of the volta: the same heaven that would not hear the poet's cries is transformed, by the memory of the beloved, into a gate before which the lark sings (TLN 404).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bootless' adj.: 'Unavailing, unprofitable, without remedy or relief'; from Old English 'bot,' remedy.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. Eagleson (1986), s.v. 'bootless': 'profitless, unavailing.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 395
OED 'bootless' (from OE 'bot', remedy) and Onions Shakespeare Glossary (Eagleson rev. 1986, s.v. 'bootless': 'profitless, unavailing') are real, accurate references that support the gloss.

The etymology of 'bootless' from OE 'bot' is correct and the reading of 'deaf heaven' as unanswered prayer is uncontroversial; the anticipatory note about the lark at TLN 404 is a reasonable structural observation, not an over-reading.

anchor_text: that man's scope
summary: 'Scope' means range, latitude, or freedom of action — the space in which someone can exercise their abilities. Envying 'that man's scope,' the poet is not just envying another's talents ('art') but the opportunity and freedom to use them, which his own outcast state denies him.
detail: OED records 'scope' (n., sense 3) as 'range of action, opportunity, or freedom; room or space to move or act.' Onions's 'Shakespeare Glossary' (s.v. 'scope') gives 'range, free play.' The pairing 'this man's art, and that man's scope' (TLN 399) contrasts two things: a specific skill ('art') and the latitude to deploy it ('scope'). The poet catalogues both because deprivation is double: he lacks the talent and the conditions in which talent can be exercised.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'scope' n., sense 3: 'Range of action or opportunity; freedom or latitude to act.'

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. Eagleson (1986), s.v. 'scope': 'range, free play, opportunity.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 399
OED s.v. 'scope' (range of action, opportunity) and Onions's gloss ('range, free play, opportunity') are standard references that accurately support the claim.

The gloss of 'scope' as 'opportunity / freedom of action' is defensible and well-attested, but the annotation subtly over-reads the line by claiming the poet lacks the talent itself ('he lacks the talent and the conditions') — the text says only that he wishes for 'this man's art, and that man's scope,' which registers envy, not a claim about his own deficiency; the core gloss is nonetheless correct.

anchor_text: death's dateless night
summary: 'Dateless' means without a fixed end-date, unlimited, perpetual. A lease or a court term has a date of expiry; death's night has none. The legal idiom of the poem makes 'dateless' especially precise: unlike a financial debt with a due date, death has no term and cannot be redeemed.
detail: The OED records 'dateless' in this sense from the 1590s: 'having no fixed or limited date; interminable' (OED s.v. 'dateless' adj., sense 1). The compound 'dateless night' also carries the older sense of undated blackness — darkness with no morning appointed. Within the sonnet's legal conceit the word captures what makes grief for the dead different from ordinary debt: a bond eventually falls due and can be paid off; death is open-ended, the account never finally closed until the speaker himself dies.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'dateless' adj., sense 1: 'Having no fixed date; undated; also, having no end, endless, perpetual.' The relevant sense is attested from the 1590s.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 412
OED s.v. 'dateless' adj., sense 1 is a real entry with the correct definition ('having no fixed date; undated; endless, perpetual') attested from the 1590s, directly supporting the summary.
'Dateless' as perpetual / without fixed end-date is the correct OED sense, and the contrast with a lease that does carry a date is coherent within the poem's legal register.

anchor_text: love's long since cancell'd woe
summary: 'Cancelled' is a legal and financial term: to cancel a bond or debt was to cross it out or void it, marking the obligation discharged. The speaker thought a past grief had been settled — cancelled like a paid debt — but finds he is weeping it 'afresh,' as if the cancellation never happened.
detail: The Elizabethan practice of cancelling a written bond was literal: the creditor drew lines through or across the document to show it was void. Shakespeare uses this sense elsewhere: in Sonnet 87 the speaker calls the relationship a 'bond' now cancelled ('When thou shalt be dispos'd to set me light, / And place my merit in the eye of scorn, / Upon thy side against myself I'll fight'). Here the cancelled grief springs back to life, suggesting that emotional debts resist the finality of legal discharge — the same point the whole sonnet's accounting imagery makes.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cancel' v., sense 3a: 'To cross out or strike through (writing); to annul or make void (a deed, bond, or obligation).' Attested from the mid-16th century in legal and commercial use.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon. Berlin, 1874-75. s.v. 'cancel': 'to annul, to make void; used of bonds and obligations.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 413

OED s.v. 'cancel' v. sense 3a and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon are real works whose entries genuinely support the legal/financial definition of 'cancel' claimed; the erroneous Sonnet 87 cross-reference appears only in the detail prose, not in sources[].

Cancellation of a written bond as the operative meaning is well-attested legal usage; the Sonnet 87 parallel (patent / bond language) is accurate in substance even though the quoted line is not the one that uses 'cancel'd' directly.

anchor_text: expense of many a vanish'd sight
summary: 'Expense' here means both expenditure (the cost paid in tears and grief) and loss (the things spent and gone). 'Vanish'd sight' means people or scenes once seen but now disappeared — things the eyes once held that are no longer visible. The line mourns not just dead friends but any cherished experience now lost.
detail: Shakespeare uses 'expense' in both its financial sense (outlay, cost) and the broader sense of loss or depletion throughout the sonnets: the most famous instance is Sonnet 129, 'The expense of spirit in a waste of shame,' where spirit (vital energy) is spent in lust. The OED records both senses active in the period: 'the action of spending or consuming; expenditure; loss' (OED s.v. 'expense' n., sense 1). The overlap between financial spending and the wastage of grief keeps the poem's legal-accounting conceit in play.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'expense' n., sense 1: 'The action of spending or using up; consumption, waste; expenditure; loss.' Multiple Shakespeare citations including Sonnet 129.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary. Oxford, 1911. s.v. 'expense': 'expenditure; loss.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 414

OED s.v. 'expense' n. sense 1 and Onions's Shakespeare Glossary are real, well-established reference works whose entries ('expenditure; loss; consumption') directly support the dual financial/depletion reading claimed.
The dual financial-and-emotional sense of 'expense' is correct, and 'vanish'd sight' as cherished persons or scenes now lost is the mainstream reading; the Sonnet 129 parallel is apt.

anchor_text: heavily from woe to woe tell o'er The sad account of fore-bemoaned moan
summary: 'Tell o'er' means to count through item by item, as an accountant goes through the entries of a ledger. 'Fore-bemoaned moan' means grief already mourned before — sorrow that has already been lamented and yet is being lamented again. The speaker is doing double accounting: paying a bill he has already paid.
detail: The OED records 'tell' in the counting sense (sense 7: 'to count, reckon') as standard in 16th-century English; 'tell o'er' was the phrase for going through a count a second time to verify it. 'Fore-bemoaned' is one of Shakespeare's characteristic compound coinages: the prefix 'fore-' ('previously') combined with 'bemoaned' ('lamented'). The compound captures the exhaustion of repetitive grief — the sense that one is wasting emotional currency, paying out again for what should already be settled. This is the third quatrain's contribution to the conceit: the previous two described specific losses; now the speaker reflects on the act of repeating the accounting itself.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'tell' v., sense 7: 'To count, reckon, enumerate.' See also sense 7b, 'tell over': 'to count through (a number or sum).' Attested throughout the 16th century.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon. Berlin, 1874-75. s.v. 'tell': 'to count; tell over, to count again.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 416

OED s.v. 'tell' v. sense 7 / 7b ('to count, enumerate; tell over: to count through') and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'tell' are real entries that directly support the accounting-register gloss.

'Tell o'er' as ledger-counting and 'fore-bemoaned' as previously-lamented grief are both correctly glossed; the 'paying a bill already paid' formulation is validated by line 418 ('Which I new pay as if not paid before').

anchor_text: Thy bosom is endeared with all hearts
summary: 'Endeared' here means made more precious or enriched in worth, not simply made dear in the modern sentimental sense. The youth's breast is enriched — as a treasury is enriched — by containing within it all the loves the poet once thought were gone. OED records this sense (enrich, make of greater value) as active in the sixteenth century.
detail: OED s.v. 'endear,' v., sense 1: 'To make dear or precious; to increase the value or worth of.' This transitive sense was common in the period; cf. sense 2 ('to make dearer in affection'), which is the modern survival. Shakespeare uses both, and the context here — 'all hearts' hoarded in a bosom — argues primarily for the 'enriched' meaning: the beloved is a casket made more valuable by what it holds. The financial metaphor runs through the whole sonnet: 'interest,' 'due,' and 'parts' (shares) belong to the same idiom of debt and inheritance.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'endear,' v., sense 1 (make precious, increase the value of), with sixteenth-century examples.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 421
OED s.v. 'endear,' v., sense 1 ('to make dear or precious; to increase the value or worth of') is a real entry with sixteenth-century citations, and the summary accurately reflects that sense.

The 'enriched / made more precious' reading of 'endeared' is well-grounded: the financial-casket metaphor runs through the whole sonnet, and OED sense 1 (increase value) fits far better than the modern sentimental sense of 'made dear in affection,' which would be almost tautological in this context.

anchor_text: holy and obsequious tear
summary: 'Obsequious' retains its older Latin meaning here: dutiful in performing obsequies, the funeral rites of the dead. A tear that is 'obsequious' is one offered in ritual mourning — the correct, reverent grief owed to the deceased. The word had not yet narrowed to its modern sense of grovelling or fawning.
detail: OED s.v. 'obsequious,' adj., sense 1: 'Of, relating to, or appropriate to obsequies or funeral rites; as is done at funerals; mournful, mourning.' OED cites examples from the 1570s and 1590s alongside Shakespeare's usages. The associated noun 'obsequies' (funeral rites) was standard: cf. Romeo and Juliet 4.5 ('All things that we ordained festival / Turn from their office to black funeral, / Our instruments to melancholy bells, / Our wedding cheer to a sad burial feast; / Our solemn hymns to sullen dirges change'). The line pairs 'holy' and 'obsequious' to stress that the mourning was both sacred (as tears for the dead should be) and formally correct — performing a religious office. The modern pejorative sense of servile flattery had begun to develop by 1600 but had not displaced the primary meaning.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'obsequious,' adj., sense 1 ('of or relating to obsequies, mournful'), with citations from 1570-1600.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'obsequious': 'relating to obsequies, obsequiousness being the show of due respect and devotion to the dead.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 425

OED sense 1 for 'obsequious' ('of or relating to obsequies; mournful') is real and confirmed with 1570s–1590s citations; Schmidt (Perseus) confirms 'especially zealous with respect to what is due to the deceased; mourning,' which the annotation paraphrases correctly.

The funeral-rites sense of 'obsequious' is the primary and well-documented Elizabethan meaning; pairing it with 'holy' and 'dear religious love' confirms the ritual-mourning register, and the Romeo and Juliet comparandum, while not a direct parallel, is illustrative rather than misleading.

anchor_text: interest of the dead, which now appear
summary: 'Interest' carries both its legal and its financial meanings. As a legal term it means the rightful claim or due that the living owe to the dead — the proper respect and mourning their memory is entitled to. As a financial term (current in the 1590s) it means an increment owed on a debt. The poet has paid this interest — tears as tribute — on loves he thought dead; the sonnet now reveals they were never truly gone but were merely 'removed' and hidden in the youth.
detail: OED s.v. 'interest,' n., senses 4 ('a legal share or right in something') and 9 ('money paid for the use of money'). Both senses were alive in the 1590s. The financial idiom dominates the sequence: Sonnet 4 calls beauty 'Nature's bequest,' warns against 'usury,' and instructs the youth to 'use' what is lent to him. Here 'interest of the dead' echoes that vocabulary: the tears were a payment of interest — a tribute owed — to a capital of dead loves that has now, it turns out, simply been deposited in the youth rather than lost. The legal sense (rightful due) reinforces 'due of many' at TLN 432.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'interest,' n., senses 4 and 9; both current in Elizabethan English and across the sonnet sequence.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'interest': 'the claim or right of a person in or to property; legal share; advantage, benefit.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 427

OED senses 4 and 9 for 'interest' are real and current in Elizabethan English; Onions (Perseus) confirms the legal-share and financial-return senses in language that closely matches the annotation's paraphrase.

The dual legal/financial valence of 'interest' is defensible and consistent with the sonnet's recurrent money-debt idiom; calling the tears a payment of 'interest' on dead loves that turn out to be 'deposited' in the youth accurately tracks the metaphor without overreaching, and the link to 'due of many' at TLN 432 is a sound contextual connection.

anchor_text: trophies of my lovers gone
summary: 'Trophies' means memorial tokens or commemorative objects, not prizes in the modern sporting sense. In the Renaissance a trophy was an emblem or monument displayed in honor of past victories or relationships — objects hung in a place of honor to keep memory alive. 'Lovers' here means those whom the poet has loved, not specifically romantic partners: friends, companions, people dear to him whom he believed lost to death.
detail: OED s.v. 'trophy,' n., sense 1b: 'A memorial of victory or achievement; a monument; a relic.' In the heraldic and funerary culture of the period, 'trophies' were the coats of arms, crests, and insignia hung in churches and great halls to honor the illustrious dead — exactly the kind of hanging monument the image invokes. OED s.v. 'lover,' n., sense 1: 'One who loves, is fond of, or has a strong attachment to; a friend, a devoted companion.' This wider sense — love as deep friendship, not only erotic attachment — is standard in the sonnets and throughout Shakespeare. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'lover': 'One who is beloved; a friend; one who has a warm attachment.' The line thus pictures the youth as a great hall hung with the heraldic emblems of all the people who ever mattered to the poet.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'trophy,' n., sense 1b (memorial, relic); and s.v. 'lover,' n., sense 1 (friend, devoted companion).

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'lover': 'one who is beloved; a friend; one who has a warm attachment to another.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 430

OED s.v. 'trophy,' n., sense 1b (memorial, relic) and 'lover,' n., sense 1 (friend, devoted companion) are real; Schmidt confirms 'lover' in the sense of 'one loving, kindly disposed; friend,' supporting the annotation's claim.

The heraldic-funerary sense of 'trophies' (memorial emblems hung in honour of the dead) is exactly right for the period, and glossing 'lovers' as 'those the poet has loved' including friends — not exclusively erotic partners — is the standard scholarly reading of this word's range in the sonnets.

anchor_text: well-contented day
summary: 'Well-contented day' means the day on which the poet is content to die — a day of peaceful, natural death accepted without resistance. The phrase marks the opening as a quietly resigned imagining of his own death, not a lament.
detail: The OED records 'well-contented' in the sense of thoroughly satisfied or at peace; the compound here functions as an adjective modifying 'day,' so the phrase means 'the day with which I am fully content' — that is, death accepted as its proper time. The tone contrasts with the bold immortality claims of Sonnets 18 and 55: here the poet neither rages against death nor defies it, but imagines it as simply satisfactory. The genitive construction ('my... day') makes death the poet's own possession rather than an external assault.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'well-contented,' adj. (obsolete): thoroughly satisfied, at peace; the compound modifying 'day' yields 'the day on which I am content [to die].' See also Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'contented.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 435

OED s.v. 'well-contented' and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon are real lexicographic sources that support the gloss; the reading of the compound as 'the day on which I am content to die' is standard and well-attested.

The gloss 'the day on which I am content to die' is one defensible reading, but 'my well-contented day' more naturally means the full life-span with which the poet is content; the death-acceptance reading is a plausible editorial inference, not the only one, and calling it 'quietly resigned imagining of his own death' over-specifies an ambiguous phrase.

anchor_text: churl Death my bones with dust shall cover
summary: A 'churl' is a rude, low-born peasant — the rudest possible social rank. Calling Death a 'churl' strips away the grand, ceremonial personifications usual in Renaissance writing and makes Death instead a graceless labourer who buries bones without ceremony.
detail: OED gives 'churl' as a serf or villager of the lowest rank, extended to mean a rude, boorish, ill-mannered person (the adjective 'churlish' survives in modern English). In classical and Renaissance poetry Death was more often personified as a mighty king or a dignified reaper; to call him a 'churl' is deliberately reductive — even Death, the great leveller, is downgraded into a clumsy farmhand shovelling earth. The move is consistent with the sonnet's broader self-deprecation: the poet undercuts the grandeur of both his death and his verse.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'churl,' n. senses 1 and 4: (1) a man of low birth, a serf; (4) a surly, ill-bred person. Cf. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'churl': 'a rude, surly fellow; a peasant.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 436
OED s.v. 'churl' senses 1 and 4 (low-born serf; surly person) are real and correctly described; Onions's Shakespeare Glossary is a genuine reference work and its entry matches the claim.
The reading of 'churl' as a rude low-born peasant stripping Death of grandeur is the standard editorial gloss (Booth, Vendler, Kerrigan) and is well supported by OED senses 1 and 4.

anchor_text: bett'ring of the time, And though they be outstripp'd by every pen
summary: 'The bett'ring of the time' means the general improvement in poetic skill that later ages will achieve. The poet predicts that by the time the youth re-reads these poems, every other writer will have surpassed them in craft. This is a pointed act of self-deprecation set against the booming Elizabethan sonnet vogue of the 1590s, when dozens of sequences were published.
detail: Samuel Daniel's 'Delia' (1592), Michael Drayton's 'Idea's Mirror' (1594), Edmund Spenser's 'Amoretti' (1595), and many lesser sequences had made the sonnet the fashionable form; Shakespeare's sequence was probably composed and circulating in manuscript during this competitive decade. 'Outstripp'd by every pen' acknowledges the competition with unusual candour — or performs unusual modesty. Whether the self-deprecation is genuine or itself a rhetorical strategy (claiming love as more durable than art is its own form of artistic claim) has been debated by editors since Malone. The phrase 'bett'ring of the time' uses 'time' in the sense of 'age' or 'era' (OED s.v. 'time' n. 12: 'the period of a person's life or of a particular age').

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bettering,' vbl. n.: the action of making better; improvement. OED s.v. 'time,' n. sense 12: a period, an era, an age. For the Elizabethan sonnet vogue see Sidney Lee, 'Elizabethan Sonnets' (1904), introduction, pp. xv-xxx.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 439

OED senses for 'bettering' and 'time' n. 12 are real; Daniel's Delia (1592), Drayton's Idea's Mirror (1594), and Spenser's Amoretti (1595) are correctly dated; Sidney Lee's 'Elizabethan Sonnets' (1904) is a real work with an introductory survey of the sonnet vogue.

'Bett'ring of the time' as poetic improvement by later ages, with 'outstripp'd by every pen' as candid acknowledgement of the competitive sonnet vogue, is the mainstream editorial reading and the historical context (Daniel, Drayton, Spenser) is factually accurate.

anchor_text: A dearer birth than this his love had brought, To march in ranks of better equipage
summary: 'Equipage' means equipment, outfit, or furnishings — here, the poetic trappings of style. 'Better equipage' means more accomplished technique, a richer and more polished verse. The military metaphor ('march in ranks') pictures poems as soldiers whose quality is measured by their gear.
detail: OED s.v. 'equipage,' n. sense 1: equipment, outfit, trappings; in a military context, the full set of arms and gear a soldier carries. The phrase 'to march in ranks of better equipage' continues a minor military metaphor latent throughout the sestet: the poet imagines a competition between poets as an army review, in which his verse falls short in 'equipage' — it lacks the polished weaponry of more accomplished writers. 'A dearer birth' means a more precious or more highly prized poetic offspring — 'birth' as the product of creative labour (OED s.v. 'birth,' n. sense 3b: a thing brought forth, a product).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'equipage,' n. sense 1: equipment, outfit, gear; in military usage, the full armament and trappings of a soldier or company. OED s.v. 'birth,' n. sense 3b: that which is produced or brought forth; a product or result of mental or creative activity.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 445
OED s.v. 'equipage' n. sense 1 (equipment, gear; military trappings) and 'birth' n. sense 3b (product of creative labour) are real entries that support the glosses given.

The military reading of 'march in ranks of better equipage' is well supported by OED and by the diction of the line itself; the slight claim of a 'latent' military metaphor throughout the sestet is a modest over-reach but does not distort the primary gloss.

anchor_text: glorious morning have I seen / Flatter the mountain tops with sovereign eye
summary: The opening eight lines build an extended metaphor — the classical 'solar conceit' — comparing the sun to an all-powerful ruler whose 'sovereign eye' bestows and withdraws favour. 'Sovereign' means supreme, kingly; the sun gazes down like a monarch granting his countenance. The poem holds this metaphor in place before revealing, at line 9, that the 'sun' is actually the person the poet loves.
detail: The solar conceit — comparing a beloved or patron to the sun — was a staple of Petrarchan verse, inherited from classical poetry and deployed by Sidney, Spenser, and Daniel. Shakespeare's innovation is structural: he withholds the vehicle of the metaphor (the Youth) for eight full lines, so the reader experiences the literal sunrise completely before the 'Even so my sun' turn arrives. The word 'flatter' is also pointed: it treats the sun's light not as a natural gift but as a courtly performance, a ruler performing favour — which prepares for the sun's later withdrawal of that favour. George Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) lists the sustained comparison (icon or allegory) as among the highest ornaments of verse.

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III, ch. 19, on the icon (sustained comparison) as a rhetorical figure.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sovereign,' adj. sense 1a: 'Supreme in power, rank, or authority; holding the position of ruler or chief.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 449

Puttenham Book III ch. 19 ('Of Figures Sententious') is real and does treat icon (resemblance by imagery) as a type of similitude, but the annotation's claim that Puttenham lists icon/sustained comparison as 'among the highest ornaments of verse' overstates what ch. 19 says — it catalogues the figure, it does not rank it as highest; the OED 'sovereign' sense 1a is accurate and uncontroversial.

The solar conceit, the Petrarchan inheritance, the reading of 'flatter' as courtly performance, and the structural claim that the vehicle is withheld for eight full lines before the 'Even so' turn are all mainstream and well-supported by the text.

anchor_text: Gilding pale streams with heavenly alchemy
summary: Alchemy was the medieval and Renaissance science that claimed to transmute base metals into gold. Here the sun literally gilds — covers with a layer of gold — the pale streams it shines on, so sunlight is 'heavenly alchemy': the one natural process that actually turns things golden. The word also carries a hint of illusion, since alchemical gold was notoriously deceptive.
detail: Alchemists (and satirists who mocked them) were commonplace in Elizabethan London. The OED records 'alchemy' used figuratively for any process of beautifying or enhancing as early as the 1590s. Shakespeare uses 'gilding' throughout the sonnets and plays as a figure for surface beauty that may not match underlying worth — 'gilded' often implies deception (compare 'gilding the lily' in King John 4.2). In the context of the solar conceit, 'heavenly alchemy' sets up the poem's own ambivalence: the transformation the sun performs is real and beautiful, but it is also transient and dependent on the sun's continued presence.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'alchemy,' n. sense 2b: 'fig. A process of transmutation; that which effects such a process.' First figurative use cited c. 1595.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'gilding,' vbl. n.: 'The action of covering with gold or a gold-coloured substance.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 452

Both OED citations (alchemy n. figurative sense, gilding vbl. n.) are real, standard lexicographic entries, and correctly support the claim that alchemy was used figuratively for beautification from the 1590s and that gilding denotes surface gold-covering.

The gloss on 'alchemy' as a beautifying/gilding process with a hint of transience and illusion is defensible; the King John cross-reference ('gild refined gold') is accurately attributed and the interpretation does not overreach.

anchor_text: Even so my sun one early morn did shine
summary: Line 9 — 'Even so my sun' — is the sonnet's volta, the turn where the argument pivots. For eight lines the poem seemed to describe an actual sunrise; this line reveals that the whole description was a vehicle for the speaker's situation: his beloved ('my sun') shone on him briefly, then withdrew into clouds. The Shakespearean volta typically arrives at line 9 or in the closing couplet; here it arrives exactly at the standard turn.
detail: Philip Sidney in 'Astrophil and Stella' (1591) and George Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) both discuss the structural hinge of the sonnet. In the Italian (Petrarchan) form the turn comes after the octave (8 lines); Shakespeare's English form allows the turn at line 9 or in the couplet. Sonnet 33 is unusual in its clean eight-line delay — the reader has had no pronoun or direct address to signal what the sonnet is actually about. The word 'Even so' (meaning 'In exactly the same way') is the formal signal of the simile's application, linking the extended solar description point by point to the personal situation. 'My sun' collapses the metaphoric vehicle (the sun in the sky) and the tenor (the beloved) into a single phrase, making them permanently fused for the rest of the poem.

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III, on the 'turne' or point of conversion in a rhetorical argument.

sources.name: Sidney, Astrophil and Stella
sources.citation: Sir Philip Sidney, 'Astrophil and Stella' (1591), sonnets 1 and 71, for the model of a delayed revelation of the beloved as the poem's true subject.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 457

Puttenham's discussion of the rhetorical 'turn' is real and relevant, but the citation of Astrophil and Stella sonnets 1 and 71 as models of 'delayed revelation of the beloved as the poem's true subject' overstates sonnet 71, which is a virtue-and-beauty praise poem and not a structurally delayed-revelation sonnet analogous to Shakespeare 33's eight-line deferral.

The reading of line 9 as the volta, the identification of 'Even so' as the formal simile-application signal, and the claim of an eight-line withheld subject are accurate and standard; the Sidney parallels cited are loose but do not constitute an overreach of the interpretation.

anchor_text: Suns of the world may stain when heaven's sun staineth
summary: 'Stain' carries two meanings simultaneously: the literal discolouration of the sun when clouds pass across it (its light is tainted), and moral staining — dishonour, shame. The couplet offers a forgiving argument: if the real sun in heaven is sometimes obscured and 'stained,' it is no surprise that a human 'sun' (the beloved) sometimes does the same. The forgiveness is genuine but tinged with sadness, since 'stain' is not a neutral word.
detail: The OED gives 'stain' in the moral sense ('to bring reproach or disgrace upon') from the early sixteenth century, so both senses were active simultaneously for Shakespeare's readers. The couplet's move is characteristically Shakespearean: the analogy that has been building across fourteen lines is now turned into an excuse or pardon. But the word 'staineth' — used of 'heaven's sun' — is quietly shocking: even the divine, sovereign source of light can be tainted. The rhetorical figure is syncrisis (a comparison that levels two apparently different things), and its effect is to lower the ideal (the celestial sun does stain) while raising the human (the beloved's fault is therefore forgivable). The pun on 'Suns / Sons' (homophones in Elizabethan English) adds another layer: the world's sons — human beings — are as fallible as heaven's sun.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'stain,' v., sense 3: 'To bring disgrace or reproach upon; to sully the honour or reputation of.' Attested from c. 1513 onwards.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., 'Shakespeare-Lexicon' (3rd ed., 1902), s.v. 'stain': both 'to discolour' and 'to tarnish morally,' both senses present in the sonnets.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 462

OED stain v. sense 3 ('to bring disgrace or reproach upon,' attested from c. 1513) is a well-established entry, and Alexander Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (3rd ed., 1902) is a real, standard reference work that records both the literal and moral senses of 'stain' in the plays and poems.

anchor_text: Hiding thy bravery in their rotten smoke
summary: 'Bravery' here means splendor or outward magnificence — the youth's radiant appearance — not courage. The clouds hiding that splendor in 'rotten smoke' continue the weather conceit: just as overcast skies blot out a beautiful day, some disgraceful conduct has obscured the youth's bright qualities.
detail: OED s.v. 'bravery' sense 2: 'showy display; ostentation; fine show or appearance; also, fine clothes or dress' — citing uses from the 1560s onward. The word carried no necessary sense of personal courage before the eighteenth century. 'Rotten' is equally pointed: OED s.v. 'rotten' sense 5 gives 'corrupt, foul, offensive to the senses or mind,' well suited to the moral coloring Shakespeare adds to the weather image. The phrase 'rotten smoke' thus does double work — natural cloud-haze and the moral taint that screens the youth from the speaker.

OED sense 2 for 'bravery' as splendor/show is well-attested in Elizabethan usage, and the double valence of 'rotten' (physical vapour + moral corruption) follows naturally from the sustained weather-and-disgrace conceit; no overreach.

anchor_text: no man well of such a salve can speak, / That heals the wound, and cures not the disgrace
summary: 'Salve' is an ointment or medicinal balm applied to a wound. The speaker concedes that the youth has tried to make amends — breaking through the cloud to dry the rain on the speaker's face — but argues that closing a cut is not enough: the scar, the shame, the public knowledge of the wrong remains. A remedy that heals the injury but not the disgrace is no remedy at all.

The medical metaphor is developed across lines 467-472: the youth's partial amends are like a physician who closes a wound but leaves the underlying infection untreated. In Elizabethan usage 'disgrace' carried its full weight of public dishonor as well as private shame (OED s.v. 'disgrace' sense 1: 'the condition of being out of favor; loss of esteem; public shame'). The distinction between healing the wound and removing the disgrace is the sonnet's central grievance.

The gloss of 'salve' as medicinal ointment is straightforward and accurate; the reading that partial amends heal the injury but not the public shame is directly supported by 'cures not the disgrace' and is the poem's plainly stated argument.

anchor_text: thy shame give physic to my grief
summary: 'Physic' means medicine or medical treatment. The speaker argues that the youth's shame — his remorse and embarrassment — cannot function as a cure for the speaker's grief. Feeling sorry is not the same as undoing the harm: the offender's regret is a treatment aimed at the wrong patient.
detail: OED s.v. 'physic' sense 1: 'the art or science of healing; medicine; also, a medicinal preparation, a drug.' The word was the ordinary Elizabethan term for medicine in general, not the more restricted modern sense. The doctor-and-patient logic runs through lines 469-473: salve (external dressing), physic (internal medicine), and grief-as-ailment form a sustained medical metaphor that cools into legal language in the following line. The turn from 'wound' to 'grief' is also significant — external injury has now been internalized as emotional suffering.

'Physic' as general medicine is uncontroversially correct for the period; the sustained medical metaphor (salve → physic → grief-as-ailment) is present in the text and the annotation does not inflate it beyond what the lines support.

anchor_text: loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud
summary: 'Canker' here means a grub or caterpillar that destroys a rosebud from inside before it can open. The line belongs to a series of natural imperfections (thorns in roses, mud in fountains, eclipses on the sun) that the speaker uses to argue the Youth's fault is simply part of nature's order.
detail: OED records 'canker' in this sense (a destructive worm, especially the caterpillar of certain moths) from the 14th century onward, noting that the rose-canker was proverbial. The word also carried the sense of a gangrenous ulcer, adding a note of inward corruption to the outward sweetness of the bud. Shakespeare uses the image elsewhere: 'For sweetest things turn sourest by their deeds; / Lilies that fester smell far worse than weeds' (Sonnet 94) and Friar Lawrence's speech on the dual nature of herbs in Romeo and Juliet (2.3).

The worm/grub sense of 'canker' is well-attested and the rose-canker imagery is standard; connecting it to Sonnet 94 and Friar Lawrence's herb speech is accurate and the gloss does not over-read the line.

anchor_text: salving thy amiss
summary: 'Salving' means applying a healing ointment or salve to a wound — here used figuratively for dressing over the Youth's wrongdoing with excuses. 'Amiss' is a noun meaning a fault or transgression. The speaker says he has been acting as a healer of wrongs he should instead be calling out.
detail: OED records 'salve' as a verb ('to apply a healing substance; to remedy or smooth over') from the 14th century. 'Amiss' as a noun — rather than an adjective or adverb — is a usage OED traces to the mid-16th century; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon cites this line specifically for the nominal use. The medical metaphor of applying salve to a moral wound was a commonplace of the period: the OED also records the figurative sense 'to excuse, palliate' for 'salve' from 1560.

'Salving' as figurative palliating and 'amiss' as a nominal fault are both defensible and well-supported by Schmidt and OED; the gloss reads the line accurately without embellishment.

anchor_text: to thy sensual fault I bring in sense
summary: The line turns on a pun: 'sensual fault' means a wrong rooted in physical desire, while 'sense' means rational argument. The speaker is saying that to a sin of the body he is adding a sin of the mind — using his reason to defend what reason ought to condemn. The opposition of sense (intellect) and sensual (appetite) was a standard moral distinction in Elizabethan thought.
detail: OED distinguishes 'sensual' (governed by bodily appetite and desire) from 'sense' (faculty of reason or understanding). The pun exploits the fact that both words share the Latin root sensus, so 'sense' used against 'sensual' is the rational faculty arrayed against the appetitive — yet here deployed in the appetitive's service. This is the speaker's most precise self-accusation: not only does he excuse the Youth emotionally, he deploys logical argument ('sense') to do it, making the intellectual faculty complicit in covering an erotic transgression.

The sensus/sense-sensual pun is plausible and the appetite-versus-reason distinction is genuinely Elizabethan, but the annotation over-specifies the pun's meaning ('sin of the mind' versus 'sin of the body') in a way that goes slightly beyond what the text plainly supports — 'sense' here may simply mean 'argument' or 'pleading' (OED sense 13) rather than 'the rational faculty' in a morally loaded sense, so the intellectual-complicity reading is defensible but not certain.

anchor_text: I an accessary needs must be, To that sweet thief which sourly robs from me
summary: An 'accessary' (spelled thus in the 1609 Quarto) is a legal term for someone who aids another's crime without committing it directly. The couplet delivers the sonnet's devastating conclusion: the speaker has not only been robbed by the Youth but has assisted the robbery. 'Sweet thief' and 'sourly robs' are a characteristic Shakespearean oxymoron — the beloved's sweetness set against the bitterness of the injury — closing the sonnet on the same paradox of mingled love and harm it began.
detail: 'Accessary' (or accessory) in English law denoted one who aided or abetted a principal offender before or after the fact, without being present at the crime itself. OED records the form 'accessary' as the standard Elizabethan legal spelling, with 'accessory' becoming more common later. The couplet thus finishes the legal narrative of lines 486-489 — prosecutor, advocate, plea, civil war — and arrives at the logical terminus: if the speaker has been arguing the Youth's case, he has aided the offence, making himself legally and morally an accomplice. The oxymoron 'sweet thief... sourly robs' (a pleasurable agent causing bitter harm) compresses the whole emotional argument of the sonnet: love makes wrong seem acceptable while still leaving its victim injured.

The legal sense of 'accessary' as an abettor not present at the crime is precisely correct and the 1609 Quarto spelling note is accurate; the oxymoron 'sweet thief... sourly robs' is a straightforward reading with no over-reach.

anchor_text: we two must be twain, Although our undivided loves are one
summary: 'Twain' means two; separate. The speaker opens with a deliberate paradox: their loves are one unified thing, yet they must live as two separate people. The whole sonnet unfolds from this contradiction between inner unity and outward division.
detail: The paradox is structural, not decorative. 'Undivided loves are one' echoes the New Testament marriage formula ('they twain shall be one flesh,' Matthew 19:6, Geneva 1599), applying it to a same-sex bond and then immediately pulling against it: the flesh may not be joined even if the love is. Shakespeare's sonnet form (three quatrains developing the problem, a couplet proposing a resolution) suits this kind of argument step by step; the first quatrain sets up the paradox, the second qualifies it, and the third names the specific social constraint. For the sonnet form see the-sonnet-form reference card.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'twain' adj. and n.: 'Separated into two, parted, severed; at variance'; in common Elizabethan use as a plain numeral and as a word carrying the sense of division or separation.

sources.citation: Matthew 19:6 (Geneva 1599): 'Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. Let not man therefore put asunder that, which God hath coupled together.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 491

Matthew 19:6 Geneva 1599 text ('Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. Let not man therefore put asunder that, which God hath coupled together.') is verbatim accurate as confirmed against the Geneva Bible, and OED s.v. 'twain' correctly records both the numeral and the separative senses.

The paradox of outward separation vs. unified love is the sonnet's central structural argument, the Matthew 19:6 echo is widely accepted by editors (Booth, Kerrigan, Duncan-Jones), and the form-follows-argument reading is mainstream and defensible.

anchor_text: those blots that do with me remain
summary: 'Blots' are stains or marks of disgrace. The speaker deliberately leaves their nature unspecified — some unidentified misconduct or scandal of his own that, if publicly associated with the Youth, would damage the Youth's standing. The vagueness is intentional and private.
detail: Onions notes 'blot' as a standard Elizabethan term for moral stain or social dishonour (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'blot': 'a spot of disgrace, a blemish on one's reputation'). The speaker takes the blots upon himself alone ('by me be borne alone') — which is at once honest acknowledgment of fault and an act of protective sacrifice toward the Youth. The nature of the blots has generated extensive editorial speculation; the sonnet offers no clue, and to supply one from outside the poem is to over-read it.

'Blots' as moral stain or social dishonour is standard Elizabethan usage; the annotation correctly resists over-specifying the blots' nature, which the text leaves deliberately vague.

anchor_text: In our two loves there is but one respect, Though in our lives a separable spite
summary: 'Respect' here means concern, regard, or quality — the love they share is of one nature. 'Separable spite' means the cruel force (whether fate, circumstance, or the speaker's own disgrace) that compels them to live apart. 'Spite' carried the older sense of harm inflicted by fortune, not merely personal malice.
detail: 'Respect' in the sense of 'regard, quality, consideration' is common in Shakespeare where modern readers expect 'aspect' or 'nature' (OED s.v. 'respect' n., sense 5: 'A particular aspect, feature, or consideration'). 'Spite' meaning adverse fortune or a hostile force of circumstance, rather than deliberate personal ill-will, is documented in OED s.v. 'spite' n., sense 3: 'Injury, harm; adverse or annoying action of things or circumstances.' The phrase 'separable spite' thus names an external condition — the social world that forces them apart — not a flaw in the love itself.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'respect' n., sense 5: 'A particular aspect, feature, or consideration viewed as part of a matter'; OED s.v. 'spite' n., sense 3: 'Injury, harm; adverse or annoying action or influence of things or circumstances.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 495

The word-senses for 'respect' and 'spite' are defensible, but identifying 'separable spite' specifically as the external social world over-specifies what the poem leaves ambiguous — lines 493-500 make the speaker's own guilt the stated cause of separation, not a generic external social force.

anchor_text: I may not evermore acknowledge thee, Lest my bewailed guilt should do thee shame
summary: The speaker cannot publicly greet or claim the Youth because his own shameful reputation would, by association, damage the Youth's standing. In Elizabethan society reputation was managed through the company one kept; to be publicly connected to a disgraced person was itself dishonoring. This is the social mechanism that enforces the separation announced at the sonnet's opening.
detail: The word 'acknowledge' here carries the force of a public act — a bow, a greeting, a declaration of friendship or patronage in front of others. In a world without mass media, public association was the primary way reputation was built or damaged. The logic runs both ways: the speaker will not acknowledge the Youth (line 499), and in lines 501-502 he instructs the Youth likewise not to honour him publicly. 'Bewailed guilt' suggests genuine remorse ('bewailed' = mourned, lamented), not mere social calculation. The situation has a class dimension common in the sequence: the Youth's 'name' — his family name and social rank — is something worth protecting, and the speaker treats it as partly his own responsibility to guard.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 499

OED s.v. 'acknowledge' v. records a sense of public recognition/greeting, and Schmidt attests the Elizabethan sense of avowing acquaintance; both citations accurately support the claim that 'acknowledge' here carries the force of a public act.

'Acknowledge' as a public act and 'bewailed guilt' as genuine remorse are both sound; the class-dimension note is standard for the sequence and the reading of the mutual-silencing instruction across lines 499-502 is accurate.

anchor_text: made lame by Fortune's dearest spite
summary: 'Lame' here means physically crippled or disabled — the poet presents himself as diminished in body or circumstance. 'Dearest' does not mean 'most beloved' but 'most severe' or 'most costly' (an archaic intensive). Fortune's 'spite' is her malicious, wilful injury — the harm a fickle goddess inflicts.
detail: The OED records 'dear' in the sense of 'grievous, dire, sore' (OED s.v. 'dear' adj. 2a), surviving in modern 'dearly bought.' Whether Shakespeare's lameness is literal or metaphorical — a real physical infirmity versus a figure for low social standing and professional vulnerability — has been debated since the nineteenth century; the poem offers no resolution, and the ambiguity is part of the conceit. Fortune as an arbitrary, spiteful power is a topos running from Boethius through the Mirror for Magistrates; here she inflicts 'spite' rather than merely withdrawing favour, which makes the wound personal. The speaker's self-description as lame, poor, and despised (line 513) sets up the reversal in which the Youth's abundance compensates for all three lacks.
