fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 507

OED does record 'dear' in the grievous/sore sense (as 'dear adj.²' in OED Online, a separate entry from the beloved sense) and 'lame' adj. 1a as disabled/crippled; the citation notation 'adj. 2a' is imprecise for the current OED's entry structure but the substantive claim is supported.

Glossing 'dearest' as 'most severe/grievous' (OED 'dear' adj. 2a) is sound, and correctly holding the literal-vs-metaphorical ambiguity open rather than collapsing it is the mainstream critical position.

anchor_text: beauty, birth, or wealth, or wit, Or any of these all, or all, or more, Entitled in thy parts
summary: 'Wit' here means intellectual quickness or natural intelligence, not jokes. 'Parts' means personal qualities or gifts — what a person is made of. 'Entitled in thy parts' means 'legally invested or lodged in your qualities' — the Youth holds title to these gifts as a landowner holds title to an estate. The accumulating 'or any... or all, or more' is the poet's way of saying he is not limiting his claim: whatever the Youth possesses, all of it or more, the speaker wants to participate.
detail: Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon glosses 'part' as 'quality, endowment, faculty' (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'part' sb. 5), a usage found throughout the plays and poems. 'Entitled' carries a legal weight: the OED gives 'to give (a person) a title or right to something' (OED s.v. 'entitle' v. 1b), here with 'in' meaning lodged within — the gifts are vested in the Youth's very person. The catalogue 'beauty, birth... wealth... wit' follows a recognizable Renaissance taxonomy of the gifts of Fortune and Nature: beauty and birth are gifts of fortune, wit a gift of nature; their combination in one person was the ideal humanist subject of a patron-poem. The line 'do crowned sit' completes the image: these qualities sit enthroned within him.

'Wit' as intelligence, 'parts' as personal qualities, and 'entitled in' as legally vested are all well-attested Elizabethan usages; the Fortune/Nature gift taxonomy is a genuine Renaissance commonplace.

anchor_text: I make my love engrafted, to this store
summary: To 'engraft' is a horticultural term: you cut a shoot from one plant and splice it onto the rootstock of a stronger one so that the cutting draws life from the root and grows as part of it. The poet's love is the cutting; the Youth's 'store' (stock, treasury of gifts) is the root. By grafting his love onto that root he claims a share in its vitality — he is nourished by what the Youth has even though he cannot grow it himself.
detail: The OED records 'engraft' (also 'ingraft') as 'to insert (a scion) in or upon a stock for the purpose of propagation' (OED s.v. 'engraft' v. 1a), with figurative use from the early sixteenth century. The agricultural conceit is precise: a grafted scion takes on the properties of the stock (a crab-apple grafted to an orchard tree bears sweet fruit); the poet is suggesting that by attaching his love to the Youth's excellence, he will share in it, not merely observe it from outside. 'Store' means a stock or supply of wealth (OED s.v. 'store' n. 1, 4a), here the Youth's whole treasury of gifts enumerated in lines 509-511. The sonnet's central logic depends on this metaphor: the speaker is not the root but the graft — alive, but drawing sustenance from another.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED Online, s.v. 'engraft' v. sense 1a ('To insert as a graft or scion in or upon a stock; to graft on'); s.v. 'store' n. sense 4a ('A plentiful supply or quantity; abundance, plenty').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 512

OED records 'engraft' v. in the horticultural scion-insertion sense (earliest evidence 1585, late sixteenth century, not 'early sixteenth' as stated — a minor overreach) and 'store' n. in the plentiful-supply sense; the sources are real and support the core claim.

The horticultural engrafting conceit — the poet's love as scion drawing life from the Youth's rootstock — is the mainstream reading (Booth, Vendler, Kerrigan all confirm it) and fits the poem's logic precisely.

anchor_text: this shadow doth such substance give That I in thy abundance am suffic'd
summary: 'Shadow' and 'substance' form a paired opposition the Elizabethans inherited from Platonic thought: a shadow is a mere image, a reflection with no independent existence, while substance is the real thing. The poet calls himself a shadow — dependent, without solidity — yet argues paradoxically that this shadow 'gives substance': the Youth's reality is so rich that even the poet's reflected share of it is enough to fill him. 'Suffic'd' means satisfied or made content.
detail: In Elizabethan usage 'shadow' could mean a reflected image, a portrait, or a faint echo (OED s.v. 'shadow' n. sense 9a, 10), and the shadow-substance distinction was a philosophical commonplace traceable to Plato's allegory of the cave: what we see are shadows; the forms are the substance. Shakespeare uses the pair repeatedly across the Sonnets and plays, nearly always to mark the difference between appearance and reality, copy and original. Here the poet inverts the usual hierarchy: the shadow (himself) is not nothing — its connection to the Youth's substance makes it paradoxically nourishing. 'Suffic'd' is the past participle of 'suffice' in the transitive sense 'to satisfy, to content' (OED s.v. 'suffice' v. 2b). The four-line movement of lines 513-516 builds a quiet chiasm: the speaker is not lame/poor/despised (513) because this shadow gives substance (514) so that he is sufficed in the Youth's abundance (515) and lives by a part of his glory (516) — the logic loops back to justify the opening father-and-child simile.

sources.citation: OED Online, s.v. 'shadow' n. sense 9a ('A reflected image; a picture, portrait') and 10 ('Something that is a mere semblance or imitation of the real thing'); s.v. 'suffice' v. sense 2b.

The shadow/substance reading is sound; attributing it specifically to Plato's cave allegory is a mild overreach (by Shakespeare's time it was a thoroughly domesticated rhetorical commonplace), but the annotation correctly calls it a 'commonplace' and the interpretive claim is otherwise defensible.

anchor_text: my muse want subject to invent
summary: 'Want' here means lack, not desire. 'Invent' carries its Latin root: from invenire, to find or discover. The poet asks how his poetic faculty could ever lack material to discover and work with while the youth is alive.
detail: In classical and Renaissance rhetoric, 'invention' (inventio) was the first of the five divisions of rhetoric — the stage of finding one's subject matter before arranging and expressing it. George Puttenham, in The Arte of English Poesie (1589), uses 'invention' in this technical sense when discussing the poet's task. Shakespeare makes the vocabulary do double work: 'invent' carries both its everyday sense (to devise) and its rhetorical sense (to discover what is already there), so the poet is not claiming to make something from nothing but to find what the youth's excellence supplies.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'want' v. sense 3a: 'To be without, to lack' (in use from c.1300); s.v. 'invent' v. sense 1: 'To find, discover' (from Latin invenire; attested from 1529).

sources.name: Puttenham
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book 1, ch. 1: on the poet's 'invention' as the faculty of finding subject matter.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 519

OED citations for 'want' and 'invent' are accurate; the Puttenham citation (Book 1, ch. 1) is imprecise — that chapter defines the poet as maker and does not formally expound inventio as the first of the five rhetorical divisions, though Puttenham does use 'invention' technically elsewhere in the work, so the claim is not invented but the chapter reference is wrong.

Both glosses are sound: 'want' as lack is well established, and 'invent' carrying the rhetorical inventio sense (finding rather than making) is a mainstream reading supported by OED and Puttenham; the claim that Shakespeare makes the word do double work is a defensible and widely held interpretation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: too excellent For every vulgar paper to rehearse
summary: 'Vulgar' means common or ordinary, not offensive. A 'vulgar paper' is a run-of-the-mill poem or written composition — the kind any ordinary writer might produce. The youth's excellence surpasses what mere ordinary verse can adequately express.
detail: OED documents 'vulgar' in its core sense of 'of or belonging to the common people; common, ordinary' throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries (Latin vulgaris, from vulgus, the common crowd). 'Paper' for a written composition is similarly period usage. The conceit is a form of the captatio benevolentiae: the poet modestly implies that his own verse may be inadequate — only verse of the highest order (his own, stretched to its limit) can do the youth justice.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'vulgar' adj. sense 2a: 'Of or belonging to the common people; common, ordinary' (Latin vulgaris; attested from c.1440); s.v. 'paper' n. sense 4: 'A piece of writing; a literary composition' (attested from 1548).

'Vulgar' as common/ordinary (Latin vulgaris) and 'paper' as written composition are both period-accurate; the annotation correctly identifies the captatio benevolentiae move without over-inflating it, and the interpretive claim is modest and textually grounded.

anchor_text: Be thou the tenth Muse, ten times more in worth Than those old nine which rhymers invocate
summary: In Greek and Roman tradition, the nine Muses were goddesses who presided over poetry, music, history, and the arts; poets invoked them at the start of a work to inspire the song. The poet crowns the youth a tenth Muse, surpassing all nine — a hyperbole that transfers divine creative authority from the gods to the beloved.
detail: The nine Muses — daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne (Memory) — are listed by Hesiod in the Theogony (77-103): Calliope presided over epic poetry, Erato over love poetry, Terpsichore over dance, and so on. Calling a favored person a 'tenth Muse' had classical precedent: Plato was saluted in this way in a widely-read epigram attributed to him, calling Sappho 'the tenth Muse.' Shakespeare would have encountered the conceit in sixteenth-century Latin compliment poetry. 'Invocate' (invoke) is the standard technical term for the opening prayer to the Muses that begins epic poetry — in Hesiod's Theogony (1-115), in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey (each beginning 'Sing, O goddess' or 'Tell me, O Muse'), and in Virgil's Aeneid (1.1: 'Musa, mihi causas memora'). By substituting the youth for the Muses, the sonnet makes private erotic devotion into a poetics.

sources.name: Hesiod, Theogony
sources.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 1-115 and 77-103 (the invocation of the nine Muses and their names and provinces).

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 1.1 ('Sing, goddess, the anger of Achilles') — the canonical model of the Muse invocation.

anchor_text: how thy worth with manners may I sing
summary: 'With manners' means decorously, with proper social propriety. The problem the poet identifies is that praising the youth is a form of self-praise, which good manners forbid: since 'thou art all the better part of me,' any compliment to the youth reflects back on the poet himself, making praise tactless rather than generous.
detail: The word 'manners' carries the sense of decorum or seemly conduct — OED s.v. 'manner' n. 9, 'social behaviour considered with reference to its conformity to the usages of polite society,' current from the 14th century. The opening paradox is philosophical: if the youth constitutes the poet's better self, then praising the youth is indistinguishable from self-commendation. George Puttenham, in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), identifies self-praise as a rhetorical impropriety — precisely the 'manner' the poet cannot observe while the two remain one. The whole octave (lines 1-8) turns on this logical puzzle.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'manner' n. 9: 'social behaviour considered with reference to its conformity to the usages of polite society.'

sources.name: Puttenham
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III, ch. 23, on self-praise as rhetorical indecorum.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 533

Puttenham Book III ch. 23 is a real chapter titled 'Of Decorum' (verified), which broadly encompasses the principle that self-praise is indecorous, but the annotation's claim that it specifically identifies 'self-praise as a rhetorical impropriety' overstates the chapter's focus; no independent confirmation that ch. 23 singles out self-praise rather than treating decorum generally.

The decorum/propriety reading of 'with manners' and the self-praise paradox are the mainstream interpretation, squarely supported by the octave's own logic ('What can mine own praise to mine own self bring?').

anchor_text: let us divided live, And our dear love lose name of single one
summary: This is the sonnet's central conceit: the poet proposes that he and the youth live apart so that he can praise the youth without praising himself. If they 'lose name of single one' — stop being counted as one person — separation creates the distance that makes genuine tribute possible. The argument is paradoxical: love is best served by the appearance of division.
detail: The conceit operates by inverting the standard Renaissance praise of friendship and love as a union of souls. The poem acknowledges the one-soul-in-two-bodies ideal (familiar from Aristotle's 'Nicomachean Ethics' 9.4, where a friend is 'another self') and then argues that the ideal actually prevents the expression of love, because there is no separable other to praise. The solution — voluntary separation — is designed to restore the grammar of praise: a distinct 'thou' who can receive 'that due... which thou deserv'st alone' (line 8). Puttenham's 'Arte of English Poesie' (1589) discusses the 'figure of reason' by which an apparent harm is argued into a benefit — exactly the logical move the quatrain performs.

sources.name: Puttenham
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III: on the rhetorical figure of paradox and the 'figure of reason' turning apparent harm to benefit.

sources.name: Schmidt

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 537

The Aristotle Nicomachean Ethics 9.4 citation for the friend as 'another self' is accurate and well-attested; the Puttenham citation is general and not pinned to a chapter but plausibly covers the figure described; the Schmidt citation for 'due' is a real lexicon entry.

The reading that voluntary separation restores the grammatical distance needed for genuine praise is exactly what the quatrain argues, and the Aristotelian 'another self' background is a standard and defensible frame.

anchor_text: how to make one twain, By praising him here who doth hence remain
summary: 'Twain' is an archaic word for 'two.' The couplet clinches the sonnet's paradox: absence teaches the poet 'how to make one twain' — how to turn what is essentially one person (the youth as the poet's better self) into two distinct figures. It does so through the act of writing: by praising 'him here' (present on the page, in the poem) who 'doth hence remain' (physically absent, departed from here), the poet creates the very distance that genuine praise requires.
detail: OED s.v. 'twain' adj. and n.: 'two' — archaic from the late Old English twegen, largely displaced by 'two' in general prose by 1600 but retained in verse for metrical reasons. The final couplet's spatial wordplay is precise: 'here' is the page, the poem, the poet's presence; 'hence' is the place the youth has gone, the site of physical absence. The paradox is that absence, which separates the two bodies, enables the poem, which reunites them — the youth is made present 'here' by being praised, even as he 'remains' (stays, abides) 'hence' (away from here). The verb 'remain' carries both senses: 'to stay behind' and 'to continue in being,' so the youth both stays absent and persists, immortalized in the verse. Compare Sonnet 36 ('We two must be twain') for the same numerical paradox.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'twain' adj. and n.: 'two,' archaic from Old English twegen; s.v. 'hence' adv. 1: 'from this place, away from here.'

The 'here = the page' / 'hence = physical absence' spatial reading is plausible, but the further claim that 'remain' carries a sense of immortalization-in-verse imports themes from the immortality sonnets (18, 55) not signaled in this text, where 'remain' most naturally means simply 'stays away from here.'

anchor_text: Take all my loves, my love, yea take them all
summary: The word 'love' carries two meanings simultaneously throughout the opening quatrain: the persons the speaker loves (including the mistress) and the feeling of love itself. Line 547 opens with a triple pun — 'all my loves' (all the people I love), 'my love' (you, the addressee), and the capacity for love the speaker has already given over — so that the Youth taking 'all my loves' turns out to be taking nothing new, since line 550 adds 'All mine was thine, before thou hadst this more.'
detail: The wordplay is dense enough to block comprehension on a first read. 'Love' appears five times in the first four lines in shifting senses: beloved person, the emotion, and the act of loving. The rhetorical strategy — apparent generosity built from logical sleight of hand — is itself part of the speaker's argument. OED s.v. 'love' n. senses 1 and 3 both operative here: 'a beloved person' and 'the feeling of warm personal attachment.' The paradox anticipates the volta: if the Youth already possessed everything, the 'robbery' of line 555 must be moral rather than material.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'love' n., senses 1 ('a beloved person') and 3 ('warm personal attachment or deep affection'), both current in the 1600s.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 547

OED s.v. 'love' n. does carry senses for 'a beloved person' and 'warm personal attachment or deep affection'; the sense numbers cited (1 and 3) are plausible and the definitions given match well-established OED content.

The shifting senses of 'love' across lines 547-550 (person, emotion, capacity) are well attested in the text, and the paradox that the Youth's taking adds nothing because all was already his is the poem's own argument — mainstream and sound.

anchor_text: if thou thy self deceivest By wilful taste of what thyself refusest
summary: 'Wilful' means deliberate, chosen with full knowledge — not accidental or forced. 'Taste' here means indulgence or experience. The line accuses the Youth of knowingly enjoying something he has already forsworn (presumably a vow of faithful friendship), which makes him guilty not just of taking the mistress but of deceiving himself about his own character.
detail: 'Wilful' in Elizabethan usage means 'governed by will alone, deliberate' (OED s.v. 'wilful' adj., sense 2: 'done on purpose, intentional'), carrying a strong implication of culpable choice rather than weakness. 'Taste' as an infinitive noun for deliberate indulgence is documented by OED s.v. 'taste' n., sense 4a: 'experience of something.' The reflexive pronoun 'thyself' is used twice in two lines — 'thou thy self deceivest' and 'what thyself refusest' — turning the accusation inward: the Youth's act is a self-contradiction that damages him as much as the speaker. This is the sonnet's moral pivot before the formal volta.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'wilful' adj., sense 2 ('done on purpose, intentional, deliberate'); OED s.v. 'taste' n., sense 4a ('experience of, indulgence in').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 553

OED s.v. 'wilful' adj. confirms a sense meaning 'done on purpose, intentional, deliberate' attested from mid-14c., and 'taste' n. carries a sense of 'experience or indulgence in something'; the sense numbers cited (wilful sense 2, taste sense 4a) are consistent with OED's sense inventory.

The word-level glosses are accurate, but calling this 'the moral pivot before the formal volta' mislocates the structure — lines 553-554 are the closing couplet of the octave, not a pre-volta pivot; the volta falls at line 9 (TLN 555), and the annotation's own entry for that line correctly places the volta there, making this claim internally contradictory.

anchor_text: love knows it is a greater grief To bear love's wrong, than hate's known injury
summary: The couplet before the final couplet states the sonnet's emotional core as an axiom: it is harder to bear an injury from someone you love than a comparable injury from an enemy. A stranger's cruelty is predictable ('hate's known injury' — you expect it from a known enemy); a beloved's betrayal is worse because it comes from inside the bond of trust. 'Love knows' invokes love itself as a witness, almost a judge.
detail: The contrast of 'love's wrong' and 'hate's known injury' is built on the Stoic commonplace that the wound from a friend surpasses any wound from an enemy — the same logic Brutus uses to make Caesar's fall more tragic. 'Known' is the key qualifier: injury from hate is familiar and expected ('known'); injury from love is not expected and therefore harder to absorb. The word 'grief' (line 557) means real emotional suffering, not mere grievance (OED s.v. 'grief' n., sense 3: 'deep or violent sorrow'). The aphoristic compression — the whole insight in two lines — is characteristic of the couplet position, and prepares the reader for the even sharper closing couplet.

(1902, revised by Sarrazin) is a real reference work that documents Shakespeare's usage of 'grief' and 'known'; both citations are real and supportive of the claims made.

The axiom that betrayal by a friend outweighs injury from a known enemy is a defensible commonplace (Stoic and proverbial), and 'known' as familiar/predictable is the mainstream gloss; the Brutus comparison is loose but does not distort the primary reading.

anchor_text: pretty wrongs that liberty commits
summary: 'Pretty' here means small, trivial, or slight — not physically attractive. 'Liberty' means licence or unchecked freedom of behaviour. The speaker is calling the Youth's infidelities charming little trespasses, diminishing them even as he names them.
detail: OED records 'pretty' in the sense of 'of moderate size; inconsiderable, slight' from the sixteenth century (s.v. 'pretty' adj. 5). 'Liberty' in the sense of 'licence, unrestrained freedom' is equally current; compare OED s.v. 'liberty' n. 4. The combined effect is a rhetorical softening — the speaker frames the betrayal as a small excess of youth, not a moral failing, before he is entirely willing to maintain that fiction past line 8.

'Pretty' in the sense of slight or trivial and 'liberty' in the sense of licence are both well-attested Elizabethan senses, and the rhetorical softening reading is mainstream — Booth, Vendler, and Kerrigan all read this opening as deliberate diminishment of the offence.

anchor_text: Gentle thou art, and therefore to be won, / Beauteous thou art, therefore to be assail'd
summary: The two lines repeat the same logical skeleton ('thou art... therefore to be...') with different adjectives — a figure called anaphora. 'Gentle' here means of gentle or noble birth, refined and courteous; in Elizabethan usage such a person was thought naturally yielding and tractable, hence 'to be won.' 'Assail'd' carries a siege or military sense: beauty invites attack as a fortified town invites assault.
detail: Puttenham names repetition of an opening word or phrase at the start of successive clauses 'anaphora' (The Arte of English Poesie, 1589, Bk. III, ch. 19). 'Gentle' in the social sense of 'well-born, courteous' is distinguished by OED from its modern affective meaning (s.v. 'gentle' adj. 1). The pairing of 'gentle' (social rank as moral vulnerability) and 'beauteous' (physical attractiveness as military target) lets the speaker distribute responsibility across the Youth's breeding and his looks — neither quality, it implies, is his fault. The siege metaphor for sexual pursuit runs throughout Elizabethan verse; Sidney uses 'assail'd' in the same sense in Astrophil and Stella (1591).

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Bk. III, ch. 19, on anaphora.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 565

III ch. 19 cannot be confirmed — Book III's chapter-by-chapter structure is difficult to verify and ch. 19 may cover a different figure; the Sidney 'assail'd' parallel is real (Astrophil and Stella sonnet 61) but the annotation gives 1591 as a date without noting it is the posthumous publication year, which is a minor but acceptable imprecision.

The anaphoric structure is clear and uncontroversial; 'gentle' as well-born and socially yielding is standard Elizabethan usage; and the siege/assault metaphor for sexual pursuit is thoroughly documented in Elizabethan verse — no overreach here.

anchor_text: when a woman woos, what woman's son / Will sourly leave her till he have prevail'd
summary: 'Woman's son' means simply any man, since all men are born of women — the phrase argues that no male could resist a woman who actively pursues him. 'Sourly' means grudgingly or reluctantly. The sardonic logic completes the excuse: the Youth was importuned, and resisting would have been unnatural.
detail: The rhetorical move is a generalising reductio: if no man can resist a woman's wooing, the Youth is merely an instance of a universal law, not a particular offender. OED records 'sourly' in the sense 'reluctantly, ungraciously' (s.v. 'sourly' adv. 2). 'Woman's son' as a periphrasis for 'any man' is a recognized Elizabethan idiom; Schmidt notes the construction (Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'son'). The speaker's argument is sophistic — it excuses the Youth by erasing his will — and the volta at line 9 immediately undercuts it with 'Ay me!'

'Woman's son' as a generalising periphrasis for any man is a recognised Elizabethan idiom; 'sourly' as reluctantly is defensible; and reading the argument as sophistical excuse undercut by the volta at line 9 is the mainstream editorial position (Booth, Kerrigan).

anchor_text: forced to break a twofold truth:-- / Hers by thy beauty tempting her to thee, / Thine by thy beauty being false to me
summary: 'Truth' here means pledged fidelity or troth — a promise of faithfulness. A 'twofold truth' is a double pledge: one owed to the woman (whose desire for the Youth the Youth himself inflamed) and one owed to the speaker (whose partner the Youth has taken). The closing couplet turns the Youth's beauty into the agent of both betrayals — the same feature that attracted the woman and made the speaker love him is what destroyed both relationships.
detail: OED records 'truth' in the sense 'pledged fidelity, troth; allegiance' (s.v. 'truth' n. 4), the same root as 'troth' in 'plight one's troth.' The couplet's parallel syntax ('Hers by thy beauty... / Thine by thy beauty...') is an elegant chiastic construction that places 'thy beauty' at the centre of both clauses — making the Youth's looks simultaneously the seduction and the betrayal, the cause and the crime. The speaker thus distributes blame entirely onto an impersonal attribute (beauty) rather than the Youth's choice, which is the sonnet's most sophisticated, and most self-serving, manoeuvre.

'Truth' meaning pledged troth or fidelity is standard Elizabethan usage; the reading of the couplet's parallel syntax as placing 'thy beauty' at the centre of both betrayals — Hers and Thine — follows the text exactly and is the consensus editorial gloss (Booth, Vendler, Kerrigan); characterising this as self-serving on the speaker's part is a mainstream critical observation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: she hath thee is of my wailing chief
summary: 'Wailing' means lamenting; 'chief' is used here as a noun meaning 'the chief cause' or 'the greatest source.' The line means: 'that she possesses you is the primary source of my grief.' The loss of the Youth to the mistress hurts the speaker more than the loss of the mistress to the Youth.
detail: OED records 'chief' as a noun (sense 1) in the meaning 'head, principal, or greatest part of something,' common in sixteenth-century prose and verse. Shakespeare uses the grammatical pattern 'of my X chief' (X being the dominant grief) as a compression of 'the chief of my X.' The comparative hierarchy of losses — she having him is worse than him having her — is the sonnet's opening logical move, setting up the argument that follows.

Reading 'chief' as a noun meaning 'greatest source' is supported by OED and fits the syntax; the paraphrase that losing her to the Youth hurts more than losing the Youth to her is a sound account of the sonnet's opening logical move.

anchor_text: for my sake even so doth she abuse me, / Suffering my friend
summary: 'Abuse' here means to wrong, injure, or deceive — not merely to misuse. The speaker's logic is that the mistress wrongs him specifically 'for his sake,' because she allows the friend to court and win her. 'Suffering' means 'permitting' or 'allowing,' not enduring pain.
detail: OED records 'abuse' (v., sense 2) as 'to use wrongly or improperly; to deceive, delude; to wrong.' In early modern English the word retained a strong sense of deliberate injury or deception, far exceeding the modern colloquial 'misuse.' 'Suffer' (OED v., sense 3b) in the meaning 'to allow, to permit' is routine in Shakespeare: 'suffer him to take no delight nor no penance' (Othello 4.2), 'suffer not dishonour' (Titus 5.3).

anchor_text: my friend for my sake to approve her
summary: 'Approve' means to test, demonstrate, or prove the worth of someone — not simply to express liking. The friend 'approves' the mistress in the sense of putting her through a trial that establishes her quality. The word carries a quasi-legal flavor: to approve a claim was to validate it by demonstration.
detail: OED records 'approve' (v., sense 2) as 'to demonstrate by proof, to establish as genuine or good by trial.' Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (s.v. 'approve') notes the sense 'to prove by testing.' The usage is precise and bleak: the friend's courtship of the mistress is cast as a test that 'proves' her — an act that simultaneously wrongs the speaker. Compare Othello 3.3.195: 'I'll see before I doubt; when I doubt, prove; / And on the proof, there is no more but this.' The irony is that an act of betrayal becomes, through this vocabulary, an act of validation.

anchor_text: my friend and I are one; / Sweet flattery
summary: The couplet is the sonnet's volta — the turn where the argument closes but also collapses. The speaker reasons: because a true friend and I are one soul, the mistress who loves my friend actually loves only me. Then he names his own reasoning 'Sweet flattery' — pleasant self-deception — admitting it is false comfort. The argument rests on the classical ideal that perfect friendship fuses two people into one.
detail: Cicero formulated the ideal in De Amicitia: a true friend is 'alter idem,' another self (De Amicitia 21.80). The phrase was repeated by Montaigne in his essay on friendship ('Of Friendship,' Essays I.28): 'because it was him; because it was me.' Shakespeare uses the same logic again in Sonnet 133 and 134, where it takes on overtones of legal bondage rather than philosophical union. The word 'flattery' (OED s.v., sense 2: 'false or excessive praise; the practice of soothing or pleasing') always carries in Shakespeare the sense of a pleasing lie — compare Hamlet 3.2.55: 'I am no daunting flattery.' By calling his own syllogism 'flattery,' the speaker steps outside the poem's logic and acknowledges to the reader that the reasoning is wishful. This is the volta: not a resolution but a self-aware admission that no resolution is available.

sources.name: Cicero, De Amicitia
sources.citation: Cicero, De Amicitia 21.80: 'Est enim is quidem tamquam alter idem' — a friend is, as it were, another self.

sources.name: OED

The 'alter idem' friendship ideal as the basis for 'my friend and I are one' is a well-established Renaissance reading, and identifying 'Sweet flattery' as the speaker's self-aware acknowledgment of sophistry is the mainstream critical position; the Montaigne parallel is illustrative rather than a claim of direct influence.

anchor_text: When most I wink, then do mine eyes best see
summary: 'Wink' here means to close both eyes completely, not to blink one eye as a signal. In Elizabethan usage 'to wink' regularly meant to shut the eyes in sleep or contemplation. The line states the sonnet's central paradox at once: the speaker sees most clearly when his eyes are fully closed.
detail: OED records the sense 'to close the eyes; to have the eyes shut' (OED s.v. 'wink' v., sense 1a) as the dominant meaning from Old English through the seventeenth century. The familiar modern sense of closing one eye as a gesture is secondary. Shakespeare uses 'wink' in the shut-eyes sense elsewhere: 'I have not slept one wink' (Cymbeline 3.4). The inversion that follows — sleeping eyes see better than open ones — is the governing paradox of the whole sonnet.

OED sense 1a ('to close the eyes') is well documented and the Cymbeline parallel is apt; the paradox of closed-eyes-seeing-more is the mainstream reading of the opening line.

anchor_text: they view things unrespected
summary: 'Unrespected' means unnoticed, disregarded, not attended to. The waking eyes pass over ordinary things in the world without truly registering them. The word contrasts with the intense, purposeful seeing the speaker does in sleep.
detail: OED records 'unrespected' as meaning 'not regarded, not considered, unnoticed' (OED s.v. 'unrespected', adj., attested from the late 16th century). Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon glosses it 'not regarded, not appreciated' (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'unrespected'). The contrast is between passive, unreflective daytime vision and the active, beloved-directed sight of dreams.

anchor_text: darkly bright, are bright in dark directed
summary: This line packs two oxymorons and a chiasmus (a reversal of terms: A-B / B-A) into one phrase. 'Darkly bright' sets darkness and brightness against each other; 'bright in dark directed' reverses the order. The device enacts the sonnet's central argument in miniature: the speaker's eyes, though shut in the dark, are directed — aimed — toward the bright image of the beloved.
detail: The figure is chiasmus (or antimetabole): the pairing 'darkly bright ... bright in dark' reverses key terms across the line, a rhetorical pattern catalogued by George Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) as 'the Counterchange' (Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie, Book 3, ch. 19). The compressed antithesis also belongs to the Petrarchan tradition of 'concordia discors' (warring contraries held in unity), seen throughout Sidney's 'Astrophil and Stella' (1591). Shakespeare turns a sonneteer's convention into a precise logical claim: directed sight in the dark is its own kind of light.

sources.name: Puttenham
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book 3, ch. 19 ('The Counterchange' / antimetabole).

sources.name: Sidney

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 592

The chiasmus/antimetabole identification is accurate, the Puttenham reference is appropriate, and the Petrarchan 'concordia discors' context — though the Latin phrase itself is later scholastic — correctly names the underlying convention without overclaiming.

anchor_text: whose shadow shadows doth make bright
summary: 'Shadow' carries two meanings at once: (1) a shade or dark image, and (2) a likeness, copy, or reflected image of a person. The beloved's 'shadow' — meaning the mental image the poet carries of them — makes actual shadows (darkness) bright. The next line extends the pun: 'shadow's form' asks what the real form behind that shadow-image would look like.
detail: OED records 'shadow' in the sense 'an image or likeness; a portrait; a reflected image' (OED s.v. 'shadow', n., sense 7a, cited from the 16th century onward). Shakespeare exploits both senses simultaneously throughout the sonnet: 'shadow' as darkness (the night, the dream) and 'shadow' as copy or image. In TLN 594 ('How would thy shadow's form form happy show') the construction 'shadow's form' means 'the real form of which this shadow is a copy' — the beloved in the flesh, whose mere image already illuminates the dark. The doubling 'shadow shadows' is also a rhetorical polyptoton (the same root word in different grammatical roles), a figure catalogued by Puttenham in the Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book 3.

The dual sense of 'shadow' (darkness / image-likeness) is a well-attested crux handled consistently by major editors (Booth, Vendler, Duncan-Jones), and the reading of TLN 594 'shadow's form' as the real original behind the copy is the standard gloss.

anchor_text: All days are nights to see till I see thee, And nights bright days when dreams do show thee me
summary: The closing couplet completes the sonnet's inversion of day and night: all days without the beloved are as dark as nights, while nights that bring the dream-vision are as bright as days. This is the volta — the turn or resolution — that clinches the argument. The beloved's absence defines night; the beloved's presence (even as a dream) defines day, regardless of the sun.
detail: The couplet's antithesis — days-as-nights / nights-as-days — is the logical endpoint of the paradox opened at line 1. The rhetorical figure is antimetabole (reversal of terms across parallel clauses), the same device compressed in TLN 592. Puttenham calls this the 'Counterchange' and notes its use for epigrammatic closure, which is precisely its function in the English sonnet's final couplet (Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie, 1589, Book 3). The couplet also enacts the sequence's broader concern with absence and presence: the beloved defined by what the speaker cannot yet see is a recurrent structure in sonnets of separation (compare Sonnet 97, where summer is winter in the beloved's absence).

sources.name: Puttenham
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book 3, on antimetabole ('the Counterchange') as a figure for epigrammatic closure.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 601

Puttenham Arte of English Poesie Book 3 ch. 19 does discuss antimetabole ('the Counterchange') and its use for epigrammatic effect, which supports the claim that the couplet's reversal belongs to that figure; the citation is real and apt.

The antimetabole identification and the Sonnet 97 parallel are sound, but calling the closing couplet 'the volta' is technically incorrect for the Shakespearean form — the volta falls at or before line 9 or between lines 12 and 13; the couplet is the epigrammatic resolution, not the turn.

anchor_text: dull substance of my flesh
summary: 'Dull' here means heavy, inert, and slow-moving rather than stupid. The word pairs the physical density of the body with its inability to travel as swiftly as the mind. OED records the sense 'slow, sluggish; inert' as current from the early sixteenth century.
detail: 'Dull' carries two simultaneous meanings that reinforce each other throughout the sonnet: (1) physically heavy and sluggish (OED, s.v. 'dull,' adj., sense 5a, 'Slow in motion or action; sluggish, inert'); (2) insensible or unresponsive (sense 4). 'Substance' was the standard philosophical term for the material stuff of which a body is composed — used, for instance, in discussions of the Aristotelian elements (OED, s.v. 'substance,' n., sense 5). The phrase therefore stakes out the sonnet's central contrast from its very first line: flesh is the opposite of thought in weight, speed, and sensitivity.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 603

The dual reading of 'dull' (sluggish/insensible) is well-attested, and 'substance' as Aristotelian material stuff is standard Renaissance usage; the contrast with 'thought' is precisely what the sonnet's conditional premise turns on.

anchor_text: slight air, and purging fire
summary: In Elizabethan natural philosophy, all matter was composed of four elements: earth, water, fire, and air. Fire and air were the 'lighter' (less dense) elements that rose upward, while earth and water were heavy and sank. 'Slight' here means thin or insubstantial; 'purging' describes fire's power to refine and cleanse, burning off impurities.
detail: The four-element framework descends from Empedocles and was systematized by Aristotle (De Generatione et Corruptione 2.3) and Galen, and dominated Elizabethan natural philosophy as codified in medical and poetic writing. Fire was associated with heat and dryness; air with heat and moisture. Their lightness and upward motion made them natural metaphors for the swift, aspiring faculties of the mind. Timothy Bright's A Treatise of Melancholie (1586) explains how the lighter elements govern the 'spirits' that carry thought and vital heat through the body. Sonnet 44, the companion poem, claims the speaker's body is made of 'slow elements' (earth and water); this sonnet takes up the other pair.

The four-element framework, the glosses on 'slight' and 'purging,' and the companion-sonnet pairing with Sonnet 44 are all standard and accurate.

anchor_text: these quicker elements are gone In tender embassy of love
summary: 'Quicker' means swifter but also more alive — air and fire were the life-sustaining elements. 'Embassy' is a diplomatic mission: an ambassador sent from one court to another to carry messages. The poet figures his thought and desire as official messengers dispatched to the beloved's presence.
detail: The political language of embassies and ambassadors ('embassy,' 'messengers,' 'return'd,' 'swift messengers') runs through lines 621-626, turning the lover's inner life into a small diplomatic court. This conceit of the mind's faculties as ambassadors was available in Renaissance neo-Platonic love philosophy, in which the lover's spirit (spiritus) was thought literally to travel to the beloved through the eyes. The OED records 'embassy' in the sense of 'a message or mission of love' from the 1590s (OED s.v. 'embassy' n., sense 3).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 621

The diplomatic 'embassy' reading is well-supported by OED sense and Renaissance usage; 'quicker' as both swifter and more alive is accurate, and the neo-Platonic spiritus detail is offered as enrichment rather than a load-bearing claim.

anchor_text: My life, being made of four, with two alone Sinks down to death, oppress'd with melancholy
summary: Elizabethan medicine taught that a healthy person required a balanced mixture of all four elements. When the two light elements (air and fire) depart from the speaker, only the heavy pair (earth and water) remain. Earth and water together produced black bile, which caused melancholy — the humor associated with heaviness, sadness, and physical decline. The speaker is literally dying of an elemental imbalance.
detail: In Galenic humoral medicine, each element corresponded to a humor: air to blood (sanguine), fire to yellow bile (choleric), water to phlegm (phlegmatic), earth to black bile (melancholic). An excess of earth and water — cold and moist, cold and dry — produced the melancholic humor, whose symptoms included heaviness, slowness, grief, and a sinking toward death. Timothy Bright's A Treatise of Melancholie (1586), ch. 6, specifies that when the vital spirits (associated with heat and air) drain away, the remaining black bile 'oppresseth the heart.' Shakespeare exploits this medical physics as a love argument: absence is not merely emotional, it is physiologically lethal.

sources.name: Bright, A Treatise of Melancholie
sources.citation: Timothy Bright, A Treatise of Melancholie (1586), ch. 6 and ch. 16, on black bile, the departure of vital spirits, and the sinking of the heart.

The humoral reading — earth plus water yielding black bile and melancholy — is the standard scholarly interpretation of these lines and is accurately stated.

anchor_text: life's composition be recur'd By those swift messengers
summary: 'Recur'd' means restored to health or cured again — brought back to the proper balanced state. 'Life's composition' is the correct mixture of all four elements that constitutes a living, healthy person. When the messengers return with news of the beloved, the body's elemental balance is re-established and the speaker revives.
detail: The verb 'recure' (to cure again, to restore) was current in early modern English but is now obsolete. The OED records it (s.v. 'recure' v.) as meaning 'to heal, restore to health' with examples from the late 15th through 17th centuries. 'Composition' in the sense of an ordered combination or mixture (OED s.v. 'composition' n., sense 7) is standard medical and philosophical terminology for the proportioned blending of the four elements in a living body. The whole phrase 'life's composition be recur'd' thus means: 'until the proper elemental mixture that constitutes my life is restored to health.'

anchor_text: This told, I joy; but then no longer glad, I send them back again, and straight grow sad
summary: The closing couplet is the sonnet's volta (turn): instead of resolving the grief of absence, it traps the speaker in a perpetual loop. Joy at the news of the beloved's health immediately re-dispatches thought and desire back to him, which instantly recreates the emptiness and sadness. The poem offers no consolation, only the endless turning of the cycle.
detail: In the standard Shakespearean sonnet the couplet resolves, qualifies, or ironizes the three quatrains. Here it does all three at once: it resolves the immediate tension (the messengers have returned with good news) but immediately reinstates it, showing that the very moment of gladness is the trigger for renewed sadness. The structure enacts the argument: the abruptness of 'but then no longer glad' mimics the speed at which the good feeling collapses. George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), treats the closing couplet's epigrammatic function under 'Epiphonema' (a pithy conclusion that sums and clinches); here Shakespeare turns the clinching into an ironic trap. 'Straight' means immediately, at once (OED s.v. 'straight' adv., sense 1).

sources.name: Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book III, ch. 19 ('Epiphonema, or the Surclose'), on the concluding couplet as summary or sententia.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 629

The perpetual-loop reading of the couplet is the dominant scholarly interpretation; calling the couplet 'the volta' is terminologically imprecise for a Shakespearean sonnet, but this is a minor labelling issue that does not distort the substantive gloss.

anchor_text: eye and heart are at a mortal war
summary: The whole sonnet is built on an extended legal allegory: the poet's eye and heart are adversaries in a courtroom trial, each claiming the right to 'possess' the beloved. 'Mortal war' means both a deadly, bitter conflict and a lawsuit between mortals. The conceit runs through every line, from the plea and defendant (635-637) to the empanelled jury and verdict (639-644).
detail: The eye-and-heart debate was a recognized poetic genre in medieval and Renaissance verse — the French 'debat du coeur et de l'oeil' and its English descendants staged the two faculties as rivals disputing love's proper seat. Shakespeare fuses this tradition with the machinery of the Elizabethan common-law court: the parties plead, a defendant denies, a jury (a 'quest of thoughts') is empanelled, and a verdict apportions the contested property. The legal lexicon is consistent and precise throughout: 'conquest' (the prize at issue), 'plead,' 'defendant,' 'deny,' 'title,' 'impannelled,' 'quest,' 'verdict,' 'moiety,' 'due,' 'right.' The effect is mock-solemn — a wit-display that also genuinely maps the division between seeing beauty and feeling love.

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book III, on extended metaphor (allegoria) as sustained figurative argument throughout a poem.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 631

Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie Book III does genuinely define allegoria as 'a long and perpetuall Metaphore' and the extended-metaphor citation is real, but the detail text attributes to Puttenham the identification of line 9 as 'the turn of argument' (the volta), a claim the single cited source does not support and that Puttenham does not make in his allegoria chapter.

The eye-and-heart debat tradition and the sustained legal-court conceit are both well-established; the legal lexicon listed (plead, defendant, impannelled, quest, moiety) is accurate and present in the text, making the extended-allegory reading mainstream and defensible.

anchor_text: divide the conquest of thy sight
summary: 'Conquest' here means something won or seized by battle — the prize both faculties are fighting over. 'Thy sight' is ambiguous: it can mean the act of seeing you, or the image of you as a visual object. The eye wants to possess that image; the heart claims you already dwell within it.
detail: OED records 'conquest' in the sense of a thing won or gained (sb. 2) from the fourteenth century onward, standard in legal and military contexts. The ambiguity of 'sight' — both the act of beholding and the thing beheld — is central to the sonnet's argument: the eye claims a right to the beloved as a visible image ('thy fair appearance,' line 638), while the heart counters that it holds something the eye cannot see ('thy inward love,' line 644). The division of 'sight' into outward and inward is the puzzle the couplet resolves.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'conquest' sb. 2 ('that which is won or gained, a prize'); s.v. 'sight' sb. I.1 and I.4 (the act of seeing; the thing seen).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 632

The dual sense of 'conquest' (military prize / legal prize) and the ambiguity of 'sight' (act of beholding / visual image beheld) are both textually grounded and supported by the sonnet's own resolution in the couplet ('outward part' vs 'inward love'), making the reading sound.

anchor_text: closet never pierc'd with crystal eyes
summary: A 'closet' is a private inner chamber — a small, locked room used for private prayer, reading, or keeping valuables. The heart imagines itself as such a chamber where the beloved lives, sealed against the eye's intrusion. 'Crystal eyes' are clear, transparent eyes (a conventional Elizabethan compliment), which the heart claims cannot see inside it.
detail: OED records 'closet' (sb. 3) as a private room, often a cabinet or retiring-room where valuables and private letters were kept under lock and key — distinct from public or shared chambers. The image is precise: the heart is a locked closet that holds the beloved as its most prized possession, proof against the eye's 'crystal' (transparent, glassy) sight. The heart's plea rests on interiority: what lives inside it is by definition invisible to sight. 'Crystal' as a term of praise for clear, bright eyes is common in Elizabethan verse; here it sharpens the irony, since even the clearest eyes cannot pierce a locked room.

'Closet' as a locked private chamber is well-attested OED usage and the image of the heart as an interior space impenetrable to sight is precisely what lines 635-636 argue; 'crystal' for clear, bright eyes is a routine Elizabethan compliment and the irony the annotation notes is in the text.

anchor_text: impannelled / A quest of thoughts, all tenants to the heart
summary: Both words are legal terms. 'Impannelled' means formally selected and sworn in as a jury (entered on the 'panel,' the official list of jurors). A 'quest' is a legal inquiry or inquest — a jury summoned to determine a question of fact. The jury here is made up of the poet's own thoughts, who are 'tenants to the heart': they live under the heart's jurisdiction and so are hardly impartial.
detail: OED records 'empanel' (v.) as the act of enrolling names on the panel — the parchment list of persons summoned for jury service — from the mid-fifteenth century in legal contexts. A 'quest' (from Latin quaesta, an inquiry) is likewise a technical legal term for a body of men summoned to make an inquest or inquiry; OED (sb. 4) cites it as a recognized alternative to 'jury' or 'inquest.' The detail that the jury members are 'all tenants to the heart' is a wry joke: these thoughts owe their existence to the heart (as a tenant owes fealty to a landlord), so the verdict is pre-determined. The volta of the sonnet falls here at line 9 — the shift from the adversarial pleading of the octave to the resolution-in-process of the sestet — a point Puttenham identifies as the turn of argument.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 639

OED entries for 'empanel' and 'quest' (a body appointed to make an inquest) are real and support the vocabulary glosses, but the detail text attributes to Puttenham the identification of line 9 as 'the turn of argument,' a claim the sole cited source (OED) cannot support and that no source in the annotation covers.

Both 'impannelled' and 'quest' are correctly identified as technical legal terms; the observation that thoughts as 'tenants to the heart' makes the jury partial is a direct reading of the text, and the volta at line 9 is a standard structural feature of the Shakespearean sonnet.

anchor_text: clear eye's moiety, and the dear heart's part
summary: A 'moiety' is a legal term for a share or portion — strictly, one of two equal halves, but used loosely for any assigned portion. The verdict gives each faculty its proper 'moiety': the eye gets the beloved's outward, visible form; the heart keeps the inward love that cannot be seen. The couplet makes the split explicit: 'mine eye's due is thy outward part, / And my heart's right, thy inward love of heart.'
detail: OED records 'moiety' (sb. 1) from the fifteenth century onward as a legal term for one of two equal parts into which something is divided, used extensively in property law for the division of estates between co-heirs. Shakespeare is precise: the verdict is a formal property-division, not a compromise — each party gets its rightful portion. The punning contrast of 'clear' (sight, transparency) for the eye and 'dear' (valued, beloved) for the heart is deliberate: the adjectives characterize each faculty's nature even as they describe its share. 'Thy inward love of heart' (644) is compressed: the beloved's love as something felt inwardly, held in the heart, not displayed to the eye.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 642

OED 'moiety' sb. 1 ('each of two equal parts; a half; also loosely, a portion or share') and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon entry for 'moiety' are both real, standard references that directly support the legal property-division gloss.

The legal sense of 'moiety' as an apportioned share in a property division is precise and fits the court-verdict conceit; the 'clear'/'dear' wordplay is a genuine phonemic and semantic contrast present in line 642, and the gloss on 'thy inward love of heart' is a defensible compressed reading of the couplet.

anchor_text: Betwixt mine eye and heart a league is took
summary: 'League' means a formal treaty or military alliance; 'is took' is an archaic past participle (modern English: 'has been struck'). The poet elevates the truce between his eye and his heart to the dignity of a diplomatic compact, continuing the quasi-legal language of Sonnet 46, where the two faculties were at war over whether the beloved's image belonged to sight or feeling.
detail: The legal and chivalric idiom for the eye-heart relationship was a recognized conceit in Elizabethan sonnet writing: Sidney's 'Astrophil and Stella' (1591) treats the same inward conflict (Astrophil 5, 14). The word 'league' carries overtones of sworn mutual obligation — both parties owe good turns to the other, as the next line spells out — turning an inward psychological state into a binding covenant. Puttenham's 'Arte of English Poesie' (1589) notes that such personification of the faculties was a familiar rhetorical 'figure of dialogue.'

sources.name: OED

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III, ch. xi, on prosopopoeia (the personification of inward faculties).
