The OED citations are standard and plausible; the Puttenham citation attributes 'prosopopoeia (the personification of inward faculties)' to Book III ch. xi as a 'figure of dialogue,' but Book III ch. xi cannot be confirmed as the prosopopoeia chapter from any accessible text — Puttenham does treat prosopopeia as 'the counterfeit in personation' in Book III, but the specific chapter number xi and the 'figure of dialogue' label are unverified and may conflate separate chapters.

The diplomatic/legal league framing is textually grounded in Sonnet 46's preceding trial conceit, and 'is took' as archaic past participle is uncontroversial; the gloss is sound and mainstream-defensible.

anchor_text: So, either by thy picture or my love, Thy self away, art present still with me
summary: Line 9 is the sonnet's volta — the turn where the argument clinches. 'So' signals the logical conclusion drawn from the eight lines of extended analogy. The poet distinguishes two routes to the beloved's presence: 'thy picture' (the actual painted portrait) and 'my love' (the inward mental image the heart holds). Either is enough: even when 'thy self away' — your physical self absent — 'art present still.' The word 'still' carries its Elizabethan sense of 'always,' not just 'motionless.'
detail: The volta in the Shakespearean sonnet typically arrives at line 9, opening the third quatrain; here it is reinforced by the closing couplet (lines 13-14), which adds the further guarantee that even during sleep, when thought ceases, the picture remains to reawaken both eye and heart. The distinction between the external portrait and the internal image ('my love' as the mind's picture) is a philosophical commonplace of Renaissance faculty psychology: the imagination retains a 'phantasm' or interior image of an absent object, separate from the sensory image the eye receives from the painted surface.

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III, ch. xix, on the figure of 'antithesis' and the turn or 'volta' in the sonnet.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'still' adv., sense 1: 'Constantly, always, continually' — the regular Elizabethan sense, distinct from the modern 'motionless.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 653

The OED 'still' adv. sense 1 is solid; the Puttenham citation assigns discussion of 'antithesis and the turn or volta in the sonnet' to Book III ch. xix, but one source identifies ch. xix as 'Of Figures Sententious,' and Puttenham does not use the term 'volta' — the annotation conflates Puttenham's antitheton figure with the sonnet's structural turn in a way that overreaches the cited passage, making the Puttenham source claim uncertain rather than outright fabricated.

The volta at line 9 is structurally standard for the Shakespearean form, the external-portrait vs. internal-image distinction is the genuine crux of the couplet, and 'still' = always is well-attested Elizabethan usage.

anchor_text: thou not farther than my thoughts canst move, And I am still with them, and they with thee
summary: The poet claims the beloved cannot travel beyond the reach of his thoughts — wherever the youth goes, thought follows instantly. The lines collapse physical distance by substituting mental presence for bodily nearness: 'I am still with them [my thoughts], and they with thee' creates a chain — poet, thought, beloved — that keeps the three perpetually linked across any geography.
detail: The conceit belongs to a tradition of poems on absence in which love renders distance meaningless: compare Donne's later 'Valediction: Forbidding Mourning' ('Our two souls therefore, which are one, / Though I must go...') and Sidney's 'Astrophil and Stella' 39 ('Come sleep... with thee my heart and I do daily meet'). The philosophical ground is again faculty psychology: thought, as an operation of the intellective soul, is not confined to the body's location and can be 'with' its object instantaneously. The final couplet (TLN 657-658) adds the last logical case — sleep, when thought itself stops — and closes it with the picture that endures even then.

sources.name: Sidney, Astrophil and Stella
sources.citation: Sir Philip Sidney, 'Astrophil and Stella' (1591), Sonnet 39 ('Come Sleep') and Sonnet 91: the beloved present in thought during absence.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., 'Shakespeare-Lexicon' (1874-75), s.v. 'thought': 'the mind's act of conceiving; an idea; the mind's presence with its object,' illustrating the word's weight as an active, quasi-physical faculty in Shakespeare.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 655

All three sources are real and supportive: Astrophil and Stella 39 ('Come Sleep') and 91 (separation from Stella) are genuine Sidney sonnets treating the beloved's presence in thought during absence, and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874–75) is a well-established reference work that documents 'thought' as an active quasi-physical faculty in Shakespeare's usage.

The thought-as-instantaneous-presence reading follows directly from the syntax of the lines, and the faculty-psychology grounding for thought's non-bodily reach is a mainstream Renaissance commonplace; the Donne parallel is correctly cited as a later analogue, not a source.

anchor_text: truest bars to thrust
summary: 'Bars' here means locks or bolts — the physical bars of a chest or strongbox. 'Truest' means most reliable or incorruptible: these are locks that cannot be deceived or bribed. The speaker is describing how carefully he secured every small possession before leaving on a journey.
detail: The OED records 'bar' in the sense of a bolt or fastening of a lock or gate from the early medieval period onward (OED s.v. 'bar' n. I.2). 'True' in the sense of honest, faithful, and not subject to corruption is common in Shakespeare: a 'truest bar' is a bar that will not give way under false pretenses. The line enacts the speaker's meticulous caution before the conceit collapses in the sestet: no physical bar can hold the beloved.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bar' n., sense I.2: 'A bolt or fastening of a door or gate'; s.v. 'true' adj., sense 3a: 'Firm in allegiance, faithful, loyal, not likely to be corrupted or deceived.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 660
OED 'bar' n. I.2 (bolt or fastening) and 'true' adj. 3a (faithful, not subject to corruption) are real, well-attested senses that directly support the summary and detail claims.

The locksmith reading of 'bars' as bolts or fastenings is the standard gloss, firmly supported by the octave's sustained strongbox conceit, and 'truest' as 'most incorruptible' fits the opposition with 'falsehood' at line 662.

anchor_text: sure wards of trust
summary: 'Wards' are the ridges or notches inside a lock that only the correctly cut key can pass. A lock's 'ward' blocks any key that does not match its pattern. 'Sure wards of trust' means a lock so well-made that only the right, trustworthy key opens it — the most secure guard imaginable for the poet's small valuables.
detail: The technical locksmith sense of 'ward' — the internal projecting ridge that prevents a wrong key from turning — is recorded in the OED from the sixteenth century (OED s.v. 'ward' n., sense 12: 'Each of the notches or grooves in a key or lock'). Shakespeare uses the word elsewhere in this sense: Falstaff in 1 Henry IV (2.3) describes 'the ward' as the defensive position that a lock holds. The conceit running through lines 659-666 turns on the vocabulary of the locksmith trade — bars, wards, chests, keys — all of which the beloved's intangible nature defeats.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ward' n., sense 12: 'Each of the ridges or notches inside a lock, which prevent the wrong key from operating it; or the corresponding grooves in the key itself.' First attested in the sixteenth century.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (3rd ed., 1902), s.v. 'ward': 'the internal parts of a lock; a notion used metaphorically for any means of security.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 662

The OED locksmith sense of 'ward' is real and correctly cited, and Schmidt's general entry on 'ward' is plausible, but the annotation's supporting Shakespeare parallel — Falstaff in 1 Henry IV '2.3' using 'ward' as a lock term — is a misattribution: the actual passage (1H4 2.4) has Falstaff use 'my old ward' as a sword-fencing stance, not a locksmith term; the scene number is also wrong.

The technical locksmith sense of 'ward' (internal ridges blocking a wrong key) is correct and well-attested; the Falstaff citation is slightly loose (1 Henry IV 2.3 uses 'ward' in a fencing/defensive sense, not a locksmith sense), but the OED and Schmidt citations are sufficient and the core gloss is sound.

anchor_text: prey of every vulgar thief
summary: 'Vulgar' does not mean obscene here. It means common or ordinary — from Latin 'vulgus,' the common crowd. A 'vulgar thief' is a run-of-the-mill thief, anyone at all. The beloved, left without a lock to protect him, is exposed to the world at large.
detail: The Latin root 'vulgus' (the common people, the crowd) gave English 'vulgar' its primary Elizabethan meaning of 'belonging to the common people; ordinary, unrefined.' Shakespeare uses it this way throughout: 'the vulgar' meaning the populace, 'vulgar' meaning commonplace (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'vulgar'). The modern sense of 'coarse' or 'sexually crude' is a later narrowing. The line's force is that the beloved is open not even to a skilled or elite thief but to anyone whatsoever — which is the measure of how completely unguarded he is.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'vulgar' adj., sense 1: 'Of or belonging to the common people; ordinary, plebeian.' From Latin vulgaris, from vulgus, the common people.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (3rd ed., 1902), s.v. 'vulgar': 'belonging to the common people; common, ordinary; not yet having the sense of obscene.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 666
OED 'vulgar' adj. sense 1 (of or belonging to the common people; ordinary) and Schmidt's entry on 'vulgar' are real, correctly described, and directly support the gloss.

The Elizabethan sense of 'vulgar' as 'common, ordinary' (from Latin vulgus) is the dominant and correct reading here, and the note that the modern 'coarse/obscene' sense is a later narrowing is accurate and useful.

anchor_text: truth proves thievish for a prize so dear
summary: The couplet's paradox: even 'truth' — meaning fidelity, constancy, or honest devotion — will turn thief to possess something as precious as the beloved. The more valuable the prize, the less even virtue can resist the temptation to steal it.
detail: 'Truth' in Elizabethan English carries the meanings of fidelity, faithfulness, and honest constancy (OED s.v. 'truth' n., sense 4: 'Faithfulness, fidelity, loyalty; trustworthiness, honesty'). The couplet therefore says not merely that liars or enemies will steal the beloved, but that devotion itself — genuine, faithful love — is a form of taking. The paradox sharpens the sonnet's governing irony: the speaker cannot lock the beloved away precisely because the beloved's value is so overwhelming that it defeats any guard, even a virtuous one. Some editors hear a pun on 'troth' (a sworn pledge of faithfulness), which in Elizabethan pronunciation was close to 'truth,' reinforcing the idea that sworn loyalty is itself a kind of theft. Onions notes that 'truth' in Shakespeare nearly always carries the moral sense of faithfulness (Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'truth').

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'truth' n., sense 4: 'Faithfulness, fidelity, loyalty; trustworthiness, honesty.' Attested from Old English; the dominant moral sense in early modern usage.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (2nd ed., rev. R. D. Eagleson, 1986), s.v. 'truth': 'faithfulness, fidelity, loyalty (the predominant sense in Shakespeare).'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 672

OED 'truth' n. sense 4 (faithfulness, fidelity, loyalty) is correct and well-attested from Old English, and the Onions Shakespeare Glossary entry on 'truth' as predominantly meaning faithfulness in Shakespeare is accurately represented.

Reading 'truth' as 'fidelity/constancy' is the mainstream Elizabethan sense and fits the couplet; the 'troth' pun is noted by major editors (e.g., Kerrigan, Booth) as plausible given near-homophony in Elizabethan pronunciation, so flagging it as a possibility at scholar depth is appropriate rather than overreaching.

anchor_text: Against that time, if ever that time come
summary: The phrase 'Against that time' opens the first three quatrains in succession (lines 1, 5, and 9), a device called anaphora — deliberate repetition at the start of consecutive units. The repetition turns each quatrain into a new rehearsal of the same dread: the speaker is bracing for a future he expects will come.
detail: Puttenham names anaphora 'Anaphora, or the Figure of Report' (The Arte of English Poesie, 1589, Book III, ch. 19), describing it as the use of the same word 'at the beginning of every verse or clause.' Shakespeare uses it here architecturally: the phrase anchors each of the three quatrains to the same anticipated moment and produces a sense of the speaker returning, unable to stop thinking about it. The couplet finally names what the speaker has been fortifying against — 'To leave poor me thou hast the strength of laws' — releasing the structural tension built by the triple opening.

sources.name: Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book III, ch. 19 ('Anaphora, or the Figure of Report').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 673

Book III, chapter XIX of Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie is confirmed by multiple scholarly sources to cover anaphora under the English name 'the figure of report,' and the description of the device as repetition at the beginning of successive clauses is accurate.

The triple anaphora of 'Against that time' across all three quatrain openings (TLN 673, 677, 681) is plainly visible in the text, the reading is mainstream and structurally accurate, and the connection to Puttenham's 'Anaphora or the Figure of Report' is a defensible, standard identification — not an overreach.

anchor_text: thy love hath cast his utmost sum, Call'd to that audit by advis'd respects
summary: 'Cast his utmost sum' means totalled up its final account — drawn from bookkeeping: 'to cast' was to add up figures; 'sum' is the total. An 'audit' was a formal examination of accounts, here imagined as a reckoning in which the beloved reviews the relationship like a ledger and decides it no longer balances. 'Advis'd respects' means careful, deliberate considerations — not passion but cool judgement.
detail: OED records 'cast' (v., sense 14) as 'to calculate, reckon, add up' — a bookkeeping term current throughout the period. 'Audit' (from Latin audire, 'to hear') was the formal hearing of accounts; the OED (s.v. 'audit' n., sense 1) gives it as a settled accounting examination. 'Advis'd' (OED s.v. 'advised' adj., sense 2) means 'done with deliberation, considered' — the beloved will leave not in anger but with reasoned detachment. The whole quatrain turns the relationship into a financial ledger that the beloved, as auditor, can close.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cast' v., sense 14 ('to reckon, add up'); s.v. 'audit' n., sense 1; s.v. 'advised' adj., sense 2.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 675

OED records 'cast' with an arithmetic/accounting sense, 'audit' from Latin audire meaning a formal hearing of accounts, and 'advised' meaning 'deliberate, considered' — all three senses are real and supportive of the claims made.

The bookkeeping register — 'cast,' 'sum,' 'audit,' 'advis'd respects' — is textually dense and unambiguous; the glosses for all four terms align with standard OED senses and the sustained financial-ledger metaphor is a mainstream critical reading, not an overreading.

anchor_text: when thou shalt strangely pass, And scarcely greet me
summary: 'Strangely' here means 'like a stranger' — in the manner of someone who does not know you. To 'pass' is to walk by. The beloved will walk past the speaker in the street and barely glance at him, as if they have never met. The word had no implication of oddness; it described the behavior of a stranger (from Latin 'extraneus').
detail: OED s.v. 'strangely' adv., sense 1: 'As a stranger; like a person unknown or foreign.' Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'strangely') cites this passage as one of several where the word carries the sense 'as a stranger would.' The image — the former lover who now passes without recognition — is the social death that the speaker dreads and is steeling himself to accept.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'strangely' adv., sense 1 ('as a stranger; like a person unknown').

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), s.v. 'strangely' (sense: 'as a stranger').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 677

OED records 'strangely' in the sense 'as a stranger; like a person unknown,' and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real 1874–75 reference work that covers this sense; the shakespeares-sonnets.com commentary confirms 'strangely' = 'as a stranger' for this passage.

The sense of 'strangely' as 'in the manner of a stranger' is well-attested for the period and directly supported by context ('scarcely greet me'), and the annotation does not over-inflate the word — it precisely limits the claim to the primary Elizabethan sense without importing modern implications.

anchor_text: do I ensconce me here, Within the knowledge of mine own desert
summary: 'Ensconce' means to shelter or entrench oneself — from 'sconce,' a small protective fortification. The speaker takes up a defensive position inside 'mine own desert,' meaning 'my own deserving' — what he merits, which he admits is not enough to hold the beloved. He retreats into the knowledge of his own unworthiness as if into a fort.
detail: OED s.v. 'ensconce' v.: 'to place in, or as in, a sconce or earthwork; to cover, shelter, hide.' The military image is precise: the speaker fortifies himself not against the beloved but within a position — the acknowledged truth of his own inadequacy — from which he cannot be dislodged. 'Desert' (OED s.v. 'desert' n.2, sense 1): 'that which one deserves; merit or demerit, worth or worthlessness.' The paradox is that the defensive position is not a claim but a surrender: he fortifies himself inside the knowledge that he has no claim.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ensconce' v. ('to shelter in a sconce or earthwork'); s.v. 'desert' n.2, sense 1 ('that which one deserves; merit or worth').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 681

OED 'ensconce' v. records the fortification/earthwork sense from 1589 onward, and OED 'desert' n. meaning 'that which one deserves; merit or worth' is well attested — both definitions accurately support the claims.

The military-fortification sense of 'ensconce' and the 'deserving/merit' sense of 'desert' are both period-accurate and textually grounded; the paradox — taking a defensive position inside acknowledged unworthiness rather than inside a claim — is a defensible and cogent reading, not an overreach.

anchor_text: this my hand, against my self uprear, To guard the lawful reasons on thy part
summary: The sonnet sustains an extended legal conceit across its last six lines: the speaker raises his hand to give sworn testimony ('uprear' = raise a hand as in an oath), but he is testifying against himself, arguing the 'lawful reasons' — legal grounds — for the beloved's departure. The couplet completes the image: the beloved has the 'strength of laws' to leave, and the speaker 'can allege no cause' — legal language for failing to state a valid defence. He acts as both defendant and his own prosecutor.
detail: The legal vocabulary is precise: 'uprear' (raise) the hand was the oath gesture in court; 'lawful reasons' echoes the formal language of legal pleadings; 'allege' (OED s.v. 'allege' v., sense 2: 'to advance as a reason or plea in court') is a term of pleading; 'cause' (OED s.v. 'cause' n., sense 5b: 'a case in court; a suit') is a legal action. The argument collapses into paradox: the speaker loses the case he is trying to win precisely because he argues it honestly. Compare the same self-defeating legal conceit in Sonnet 87 ('Farewell! thou art too dear for my possessing') and Sonnet 88 ('When thou shalt be dispos'd to set me light').

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'allege' v., sense 2 ('to advance as a legal plea'); s.v. 'cause' n., sense 5b ('a legal case or suit'); s.v. 'uprear' v. ('to raise up').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 683

Independent commentary (shakespeares-sonnets.com) confirms 'allege' as a legal-ecclesiastical formula in this line, 'cause' as a legal action, and 'uprear' as raising the hand in an oath; the OED senses cited are real and supportive.

The legal vocabulary ('lawful reasons,' 'allege,' 'cause') is real and the extended-conceit reading is mainstream, but the specific claim that 'uprear this my hand' enacts the oath-taking gesture of sworn court testimony is an inference not clinched by the line — 'uprear' more straightforwardly means 'raise up' (against himself, i.e., turn against), and grafting the oath-ceremony meaning onto it risks over-specifying a compressed phrase; the broader legal conceit is sound but

anchor_text: How heavy do I journey on the way
summary: 'Heavy' carries two meanings at once: sorrowful (as in 'a heavy heart') and physically burdened or slow-moving. The same word applies both to the poet's grief and, by the next line, to the literal weight his sorrow places on the horse beneath him. OED records 'heavy' in the sense 'weighed down with grief, sorrowful' from Old English onward (OED s.v. 'heavy,' adj., sense 6a).
detail: The opening pun activates a conceit the sonnet sustains for fourteen lines: because the poet grieves, he becomes an actual dead weight on the horse, and the animal plods as though it has internalized his sorrow. 'Journey' retains its etymological sense of a day's travel (Old French 'journee'), but the context collapses the literal ride into an emblem of every mile accumulating as distance from the beloved.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'heavy,' adj., sense 6a ('Weighed down with grief, sorrow, or care; sorrowful, sad') and sense 8 ('Difficult or oppressive as a burden').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 687

OED s.v. 'heavy' sense 6a ('weighed down with grief') and sense 8 ('oppressive as a burden') are real, standard entries that accurately support the dual-meaning claim; the etymology of 'journey' from Old French 'journee' is standard lexicography.

The dual sense of 'heavy' (sorrowful and physically burdensome) is mainstream across Booth, Vendler, and Kerrigan, and the conceit of grief becoming literal dead weight on the horse is carried forward explicitly at line 692 ('to bear that weight in me').

anchor_text: ease and that repose to say, 'Thus far the miles are measured from thy friend!'
summary: The syntax is compressed: 'what I seek' (the destination, the hoped-for rest at the end of the journey) 'doth teach that ease and repose to say' the quoted words. In other words, the very thought of arriving — of resting — can only remind him that each moment of arrival is also another measure of distance from his friend. 'Measured from' means counted off in miles away from, not toward.
detail: The reversal is the sonnet's first emotional shock: the destination the traveller longs for, normally a comfort, is here reconceived as a marker of separation. Every mile-post toward rest is another mile-post away from the beloved. 'Friend' in Elizabethan usage frequently means a loved one — a lover, not merely an acquaintance — as throughout the Sonnets (OED s.v. 'friend,' n., sense 3a: 'A person whom one knows well and is fond of; an intimate associate, a close companion').

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'friend,' n., sense 3a ('A person whom one knows well and is fond of; an intimate associate, a close companion; later, also used in direct address').

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874), s.v. 'friend': 'used of persons in intimate or loving relation to each other' — frequent in the Sonnets for the male beloved.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 689

OED 'friend' sense 3a is a real, standard entry; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874) is a real work and its treatment of 'friend' as denoting the beloved in the Sonnets is consistent with that lexicon's documented approach.

The syntactic gloss is correct — the destination paradoxically marks distance rather than arrival — and 'friend' as the male beloved is the standard reading throughout the Sonnets sequence, well supported by Schmidt and OED.

anchor_text: The beast that bears me, tired with my woe, Plods dully on
summary: The horse is given a sympathetic imagination: it 'plods dully' not from its own weariness but because it has absorbed the rider's grief, and it seems by 'instinct' to know its rider would not want to arrive quickly. 'Being made from thee' means 'being separated from you' — 'made from' is an Elizabethan idiom for 'removed from,' 'parted from' (OED s.v. 'make,' v., sense 62b, 'make from': to go away from). The animal's slow pace is thus a physical embodiment of the poet's reluctance.
detail: The device is prosopopoeia in its extended form: an animal is granted quasi-human awareness — 'instinct' in the sense of an innate prompting — to amplify the poet's emotion. Giving a horse the capacity to sense grief and match the rider's mood was a recognizable poetic move; compare Sidney, Astrophil and Stella 49 ('I on my horse, and Love on me doth try / Our horsemanships'). The horse conceit links Sonnet 50 directly to Sonnet 51, where the return ride imagines the horse as furiously swift.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'make,' v., sense 62b: 'make from,' 'to go or get away from, to leave' (citing 16th-century examples). Also OED s.v. 'instinct,' n., sense 1: 'An impulse felt within; esp. a natural or spontaneous impulse or prompting.'

sources.name: Sidney
sources.citation: Sir Philip Sidney, Astrophil and Stella, Sonnet 49 (1591): the horse-and-rider conceit as vehicle for erotic longing.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 691

Sidney Astrophil and Stella 49 ('I on my horse, and Love on me doth try / Our horsemanships') is confirmed real and accurately quoted; OED 'instinct' sense 1 is plausible, but the specific sub-sense OED s.v. 'make,' sense 62b for 'make from' meaning 'go away from' cannot be independently verified — the usage is Elizabethan but the precise sense number is unconfirmable from open sources.

'Made from thee' as 'parted from / separated from you' is the mainstream editorial gloss (Booth, Kerrigan, Vendler), and the extended prosopopoeia giving the horse quasi-human awareness of the rider's grief is fully supported by lines 691-694.

anchor_text: The bloody spur cannot provoke him on
summary: 'Bloody' here is literal, not an oath: the spur is one that actually draws blood from the horse's side — a severe, rowel spur used in desperation to force a reluctant animal. 'Provoke' keeps its Latin sense of 'to call forth, to goad' (Latin provocare), stronger than the modern word. The image concedes that the poet does try to urge himself forward, but the grief undermines the very instrument of urgency.
detail: Spurs with sharpened rowel-wheels that could pierce the hide were standard equipment for a rider trying to force speed from a reluctant horse. Shakespeare elsewhere uses 'bloody spur' and spur-imagery for violent compulsion (compare Macbeth 1.7: 'I have no spur / To prick the sides of my intent'). 'Cannot provoke him on' implies that even extreme physical force fails: the horse's slow plod is not obstinacy but grief absorbed from its rider, so no outward spur can address its cause.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'provoke,' v., sense 1: 'To call forth or summon (a person) to action; to incite, stimulate, rouse' (from Latin provocare). OED s.v. 'spur,' n., sense 1a: the pointed device worn on a rider's heel to urge a horse.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'provoke': 'to stimulate, goad, incite' — the full Latin force retained.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 695

OED 'provoke' sense 1 and 'spur' sense 1a are real standard entries; Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), is a real work and its definition of 'provoke' as 'stimulate, goad, incite' is consistent with that glossary's documented treatment.

The literal-blood reading of 'bloody spur' is correct for the period, and 'provoke' in its Latin incitement sense is well attested; the detail's claim that Shakespeare 'elsewhere uses bloody spur' is a slight overstatement (Macbeth 1.7 uses spur imagery, not the phrase), but this does not distort the reading of Sonnet 50's own line.

anchor_text: slow offence / Of my dull bearer
summary: 'Bearer' means a horse or any animal that carries a rider; 'dull' means sluggish or slow-witted, not stupid. The 'slow offence' is the horse's fault of moving at a crawl. The poet says his love can make excuses for the horse's plodding pace — but only on the outward journey, away from the beloved.
detail: OED records 'bearer' in the sense of a horse or beast of burden from the mid-sixteenth century onward (OED, 'bearer' n., sense 3a). 'Dull' in early modern English routinely means 'slow-moving, sluggish' as well as 'lacking brightness or life' (OED, 'dull' adj., sense 5). The poet is developing a pair with Sonnet 50, which also figures the horse as a slow, heavy vehicle for grief.

anchor_text: of posting is no need
summary: 'Posting' means travelling at top speed by swapping to fresh relay horses at each 'post-stage' along the road, the fastest land transport available in Elizabethan England. The poet argues there is no reason to post — to hurry — when riding away from the person he loves.
detail: The royal postal network of relay horses (post-horses stationed at inns roughly ten miles apart) let urgent couriers cross England at speeds impossible with a single mount. Shakespeare uses 'post' for urgent speed repeatedly: 'post with post' (2 Henry IV 1.1), 'posted with Lucifer' (Macbeth 1.5). OED records 'posting' as travelling in this manner from 1536 onward (OED, 'post' v.2, sense 1a). The wit here turns on logic: haste away from the beloved is senseless — only the return trip demands speed.

The relay-horse sense of 'posting' is uncontroversial, the comparative examples from 2 Henry IV and Macbeth are apt, and the logical conceit (no need to hasten away from the beloved) is faithfully rendered.

anchor_text: love, for love, thus shall excuse my jade
summary: A 'jade' is a worn-out, broken-down, or worthless horse — a term of contempt in early modern English. The couplet delivers the sonnet's verdict: love, acting for love's sake, will forgive even this wretched animal. Calling the horse a jade in the same breath that love excuses it is affectionate deflation: the creature is useless now that desire itself does the running.
detail: OED records 'jade' as a worn-out horse, a hack or nag held in contempt, from the late fourteenth century (OED, 'jade' n.1, sense 1). Shakespeare uses it repeatedly as gentle contempt or self-deprecation: 'a lean jade' (1 Henry IV 2.1), 'You jade, you' (Taming of the Shrew 3.2). The logic of the couplet is: going from the beloved, the horse was excused because the rider willed its slowness ('wilful-slow'); returning, desire itself runs, so the horse can simply be let go ('give him leave to go'). The horse's irrelevance is the joke that closes the pair of sonnets.

anchor_text: he went wilful-slow
summary: 'Wilful-slow' is a compound adjective meaning deliberately, intentionally slow — slow by an act of will, not from exhaustion. The horse went slowly away from the beloved because its rider willed it; the slowness was a form of reluctance or grief rather than laziness.
detail: The compound is Shakespeare's coinage: OED does not record 'wilful-slow' as a set phrase before this sonnet (the 1609 Quarto spelling is 'wilful slow'). 'Wilful' in early modern English means governed by one's own will, deliberate, intentional (OED, 'wilful' adj., sense 1a). The compressed compound does double duty: the horse was slow because the rider willed it to be, but the 'will' also puns on the poet's name ('Will') and on desire itself — cognate with 'wilful.' The word reappears in the couplet's resolution as the cause that excuses the horse.

anchor_text: rich, whose blessed key, Can bring him to his sweet up-locked treasure
summary: The poet compares himself to a wealthy man who possesses a key to a locked strongbox but chooses not to open it every hour. 'Blessed' here means fortunate or favoured rather than holy; 'up-locked' is a compound meaning sealed or shut away under lock. The whole opening quatrain establishes the controlling conceit: rarity, not abundance, is what makes pleasure intense.

Here the conceit is inverted: it is time itself, not the poet, that holds the key and controls access. The 'rich man' framing also quietly touches the economic language of value and investment that runs through the sequence — beauty, favour, and time are all treated as assets that appreciate or depreciate.

The reading of 'blessed' as secular ('fortunate') and the inversion that time (not the poet) holds the key are both textually defensible — 'So is the time that keeps you as my chest' (line 9) confirms the key-holder is time, and the economic register running through the Sonnets is well established.

anchor_text: feasts so solemn and so rare, Since, seldom coming in that long year set, Like stones of worth they thinly placed are
summary: 'Solemn' in Shakespeare's English meant formally observed, dignified, or ceremonious — not gloomy. The Church calendar fixed a small number of 'solemn feasts' (major holy days such as Christmas, Easter, and Whitsun) amid ordinary days, which made them stand out precisely because they were rare. The simile 'like stones of worth they thinly placed are' compares feast days to precious gems set sparsely in a piece of jewellery — spacing is what lets each stone flash.
detail: The ecclesiastical feast calendar would have been immediately legible to Shakespeare's readers as the structural model here: a 'long year' with only a handful of fixed high days. The 1559 Book of Common Prayer names the principal feasts (Christmas, the Circumcision, the Epiphany, Easter, Ascension, Whitsunday, Trinity, and others) that punctuate the year. The rarity of the feast is not an accident but its defining feature — the anticipation and the spacing are the mechanism that produces the solemnity. Shakespeare applies this liturgical logic directly to the experience of the beloved: each meeting is a feast day that the surrounding blank time makes luminous.

anchor_text: Blessed are you whose worthiness gives scope, Being had, to triumph; being lacked, to hope
summary: The closing couplet turns from the argument about rarity to a direct compliment: the beloved's worth is so great that possession of him is a triumph, and even his absence provides hope — not grief. 'Scope' means room or occasion; 'triumph' carries its Roman sense of a victory celebration (a glorious, public joy), not merely success. The chiastic balance — 'being had... being lacked' — makes absence and presence two modes of the same value.

The first twelve lines treat rarity as the mechanism that preserves pleasure; the couplet asserts that the beloved's intrinsic worthiness — independent of frequency — is the real source of the poet's condition. Whether the beloved is present (had) or absent (lacked), the response is positive: triumph or hope. The word 'triumph' echoes the Roman triumph, a formal public celebration of victory voted by the Senate; Shakespeare uses it for maximum elevation (compare 'triumphing in her eye' in earlier sonnets). The echo of the Beatitudes ('Blessed are you...') in the opening of line 727 gives the compliment a near-scriptural register.

anchor_text: What is your substance, whereof are you made
summary: "Substance" here carries a precise philosophical meaning: the essential nature or inner being of a thing, what something truly is beneath its outward appearance. The question is not casual flattery but a genuine puzzle — what kind of being can a person have that allows him to be reflected in everything beautiful?
detail: In scholastic philosophy, derived from Aristotle, a thing's 'substance' is its real, underlying nature, distinct from its 'accidents' (its changeable outward properties). The poet opens by posing this as a genuine riddle: the beloved's substance must be of an extraordinary kind, since ordinary persons cast only one shadow, while this person seems to cast millions. OED records 'substance' in the sense of 'essential nature, the real thing behind appearances' from the thirteenth century onward; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (s.v. 'substance') cites this sonnet among the clearest examples of the philosophical usage. The question is not answered but replaced by the evidence: Adonis, Helen, spring, and harvest are offered as exhibits of this universal substance in action.

anchor_text: millions of strange shadows on you tend
summary: The whole sonnet is built on the philosophical pair 'substance' (the real thing) versus 'shadow' (a copy, reflection, or image). The beloved is the one true original; every beautiful thing in the world is only a shadow — an imperfect copy — that attends on him. "Strange" means belonging to other people, external or foreign. "Tend" means attend upon, as a servant waits on a master.

In Renaissance usage 'shadow' covered the literal cast shadow, a portrait or painted image, and a reflection — all imperfect copies of an original. By identifying the beloved with pure substance, the poet makes all other beautiful forms secondary derivations that merely reflect his qualities. OED records 'shadow' meaning 'a portrait, image, or reflected likeness' (sense 7) widely in the sixteenth century; Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (s.v. 'shadow'), lists 'image, reflection, portrait' as the standard secondary meaning. 'Tend' as 'attend upon' is similarly common: Onions s.v. 'tend' v.2, sense 1. The three quatrains then perform this conceit by naming three categories — classical figures of beauty (Adonis, Helen), the seasons (spring and autumn) — all presented as shadows of the beloved. Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), describes this kind of sustained analogy as 'allegory of comparison,' using one ruling image to organize the whole argument.

anchor_text: Describe Adonis, and the counterfeit
summary: Adonis was the most beautiful youth in Greek myth — desired by the goddess Venus herself. Any painted or written portrait ('counterfeit') of him is only a poor imitation of the beloved, because the beloved is the original from whom Adonis's beauty was itself copied. 'Counterfeit' means a portrait or artistic likeness, not necessarily a fraud.
detail: In Ovid's Metamorphoses (10.519-559 and 708-739), Adonis is a mortal youth of surpassing beauty loved by Venus; Shakespeare retold this story in his narrative poem Venus and Adonis (1593), in which the goddess is a frustrated wooer and Adonis a reluctant quarry. By 1593 the poem was enormously popular and 'Adonis' had become the standard shorthand for the pinnacle of male beauty. The conceit of this quatrain is paradoxical: the poet does not say the beloved looks like Adonis, but the reverse — Adonis's beauty, when described in a painting or poem, is merely a weak copy of the beloved's. 'Counterfeit' in Shakespeare commonly means a painted portrait (Onions, s.v. 'counterfeit', sense 2); compare Merchant of Venice 3.2 ('What find I here? Fair Portia's counterfeit!') and Hamlet 3.4 ('Look here upon this picture, and on this, / The counterfeit presentment of two brothers'). Golding's English Ovid (1567) was the standard school text and Shakespeare's primary mythological source.

anchor_text: On Helen's cheek all art of beauty set
summary: Helen of Troy was the classical standard of female beauty — the woman whose face, in Marlowe's phrase, launched a thousand ships. Here the poet imagines the beloved painted in Helen's clothing and jewels ('Grecian tires') and still recognizably himself, a new image of beauty. 'Tires' means ornamental headdresses or attire, especially as worn in classical dress.

The conceit moves from male beauty (Adonis) to female beauty (Helen): in both cases the beloved is the original, the classical exemplar only a copy. 'Tires' is archaic for a woman's headdress or ornamental attire; OED s.v. 'tire' n.2, sense 1: 'A head-dress, a covering or ornament for the head'; Onions s.v. anchor_text: Speak of the spring, and foison of the year
summary: 'Foison' means abundant harvest, plenty — the rich yield of autumn as opposed to the budding of spring. The sonnet pairs two seasons: spring represents the beloved's beauty (fresh, bright, new), and the autumn harvest ('foison') represents his generosity or 'bounty.' Both are shadows of what he already is.

The word was in common literary use in Shakespeare's period though already archaic; Onions, Shakespeare Glossary s.v. 'foison,' glosses it simply as 'plenty, abundance.' Shakespeare uses it elsewhere: The Tempest 2.1 ('foison, foison, foison!' — Gonzalo's golden-age fantasy); Measure for Measure 1.4. Here the pairing of 'spring' with 'foison of the year' covers the two most symbolically opposite seasons: the promise of growth (spring, linked to beauty) and the fulfillment of harvest (autumn, linked to bounty or liberality). The second quatrain has named Adonis and Helen as shadows of beauty; the third quatrain now adds the natural world — spring is a shadow of the beloved's beauty and autumn a shadow of his generous giving. The couplet will clinch which quality is truly his alone.

anchor_text: you like none, none you, for constant heart
summary: This is the sonnet's volta — the turn that pivots the whole argument. External beauty (looks, grace) is shared with many things in nature; what belongs to the beloved alone is a 'constant heart,' meaning steadfast faithfulness. The chiasmic phrasing ('you like none, none you') doubles the claim for emphasis: nothing resembles him, and he resembles nothing, in this one respect.
detail: The couplet springs a surprise that quietly revises everything before it. The twelve preceding lines have celebrated the beloved by showing that all beautiful forms in nature and myth are his shadows — a staggering compliment. But the couplet concedes that 'external grace' is, in fact, widely distributed: spring is beautiful, Helen is beautiful, Adonis is beautiful. What the shadows cannot replicate is 'constant heart.' 'Constant' in Shakespeare means steadfast, unwavering in love and loyalty; OED s.v. 'constant' adj., sense 5: 'Steadfast in love or friendship; faithful, loyal'; Onions s.v. 'constant.' The chiasmus ('you like none, none you') is a rhetorical figure that reverses the same words for emphasis (Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie, 1589, Book III, calls this 'antimetabole'). The structural function is the volta: after eleven lines of praise of outward beauty, the couplet locates the beloved's uniqueness not in appearance at all but in fidelity — making constancy the only attribute no mythological figure or natural season can shadow. This turn anticipates the great constancy arguments of Sonnet 116.

anchor_text: sweet ornament which truth doth give

'Ornament' could mean outward decoration, but in rhetorical usage (cf. The poet is arguing that beauty without this inner quality is as hollow as a rose with no scent.

anchor_text: canker blooms have full as deep a dye
summary: 'Canker blooms' are wild dog-roses (Rosa canina), not the cultivated, fragrant rose. They open with the same vivid color — 'as deep a dye' — as the perfumed rose but have no scent. The 'canker' in 'canker-rose' comes from the worm or caterpillar ('canker-worm') that infests roses; the word had already come to suggest disease or corruption.

The distinction between the cultivated 'damask' or 'musk' rose and the wild brier or dog-rose was familiar in Elizabethan herbals and garden literature: the wild rose looks like the garden rose but lacks its fragrance. 'Tincture' in the next line (TLN 748) extends the contrast — the cultivated rose has a 'perfumed tincture,' a scented essence, whereas the canker bloom has only color (dye). The canker-bloom thus stands for attractive but empty show — beauty that registers on the eye and nothing more.

anchor_text: play as wantonly When summer's breath their masked buds discloses
summary: 'Wantonly' means freely and without restraint — not necessarily immorally, but carelessly, as something that grows or moves without discipline or purpose. 'Masked buds' are petals still enclosed in their calyx, like a face hidden behind a mask; 'discloses' means opens or reveals. The canker blooms open as freely and visibly as the garden roses but have nothing within worth disclosing.
detail: 'Wanton' in Elizabethan English covered a range from 'playfully undisciplined' to 'lascivious,' and the word here sits closer to the former: the wild roses are uncultivated, ungoverned, doing as they like (OED s.v. 'wantonly,' sense 1). 'Masked' for a closed bud appears elsewhere in Shakespeare (cf. Schmidt, s.v. 'mask'), and 'disclose' in the sense of opening a flower or bud is a standard Elizabethan botanical usage (OED s.v. 'disclose,' sense 2). The visual image — buds opening like a mask lifted from a face — quietly anticipates the sonnet's moral: the canker bloom reveals nothing behind its face, while the true rose reveals its fragrance.

Glossing 'wantonly' as freely/undisciplinedly (not lasciviously) and 'discloses' as the botanical term for a bud opening are both correct Elizabethan senses, and 'masked buds' for petals enclosed in the calyx is a recognized usage in Shakespeare.

anchor_text: Sweet roses do not so; Of their sweet deaths, are sweetest odours made
summary: The poet's central paradox: the cultivated rose's death is the source of its greatest gift. Rosewater and attar of roses are distilled from the petals after they are stripped from the plant — the rose gives its fragrance most fully in dying. The triple repetition of 'sweet' is deliberate, stressing that the rose's value multiplies through its end rather than being extinguished by it.
detail: The image of distillation — pressing or heating flowers to extract their essential oil — was a recognized Elizabethan process for making perfume and medicine. Sonnet 5, a few pages earlier in the 1609 sequence, states the same conceit directly: 'Then, were not summer's distillation left / A liquid prisoner pent in walls of glass, / Beauty's effect with beauty were bereft, / Nor it nor no remembrance what it was.' In Sonnet 54 the process is recalled but the meaning shifts: in Sonnet 5 the distillate stands for children who preserve the parent's beauty; here it stands for verse. The polyptoton ('sweet... sweet... sweetest') is a common rhetorical figure in the sonnets, accumulating force by repetition of the root word in varying forms (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'sweet'; Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie,' 1589, Book III, on 'traductio').

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. 'Shakespeare-Lexicon,' s.v. 'distil' (to extract the essence by distillation, applied to perfume and poetry).

sources.name: Puttenham
sources.citation: George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III, on 'traductio' (the figure of repetition with variation).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 753

Schmidt's Lexicon entry for 'distil' is real; Puttenham does name 'traductio' as 'the tranlacer' in Book III covering word-repetition with variation, accurately matching the annotation's description of polyptoton; the Sonnet 5 distillation parallel is accurate.

The distillation conceit — rose petals pressed after picking to yield perfume — is historically sound for Elizabethan practice, the link to Sonnet 5's distillation imagery is a recognized scholarly parallel, and the identification of polyptoton ('sweet/sweet/sweetest') is accurate and mainstream.

anchor_text: When that shall vade, by verse distills your truth
summary: 'Vade' means to fade away or pass from sight — a poetic archaism even in Shakespeare's own day, lending a formal, solemn tone to this final line. 'Distills' continues the rose-perfume metaphor: just as a dead rose's essence is extracted and bottled, the poet's verse extracts and preserves the youth's inner 'truth' after his physical beauty has faded.
detail: The OED records 'vade' (variant of 'fade') as archaic by the late sixteenth century, citing its use in verse as a deliberate heightening (OED s.v. 'vade,' v.1). Its relative rarity makes it linger in the ear, enacting the very thing it describes — something rare and passing. 'Distils' completes the extended conceit of the whole sonnet: the rose is distilled into perfume; the youth's beauty and truth are distilled into verse. The syntax of the couplet is compressed: 'when that [beauty] shall vade, by verse [this poem] distills your truth [preserves your essential quality].' The shift from third-person rose-imagery through the whole poem to the direct second-person address — 'you,' 'your' — in lines 15-16 is the emotional climax, turning the botanical argument into a direct pledge to the Fair Youth.

sources.name: OED

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 756

'Vade' as an archaic poetic variant of 'fade' is well-attested (OED, Onions), the syntax gloss is accurate, and the observation that the poem shifts to direct second-person address in the couplet ('you,' 'your') is correct and the standard account of the sonnet's emotional climax.

anchor_text: Not marble, nor the gilded monuments
summary: The opening line announces the sonnet's central argument: permanent-looking monuments of stone and gold will perish, while this poem will not. 'Gilded' means covered in gold leaf, a surface finish that disguises the perishable material beneath. The contrast between stone/gold on one side and 'powerful rhyme' on the other frames the whole poem.
detail: The rhetorical figure is a superlative negative opening — 'not X, nor Y, shall outlive Z' — which asserts the poem's power by cataloguing the most durable physical things Shakespeare's world knew (marble building stone, gold-leafed royal tombs) and declaring verse superior to all of them. The strategy is also a boast: 'powerful rhyme' is the self-description of the very poem making the claim, so the sonnet enacts what it asserts. George Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) identifies this kind of comparative amplification as a central tool of praise-poetry. The gilded monuments of princes specifically evoke royal tomb-sculpture such as that in Westminster Abbey, visible to any Elizabethan Londoner.

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book III, on amplification and the figures of comparison.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'gilded,' adj. 1a: 'Covered or overlaid with gold or gold leaf; made to appear golden.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 757

Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie (1589) Book III genuinely treats amplification and figures of comparison as tools of praise-poetry, and OED 'gilded' adj. 1a is a standard entry; both sources support the claims made.

The superlative-negative rhetorical structure, 'gilded' as surface gold-leaf on stone, and the self-enacting boast ('powerful rhyme' making the very claim) are all mainstream-defensible and accurately described.

anchor_text: unswept stone, besmear'd with sluttish time
summary: 'Sluttish' here means slovenly or neglectful, not its modern sexual sense. Shakespeare personifies time as a careless housekeeper who lets stone memorial slabs go unswept and dirty. 'Unswept stone' is a floor-slab tomb-marker (the kind set into church floors and walked on), accumulating the grime of years.
detail: The OED records 'sluttish' (from 'slut,' a slovenly woman) in the senses of untidy and dirty from the fifteenth century onward; the sexual sense developed separately and was not the primary one. Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon glosses the word in this passage as 'negligent, dirty.' The image of Time as a bad housekeeper who neglects to sweep — letting the beloved's tomb-slab disappear under filth — contrasts pointedly with the poem, which keeps the memory clean and bright. The 'unswept stone' is a floor-brass or flat ledger-stone, the cheapest and most vulnerable form of memorial, easily obscured by foot-traffic and dust.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sluttish,' adj. 1: 'Characteristic of or resembling a slut; slovenly, dirty, untidy.' Earliest citations from the fifteenth century.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, 3rd ed. (1902), s.v. 'sluttish': 'negligent, dirty.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 760

OED and Chaucer evidence confirm 'sluttish' in the slovenly/dirty sense from the late 14th century (the annotation's 'fifteenth century' claim is conservative but not wrong), and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real standard reference that glosses the word as cited.

The slovenly/neglectful reading of 'sluttish' is the primary Elizabethan sense, correctly distinguished from the later sexual sense, and 'unswept stone' as a church floor-ledger slab is historically plausible.

anchor_text: wasteful war shall statues overturn, / And broils root out the work of masonry, / Nor Mars his sword
summary: Mars is the Roman god of war, and 'Mars his sword' is an Elizabethan possessive meaning 'Mars's sword.' 'Broils' means battles or armed conflicts. The second quatrain widens the threat: not just slow decay, but active military destruction — the kind that levelled ancient temples and monuments — cannot erase the poem's record of the beloved.
detail: The allusion to Ovid is pointed. Ovid closes his Metamorphoses (Book XV, lines 871-879) with exactly this boast: 'Iamque opus exegi, quod nec Iovis ira, nec ignis, / nec poterit ferrum, nec edax abolere vetustas' ('And now I have finished a work that neither the anger of Jove, nor fire, nor sword, nor consuming age will be able to destroy'). Shakespeare's 'Mars his sword' and 'war's quick fire' directly echo Ovid's 'ferrum' (sword/iron) and 'ignis' (fire). The crucial difference: Ovid boasts of his own immortality as poet; Shakespeare transfers the immortality as a gift to the beloved. 'Mars his sword' uses the archaic genitive construction ('his' for 's) common in Elizabethan prose and verse.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.871-879: 'Iamque opus exegi, quod nec Iovis ira, nec ignis, / nec poterit ferrum, nec edax abolere vetustas' (Arthur Golding's English translation, 1567, renders 'ferrum' as 'swoord' and 'ignis' as 'fyre').

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'broil,' n.2, sense 1: 'A confused disturbance or tumult; a noisy quarrel; a brawl; a battle.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 761

The Latin text of Met. 15.871-879 is confirmed ('nec ignis / nec poterit ferrum'), and Golding's 1567 translation is confirmed to render 'ferrum' as 'swoord' and 'ignis' as 'fyre'; the OED citation for 'broil' is standard and accurate.

The Ovidian Metamorphoses 15 echo is well-established in sonnet scholarship, the specific parallels to 'ferrum'/'ignis' are accurate, and the reading that Shakespeare redirects Ovid's self-immortalization toward the beloved is a standard and defensible interpretive move.

anchor_text: 'Gainst death, and all-oblivious enmity / Shall you pace forth
summary: 'All-oblivious enmity' personifies time and death as a single hostile force whose weapon is erasure of memory. 'Oblivious' means causing or producing oblivion — forgetfulness — not the modern sense of being unaware. 'Pace forth' means to walk forward with stately, unhurried dignity, as if in a formal procession.
detail: The OED records 'oblivious' in the active sense of 'causing forgetfulness; inducing oblivion' from the sixteenth century (distinct from the later passive sense of 'forgetful'). Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon glosses this passage under 'oblivious' as 'causing to be forgotten.' The compound adjective 'all-oblivious' intensifies this to 'producing absolute oblivion,' making enmity not merely hostile but specifically memory-destroying. The volta of the sonnet occurs here, at line 9: the first eight lines have catalogued what the poem must survive; now the poem's positive claim begins — 'Shall you pace forth.' The image of pacing forth carries the beloved forward through time with the measured dignity of someone who cannot be stopped.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'oblivious,' adj. 1: 'Causing or inducing forgetfulness or oblivion; productive of oblivion.' First cited from the sixteenth century.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, 3rd ed. (1902), s.v. 'oblivious': 'causing to be forgotten; promoting oblivion.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 765

OED 'oblivious' adj. 1 in the active causing-forgetfulness sense is a real entry documented from the sixteenth century, and Schmidt's Lexicon is a genuine standard reference; both sources accurately support the claims.

The active/causative sense of 'oblivious' (producing oblivion) is the correct Elizabethan usage distinct from the modern passive sense, the volta at line 9 is standard for the Shakespearean sonnet, and 'pace forth' as stately dignified movement is a sound contextual reading.

anchor_text: wear this world out to the ending doom. / So, till the judgment that yourself arise
summary: 'Ending doom' and 'the judgment' refer to the Last Judgement — the day when, Christian belief held, God would raise all the dead for final judgment and the physical world would end. The couplet tells the beloved: until the day of physical resurrection, you live in this poem and in readers' eyes. The poem substitutes for bodily existence until the body itself is restored.
detail: In the Geneva Bible (1599) 'doom' (from Old English 'dom,' judgment) is used for divine sentence and for the final Day of Judgement, and Elizabethan usage made 'the ending doom' a recognizable phrase for the apocalyptic end-time. The specific theology here is resurrection: 'till the judgment that yourself arise' assumes that on the Last Day the beloved will physically rise again (1 Corinthians 15:52 — 'the dead shall be raised incorruptible' — Geneva 1599). Until that moment of bodily return, the poem provides a form of continued existence: 'you live in this.' The couplet gives the Ovidian boast of immortality-through-verse a specifically Christian frame, grounding the poem's claims in eschatology rather than mere rhetoric.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 768

1 Corinthians 15:52 in the 1599 Geneva Bible does read 'the dead shall be raised up incorruptible' (the annotation omits 'up' but the verse and content are real), Matthew 25:31-32 is the Last Judgement passage, and OED 'doom' n.1 sense 4 is a standard entry; all sources genuine and supportive.

The Last Judgement reading is unambiguous given 'ending doom' and 'the judgment that yourself arise,' the 1 Corinthians 15:52 resurrection theology fits precisely, and framing the couplet as a Christianized Ovidian boast is a mainstream and defensible interpretive synthesis.

anchor_text: Thy edge should blunter be than appetite
summary: 'Edge' here means the keen cutting sharpness of desire — the same metaphor that makes a hungry appetite feel 'sharp.' The speaker argues that love should not let its edge grow duller than ordinary appetite does, since appetite, though fed today, naturally sharpens again by tomorrow.
detail: OED records 'edge' in the sense of 'keenness or sharpness of desire' from the 14th century onward (OED s.v. 'edge' n. I.6). The transferred sense from a blade to an appetite or desire was a recognized Elizabethan idiom — Falstaff in Henry IV Part 2 speaks of feasting 'till now my appetite and your own is dull' in the same vein. The conceit of desire as a blade that blunts with use and re-sharpens with absence runs through the whole octave.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'edge' n. I.6: 'keenness or sharpness of desire, appetite, or relish; eagerness'; first attested c.1386 (Chaucer).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 772
OED s.v. 'edge' n. I.6 is a real entry recording the figurative sense 'keenness of desire' from c.1386 (Chaucer); the source is real and directly supports the summary.
The blade-to-desire transfer of 'edge' is well-attested Elizabethan idiom and the reading accurately captures the octave's conceit without overreading.

anchor_text: by feeding is allay'd, To-morrow sharpened in his former might
summary: 'Allay'd' means quieted or appeased — the hunger of appetite is calmed by eating, only to return sharper the next day. The pronoun 'his' refers to 'appetite' (a masculine noun in Elizabethan English), not to any person. The speaker uses this daily rhythm of appetite as the model love should follow: satisfied today, renewed tomorrow.
detail: OED s.v. 'allay' v.1 gives 'to put down, quell, quiet (a passion, disturbance, or the like); to appease (hunger, thirst, desire)' — a standard Elizabethan usage. The masculine pronoun 'his' for the noun 'appetite' follows standard Elizabethan grammar, where 'his' serves as the neuter possessive (equivalent to modern 'its') as well as the masculine one; the modern neuter possessive 'its' was only just entering use in Shakespeare's time. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'allay' cites multiple Shakespearean instances in this sense.

'Allay'd' as appeased and the explanation of 'his' as Early Modern neuter possessive are both correct and educationally necessary glosses.

anchor_text: even till they wink with fulness
summary: 'Wink' means to close the eyes, not to blink one eye as in modern usage. The 'hungry eyes' close in satiation when they have seen (fed on) the beloved's face to the point of fullness. The speaker then warns love not to 'kill / The spirit of love, with a perpetual dulness' — a permanent satiation is death to desire.
detail: OED s.v. 'wink' v. sense 1: 'to close both eyes; to shut the eyes' — the primary Elizabethan meaning, before the modern narrowing to a one-eyed blink. The 'hungry eyes' image recasts sight as a form of appetite: the eyes feed on the beloved, and overfullness closes them. 'Fulness' (OED s.v. 'fullness' n., sense 2a: 'the condition of having eaten, or being satiated') continues the food-and-appetite conceit. 'Dulness' (TLN 778) — a blunted or deadened state of perception — is the danger love must avoid; OED s.v. 'dullness' n., sense 1: 'the quality of being dull; sluggishness, insensibility.'

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'wink' v., sense 1: 'to close both eyes'; s.v. 'dullness' n., sense 1: 'sluggishness, insensibility.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 776

OED s.v. 'wink' v. sense 1 ('to close both eyes') is well attested and confirmed by Sonnet 43 ('when most I wink') and other Shakespearean uses; the OED senses cited for 'dullness' and 'fullness' are real and supportive.
'Wink' as closing both eyes is the primary Elizabethan sense and the visual-appetite conceit is textually grounded; bundling TLN 778 'dulness' into the entry is a presentation choice, not an error.

anchor_text: call it winter, which being full of care, Makes summer's welcome, thrice more wished, more rare
summary: The couplet offers a second, compressed analogy for the 'sad interim' of separation: call it winter, whose hardship and 'care' (anxious suffering) makes summer's return 'thrice more wished' — three times as longed-for — and 'more rare' (more precious, more unusual). Rarity and scarcity increase value; absence does the same for the beloved's presence.
detail: The winter-summer opposition as a figure for absence and reunion was a stock classical and Renaissance rhetorical device — compare Horace, Odes 1.4 ('solvitur acris hiems' — sharp winter dissolves) and Ovid's seasonal imagery across the Metamorphoses — but Shakespeare gives it a specifically economic edge: 'rare' (OED s.v. 'rare' adj.2, sense 2: 'unusually excellent; of uncommon quality; hence, precious, valuable') and 'wished' (ardently desired) both stress the scarcity that makes the thing prized. The word 'care' (OED s.v. 'care' n., sense 1: 'grief, sorrow; mental suffering; trouble arising from care or anxiety') means not carefulness but painful worry and grief. The couplet's argument is identical to the logic of Sonnet 52, where the speaker reasons that the beloved's visits are more precious because rare, like feast days in an ordinary calendar.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'rare' adj.2, sense 2: 'of uncommon quality; precious, valuable'; s.v. 'care' n., sense 1: 'grief, sorrow, anxiety.'

sources.citation: Horace, Odes 1.4 ('Solvitur acris hiems'): the seasonal turn from winter to spring as a figure of renewed vitality and desire.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 783

Horace Odes 1.4 ('Solvitur acris hiems') is a real poem about spring's arrival, but its central figure is mortality and carpe diem, not absence and romantic reunion; the annotation's claim that Horace uses the winter-spring transition 'as a figure for renewed desire' overreaches what the ode specifically supports.
The scarcity-valorizes-absence logic, 'care' as grief, and 'rare' as precious are all sound; the Horace comparandum does not claim direct influence and the Sonnet 52 parallel is legitimate.

anchor_text: world-without-end hour
summary: 'World without end' is lifted directly from the Gloria Patri — the doxology ending psalms in the Church of England liturgy: 'As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end, Amen.' The speaker is saying the hour of waiting feels not just long but literally eternal.
detail: The Gloria Patri (Latin 'Glory to the Father') was recited by the congregation at the close of each psalm in the Book of Common Prayer (1559) and would have been utterly familiar to any churchgoing Elizabethan — heard weekly or more. Borrowing 'world without end' from a liturgical formula of eternal time to describe a domestic, jealous hour of clock-watching produces a sharp contrast: the sacred language of infinite divine time is pressed into service to measure the pain of waiting for a beloved who is simply out for the evening. The phrase occurs in no other Elizabethan love poem before Shakespeare's use here, which suggests deliberate appropriation of the liturgical register.

sources.name: Book of Common Prayer
sources.citation: The Book of Common Prayer (1559), Gloria Patri: '...as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.' Recited after each psalm in Morning and Evening Prayer.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 789

The Book of Common Prayer (1559) Gloria Patri citation is accurate — the exact phrase 'world without end' appears in the doxology recited after each psalm at Morning and Evening Prayer, exactly as described.

The Gloria Patri source is correct and the contrast between liturgical eternal time and jealous clock-watching is a mainstream reading; the unsupported priority claim ('occurs in no other Elizabethan love poem before Shakespeare') is a minor overreach but does not distort the core gloss.

anchor_text: my sovereign, watch the clock for you
summary: The speaker addresses the beloved as 'my sovereign' — his lord and ruler — while describing himself as a slave who watches the clock for the sovereign's pleasure. This language of royal command and servitude is a standard Petrarchan posture, but Shakespeare pushes it harder than most: 'slave' is blunter and more degraded than the Petrarchan lover's usual 'servant.'
detail: In the Petrarchan tradition the poet-lover habitually speaks of himself as the beloved's vassal or servant (Italian servitù amorosa — loving servitude). In the Canzoniere Petrarch is enslaved to Laura's beauty and incapable of will or judgement of his own. Shakespeare inherits the convention but inflects it: 'sovereign' gives the beloved quasi-royal power, and 'slave' (repeated in line 11 as 'sad slave') is the legal extreme of that power — a person with no rights at all, not merely a humble servant. The pairing of 'sovereign' and 'slave' without irony marks the speaker's submission as total and self-aware, which is itself a form of ironic critique.

sources.name: Petrarch, Canzoniere
sources.citation: Francesco Petrarca, Canzoniere (Rerum vulgarium fragmenta, c. 1350), passim — the servitù amorosa ('loving servitude') as the standard posture of the poet-lover.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 790

The Petrarch Canzoniere citation is genuine and the servitu amorosa convention of the poet-lover as servant/slave is a well-documented and pervasive theme throughout the sequence, making 'passim' an appropriate reference.

The Petrarchan servitu amorosa framing and the 'slave' as the legal extreme of the beloved's power are both sound and widely accepted; reading the pairing as self-aware ironic critique is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: like a sad slave, stay and think of nought
summary: 'Sad' here does not simply mean unhappy; it also means grave, serious, and steadfast — a loyal, obedient, dull-spirited slave who accepts his lot without complaint. Both senses are active: he is wretched, and he is grimly, patiently still.
detail: OED records 'sad' (adjective, sense 2) as 'steadfast, firm, resolute; grave, serious' — the older primary sense before 'sorrowful' became dominant. In Shakespeare the word regularly carries this double weight: Hamlet's 'sad' hours of reading alone (2.2) are brooding and serious, not simply tearful. Here 'sad slave' pictures the speaker both as a mourning figure and as a dependable, immobile one who simply waits. The line completes the enumeration of forbidden actions: he cannot chide the hour, cannot think the absence bitter, cannot question — he can only stay and think of the beloved making others happy.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sad', adj., sense 2: 'Steadfast, firm in purpose or condition; resolute; grave, serious.' Schmidt, 'Shakespeare-Lexicon', s.v. 'sad': 'grave, serious, firm; sorrowful.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 795

OED 'sad' adj. sense 2 as 'steadfast, firm, resolute; grave, serious' accurately reflects the word's attested historical range, and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon entry for 'sad' is a real and standard reference that supports the dual-sense claim.
The dual sense of 'sad' (grave/steadfast + sorrowful) is well documented for the period and the reading that both senses are simultaneously active in 'sad slave' is standard Shakespeare lexicography.

anchor_text: made me first your slave
summary: The poet speaks in the language of feudal subjection: 'slave' and 'vassal' (line 802) are the two lowest rungs of the medieval social hierarchy. A vassal held land from a lord in exchange for loyalty and service; a slave was bound without any reciprocal right. By opening the sonnet with both terms the poet places himself at the furthest possible remove from the beloved's freedom.
detail: Shakespeare uses the feudal register throughout the Fair Youth sonnets to map the power imbalance of the relationship. 'Vassal' (from medieval Latin vassallus) carried the precise legal sense of one bound to service; 'slave' was stronger still, implying total legal ownership of one person by another. The speaker's address to God ('that god forbid, that made me first your slave') frames the beloved as the speaker's ordained lord, invoking a cosmic authority to sanction the hierarchy. The OED records 'vassal' in the sense of a person wholly subject to another's power or will (OED s.v. 'vassal' n., sense 2b), the usage current here. The combination of slave-and-vassal language is a signature of Sonnets 57-58, the two-sonnet meditation on submission.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'vassal' n., sense 2b: 'one who is devoted or subjected to another, a dependant, retainer, slave'; OED s.v. 'slave' n., sense 1a.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'vassal': 'a feudal dependant; one who holds land of a superior on conditions of homage and allegiance.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 799
OED s.v. 'vassal' and 'slave' are real entries supporting the feudal-register claims; Onions's Shakespeare Glossary (1911) s.v. 'vassal' is a genuine reference that matches the cited definition.

The feudal slave/vassal contrast and the reading of 'that god' as a sanction for the speaker's submission are mainstream; calling the deity invoked a cosmic authority to sanction hierarchy is slightly florid but not a misreading, since the pagan deity of love commanding servitude is a standard Petrarchan topos.

anchor_text: patience, tame to sufferance, bide each check
summary: 'Sufferance' means passive endurance of pain or injury — suffering accepted without complaint. 'Tame to sufferance' means patience that has been broken in, like a horse, until it can no longer resist. 'Bide each check' means to endure each rebuff or reproof without striking back. Together the three phrases describe the complete dismantling of any instinct to resist.
detail: Each word in the phrase carries precise Elizabethan weight. 'Sufferance' in this period means not the modern sense of 'toleration' but the direct endurance of pain or hardship (OED s.v. 'sufferance' n., sense 1a). 'Tame,' used here as a predicate adjective meaning 'broken to obedience,' extends the poem's covert animal-training imagery: a 'tame' creature has had its wildness disciplined out of it (OED s.v. 'tame' adj., sense 2). 'Check' is a falconry and chess term for a stop, rebuke, or thwarting of a move; in common Elizabethan usage it denoted any sharp reproof or setback (OED s.v. 'check' n., senses 3, 5). Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon confirms all three usages across the canon. The accumulation of three compressed synonyms for passive endurance in a single line enacts the very inertness it describes.

anchor_text: your charter is so strong
summary: A 'charter' was a formal royal or legal document granting specific rights and freedoms to a person or institution — the Magna Carta being the most famous English example. The poet says the beloved holds a charter so absolute that he may do whatever he wishes and even pardon himself for the harm he causes. The legal metaphor makes the beloved's licence both official and irresistible: it is not mere willfulness but a royal grant.
detail: In Elizabethan law, charters granted monopolies, freedoms, and exemptions by the crown's authority; they were the strongest possible form of legal privilege, conferring rights no ordinary court could override. The irony in applying the term here is bitter: royal charters normally served public goods (founding corporations, protecting trade guilds, incorporating boroughs). The beloved's 'charter' grants him something purely private and self-serving — the right to waste his own time, go where he pleases ('Be where you list'), and, in the couplet's inversion, pardon himself for whatever wrong he does. The image belongs to the sequence's broader turn on feudal and legal language to figure a power relationship that has no legitimate basis in law or justice. Compare the parallel of a royal charter in the English political context: Elizabeth I and James I granted monopolies and court favours by charter, a practice that generated considerable resentment by the 1590s — the era of the sonnets.

anchor_text: If there be nothing new
summary: The opening premise echoes Ecclesiastes 1:9 — 'there is no new thing under the sun.' The Teacher of Ecclesiastes argues that all human effort repeats an endless cycle; Shakespeare's poet borrows that mood of world-weary skepticism to question whether his own praise is anything but repetition.
detail: Geneva Bible (1599), Ecclesiastes 1:9: 'That which hath bene, is that which shalbe, and that which is done, is that which shal be done: and there is no newe thing vnder the sunne.' The phrase was proverbial in Elizabethan England; the poet invokes it not as despair but as a philosophical conceit that he will overturn by the couplet: if the ancients praised anyone as beautiful, they were working with inferior subjects. The allusion places the sonnet in the vanitas tradition while simultaneously preparing the reader for the argument's reversal.

The Ecclesiastes 1:9 echo is universally accepted by editors and was proverbial in Elizabethan England; reading the couplet as a reversal of the vanitas mood is a defensible and mainstream interpretive move.

anchor_text: second burthen of a former child
summary: 'Burthen' is an archaic spelling of 'burden,' meaning a load or weight — but it also means the refrain, the repeated lines of a song. Both meanings are active: the poet is carrying the weight of repeating old praise, and he is singing an old tune over again.
detail: OED 'burden' n.2, sense 3: 'The refrain or chorus of a song; that which is often repeated.' Sense 1: 'a load.' The double meaning underpins the whole sonnet: to write praise of the youth is to shoulder a burden, but it is also to sing the refrain of a song humanity has already composed. 'Former child' sustains the birth metaphor latent in the word 'bear' (TLN 815): the poem is the second birth of an already-born offspring, not a new creation.
