anchor_text: Since mind at first in character was done
summary: 'Character' here means written letters or inscription, not personality. The line means 'since thought was first set down in writing' — that is, from the very beginning of written history. The poet wishes he could search all of recorded time for an image of the youth.
detail: OED 'character' n., sense 5: 'A distinctive mark, sign, brand, or stamp' and sense 6: 'A graphic symbol... a letter of the alphabet.' The word retains its etymological Greek meaning (kharakter: engraved mark) in Elizabethan usage. Schmidt, 'Shakespeare-Lexicon,' s.v. 'character': 'handwriting, writing.' The phrase compresses: 'since thought [i.e., intellectual content] was first fixed in letters' — the beginning of literacy is the outer limit of the poet's imagined search.

anchor_text: Wh'r we are mended, or wh'r better they, Or whether revolution be the same
summary: 'Wh'r' is a contracted form of 'whether,' used twice for rapid rhetorical enumeration. 'Revolution' carries its Elizabethan astronomical sense: the orbital return of a planet to its starting point, and so the turning of time's cycle back to where it began. The three alternatives — we have improved, they were better, or history simply repeats — are the sestet's open question, resolved dismissively by the couplet.
detail: OED 'revolution' n., sense 2: 'The action of revolving or moving round in an orbit; the motion of a celestial body in its orbit.' This sense was primary in Elizabethan scientific discourse (Copernicus's great work was 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium,' 1543). 'Wh'r' (also spelled 'whe'r') is a metrically convenient contraction of 'whether'; its triple deployment in two lines gives the verse a breathless, list-like quality — a classical anaphora — before the couplet shuts down the question. The poem's cyclical-time argument (five-hundred-year backward look, revolution as orbital return) draws on the same conceptual world as Shakespeare's Sonnet 123.

The astronomical sense of 'revolution' (orbital return of a celestial body) is mainstream and well-supported; calling the 'wh'r...wh'r...whether' pattern 'anaphora' is defensible even though the third instance uses the full form, as the word-repetition effect is real and recognized by editors.

anchor_text: the wits of former days, To subjects worse have given admiring praise
summary: The couplet delivers the sonnet's volta: the poet stops wondering whether antiquity was better and declares that ancient writers, whatever their skill, were praising inferior subjects. The youth surpasses anyone the old world could have praised — a backhanded compliment that redeems the entire twelve-line meditation on repetition.
detail: The turn here is doubly compressed. First, the couplet resolves the three-way question of TLN 823-824 by superseding it: comparison is irrelevant because the youth's beauty defeats every historical benchmark. Second, the word 'wits' (OED 'wit' n., sense 7: 'a person of superior intellect; a talented or gifted person') carries a note of competitive rivalry — those ancient wits, however clever, were outclassed by their subject matter, not their talent. The device is a form of the rhetorical praeteritio: the poet seems to concede the ancients' greatness and then uses the concession to magnify the youth. The same move appears in Sidney, 'Astrophil and Stella' 3 ('Let dainty wits cry on the sisters nine'), where praising rival poets' skills is the launch-pad for a bolder claim.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 825

The general interpretation of the couplet as magnifying the youth by outdoing ancient precedent is sound, but labelling the device 'praeteritio' is a mislabelling — praeteritio means passing over by mentioning; the actual move here is synkrisis (comparative surpassing), so the rhetorical term overstates what the text does.

anchor_text: Like as the waves make towards the pebbled shore
summary: The sonnet's central image — time as waves endlessly displacing one another — draws on the speech of Pythagoras in Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book 15, where time is compared to a river: 'Our bodies also are always in movement, never the same.' Ovid's Pythagoras argues that nothing in the world is permanent; Shakespeare compresses this into fourteen lines and turns philosophical equanimity into an assault.
detail: Ovid gives Pythagoras a long speech in Metamorphoses 15.176-452 expounding metempsychosis and universal flux; the passage includes the comparison of time to flowing water (Met. 15.178-185 in Golding's 1567 translation: 'As every wave drives other forth, and that that comes behind / Both thrusteth and is thrust itself...'). Golding's English was Shakespeare's working text. The sonnet's closing boast — that verse will outlast Time's destruction — also answers Ovid's conclusion to the Metamorphoses (15.871-879), where the poet declares his 'work' finished and proof against 'the wrath of Jove... nor fire, nor sword, nor consuming age' (Golding's version). Shakespeare picks up that defiance and makes it personal and lover-directed. The Ovidian subtext is what gives Sonnet 60 its unusual density: it is not merely a meditation on time but a conscious reply to the greatest classical meditation on time in verse.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.176-452 (universal flux and time as river); 15.871-879 (the poet's defiance of oblivion); Arthur Golding's English translation (1567).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 827

The Ovid Metamorphoses 15 Pythagoras-flux source and the couplet's echo of Met. 15.871-879 are the mainstream scholarly identification (Burrow, Booth, Duncan-Jones), and the Golding-as-working-text claim is widely held; calling this a 'conscious reply' is interpretively strong but within the range of accepted scholarship.

anchor_text: Each changing place with that which goes before, In sequent toil all forwards do contend
summary: 'Sequent' means following in an unbroken series; 'toil' is laborious effort. The lines say that each moment displaces its predecessor and is itself displaced, every minute straining forward in a ceaseless relay. The wave image renders time not as smooth flow but as relentless mechanical effort.
detail: OED records 'sequent' (adj.) meaning 'following in regular succession' from the 16th century (OED s.v. 'sequent', adj. 1). 'Contend' carries a sense of striving against resistance (OED s.v. 'contend', v. 4), so the line personifies each minute as a competitor elbowing forward. The effect is of time experienced not as gliding but as grinding, anticipating the violent verbs that fill the third quatrain ('transfix', 'delves', 'mow').

Reading 'sequent' as successive and 'contend' as striving against resistance is OED-supported and the wave-as-relay gloss is the mainstream reading; the contrast of grinding vs. gliding time is a defensible interpretive inference from the diction, not an overreach.

anchor_text: Nativity, once in the main of light, Crawls to maturity
summary: 'Nativity' here means a person at the moment of birth. 'The main of light' means the open expanse of daylight — the same 'main' used for the open sea. The image is of a newborn launched into the full flood of life and sunlight, only to crawl through it toward decay.
detail: OED gives 'nativity' in the sense of 'a newly born person; a person regarded as newly born' (OED s.v. 'nativity', n. 3). In Elizabethan astrology a person's 'nativity' also denoted the horoscope drawn at birth — the configuration of the heavens that determined one's fortune — which sharpens the resonance: at birth one is at the crown of one's astrological moment, already subject to what the stars ordained. 'Main' meaning 'open expanse' (of sea or sky) is OED s.v. 'main', n.2, sense 3. The verb 'crawls' is precise: the infant's first motion sets the pace for a life that, though it reaches the 'crown'd' height of maturity, is already declining.

Both the literal birth-person sense and the astrological nativity-as-horoscope sense are well-attested period meanings; the claim that 'crawls' anticipates decline is warranted by the poem's logic (eclipse imagery follows immediately), and no folk etymology or anachronism is present.

anchor_text: Crooked eclipses 'gainst his glory fight, And Time that gave doth now his gift confound
summary: 'Crooked' means malignant or perverse — the standard Elizabethan epithet for anything hostile and twisted. Eclipses were widely feared as bad omens portending disasters for rulers and kingdoms. 'Confound' means to destroy utterly or bring to nothing. Time that first gives the gifts of youth turns and annihilates them: giver becomes wrecker.
detail: OED gives 'crooked' in the figurative sense 'deviating from rectitude; perverse, wrong; (of persons, also) dishonest, deceitful; (of things) evil, ill-omened' (OED s.v. 'crooked', adj. 6). Elizabethan natural philosophy held that eclipses disturbed the elemental order and presaged political upheaval — the view Gloucester voices in King Lear 1.2 and Ulysses invokes in Troilus and Cressida 1.3. Here the eclipses are Time's instruments, shadowing the matured life that was once in 'the main of light.' 'Confound' in the sense 'to destroy, bring to ruin' is OED s.v. 'confound', v. 5, and was in common Elizabethan use.

'Crooked' as ill-omened and the Elizabethan fear of eclipses as political portents are uncontroversial; the King Lear and Troilus parallels are apt and the reading of 'confound' as destroy is standard.

anchor_text: Time doth transfix the flourish set on youth And delves the parallels in beauty's brow
summary: 'Transfix' means to pierce through or impale; 'flourish' here means the bloom or ornamental prime of youth. 'Delves' means digs or ploughs; 'parallels' means lines running side by side — that is, the furrows of wrinkles on a face. Time stabs the flower of youth and then ploughs wrinkle-lines into the brow as a farmer digs furrows in a field.

'transfix', v. 1a), and 'flourish' in the sense 'the state or period of greatest vigour or beauty; the prime, the bloom' (OED s.v. 'flourish', n. 4). The violence of 'transfix' is not accidental: it turns Time's action from gradual erosion into an act of stabbing. 'Delve' in the sense 'to dig, to plough' is OED s.v. 'delve', v. 1; 'parallels' for wrinkles exploits the geometric term (parallel lines that never meet), giving the metaphor of the face as a field ploughed into permanent furrows. Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon) and Onions (Shakespeare Glossary) both gloss 'parallels' here as wrinkles.

anchor_text: thy image should keep open
summary: 'Image' here does not mean a painted or carved likeness; it means the mental apparition — the inward picture of the beloved that the poet cannot banish from his mind. The poet asks whether the youth is deliberately making his own image haunt the poet's sleepless nights.
detail: OED records 'image' in the sense of a mental representation or phantasm formed by the imagination (OED s.v. 'image' n. 5a, citing uses from the 14th century onward). The word carried genuine psychological weight in Renaissance faculty psychology: the imaginative faculty retained impressions that could return involuntarily, especially in darkness. The question 'Is it thy will' — is this an act of the beloved's will? — frames the image as a supernatural projection, almost a spirit sent from the youth, which the sestet then retracts.

anchor_text: shadows like to thee do mock my sight
summary: 'Shadows' means insubstantial phantoms or likenesses — not cast shadows but false semblances that look like the beloved but are not him. 'Mock my sight' means deceive or delude my eyes. The poet lies awake and sees the beloved's face everywhere, in shapes that counterfeit him but vanish.

Shakespeare uses the word in this sense throughout the canon — 'the best in this kind are but shadows' (A Midsummer Night's Dream 5.1), where actors and their art are all unreal semblances. In the sonnet tradition the beloved's 'shadow' or image haunting the lover at night is a Petrarchan commonplace; Shakespeare literalizes it into specific, tormented insomnia.

anchor_text: The scope and tenure of thy jealousy
summary: 'Tenure' is a legal term for the terms or conditions under which something is held — here, the full terms and extent of the youth's jealous surveillance. 'Jealousy' in this period meant watchful suspicion or zealous guarding, not simply the emotion of romantic envy. The poet imagines the youth sending his spirit to pry into the poet's 'shames and idle hours' — the scope (reach) and tenure (terms) of that spying mission.

The legal flavor is apt: the poet frames the imagined spying as though the youth holds some right of inspection over him. 'Jealousy' in Elizabethan usage regularly meant watchful suspicion or zealous concern rather than the modern narrower romantic sense (OED s.v. 'jealousy' n., sense 2: 'vigilance in guarding a possession... anxiety lest some evil befall'). The same usage appears in Othello, where Iago warns of 'the green-eyed monster' jealousy that guards what it loves possessively.

anchor_text: To play the watchman ever for thy sake
summary: A watchman was a parish or ward officer who walked the streets through the night, keeping guard against fire and crime. The poet transforms his sleepless love into the same kind of vigilant, duty-bound service — not passive suffering but an active watch kept on the beloved's behalf. The word 'play' acknowledges the role is performed as well as felt.
detail: Night watchmen were a familiar civic institution in Elizabethan England: householders took turns (or paid deputies) to patrol their ward from dusk to dawn, with authority to challenge strangers and raise the hue and cry. The post is treated as a comic figure in Much Ado About Nothing (Dogberry's watch) but in the sonnet it is elevated into a type of faithful devotion — the soldier who stands guard while others sleep. The poet's insomnia, reframed as a watchman's tour of duty, becomes an act of love rather than a torment; yet the framing also implies the beloved, awake elsewhere, needs no such guarding from his own side.

The Elizabethan ward-watchman context is accurate, the Dogberry parallel apt, and the interpretive payoff — devoted watch met by the beloved's absence — is directly licensed by the couplet's plain sense.

anchor_text: whilst thou dost wake elsewhere, From me far off, with others all too near
summary: 'Wake' plays on two senses: to be awake (as the insomniac poet is) and to keep lively company, to carouse. The poet keeps watch in sleepless loyalty while the youth stays awake in a very different way — at ease, sociable, and 'with others all too near.' The phrase 'all too near' carries a sting of jealousy: the others have a physical closeness that the absent poet is denied.
detail: OED records 'wake' in the sense of to be awake or to stay up at night (OED s.v. anchor_text: Methinks no face so gracious is as mine
summary: The second quatrain (lines 5-8) is a sustained exercise in comic self-praise: the poet ranks his own face the most 'gracious' (beautiful, pleasing), his 'shape' (physique) the most 'true' (well-proportioned), and his overall worth greater than all others. 'Gracious' in Elizabethan usage could mean both spiritually favored and physically handsome; 'truth of such account' pairs bodily symmetry with moral worth, so the poet is claiming total superiority. The reader is set up to enjoy the collapse. Puttenham's 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) discusses auxesis (gradual amplification) as a scheme suited to praise and censure alike.

anchor_text: 'Tis thee,--myself,--that for myself I praise
summary: The couplet springs the paradox the poem has been building toward: the poet's self-love was never really about himself. The dashes around '--myself,--' enact a hesitation and correction — it was 'thee' (the youth) he was praising all along, projecting the youth's beauty onto his own reflection. Both senses are in play: the poet's inner image of his own face has been painted over with the youth's colors, a flattering but delusional portrait. The couplet thus resolves the moral problem raised in line 16 ('Self so self-loving were iniquity'): genuine self-love of the poet's actual aging face would be absurd vanity; but what looked like self-love was actually displaced love of another — which the sequence as a whole insists is the poet's defining relationship. This is the sequence's recurring turn: the poet loves the youth so completely that the youth becomes the poet's better self. anchor_text: Time's injurious hand crush'd and o'erworn

anchor_text: his youthful morn Hath travell'd on to age's steepy night
summary: 'Steepy' means 'steep' — a precipitous or abrupt drop. The youth's life is imagined as a single day: morning (youth) gives way to night (old age) not gradually but over a cliff edge. anchor_text: do I now fortify Against confounding age's cruel knife
summary: 'Confounding' means 'destroying utterly, ruining.' The word comes from Latin confundere, 'to pour together, to ruin,' and in Elizabethan English meant to overthrow or bring to nothing. anchor_text: rich-proud cost of outworn buried age
summary: 'Cost' here means costly display or magnificence — the grand monuments and ornaments of civilizations long dead (OED 'cost' n. 3, 'pomp, magnificence, splendour'). Elizabethan audiences would have recognised this immediately — the dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII (1536-41) had left hundreds of abbeys roofless across the landscape, making the ruins of a 'buried age' a present visual fact rather than a bookish abstraction.

anchor_text: brass eternal slave to mortal rage

anchor_text: hungry ocean gain / Advantage on the kingdom of the shore
summary: The second quatrain watches sea and land trade ground in a ceaseless, purposeless exchange: the ocean erodes the shore, then the shore reclaims from the sea. This was Ovid's great image of universal flux. In 'Metamorphoses' XV, Pythagoras observes that what was once dry land is now sea, and what was once sea is now land — nothing stays fixed.

The phrase 'kingdom of the shore' personifies the land as a sovereignty vulnerable to invasion — a metaphor that makes the geological process feel like political conquest, sharpening the final fear that love too will be 'taken.' 'Increasing store with loss, and loss with store' (line 890) renders the balanced chiasmus of the exchange: what one side gains the other loses, and the process simply reverses, without winner or end.

anchor_text: shall beauty hold a plea, Whose action is no stronger than a flower
summary: The poet casts beauty's struggle against time as a lawsuit it cannot win. 'Hold a plea' means sustain a legal case in court; 'action' is a legal term for a formal suit. Beauty's case collapses because its only evidence — a flower — will not last long enough for the hearing.

The legal conceit was a commonplace of the sonnet tradition — Sidney's 'leave me, O love' and Daniel's Delia use legal imagery of appeals and verdicts — but Shakespeare presses it into the poem's structure: the three quatrains are beauty's failing arguments, and the couplet the only counter-verdict the court will allow.

anchor_text: Time's best jewel from Time's chest lie hid
summary: The poet imagines beauty as a jewel that belongs to Time — kept in Time's chest (treasure-box), from which there is no escape. The sestet's central question is whether anything can be hidden away from Time, which owns and ultimately claims everything beautiful.

anchor_text: desert a beggar born
summary: 'Desert' here means merit, worth, or deserving talent — not the wasteland. The line says that genuine virtue and ability are born into poverty and social obscurity, denied the recognition they earn. The injustice is foundational: the world does not reward what is good.

anchor_text: needy nothing trimm'd in jollity
summary: 'Needy nothing' means a person of no worth or substance who nonetheless lacks nothing materially. anchor_text: maiden virtue rudely strumpeted
summary: 'Strumpeted' means made into a strumpet — publicly dishonoured and prostituted. A strumpet was a prostitute; to strumpet a person is to treat their virtue as something that can be bought, sold, or defiled. The adverb 'rudely' adds violence: innocence is not merely neglected but actively degraded.

The form 'strumpeted' converts a noun of sexual dishonour into a verb of violent action against female virtue. The word 'maiden' (meaning not merely unmarried but chaste and uncorrupted) heightens the violence: it is specifically innocent, uncorrupted virtue that is being degraded, not merely ordinary compliance. Of the twelve items in the sonnet's catalogue, this is the only one cast as an act of sexual violation, which gives it particular force among the more institutional grievances around it (misplaced honour, disabled strength, tongue-tied art).

anchor_text: simple truth miscall'd simplicity
summary: 'Simplicity' in this period carried a derogatory second meaning: foolishness, feeble-mindedness, or lack of sophistication. The line complains that honest, plain speaking ('simple truth') gets dismissed as stupidity. The wordplay turns the insult back on the accusers: the world mistakes directness for dimness.

The punning clash between 'simple' as honest/plain and 'simplicity' as foolish drives the line's bitterness: the adjective that should praise ('simple truth' = truth unadorned, without guile) becomes a noun of contempt when the world relabels it. The line is the sonnet's sharpest compression of social hypocrisy — a world in which being honest and direct is counted against you as a social deficiency rather than recognised as a virtue.

anchor_text: Tir'd with all these, from these would I be gone, Save that, to die, I leave my love alone
summary: The closing couplet is the sonnet's volta — its turn. The first line of the couplet echoes the opening line almost word for word, sealing the catalogue; 'Save that' then provides the single exception that reverses everything. The poet would welcome death, but dying means abandoning his beloved — and that one fact is enough to keep him alive in a world he has spent twelve lines condemning.
detail: The volta (Italian for 'turn') is the structural hinge of the sonnet form: after the three quatrains have built the argument, the couplet pivots it. Here the pivot is unusually stark: the opening line of the couplet reprises TLN 911 almost verbatim ('Tired with all these' / 'Tir'd with all these'), a ring-closure that makes the whole twelve-line catalogue feel like a closed list before the two-word phrase 'Save that' breaks it open. 'Save' means 'except' — it is the one condition that defeats the argument for dying. The grammar of the last line is carefully compressed: 'to die, I leave my love alone' means that if he were to die, he would be leaving his love solitary and unprotected in the very world whose twelve injustices he has just catalogued. Love — not fear, not hope, not ambition — is the poet's only reason to stay. Structurally, this couplet belongs to the type Puttenham calls 'epiphonema,' a summarizing concluding exclamation that gathers and resolves, though here the resolution is deliberate irony: the world is intolerable, and yet love makes it necessary.

sources.name: Puttenham

The ring-closure and volta observations are sound, but labelling the couplet 'epiphonema' (Puttenham's summarising exclamation) misfires — the couplet is a conditional exception, not an exclamation — and glossing 'to die, I leave my love alone' as leaving the beloved specifically 'unprotected' in a hostile world over-reads what the line simply says (leaving the beloved without the speaker's company).

anchor_text: wherefore with infection should he live
summary: 'Infection' means moral corruption or contamination, not physical disease. The poet asks why the youth should live alongside a world diseased by sin — as if mere proximity to vice might taint genuine virtue.
detail: OED 'infection' n. sense 4 records the figurative moral use — 'the communication of corrupt moral influence' — active throughout the sixteenth century. The opening 'Ah! wherefore' frames the whole sonnet as a kind of lament or rhetorical complaint: not a direct address to the youth but a meditation on why purity should have to coexist with corruption at all. The question is never resolved with an answer; the couplet instead offers a different framing — the youth is preserved not for his own sake but as Nature's last exhibit.

anchor_text: lace itself with his society
summary: 'Lace' here means to adorn or trim — as lace was stitched onto clothing to embellish it. Sin borrows the youth's company to dress itself up and appear respectable. 'Society' means companionship or association, not a social organization.

'Society' is used in the Elizabethan sense of 'the state of being associated with another; company, fellowship' (OED 'society' n. sense 1a). The image is precise: sin does not merely tolerate the youth — it actively attaches itself to him as ornamentation, exploiting his presence to look better than it is. The metaphor anticipates the 'false painting' imagery of the next quatrain.

anchor_text: steel dead seeming of his living hue
summary: 'Steel' means to fix or confirm — to make as hard and permanent as steel. 'Dead seeming' means a lifeless appearance or imitation. 'Hue' means complexion or color. The line says: why should false cosmetics work to confirm and preserve a dead copy of the youth's living complexion?

'Seeming' as a noun meaning 'outward appearance, semblance' is common in Shakespeare: compare Hamlet's 'I know not seems' (1.2) and Othello's 'seeming' as a key term for Iago's deception. The opposition of 'dead seeming' against 'living hue' crystallizes the sonnet's central contrast: cosmetics achieve only lifeless reproduction of what the youth embodies as a living reality. 'Hue' carries both 'color' and 'form or aspect' (OED s.v. 'hue' n.1, sense 1).

Schmidt's 'to make firm/hard' sense for 'steel' is well-supported, 'seeming' as a substantive meaning outward appearance is common in Shakespeare, and the dead-vs.-living opposition is the sonnet's genuine central contrast; the Hamlet and Othello comparisons are illustrative rather than load-bearing and do not overreach.

anchor_text: Nature bankrupt is, Beggar'd of blood to blush through lively veins
summary: Lines 9-12 build an extended financial conceit: Nature has gone bankrupt — exhausted her treasury of genuine beauty — and now survives on the youth's credit. 'Beggar'd of blood' means stripped of the vital blood that made real color in living cheeks. 'Exchequer' (line 11) is the royal treasury; 'lives upon his gains' means Nature draws her income entirely from the youth's surplus. The conceit maps economics onto beauty: the youth is Nature's only remaining asset.
detail: The volta (the turn in sonnet argument) falls here at line 9 — 'Why should he live, now Nature bankrupt is' — shifting the poem's question from 'why must purity share a corrupt world?' to 'why does Nature still need him alive?' The financial register — bankrupt, beggared, exchequer, gains — is sustained and precise. 'Exchequer' was the English government's treasury department, the repository of the Crown's financial reserves; to say Nature has 'no exchequer now but his' makes the youth her entire capital. 'Proud of many' at line 936 means Nature was once rich with many beautiful people; she is now reduced to this one. Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) discusses extended metaphor (allegoria) — sustaining a single figurative comparison across multiple lines — as a mark of sophistication.

The sustained financial conceit (bankrupt, beggared, exchequer, gains) is accurately mapped; placing the volta at line 9 is correct for the Shakespearean form and the argument does shift there; the gloss of 'proud of many' as Nature's former richness is the standard reading; the Puttenham allegoria citation is loosely applied but does not misrepresent the poem.

anchor_text: him she stores, to show what wealth she had
summary: The couplet completes the financial conceit with a darker implication: Nature keeps the youth alive as a preserved specimen — a museum piece — to demonstrate what genuine beauty once looked like 'in days long since, before these last so bad.' 'Stores' means to lay up in store, to keep in reserve. The compliment is also an isolation: he is remarkable precisely because he belongs to a lost better age that the corrupt present cannot reproduce.
detail: The phrase 'days long since, before these last so bad' encodes the classical and Renaissance myth of temporal decline — the idea that the world is deteriorating from a golden past. Compare Ovid, 'Metamorphoses' 1.89-150, on the four ages (gold, silver, bronze, iron), where each age is worse than the last; by the Iron Age the earth is full of deceit and fraud. Shakespeare need not invoke Ovid explicitly: the assumption that the present is degenerate compared to an idealized past saturates Elizabethan moral writing. 'Stores' (OED s.v. 'store' v., sense 2: 'to lay up in store, to preserve, to keep') turns Nature into a keeper of archives — the youth is her only surviving record of what beauty used to be. This couplet does not celebrate or rescue the youth; it memorializes him, and the elegiac note is quietly ominous.

The archival/specimen reading of 'stores' is defensible and widely held; invoking Ovid's four ages for the 'days long since' temporal-decline framework is appropriate (with honest hedging that Shakespeare need not cite Ovid directly); characterizing the couplet as 'elegiac and quietly ominous' rather than celebratory is a legitimate critical position, not a fringe overreach, though the text itself is ambiguous enough that 'uncertain' would also be defensible.

anchor_text: map of days outworn
summary: 'Days outworn' means the past ages, the worn-out days of long ago. The poet calls the youth's face a 'map' — a chart containing all the information of a larger territory — of that earlier world when beauty was genuine and unadorned. His face is a surviving record of what true beauty looked like before cosmetics and wigs corrupted it.

The 'map' conceit belongs to a cluster of Elizabethan metaphors in which a face, a poem, or a landscape is a compressed image of something larger; Puttenham's 'Arte of English Poesie' (1589) treats such 'resemblance by imagery' as a recognized rhetorical figure. The conceit recurs in Sonnet 106, where old chronicles are read as imperfect records of the beloved.

The 'map' as compressed record of a larger territory is a well-attested Elizabethan conceit, and the Sonnet 106 parallel (old chronicles as imperfect records of beauty) is a sound intra-corpus comparison; the gloss of 'outworn' as 'past, exhausted' fits the context without overreach.

anchor_text: bastard signs of fair were born
summary: 'Bastard' means illegitimate — not born of genuine parentage. 'Signs of fair' are outward displays of beauty. Together, 'bastard signs of fair' denotes counterfeit or artificial beauty — cosmetics and wigs that mimic natural looks without being natural. These devices 'durst inhabit on a living brow' means they dared to take up residence on a person's face.

'Signs of fair' follows a standard Elizabethan idiom in which 'fair' is used as a noun meaning 'beauty' or as an adjectival noun (OED, s.v. 'fair,' n.1, sense 1: 'beauty, fairness'). The phrase directly contrasts with the youth's authentic beauty elsewhere in the sonnet.

'Bastard' as 'counterfeit, not genuine' and 'fair' as a noun meaning 'beauty' are both mainstream Elizabethan usages that fit lines 41-42 cleanly; the reading of the phrase as denoting artificial cosmetics and wigs is the consensus interpretation and is directly supported by the cosmetics-wig context of lines 43-46.

anchor_text: golden tresses of the dead, The right of sepulchres, were shorn away, To live a second life on second head
summary: The poet objects to the Elizabethan trade in wigs made from hair cut from corpses. 'The right of sepulchres' means what belongs by right to the tomb — the hair of the dead. 'Shorn away' means shaved off before burial and sold so the dead person's hair could 'live a second life on second head' as a wig on someone else. The practice is treated as a desecration of the dead.
detail: The human-hair wig trade was substantial in late Elizabethan England; wealthy patrons paid significant sums for high-quality wigs of natural human hair. Philip Stubbes attacked it in 'The Anatomie of Abuses' (1583), condemning the cutting of dead people's hair for wigs as ungodly vanity. 'Sepulchre' derives from Latin sepulcrum (burial place); OED records it as the standard English word for a tomb or grave from the medieval period onward (OED, s.v. 'sepulchre,' n.). Shakespeare returns to the wig as a mark of inauthenticity in Sonnets 67 and again here, and in the plays (e.g., The Merchant of Venice 3.2 on cosmetic borrowings). 'Beauty's dead fleece' (line 11) compounds the image: the hair of the dead is 'fleece' — the clipped coat of a shorn animal — emphasizing its transformation from something personal and human into mere commodity.

The corpse-hair wig trade is historically attested, Stubbes's attack on it in Anatomie of Abuses is real, and the text's 'right of sepulchres' / 'shorn away' / 'live a second life on second head' makes the interpretation unambiguous; the 'fleece' reading as animal-commodity metaphor is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: him as for a map doth Nature store, To show false Art what beauty was of yore
summary: The closing couplet completes the sonnet's argument. Nature preserves the youth as a living demonstration — a map — to expose what 'false Art' (artificial cosmetics, wigs, and cosmetic craft) can only counterfeit. 'Of yore' means of old, in former times. The couplet turns the youth from a private beloved into a public standard: he is what beauty used to be before the world's corruption, and Nature keeps him on display to shame the imitators.
detail: The couplet reactivates 'map' from line 1, closing the sonnet's frame. 'Store' in the sense of 'to keep, preserve, lay up in reserve' is attested from the early sixteenth century (OED, s.v. 'store,' v., sense 1b). 'False Art' sets cosmetic craft directly against Nature: 'art' here carries its older sense of any human skill or artifice (OED, s.v. 'art,' n., sense 4), not fine art in the modern sense. 'Yore' is an archaism meaning 'a long time ago, in former times' (OED, s.v. 'yore,' n. and adv.), already slightly old-fashioned in Shakespeare's day and used here to reinforce the contrast between a pure and distant past and a fallen present. The epigrammatic snap of the couplet — the final clinching statement that the sonnet form builds toward — is the 'close' in Puttenham's sense.

anchor_text: Want nothing that the thought of hearts can mend
summary: 'Want' here means 'lack,' not 'desire.' The line says your outward appearance lacks nothing that even the most searching inner judgment of any observer could improve upon or find fault with. 'Mend' means to repair or correct a deficiency.
detail: The OED records 'want' in this sense (to be without, to lack) as the dominant meaning in early modern English; the sense of 'desire' or 'wish' is secondary. Shakespeare uses the construction elsewhere — 'I want that glib and oily art / To speak' (King Lear 1.1). 'Mend' equally means to correct or improve something defective; both words together say that no critical scrutiny could find a flaw to fix.

anchor_text: churls--their thoughts, although their eyes were kind, To thy fair flower add the rank smell of weeds
summary: 'Churls' are rough, low-bred, discourteous people — the poet's rueful admission that the judges making this inner verdict may themselves be coarse in manner, even while their judgment is right. 'Rank' means foul-smelling, coarse, and overgrown. The flower-and-weed image compresses the sonnet's whole argument: the fair outward flower (the youth's beauty) is now tainted by the rank inner smell (his conduct).

The parenthetical dash construction ('Then--churls--their thoughts') marks an interjection of the poet's own aside — acknowledging the vulgarity of the accusers while conceding that they are right. 'Rank' (OED s.v. 'rank,' adj., sense 4: 'strong and offensive in smell or taste; rancid') sets up the antithesis with 'fair flower': the language moves from visual beauty to olfactory corruption, a compression typical of the late-sequence sonnets.

anchor_text: But why thy odour matcheth not thy show, The soil is this, that thou dost common grow
summary: 'Soil' is a pun: it means both 'reason, explanation' (as in 'to soil a question,' i.e. to resolve it) and the literal earth or ground from which weeds grow — completing the flower-and-weed conceit. 'Common grow' means to become ordinary, base, and promiscuous — to lose what made you exceptional by associating with low company or low behaviour.

The couplet exploits both at once: 'The soil [resolution/diagnosis] is this, that thou dost common grow' while soil also names the ground where the rank weeds root. 'Common' in early modern English carried sharp social and moral weight: OED s.v. 'common,' adj., sense 3b: 'belonging to or shared by the general mass of people; of low social rank'; sense 9: 'of loose character, unchaste.' To 'grow common' was to descend from singular worth into base, undistinguished, or promiscuous conduct. The couplet functions as the sonnet's volta, pivoting from descriptive praise to pointed diagnosis.

The 'soil' = solution pun and 'common' = base/promiscuous readings are established, but the gloss misidentifies the couplet as 'the sonnet's volta' — the volta of a Shakespearean sonnet falls at line 9, not the couplet; the couplet is the epigrammatic resolution, and this terminological error risks confusing students about sonnet structure.

anchor_text: slander's mark was ever yet the fair
summary: The poet argues that beautiful or virtuous people have always attracted slander, so being blamed is not a sign of guilt but of distinction. 'The ornament of beauty is suspect' — suspicion is the inevitable shadow that follows genuine excellence, like a crow appearing against a clear sky.
detail: The argument draws on a classical commonplace: Socrates was condemned, Aristides exiled, Joseph falsely accused — the greatest are always targets. The crow image (line 970) works as a rhetorical illustration: no matter how pure the sky, a black bird can appear in it. That appearance does not taint the sky; it proves the sky's clarity. The logic inverts ordinary expectation — being slandered is recast as a mark of honour rather than shame.

The reading that 'slander's mark was ever yet the fair' reframes blame as a badge of distinction is textually sound and the crow simile (TLN 970) directly supports it; the classical commonplace of Socrates/Aristides is legitimate but goes beyond what the sonnet itself invokes, so the detail is slightly over-elaborated but not wrong.

anchor_text: canker vice the sweetest buds doth love
summary: 'Canker' is a disease that eats rose buds from the inside — a worm or fungal rot that destroys the most perfect flowers first. 'Canker vice' is corruption conceived as this bud-rot: evil targets what is most fresh and valuable, so the youth's purity ('unstained prime') is itself the reason he draws attack.
detail: In Elizabethan garden writing the canker or cankerworm was notorious for destroying roses at their peak. OED s.v. 'canker' n.2a cites the sense 'a caterpillar or worm that preys on plants,' especially roses. The image runs through the Sonnets: compare Sonnet 35.4 ('Roses have thorns, and silver fountains mud; / And loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud'). 'Prime' in the following line ('unstained prime') means the spring-time period of freshest growth — OED s.v. 'prime' n.1: 'the first season of the year; spring.' Together the two lines make the botanical argument: the most perfect bud draws the canker, the most virtuous youth draws slander.

anchor_text: pure unstained prime
summary: 'Prime' means the springtime of life — the earliest period of youth, when vigor and freshness are at their height. 'A pure unstained prime' says the youth's young years have not been morally corrupted: he is still at his spring, unmarked by vice.
detail: OED s.v. 'prime' n.1a: 'The first season of the year; spring' and n.5: 'The spring or early part of (a person's) life.' The botanical sense of prime (the spring season when buds are freshest) ties back directly to 'sweetest buds' and 'canker' in the line above, making the whole quatrain one extended garden metaphor: youth = spring bud, vice = canker, purity = the bud's unstained first growth. The word also carries the sense of 'first in quality' (OED n.6), so 'pure unstained prime' packs three ideas: earliest season, greatest vigor, and top quality — all as yet uncontaminated.

anchor_text: the ambush of young days
summary: Youth is figured here as a military campaign full of hidden dangers. 'Ambush of young days' means the temptations and moral hazards that lie in wait for young men, ready to ambush them before they can build any moral resistance. The youth has passed through this danger zone either untested or victorious when he was attacked.
detail: The extended military metaphor — ambush, assail, charg'd, victor — casts the moral life of a young man as a series of engagements with an unseen enemy. 'Assail'd' and 'charg'd' are terms from siege and battle. 'Charg'd' means 'attacked, charged by an enemy' (OED s.v. 'charge' v. 3a: 'to make an attack upon'). The two alternatives the poet offers — 'Either not assail'd, or victor being charg'd' — represent two kinds of safe passage: exemption from temptation, or resistance to it. Scholars note that the ambiguity is deliberate: the poet is not certain which applies, and the uncertainty subtly reopens the question the sonnet appeared to close.

anchor_text: surly sullen bell / Give warning to the world
summary: The 'bell' is the passing bell or death-knell, tolled by a parish church when someone in the community had died, to announce the death and call neighbours to pray for the soul. 'Surly sullen' gives the bell a bitter, resentful character rather than merely a mournful one. The sound would carry across the town and was the first public notice of a death.
detail: In Elizabethan England, bells served as the community's news system. The passing bell was rung as a person was dying (to summon prayers) and again at death to announce the fact. The poet uses its brevity against itself: mourn no longer than the bell rings, he says, and since the bell stops tolling within hours, that is almost no time at all. The word 'sullen' in Shakespeare's usage carried a sense of gloomy brooding or heavy darkness rather than mere sadness (OED s.v. 'sullen' adj. 2: 'dull, heavy, dismal'); 'surly' adds a quality of hostile roughness (OED s.v. 'surly' adj. 1: 'lordly, imperious,' then 'churlish, morose'). Together they personify the bell as a harsh authority rather than a comforting voice.

anchor_text: compounded am with clay
summary: 'Compounded' means mixed together and dissolved into a substance. The body after death was thought to return to the elemental matter of the earth — clay, dust — and 'compound' was the technical term for such a chemical or philosophical mixing. 'Clay' for the body of the dead appears throughout Elizabethan writing and draws on Genesis, where God forms Adam from the 'dust of the ground.'
detail: OED records 'compound' (v., sense 3) as 'to put together, combine (elements or ingredients) to form a compound substance.' Applied to the corpse it means the body has been broken down and folded into the soil's constituent matter, losing its form entirely. The philosophical background is the Galenic and Aristotelian doctrine of the four elements: a body decomposes back into earth, water, air, and fire. 'Clay' (OED s.v. 'clay' n. 2: 'the material of the human body; earth as the substance of which man is formed') echoes Genesis 2:7 — 'And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground' (Geneva 1599) — and the burial formula 'earth to earth, ashes to ashes.' The phrase 'compounded am with clay' is a passive construction that enacts the poet's loss of self: he is not a subject acting but a substance acted upon.

anchor_text: my poor name rehearse
summary: 'Rehearse' here means to repeat, go over, or recite — not to practise for a performance. The poet asks the beloved not even to say his name aloud. In Elizabethan usage 'rehearse' routinely meant any kind of repetition of words or facts, and the context of a spoken name makes the request stark: absolute silence, not even one syllable.
detail: OED s.v. 'rehearse' v. sense 1a: 'to say over, repeat (what has been said or written); to recite.' This older sense was the primary one before the theatrical meaning (to practise a play) became dominant in later English. In the sestet the poet has already asked the beloved not to 'look upon this verse' in a way that causes grief; here he extends the prohibition to speech itself. Even the utterance of a name is too much, because it would make the beloved's grief visible to 'the wise world' that might mock it (line 993).

anchor_text: the wise world should look into your moan, / And mock you with me after I am gone
summary: 'The wise world' is bitter irony: the world that considers itself knowing and shrewd is actually cold and ready to ridicule grief. The couplet gives the poet's practical reason for urging forgetting: if the beloved is seen to mourn excessively for someone the world deems unimportant, the world will mock him for it. The poet's love is so thoroughgoing that protecting the beloved from ridicule matters more than being remembered.
detail: The 'wise world' recurs across the Sonnets as a cynical social audience, quick to scorn lovers who display their feelings — see Sonnet 66 ('art made tongue-tied by authority') and Sonnet 121 ('Tis better to be vile than vile esteemed'). 'Look into' means to peer into, scrutinize, expose — the world as an intrusive observer of private grief. 'Mock you with me' means mock you by associating you with me: the poet implies he is someone the world would think unworthy of grief, and that grief for him would dishonour the beloved. This self-deprecation is deliberate — it is the same impulse that makes him ask for his 'poor name' not to be repeated. The couplet thus resolves the sonnet's argument by anchoring the self-sacrifice in a social reality: the mocking world is the final reason love should not be displayed.

anchor_text: lest the world should task you to recite
summary: 'Task' here means to call to account, to challenge someone to perform a duty. The poet fears the world will demand that the beloved explain what merit the poet possessed to deserve such love. OED records 'task' as a verb meaning 'to impose a task or burden on' and 'to call to account' from the sixteenth century.

'task' (to burden, to put to the proof). The fear of public scrutiny — of being 'tasked' to justify the love — establishes the sonnet's anxious logic: the only safe escape from that scrutiny is the beloved's silence or forgetting.

anchor_text: devise some virtuous lie, To do more for me than mine own desert
summary: A 'virtuous lie' is a deliberate falsehood told for a kind purpose — praising a man who deserves no praise. The phrase is an oxymoron, pairing a moral virtue with a moral wrong, and it captures the whole sonnet's predicament: genuine love for a worthless person can only express itself dishonestly. 'Desert' means what one deserves by right, here the poet's honest (and poor) due.
detail: The moral status of the 'pious fraud' or benevolent lie was debated in Renaissance ethics, but Shakespeare's phrasing does not endorse it — the word 'devise' (meaning to contrive or scheme) adds a note of effort and even artifice, while 'mine own desert' sets the honest standard the lie must exceed. Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) describes the figure of 'Oxymoron' (the coupling of contradictory terms) as producing sharp wit; Shakespeare here uses it to expose the paradox of self-deprecating love. OED s.v. 'desert' (n.1) cites Elizabethan use for 'what one merits or deserves by conduct.'

Reading 'virtuous lie' as an oxymoron exposing the paradox of praising a worthless man is the mainstream editorial position; the gloss on 'desert' and 'devise' is defensible, and the Puttenham reference is used loosely but not misleadingly for interpretive colour rather than as a load-bearing claim.

anchor_text: hang more praise upon deceased I Than niggard truth would willingly impart
summary: 'Niggard' means miserly, stingy, begrudging. 'Niggard truth' is honest assessment figured as a miser who doles out praise only where it is strictly owed — and, the poet implies, would owe him almost none. To 'hang more praise upon' someone is to add, as ornaments, tributes beyond what is warranted. OED records 'niggard' as an adjective meaning 'meanly sparing, grudging' from the fifteenth century.
detail: The personification of Truth as a reluctant or stingy giver was a recognized rhetorical figure. Onions ('A Shakespeare Glossary,' s.v. 'niggard') glosses the word as 'miserly, sparing.' The image of praise as something to be 'hung upon' a person — like garlands or votive offerings on a tomb — turns the couplet's worry about post-mortem reputation into something almost sculptural: will honest epitaphs leave the tomb bare? The syntactic boldness of 'deceased I' (see separate annotation) sharpens the shock of the phrase.

anchor_text: That time of year thou mayst in me behold
summary: The poet opens with the first of three sustained comparisons for his own aging: late autumn, twilight, and a dying fire. Each of the three quatrains introduces a new image, and each tightens the sense of approaching extinction. The repetition of 'In me thou see'st' at lines 5 and 9 drives the sequence forward and keeps the beloved as the observer throughout. This triple-metaphor structure is a classical device called tricolon, here adapted to the sonnet's three-quatrain form.
detail: Puttenham's 'Arte of English Poesie' (1589) codifies the tricolon (three matched members) as a figure of amplification. Shakespeare builds one at the structural level: each of the three quatrains is a complete simile (the poet IS autumn, IS twilight, IS a dying fire) rather than a passing comparison. The volta, or turn, comes not at line 9 but deferred to the couplet, so all three images accumulate before the emotional payoff. The anaphora 'In me thou see'st' (lines 5, 9) makes the progression feel inexorable. George Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589), Book III, discusses both anaphora and the cumulative amplification of tripartite structures.

anchor_text: Bare ruin'd choirs, where late the sweet birds sang
summary: A 'choir' is the chancel of a church — the section where the choir sang the daily offices. After Henry VIII dissolved the English monasteries between 1536 and 1541, more than 800 religious houses were stripped of their lead roofing and left roofless and open to the sky. Their bare stone vaults, once filled with choral singing, were a common sight across the English countryside throughout the late sixteenth century. The poet fuses the bare winter branches with those empty stone arches: both are stripped, silent, and a record of what was.
detail: Henry VIII's dissolution of the monasteries is documented in Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) and in the records of the Court of Augmentations established to administer the seized properties. By Shakespeare's day the roofless chancels were familiar landmarks in many counties; John Leland, writing a survey of England in the 1540s, described ruin after ruin still smoking from the stripping of their lead. The image is compressed: the bare boughs ARE the broken arched vaults, which WERE filled with birdsong (the choir-boys and monks who sang Matins, Vespers, and the other hours). The three elements — tree, ruin, silence — are collapsed into a single line. The historical resonance also carries a mild religious melancholy: it is not just age but a specific, violent human destruction that has silenced these 'sweet birds.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1012

The dissolution-of-the-monasteries reading is a plausible and widely discussed interpretation (Malone, Booth, Vendler all engage it), but the annotation presents it as settled fact rather than one defensible possibility among others, overstating scholarly consensus on one of the most contested lines in the Sonnets.

anchor_text: glowing of such fire, That on the ashes of his youth doth lie
summary: The third quatrain's image of a fire dying on its own ash is a paradox: the fuel that fed the fire has become the ash that smothers it, so what nourished life is now what extinguishes it. 'His' here means 'its' (the fire's own); 'expire' means both to go out — as a flame expires when it exhausts its fuel — and to breathe one's last breath, since 'expire' comes from Latin exspirare, to breathe out. The dying fire is simultaneously the poet's aging body and the consumed fuel of youth.
detail: OED records 'expire' v. in both senses from the sixteenth century: 1a, 'to breathe out'; 1b, 'to die'; and 3, '(of fire, light, etc.) to go out, become extinct.' The word applies to both tenor and vehicle at once: the fire expires (goes out) and the poet expires (dies). The paradox of 'consum'd with that which it was nourish'd by' is also physical fact — a fire generates the ash that ultimately banks and smothers it — given an existential turn: life destroys itself in the act of living, the body consuming its own vitality as fuel. The rhetorical figure is oxymoron combined with chiasmus: the nourishing agent is reidentified as the consuming one.

The core paradox reading (fuel becomes smothering ash), the 'his' = 'its' pronoun gloss, and the dual sense of 'expire' are all sound; labeling the figure 'oxymoron combined with chiasmus' is slightly overschematic but does not misread the line.

anchor_text: As the death-bed, whereon it must expire
summary: 'Expire' means both to go out (as a fire exhausts its fuel) and to breathe one's last and die, from Latin exspirare, 'to breathe out.' The word applies simultaneously to the fire and to the poet: the fire expires on its ash-bed and the poet expires on his death-bed. The 'death-bed' in this line is literally the bed of ash on which the dying embers rest, and figuratively the poet's own deathbed.

anchor_text: fell arrest / Without all bail
summary: 'Fell' means fierce or savage (OED fell, adj. 1a: 'cruel, savage, ruthless'). 'Arrest' here is a legal term: a seizure of a person by authority. The poet imagines death as a brutal bailiff or sheriff who carries the body away and accepts no bail — no payment or surety can secure release. Death is the one arrest from which there is no legal remedy.
detail: The legal metaphor of death-as-arrest was a commonplace in sixteenth-century English verse, but Shakespeare sharpens it by pairing 'fell' (which could describe a wolf or a tyrant) with the routine bureaucratic procedure of arrest. 'Without all bail' means 'without any possibility of bail whatsoever' — the word 'all' functioning as an intensifier (OED all, adv. 4: 'entirely, completely'). The conceit sets up the rest of the sonnet: if the body is what death arrests and carries off, it is only the body — the 'dregs' — that is lost. See also Sonnet 107: 'The mortal moon hath her eclipse endured.'

The death-as-bailiff legal conceit is well-attested in sixteenth-century verse and the reading of 'fell' as savage/cruel is the standard gloss; the claim that 'all' functions as an intensifier is textually sound and the OED supports it.

anchor_text: My life hath in this line some interest
summary: 'Interest' carries a double meaning: a legal share or claim (OED interest, n., sense 5a: 'a legal concern, title, or right in property'), and the plain sense of significance or importance. 'This line' means both the line of verse the reader holds and the poet's lineage or line of life. The poet is saying that his life has a legal stake — a surviving claim — in this very poem, which will remain with the beloved as a memorial after his death.
detail: The word 'interest' was already in active use in financial and legal senses by the 1590s (OED dates the legal-property sense to the fifteenth century). The pun on 'line' — a line of poetry and a thread of life — is characteristic of the mortality sonnets (compare Sonnet 63, 'his beauty in these black lines be seen'). 'Memorial' (line 1026) is the noun form of 'memory': the poem will serve as the monument that keeps the poet present in the beloved's mind, a function claimed more boldly in Sonnet 55 ('Not marble, nor the gilded monuments / Of princes, shall outlive this powerful rhyme').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1025

The double meaning of 'interest' (legal stake / significance) is defensible, but the pun on 'line' as both verse-line and lineage is an overreach — the context ('this line some interest / Which for memorial still with thee shall stay') points unambiguously to the line of verse, not to lineage, and imposing the genealogical sense muddies a clean legal-poetic conceit without textual warrant.

anchor_text: The earth can have but earth, which is his due
summary: The line echoes the burial formula drawn from Genesis: God tells Adam that because he sinned, 'dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return' (Genesis 3:19, Geneva 1599). The body is made of earth and belongs to the earth as a debt ('his due'); only the spirit is exempt from this repayment. The following line makes the contrast explicit: 'My spirit is thine, the better part of me.'
detail: The Geneva Bible's marginal note on Genesis 3:19 glosses 'dust' as referring to the material body formed in Genesis 2:7 ('the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground'). The burial service in the 1559 Book of Common Prayer rendered this as 'earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust' — a formula every Elizabethan churchgoer heard at gravesides, making the allusion instantly recognizable without requiring biblical literacy. The pronoun 'his' in 'which is his due' refers back to 'The earth' — the earth is owed the body as its rightful portion. Shakespeare uses the same conceit in Hamlet's 'Alexander returneth into dust' (5.1) and in Sonnet 146, where the body is called the 'earth' that the soul should not overfeed.

The Genesis 3:19 echo and the BCP burial formula are both unambiguously active here; the reading of 'his due' as the earth's rightful portion is the standard gloss and is supported by the explicit contrast with 'My spirit' in the following line.

anchor_text: sweet-season'd showers are to the ground
summary: 'Season'd' here means timely or occurring at the proper season — rains that arrive when the earth can use them for growth, not merely pleasant rains. The simile sets the beloved not as a luxury but as something the poet literally cannot thrive without, like rain to dry ground.

This quietly elevates the comparison above conventional Petrarchan praise of beauty.

anchor_text: Sometime all full with feasting on your sight, / And by and by clean starved for a look
summary: 'Clean' is an intensifier meaning 'completely' or 'entirely' — 'clean starved' means utterly famished, not merely a little hungry. The pair 'feasting / starved' extends the food metaphor from the opening: the poet gorges on a sight of the beloved, then is instantly, completely deprived. 'By and by' means 'shortly afterward' or 'soon.'
detail: OED records 'clean' as an adverbial intensifier ('quite, entirely, wholly') from Old English through the 17th century; it appears in this force throughout Shakespeare (e.g. 'I have forgot all' — 'the time is clean forgot,' 2 Henry IV). The rapid oscillation ('Sometime... And by and by') mimics the miser's restless anxiety; the shift from full to starved in a single line is the formal enactment of the instability described. 'Feasting on your sight' continues the literalized food conceit of lines 1-2.

anchor_text: barren of new pride
summary: 'Pride' here means showy ornament or finery — outward display rather than the emotion. The poet is asking why his verse carries no new decorative flourishes, no fashionable novelty. OED records 'pride' in the sense of fine or splendid adornment from the thirteenth century onward (OED s.v. 'pride' n., sense 4a).

Calling verse 'barren of new pride' is a self-deprecating paradox: the conventional praise-word for poetic ornament is turned into a lack. The line opens three consecutive 'Why' questions that run through line 5, a rhetorical device called anaphora, making the self-interrogation feel almost compulsive.

anchor_text: keep invention in a noted weed
summary: 'Weed' is an archaic word for garment or clothing — 'widow's weeds' (mourning clothes) preserves the same usage. 'Noted' means well-known or recognizable. So 'a noted weed' is a recognizable costume: the poet dresses his creative material ('invention') always in the same style, instantly identifiable as his own.
detail: OED traces 'weed' in the sense of a garment from Old English 'waed' (OED s.v. 'weed' n.2, sense 1a); it was already archaic-sounding by 1609, giving the image a slightly formal, heraldic tone. 'Noted' carries the sense of 'marked,' 'observed,' 'well-known' (OED s.v. 'noted' adj., sense 2). The metaphor of style as clothing — dressing thought in words — is a standard Renaissance figure drawn from classical rhetoric (Cicero, 'De Oratore' 3.25.96: thought and expression as body and garment). The poet turns it self-critically: his style is so consistent it is a uniform, not a choice.

anchor_text: you and love are still my argument
summary: 'Argument' does not mean a quarrel. It is a technical literary term for the subject matter or theme of a work — what the poem is about. 'Still my argument' means 'always my subject.' OED records this sense from the fifteenth century onward (OED s.v. 'argument' n., sense 5).
detail: The word was standard in Renaissance literary usage: prefatory 'Arguments' (prose summaries of a poem's subject) appeared before books of Spenser's 'Faerie Queene' and before Shakespeare's own 'Venus and Adonis.' To say 'you and love are still my argument' is to say that the beloved is the entire scope of the poet's creative enterprise — not just one topic among many but the only topic, a claim that recasts repetition as dedication. 'Still' throughout this sonnet consistently means 'always' (OED s.v. 'still' adv., sense 7) rather than 'at this moment,' reinforcing the theme of unvarying constancy.

'Argument' as subject-matter or theme is a well-attested Renaissance literary term and 'still' as 'always' is correct; both glosses are confirmed by OED and Onions and are essential to any plain reading of the line.

anchor_text: Thy glass will show thee how thy beauties wear
summary: 'Glass' here means a looking-glass, i.e. a mirror. 'Beauties wear' means 'your good looks wear away' — fade and erode over time, as cloth wears thin. The poet presents the mirror not as a flattering object but as a brutal instrument of self-knowledge: it shows the youth what time is doing to his face.
detail: The mirror (glass) is a recurring instrument in the Sonnets: Sonnet 3 opens 'Look in thy glass and tell the face thou viewest,' where it is pressed into the procreation argument; here it shifts from that argument toward mortality. The OED records 'glass' for mirror from the 14th century (OED s.v. 'glass' n. 4a), and 'wear' for gradual deterioration from at least 1300 (OED s.v. 'wear' v.1 9a). The memento mori function of the mirror — show the viewer not beauty but its transience — belongs to a long tradition of vanitas imagery. George Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie (1589), notes that mirrors and dials were stock emblems of time's passage in contemporary verse.

Glass = mirror and wear = gradual deterioration are both mainstream, well-attested senses, and the vanitas framing is a defensible scholarly commonplace.

anchor_text: Thy dial how thy precious minutes waste
summary: 'Dial' means a sundial (or clock-dial). 'Precious minutes waste' means your valuable minutes are being used up — squandered, drained away. The sundial, companion gift to the mirror and the blank book, shows time passing not in sudden leaps but in the almost imperceptible crawl of a shadow across the face.
detail: OED records 'dial' for a sundial from the 15th century (OED s.v. 'dial' n. 1); by the 1590s it could also mean any clock-face. 'Waste' here carries the senses of 'consume' and 'make desolate': the minutes are being emptied of their substance (OED s.v. 'waste' v. 3a, 4). The sundial is the poem's second instrument of temporal self-knowledge — more suited than the mirror to showing time's motion, because the shadow moves continuously but too slowly to see in any single moment, a quality the sonnet exploits in 'shady stealth' (TLN 1071).

anchor_text: These offices, so oft as thou wilt look
summary: 'Offices' here means duties or assigned functions — not rooms in a building. The three objects (mirror, sundial, blank book) each perform an 'office': a task appointed to them. Looking into them repeatedly ('so oft as thou wilt look') will profit the youth and fill the book with his own recorded thoughts. The couplet makes the gift interactive: the book becomes richer the more the youth uses all three.
detail: OED s.v. 'office' n. 4 records the sense of 'duty, function, or service appointed to a person or thing' from the 13th century; the word is used this way throughout Shakespeare (e.g., 'the office of a wall' in A Midsummer Night's Dream 5.1). The elegance of the closing couplet is that all three offices are unified by the verb 'look': look in the glass (mirror), look at the dial (sundial), look at the page (blank book). The promise that these offices will 'profit thee and much enrich thy book' echoes the language of accounting — time spent with these objects yields a return, like a sound investment of the 'precious minutes' mentioned at TLN 1066.

anchor_text: every alien pen hath got my use
summary: 'Alien' here means foreign, outside, belonging to another — not a stranger from another country but a rival who has no prior claim on the young man's favor. 'Pen' stands for the poet who wields it, a common metonymy. 'Got my use' means adopted my practice: the other poets have picked up the speaker's habit of drawing inspiration from the youth.
detail: OED 'alien' adj. 1: 'Belonging to another person, place, or family; not one's own.' The word carries a note of intrusion: these pens occupy a space the speaker once had to himself. 'Use' (OED sb. 13) means customary practice or habit; 'got my use' is therefore 'taken on my custom.' The phrase 'under thee their poesy disperse' (line 1082) reinforces the patronage frame: the rival poets scatter their verse abroad under the youth's name and sponsorship. The situation is the first sonnet in the Rival Poet cluster (78-86) and establishes the competitive anxiety that drives the sequence forward.

anchor_text: taught the dumb on high to sing, And heavy ignorance aloft to fly, Have added feathers to the learned's wing
summary: The second quatrain builds a contrast: the youth's eyes lift the speechless ('dumb') to sing and the uneducated ('heavy ignorance') to soar, while also giving the already-gifted poet extra lift ('added feathers to the learned's wing'). The flight imagery runs in two directions at once — it raises the low and supercharges the high — making the youth's influence universal.
detail: The flight conceit draws on Ovid's Daedalus and Icarus story as a background image of wings enabling poets to soar, but the main work here is antithesis: 'dumb' versus 'the learned's wing.' 'Heavy ignorance' is an oxymoron — ignorance is characteristically slow and earthbound, yet the youth's beauty makes it airborne. 'Feathers' added to the learned's wing implies the rival poets already had wings (skill, education) but the youth gilded them further. The phrase 'given grace a double majesty' (line 1086) closes the quatrain with a rhetorical doubling: what was already graceful becomes doubly so. Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) calls the device of raising low things by comparison 'auxesis' (amplification).

The antithesis reading (dumb/ignorant raised versus learned already-winged further elevated) is the correct mainstream interpretation; the Daedalus allusion is a loose background gesture rather than an overreach, and the Puttenham auxesis identification fits the amplifying structure.

anchor_text: that which I compile, Whose influence is thine
summary: 'Compile' in Elizabethan usage meant to compose or put together in writing — not yet narrowed to the modern sense of assembling others' work. The poet is simply saying 'what I write.' 'Influence' retains its astrological sense: a power flowing from the youth into the poem, the way stars were thought to pour invisible force down onto earthly life.

Shakespeare uses it for straightforward authorship: the compiled poem is the speaker's own composition, not an anthology. 'Influence' (OED sb. 2): in Renaissance thought, an ethereal fluid flowing from celestial bodies into earthly things, shaping temperament and events. Applied to the youth, it elevates him to near-stellar status — his beauty pours into the poem the way a planet's force pours into a human life. The coupling of the two archaic senses deepens the speaker's point: he does not merely use the youth decoratively; the youth's force is the poem's animating principle.

anchor_text: My verse alone had all thy gentle grace; But now my gracious numbers are decay'd

anchor_text: Deserves the travail of a worthier pen

anchor_text: Then thank him not for that which he doth say, Since what he owes thee, thou thyself dost pay.
summary: The closing couplet delivers the logical conclusion of the paradox: the youth owes the rival poet no gratitude, because the youth has effectively paid for every compliment himself — the raw material (his beauty, his virtue) was always his own. 'What he owes thee' means the debt the rival incurred by borrowing those qualities; the youth 'pays' it by being what he already is.

The construction is chiastic — 'what he owes thee' / 'thou thyself dost pay' — placing the rival and the youth at opposite ends of a sentence that collapses back on itself. The witty economy of the couplet is characteristic of the Shakespearean sonnet form, where the final two lines are expected to close or overturn the argument of the preceding twelve.

anchor_text: Your shallowest help will hold me up afloat, Whilst he upon your soundless deep doth ride
summary: 'Soundless' does not mean silent here: it means impossible to sound — too deep to measure with a lead-and-line, the Elizabethan navigator's tool for gauging depth. The rival poet sails the profound depths of the young man's worth; the speaker manages only the shallows. The contrast positions the two poets at opposite ends of the ocean of the youth's excellence.

'Sounding' was the standard method of depth measurement: a weighted line lowered from the ship until it struck bottom; if no bottom was found the water was 'soundless.' The contrast between the patron's 'shallowest help' (enough to keep the poet afloat) and the rival's access to 'soundless deep' carries the sonnet's central social as well as poetic argument: depth of patronage corresponds to depth of poetic ability.

anchor_text: without attaint o'erlook

anchor_text: their gross painting might be better us'd Where cheeks need blood

anchor_text: barren tender of a poet's debt
summary: 'Tender' is a legal term meaning a formal offer of payment of what is owed. A poet owes praise to a patron who inspires him; that praise-tribute is the 'poet's debt.' anchor_text: affable familiar ghost Which nightly gulls him with intelligence

anchor_text: injuries that to myself I do, Doing thee vantage, double-vantage me
summary: 'Vantage' means advantage or gain (from Old French 'avantage'). The logic — that self-abnegation earns a double profit — is worked out in two parallel moves: (1) injuring myself helps you (one vantage); (2) the very act of love directed at you enriches me spiritually (a second vantage). anchor_text: Speak of my lameness, and I straight will halt

anchor_text: Thou canst not love disgrace me half so ill, To set a form upon desired change
summary: This compressed couplet means: 'You cannot disgrace me half as badly (even to give a plausible appearance to the separation you want) as I will disgrace myself.' The poet then offers to make that effort unnecessary by destroying his own reputation so thoroughly that no further justification is needed. The logic is one of competitive self-abasement.

anchor_text: Thy sweet beloved name no more shall dwell, Lest I, too much profane, should do it wrong
summary: 'Profane' means to treat something sacred with contempt or defilement — here, to degrade the youth's name by letting it be associated with someone as unworthy as the poet. The poet borrows this register deliberately: the youth's name has the sanctity of a divine name, and his own contaminated mouth would defile it. The construction 'Lest I, too much profane, should do it wrong' — with 'profane' used as an adjective modifying 'I' — means 'lest I, being too much a profaner (i.e. one who defiles holy things), should dishonour it.' anchor_text: Give not a windy night a rainy morrow
summary: This is the sonnet's central image: a stormy night is hard to endure, but waking to a rainy day afterward is what breaks the spirit by prolonging misery. anchor_text: Some glory in their birth, some in their skill, / Some in their wealth
summary: The opening eight lines build a catalog (the rhetorical device of enumeratio) — listing seven things men pride themselves on: birth, skill, wealth, physical strength, fashionable clothes, hawks, and horses. This anaphoric repetition of 'Some in their...' creates a drumbeat that the poet then dismisses all at once. Puttenham calls such accumulation 'congeries' or 'heaping'; its purpose here is to make the dismissal in the sestet feel total.

The anaphora ('Some... Some... Some...') is the figure Puttenham calls 'Anaphora or the Figure of Report' in The Arte of English Poesie (1589), where the same word begins each clause. Its effect is both comic (the sheer accumulation) and rhetorical (it sets up a unified target for the turn in line 9). Horace uses a similar priamel — a catalog of what others prize, swept away by what the poet prizes — in the opening of Odes 1.1 ('Some delight in the Olympic dust... I rank the ivy crown of learned poets higher'); the structure is a classical lyric commonplace.

anchor_text: every humour hath his adjunct pleasure
summary: 'Humour' here means a person's dominant temperament or inclination — whatever they happen to be drawn to. Elizabethan medicine taught that four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, choler, black bile) governed personality; by extension 'humour' came to mean any governing mood or taste. 'Adjunct' means something attached as a companion or accessory to it.

By Shakespeare's time 'humour' had broadened to cover any personal taste or idiosyncratic preference, which is the sense here: every man's particular bent finds its own matching pleasure. Ben Jonson's Every Man in His Humour (1598) shows the word at the height of its fashionable currency.

anchor_text: these particulars are not my measure, / All these I better in one general best

anchor_text: For term of life thou art assured mine

anchor_text: supposing thou art true, Like a deceived husband
summary: The poet casts himself as a cuckold — a husband whose wife has taken another lover without his knowing. The comparison is precise, not merely insulting: the cuckold's defining feature is his structural inability to detect change, which is exactly the predicament the rest of the sonnet examines.

Shakespeare uses the image to isolate an epistemic condition rather than to mock: the cuckold does not fail to see the signs — he has no signs to see. That incapacity is the sonnet's subject. The image is reinforced by the closing couplet of Sonnet 92, which ends on the fear that the youth may be 'false' in ways the poet will never detect; Sonnet 93 opens by following that fear to its logical conclusion.

anchor_text: How like Eve's apple doth thy beauty grow, If thy sweet virtue answer not thy show
summary: The closing couplet compares the youth's beauty to the fruit Eve took from the forbidden tree in Genesis: beautiful to look at, but the means of human ruin. If the youth's inner virtue does not match his outward 'show' (appearance), then his lovely face is exactly like that apple — perfect on the surface, concealing catastrophe. 'Show' means outward appearance as distinct from inner truth.

Shakespeare's couplet applies that structure exactly: the beauty that draws you in may be the instrument of your undoing if it conceals the opposite of what it promises. The conditional form ('If...') is deliberately unresolved — the poet does not accuse, he raises the possibility and leaves it open, which is more destabilizing than an accusation would be. 'Show' is a charged word throughout the sonnets: OED records it as 'outward appearance as opposed to inner reality.' The Eve's apple image also glances at the youth's position in the Petrarchan tradition — where the beloved's beauty was supposed to be a sign of inner virtue (Platonic beauty theory), this couplet asks whether that equation can be trusted.

anchor_text: husband nature's riches from expense
summary: 'Husband' here is a verb meaning to manage frugally, to save and conserve. 'Expense' means spending or expenditure (from Latin 'expensa,' laid out). The line says the self-contained person carefully preserves what nature has given him rather than squandering it. The agricultural sense of 'husbandry' — careful management of land and resources — is present throughout the early sonnets as a running metaphor for how one's gifts should be used.

'Expense' in the sense of 'spending, expenditure, waste' (OED n. 1a) runs through the sonnets: compare Sonnet 30 ('sessions of sweet silent thought / I summon up remembrance of things past... with old woes new wail my dear time's waste') and Sonnet 129 ('Th'expense of spirit in a waste of shame'). The cluster of economic terms — 'inherit,' 'husband,' 'expense,' 'lords and owners,' 'stewards' — builds the poem's governing metaphor: personal virtue as an estate to be managed wisely or squandered.
