anchor_text: lords and owners of their faces
summary: The poem draws a sharp legal contrast between two kinds of person: 'lords and owners,' who possess their gifts outright, and mere 'stewards,' who hold them in trust for another and must render account. A steward in Elizabethan law and household practice managed a great estate on behalf of its owner but had no personal claim to what he administered. The distinction reframes personal beauty and talent as forms of property that some people genuinely hold while others only borrow.
detail: The vocabulary is drawn from property and estate management. 'Lord' in the period denotes the holder of a freehold — one who owns absolutely. A 'steward' was the officer who ran a nobleman's household or estate, controlling its revenues and disbursements but always acting as an agent of the true owner (compare the steward Malvolio in Twelfth Night, or Joseph as steward of Potiphar's house). The parable invites the reader to ask which type the youth is: one who truly possesses his own excellence, or one who merely administers a gift that belongs to nature or heaven, and who may be called to account for its use. The distinction quietly anticipates the sestet's warning.

The lord/steward property-law contrast is grounded directly in the text and the Elizabethan estate-management vocabulary; the reading that 'faces' stands synecdochically for all outward gifts is mainstream and defensible.

anchor_text: if that flower with base infection meet
summary: 'Base' means low, ignoble, or morally degraded. 'Infection' in Elizabethan usage could mean any corrupting disease or moral contamination, not only bacterial illness. 'Outbraves' means surpasses in fine appearance or display — the infected lily is actually outdone in dignity by the humblest weed. The comparison turns the social hierarchy of the octave (lords versus stewards) into a natural hierarchy that the corrupted can fall below entirely.
detail: OED records 'base' in senses of 'of low moral quality, mean, vile' (adj. 5a) and 'infection' as 'moral corruption, depravation' (n. 4a) as well as physical disease. 'Outbrave' (OED v. 1: 'to surpass in bravery, fineness, or ostentation') is a Shakespearean formation. The corrupted lily does not merely equal the weed — it falls below it, because the greater the original beauty, the more conspicuous its corruption. The Elizabethan language of 'infection' routinely moved between physical and moral registers without distinction, so readers would hear both senses simultaneously.

The dual physical/moral register of 'infection,' the sense of 'base,' and 'outbraves' are all correctly glossed and the logic that greater original beauty makes corruption more conspicuous is a sound reading of the sestet's argument.

anchor_text: canker in the fragrant rose, Doth spot the beauty
summary: A 'canker' is a plant disease — a spreading rot or blight that eats into stems and buds from within. Here the youth's shame is the hidden corruption inside an otherwise beautiful flower: the rose still looks and smells lovely to the world, but the rot is real. 'Spot' means to blemish or stain.
detail: The canker-in-the-rose image recurs in Shakespeare as the emblem of concealed corruption that beauty cannot cure: 'Loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud' (Sonnet 35); 'the canker galls the infants of the spring' (Hamlet 1.3). OED records 'canker' in the plant-disease sense from the sixteenth century onward, distinct from the ulcer sense. The poet's point is not that the youth is wholly corrupt, but that the rot is real even when it cannot be seen — which makes the beauty more, not less, troubling.

The canker-in-the-rose gloss is textually grounded, the image is recurrent in Shakespeare (Sonnet 35 is correctly cited), and the reading that concealment makes the corruption worse — not lesser — is the mainstream scholarly interpretation.

anchor_text: what a mansion have those vices got, Which for their habitation chose out thee
summary: The poet personifies the youth's vices as tenants who have found an extraordinarily grand lodging. A 'mansion' is simply a large, fine dwelling place — the youth's beauty is so magnificent a house that even vices are elevated by living in it. 'Habitation' means dwelling or place of residence. The device is ironic: the vices are lucky to have found such distinguished quarters.
detail: OED records 'mansion' in the sense of 'a place of abode, a dwelling-place, an abode' (sense 1a) long before it narrowed to its modern sense of a large country house; the word carries no necessary implication of grandeur in Elizabethan usage beyond 'a place where one stays.' Shakespeare uses it in this neutral-to-elevated sense in the sonnets: 'beauty's mansion' (Sonnet 3). The personification of vices as house-hunters who inspect properties and choose the finest is a miniature allegory — a compressed version of the morality-play convention in which abstract qualities inhabit a human being like lodgers. The irony is that the youth's beauty has made him attractive real estate for sin.

The reading of vices as tenants in the youth's beauty is the plain sense of lines 1325-1326; noting that 'mansion' simply means 'dwelling' (not necessarily a grand house) is a legitimate clarification, and the morality-play lodger comparison is a standard gloss for this conceit without over-reaching.

anchor_text: beauty's veil doth cover every blot, And all things turns to fair that eyes can see
summary: This is the central conceit of the sonnet. A 'veil' is a covering that hides what is beneath it; a 'blot' is a stain or moral blemish. The poet says the youth's beauty acts like a veil that transforms every fault into something the world reads as attractive. Because people can only see the surface, everything about the youth appears fair — the beauty literally converts the ugly to the beautiful for any observer.
detail: The image is darker than it first sounds. In Renaissance moral thought, a veil that conceals vice from sight is itself a moral problem — the danger is not just that the youth gets away with his faults but that beauty is functioning as a systematic deceiver, seducing both the world and (by implication) the poet into false judgments. This sets up the volta in the couplet: the word 'Take heed' at line 13 is the turn, signalling that the poet steps back from admiring the deception to warn against depending on it. Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) describes the conceit (the sustained metaphor or 'allegoria') as the figure that allows the poet to praise and blame simultaneously by clothing meaning in an image.

The veil-as-deceiver gloss is defensible, but identifying line 1329 ('Take heed') as the sonnet's volta is an interpretive claim that overreaches slightly — in a Shakespearean sonnet the couplet is a structural unit distinct from the Petrarchan volta, and the shift of argument here is an expected formal feature, not a special dramatic reversal; the annotation conflates Petrarchan and Shakespearean form distinctions after correctly distinguishing them, creating a minor interna

anchor_text: The hardest knife ill-us'd doth lose his edge
summary: The closing couplet ends on a proverb: even the finest knife, if used carelessly or for the wrong purpose, will go dull. 'His' is the Elizabethan possessive for 'its.' The lesson is that the youth's beauty — however exceptional — has limits. Misuse wears out even the best instruments. The couplet makes the warning of 'Take heed' specific: the privilege of beauty is not permanent.
detail: The proverb was current in Elizabethan England; Tilley records the analogous 'The best things, if abused, hurt most' (M 462) and related sayings about tools worn out by misuse. The knife metaphor is a deliberate change of register: the preceding twelve lines work in the organic language of roses, beauty, and mansions; the couplet introduces something hard-edged, mechanical, and deliberately unromantic. The 'hardest knife' — the best steel — going dull from ill-use is the plainest possible way of saying that exceptional gifts cannot indefinitely absorb their own abuse. The use of 'his' as a possessive for an inanimate object ('its' was still settling into English; 'his' was the older form) is standard Elizabethan usage, not a personification.

The proverb reading is the unanimous scholarly gloss; the register-shift observation (organic imagery yielding to hard-edged mechanical imagery) is a well-established critical point; and the note on 'his' as the Elizabethan genitive of 'it' is accurate and helpfully pre-empts a common misreading.

anchor_text: thy fault is youth, some wantonness
summary: 'Wantonness' meant reckless, undisciplined behavior — pleasure-seeking without self-restraint, and often specifically sexual license. The word set the charge the speaker is weighing: some critics call the youth's conduct mere youthful excess, others call it deliberate lewdness.
detail: OED records 'wantonness' from the fourteenth century with the core sense of unrestraint or lack of discipline; by Shakespeare's time it had gathered a strong secondary sense of lascivious or lewd conduct ('wanton' as an adjective meaning unchaste is common across the canon). The two diagnoses — 'youth' (innocent immaturity) and 'wantonness' (culpable license) — set up the sonnet's argument: observers disagree, yet the youth's charm somehow overrides the distinction. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'wantonness,' distinguishes the sense of playful recklessness from the explicitly sexual sense; both may be in play here, the ambiguity being part of the point.

anchor_text: lov'd of more and less
summary: 'More and less' is an Elizabethan idiom meaning 'great and small' — that is, people of high rank and people of low rank alike. The line says the youth is loved by everyone across the entire social order, not just by one class of admirer.

The phrase is not about degree of feeling but about social degree. The sonnet's claim is thus surprisingly sweeping: the youth's simultaneous 'faults' and 'graces' attract not a particular type of admirer but the whole human range.

anchor_text: lambs might the stern wolf betray, / If like a lamb he could his looks translate
summary: The image of a wolf disguised as a lamb comes from Jesus's warning in Matthew 7:15: 'Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheepes clothing, but inwardly they are rauening wolues' (Geneva 1599). The speaker turns the image on the youth: because he already looks innocent, he could, if he chose, deceive any number of unsuspecting admirers as effectively as a wolf in a fleece.
detail: The wolf-in-lamb's-clothing was among the most widely recognized biblical images in Elizabethan England, preached from pulpits and cited in the official Homilies. Shakespeare typically inverts or complicates standard typology: here the youth is not the deceiver-wolf but a person whose natural appearance of innocence gives him the wolf's potential power of deception without the wolf's malicious intent. The conditional framing ('might... if... could') leaves the youth's moral character ambiguous — the speaker imagines the danger without accusing him of it. The word 'betray' confirms the biblical register: in Matthew the false prophet's deception is a betrayal of the flock he pretends to shepherd.

anchor_text: the strength of all thy state
summary: 'State' here means the full weight of the youth's social standing, personal authority, and physical magnetism combined — the total power his rank and presence give him over those who see him. 'The strength of all thy state' is the maximum force he could bring to bear if he chose to use it deliberately.

In the Sonnets 'state' often fuses social rank with the physical bearing that embodies it — as in Sonnet 94, where those who 'have power to hurt and will do none' are described through a similar vocabulary of latent, restrained authority. The line implies that the youth currently holds back: his charm operates incidentally, not as a calculated seduction. The speaker's unease is that the full, deliberate deployment of that power would be irresistible.

anchor_text: I love thee in such sort, / As, thou being mine, mine is thy good report
summary: The closing couplet of Sonnet 96 is nearly word-for-word identical to the closing couplet of Sonnet 36 ('As thou being mine, mine is thy good report'). Whether this repetition was intentional — an echo signaling that the two sonnets share a theme about the intertwining of the poet's and the youth's reputations — or a scribal or compositorial accident in the 1609 printing, has been debated for centuries.
detail: Sonnet 36 closes: 'As thou being mine, mine is thy good report.' Sonnet 96 closes: 'As, thou being mine, mine is thy good report' — differing only in the comma after 'As.' The repetition is unique in the 1609 Quarto; no other couplet is duplicated. Editors have proposed three explanations: (1) intentional echo, reinforcing a shared subject across the two sonnets and the surrounding cluster (93-96 all circle around the youth's power of appearance); (2) scribal error in the manuscript, with the copyist importing the couplet from memory; (3) compositorial error in Thomas Thorpe's print shop. Because the 1609 Quarto is the sole text and there is no manuscript evidence, the question cannot be resolved. A reader who takes the repetition as intentional will hear the couplet as a kind of refrain, gathering the poet's exposure of vulnerability each time: his own reputation is mortgaged to the youth's conduct. See the-1609-quarto-and-mr-wh for the publication context.

The duplicated couplet is a well-established textual fact, and the three standard explanations (intentional echo, scribal error, compositorial error) fairly represent mainstream editorial debate without overclaiming.

anchor_text: the pleasure of the fleeting year
summary: The poet addresses the Fair Youth as the thing that gives the year its meaning -- the one pleasure that makes the passing seasons worthwhile. 'Fleeting' (rapidly passing) names the year as something that slips away; the youth is what redeems it. This opening sets up the sonnet's central paradox: summer passed, and with it any pleasure the year contained.
detail: The construction is an appositive: 'thee, the pleasure of the fleeting year' -- 'the pleasure' stands in apposition to 'thee,' equating the person with the year's whole significance. 'Fleeting' carries its full force of swift, unstoppable motion (OED s.v. 'fleeting,' adj. 1: 'That passes or disappears rapidly; transient, transitory'). The line establishes why the absence registers as winter: if the youth is the year's pleasure, his absence empties the year of whatever made its seasons feel like anything at all.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1346

anchor_text: teeming autumn, big with rich increase, Bearing the wanton burden of the prime
summary: 'Teeming' means heavily productive, swarming with fruit -- its root sense is 'pregnant' or 'bringing forth young.' 'Prime' here means spring, not primacy: autumn 'bears the wanton burden of the prime' because it carries to harvest the offspring that spring generated freely ('wanton' = unrestrained, freely given). The cluster turns the season into a pregnant figure bringing another season's children to term.
detail: 'Teeming' (OED s.v. 'teem,' v.2: to bring forth, to be prolific, from Old English team, offspring) keeps its biological sense active in Shakespeare: compare 'the teeming earth' (Richard II 3.2). 'Wanton' in this period means unrestrained, freely bestowed, without governance -- not always with a sexual connotation, though here spring's generative excess carries that charge. 'Burden' can mean both a load carried and, in music, a refrain -- both senses press: autumn heaves the weight of spring's produce. The lines build the central irony: a visibly fecund autumn should feel like abundance, but without the youth the poet experiences it as hollowness.

anchor_text: widow'd wombs after their lords' decease
summary: Autumn's harvests are compared to children born to widows after their husbands have died. The 'lords' are the summer sun and spring -- the generating seasons, now dead and gone -- and the autumn fruit is their posthumous issue. The comparison makes abundance feel like grief: the harvest is real, but the force that made it possible is absent.
detail: The legal and emotional resonance of 'widow'd wombs after their lords' decease' is precise: in Elizabethan law, children born up to ten months after a husband's death could be legitimate and inherit; such posthumous children belonged to a dead man and bore his name, yet he never saw them. The analogy maps onto the sonnet's situation: just as the widow's child is orphaned before birth -- rich with its father's nature but fatherless -- so autumn's fruit ('unfather'd fruit,' line 1354) exists in full physical abundance but without the presiding principle that gives it meaning. 'Lords' puns on 'lord' as master and as husband, both senses applicable to the dominant summer sun.

anchor_text: hope of orphans, and unfather'd fruit
summary: 'Unfather'd' means fatherless -- the harvest exists but is orphaned from the summer that generated it. 'Hope of orphans' means the kind of hope orphans have: thin, dependent, easily crushed. The paired images say that autumn's abundance, for all its visual richness, feels like the anxious hope of children who have no father to secure their future.

The metaphysical extension is that the fruit is fatherless because 'summer and his pleasures wait on thee' (line 1355): summer itself follows the youth, so wherever the youth is not, summer is not, and the fruit summer generates is parentless. 'Hope of orphans' glosses the fruit's condition in emotional rather than physical terms: orphans' hope is real but fragile, dependent on the goodwill of the world rather than the certainty of parental support. anchor_text: figures of delight, / Drawn after you, you pattern of all those
summary: 'Figures' here means copies or representations. The poet inverts the standard praise comparison: the lily and the rose are not models the beloved resembles, but copies 'drawn after' him. Sonnet 18 ('Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?') says the youth surpasses nature; here the logic goes further: the youth is nature's original source. anchor_text: with your shadow I with these did play
summary: 'Shadow' in Elizabethan English regularly meant a copy, image, or reflected likeness — something that resembles an original without being it. The flowers are the beloved's 'shadow': representations of him without his substance. The speaker has been amusing himself with pale imitations, not the real person.

The verb 'play' also carries a theatrical undertone: the speaker has been staging a performance of delight using stand-ins, understudies for the absent original. The couplet thus admits the futility of the whole twelve lines: spring's display was a shadow-play, and the speaker knew it all along.

anchor_text: The forward violet thus did I chide
summary: 'Forward' here means bold, presumptuous, or premature. The violet has bloomed early and dared to smell sweet before earning the right -- its forwardness is an affront, which is why the poet 'chides' (scolds) it.

'Chide' (OED 'chide' v. 1) means to scold or rebuke, usually from a position of authority -- so the poet plays mock-magistrate to the offending flower.

anchor_text: buds of marjoram had stol'n thy hair
summary: Marjoram is a fragrant herb with small, densely clustered buds and a soft, downy texture. The poet sees its buds as resembling the youth's hair in color and softness -- close enough that the plant must have stolen the look.
detail: Sweet marjoram (Origanum majorana) was a common English garden herb, well known for its sweet scent and the small, velvety, closely packed buds that appear before the tiny flowers open. John Gerard's Herball (1597) describes marjoram's soft, woolly leaves and notes its garden familiarity. The color of the fresh buds ranges from pale green to soft brownish-gold -- easily figured as resembling fair or light-brown hair in its texture and close-set quality. Shakespeare uses marjoram elsewhere as an emblem of delicacy and sweetness (All's Well That Ends Well 4.5: 'the sweet marjoram of the sallet'). The theft-conceit allows a tactile comparison (softness) that a straightforward blazon simile could not as easily achieve.

anchor_text: More flowers I noted, yet I none could see
summary: Sonnet 99 is the only poem in the entire 1609 sequence with fifteen lines instead of fourteen. The extra line extends the opening address to the violet, creating a five-line opening. Whether this is deliberate formal excess or a scribal or printing error is unresolved.
detail: The 1609 quarto (Shake-speares Sonnets, Thomas Thorpe, Q1609) prints the poem as fifteen lines with no indication of error. Editors have proposed three explanations: (1) an authorial surplus line that Shakespeare never cut; (2) a scribal interpolation in the manuscript before it reached Thorpe; (3) a deliberate choice, in which the poem's own proliferating logic -- flowers that cannot stop stealing -- is enacted by a poem that cannot confine itself to fourteen lines. Some editors read the opening line ('The forward violet thus did I chide:') as a separate exordium standing outside the quatrain structure, after which a standard 14-line sonnet follows from line 2. All editors retain the fifteen-line text from Q1609; none has commanded consensus on the question of intention.

anchor_text: Where art thou Muse that thou forget'st so long
summary: The poet directly addresses his Muse -- the divine source of poetic inspiration. In classical tradition, the nine Muses were daughters of Zeus and Memory who presided over the arts; invoking them was the standard opening gesture of epic poetry. Shakespeare here adapts the device from solemn invocation to affectionate reproach, treating his Muse as a truant who has wasted her 'fury' -- her sacred frenzy -- on lesser subjects.
detail: Homer opens both the Iliad and the Odyssey by calling on the Muse to sing; Virgil opens the Aeneid the same way. The convention was so standard that Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) notes that English poets inherited the invocation from 'the old Poets.' The word 'fury' for poetic inspiration (Latin furor poeticus) was transmitted to Renaissance readers through Cicero; Sidney in 'The Defence of Poesy' (1595) discusses the 'divine force' the Muse gives the poet. Shakespeare's turn is to make the Muse not a lofty cosmic power but a delinquent who needs scolding back to her duty.

The classical-invocation-as-reproach reading is mainstream and well-supported; describing the poem as 'affectionate' scolding rather than solemn invocation accurately captures the tone of the sestet's commands.

'Darkening thy power to lend base subjects light' means that pouring her inspiration into trivial poems dims the Muse's own creative force while illuminating unworthy material: the Muse's power is finite and spent on the wrong thing.

'Gentle' means both polished and worthy of the beloved's refined nature.

anchor_text: prevent'st his scythe and crooked knife
summary: 'Prevent'st' means forestall or arrive before -- to 'prevent Time's scythe' is to get there first, to immortalize the beloved in verse before Time destroys him. 'His scythe and crooked knife' are the traditional tools of Time personified as the harvester of life: the scythe cuts down the living like grain, and the crooked knife (a pruning sickle) trims what regrows. The couplet frames the poem itself as a race against death.

The image of Time as a harvester with a scythe was the dominant visual shorthand of the period, present in emblem books such as Whitney's 'A Choice of Emblemes' (1586). The same image appears across the sequence: Sonnet 60 has 'nothing stands but for his scythe to mow' and Sonnet 12 offers 'nothing 'gainst Time's scythe can make defence.' Here, poetry has replaced procreation as the means of outrunning Time.

anchor_text: O truant Muse what shall be thy amends
summary: 'Truant' means one who shirks a duty or deserts a post without leave. The poet addresses his own Muse as a defaulting pupil who owes reparation ('amends'). The schoolroom reproach reverses the usual convention in which the poet humbly petitions the Muse for help; here the poet is her judge.

The apostrophe to the Muse -- addressing a personified figure as if present -- is standard in classical and Elizabethan verse invocations; Puttenham classifies it as 'apostrophe' and notes its compulsive rhetorical force (The Arte of English Poesie, 1589, Book III, ch. 19). Sidney's Astrophil and Stella Sonnet 1 uses the same device but in the opposite direction: the Muse commands the poet ('Fool, said my Muse to me, look in thy heart and write'). Shakespeare's inversion -- poet commanding Muse -- frames the whole sonnet as a demand for professional reparation, not a prayer for inspiration.

anchor_text: truth in beauty dy'd
summary: 'Dy'd' is the past tense of 'to dye' -- to color by steeping -- not of 'to die.' Truth has been dyed into beauty: the beloved is a living fusion in which truth takes a beautiful outward form, and beauty is given inward substance by truth. The 16th-century spellings of 'dye' and 'die' overlapped, so the shadow of mortal dying quietly presses on the image.

The metaphor carries into lines 7-8, where beauty is said already to have its colour 'fix'd' -- permanently dyed in the beloved rather than applied from outside. The audible pun on mortal 'die' introduces the time-and-mortality anxiety that the couplet then resolves by asserting the verse's power to preserve.

Reading 'dy'd' as 'dyed' (primary) with the audible secondary pun on 'die' is the mainstream editorial consensus (Booth, Kerrigan, Duncan-Jones), and the extension into the 'colour fix'd' imagery of lines 7-8 is accurate to the text.

anchor_text: Truth needs no colour, with his colour fix'd; Beauty no pencil, beauty's truth to lay
summary: 'Colour' carries two meanings: the natural hue already in the beloved, and rhetorical embellishment -- the verbal 'colours' a poet applies. 'Pencil' is a painter's fine brush (not a writing implement), and 'to lay' means to apply pigment to a surface. The Muse's imagined excuse is that perfect natural beauty needs no cosmetic paint and no poetic ornamentation, because truth is already 'fix'd' (permanently stained) in the beloved.
detail: Elizabethan rhetoric used 'colours' (Latin colores) as a technical term for verbal ornaments: Puttenham devotes much of Book III of The Arte of English Poesie (1589) to cataloguing rhetorical 'colours.' 'Pencil' in the period meant exclusively a fine-tipped brush used by portrait painters (OED s.v. 'pencil', n., sense 1a: 'a small fine brush used in painting'), not a graphite writing stick; the modern sense only emerged later. 'To lay' colour is the painter's verb for applying a coat of pigment (OED s.v. 'lay', v., sense 42). The Muse is imagined to argue that the beloved's beauty is so inherently truthful that adding poetic 'colour' would be as redundant as painting a lily; the couplet clinches it -- 'But best is best, if never intermix'd.' The poet then demolishes this logic: the Muse's duty is not improvement but preservation.

anchor_text: for't lies in thee To make him much outlive a gilded tomb
summary: A 'gilded tomb' is a stone monument covered in gold leaf -- the most expensive memorial the Elizabethan wealthy could commission. Gilding -- applying gold leaf to alabaster or stone effigies -- was the standard finish for high-status Tudor and Jacobean church monuments; the families of noblemen and bishops paid craftsmen to maintain these gilded surfaces against weathering. The Muse, the poet argues, has the one power that no sculptor has: to make the beloved legible to readers 'of ages yet to be.'

anchor_text: sweets grown common lose their dear delight

anchor_text: when first your eye I ey'd

anchor_text: Let not my love be call'd idolatry
summary: Idolatry is the worship of an idol — an image or object treated as divine — and by extension any excessive devotion to something that does not merit it. Shakespeare makes the charge explicit here and builds the whole sonnet as a refutation: devotion to one person who is genuinely 'fair, kind, and true' is not idolatry but something closer to the right worship of a real excellence.

anchor_text: they looked but with divining eyes, / They had not skill enough your worth to sing
summary: 'Divining' means prophesying or seeing the future; a 'diviner' was a prophet or seer. The old poets looked at their contemporaries with eyes that were, without knowing it, prophetic — they sensed something ideal they could not fully articulate. The couplet that follows completes the thought: even the speaker, who has the actual beloved in front of him, lacks the words to praise adequately. Past poets lacked the original; the present poet lacks the tongue.
detail: OED records 'divine' (v.) in the sense 'to have a presentiment of, to conjecture or guess at beforehand' (sense 5a) throughout the sixteenth century. The word-group — 'divining,' 'prophecies,' 'prefiguring' — sustains the theological register throughout the sestet. The implied argument is a paradox: the closer you are to the beloved, the more speechless the encounter makes you. Distance gave the old poets freedom to approximate; nearness leaves the speaker wordless. This is the 'inexpressibility topos' — the classical and Renaissance convention of claiming the subject exceeds what language can hold — but it is turned with particular precision: not 'I cannot praise you adequately' in the abstract, but 'I, who can see you, am worse placed than those who could only guess.'

anchor_text: lease of my true love control
summary: 'Lease' is a contract giving a tenant use of property for a fixed term; when the term ends, the property reverts to the landlord. The poet says that neither his own fears nor the world's prophetic dread could 'control' (govern, put a limit on) his love, even though it was 'supposed as forfeit to a confin'd doom' — assumed to be lost when its short legal term ran out. 'Confin'd doom' means a limited or predetermined ending — the 'doom' (judgment, fate) that was supposed to end the love. The opening conceit positions love's survival as a legal miracle: the lease should have lapsed, but it stands.

anchor_text: sad augurs mock their own presage
summary: 'Augurs' in Rome were priests who predicted the future by reading the flight of birds and the entrails of sacrificed animals. By Shakespeare's day the word had widened to mean any prophet of doom. 'Presage' means a prophecy or forewarning. Here the gloomy predictors who had forecast catastrophe at Elizabeth's death find their own prophecies mocked — proven false — by the peaceable succession. The 'sad' means 'grave, grim' rather than sorrowful.

Shakespeare uses the same semantic field in Hamlet's 'we defy augury' (5.2), where Hamlet dismisses omen-reading before his fatal duel. Here the tone is triumphant rather than defiant: the prophets did not merely fail but are made to look foolish. The word 'mock' carries its full Elizabethan force of exposing something as a sham.

anchor_text: Death to me subscribes
summary: 'Subscribes' means yields, concedes, or submits — literally 'writes beneath,' as a defeated party signs below an agreement. The word belonged to the language of legal instruments and formal submission; to subscribe was to acknowledge another's authority.

anchor_text: like prayers divine, I must each day say o'er the very same
summary: The speaker answers his own question with an analogy to daily prayer: repetition is not staleness but ritual fidelity. The sonnet quietly answers the Puritan objection: prayer's power comes not from novelty but from the constancy of the heart that repeats it. The phrase 'say o'er' means to recite or repeat, especially of prayers (OED s.v. 'say,' v., sense 10b).

anchor_text: if I have rang'd, / Like him that travels
summary: 'Rang'd' means wandered or strayed from a fixed point — used of hunting hounds running wide of the pack, or of a person roved from home. The poet openly concedes he has been away and unfocused, but frames it as a traveler's detour, not a permanent departure.

The analogy to the traveler who 'return[s] again / Just to the time' converts the admission into evidence of faithfulness — a traveler always comes home, so ranging is not betrayal.

anchor_text: Just to the time, not with the time exchang'd
summary: A compressed, antithetical line: 'just to the time' means punctual, arriving on time; 'not with the time exchang'd' means not altered by the time away — the speaker returns when expected and returns unchanged. 'Exchang'd' means transformed or swapped out for something different.

'Exchang'd' carries its period sense of transformed or substituted: to be 'exchang'd with the time' would mean to have been reshaped by one's experiences during absence, as if a different person came back. The line denies both lateness and alteration, and the chiastic structure (time / exchanged with time) signals the volta turning from concession toward vindication.

anchor_text: it could so preposterously be stain'd
summary: 'Preposterously' does not simply mean absurdly. Its Latin root is 'praeposterus' — 'with the last before the first' — and it means against natural order, the wrong thing put first. To abandon the beloved's 'sum of good' for nothing would invert all proper valuation, putting worthlessness above worth.

The etymological force (Latin prae, 'before' + posterus, 'coming after': thus, the posterior before the prior) was felt strongly in Shakespeare's day as a term meaning contrary to nature and right order. The word's logic reinforces the argument of the third quatrain: all ordinary human frailties ('all frailties that besiege all kinds of blood') might affect the speaker, but none could reverse the fundamental order in which the beloved's 'sum of good' is the highest value. anchor_text: guilty goddess of my harmful deeds
summary: Fortune was a Roman goddess imagined as turning a great wheel that raised and cast down men without reason or mercy. The poet calls her 'guilty' because she assigned him a low, public trade rather than a station of dignity — making her responsible for what he has become. Calling her 'guilty' is unusual; it shifts blame from the poet to the force that placed him.
detail: Boethius's Consolatio Philosophiae (II, prose 1-2) gave the Middle Ages and Renaissance their central image of Fortune spinning her wheel, indifferent to merit. The Roman Fortuna was proverbially blind and capricious — a 'strumpet' in Hamlet's terms — dispensing luck without judgment. To address Fortune directly and charge her with guilt inverts the standard consolation (which tells the sufferer to detach from Fortune's gifts); the poet accuses her rather than submitting to her. The accusation frames the whole octave: Fortune chose his livelihood, Fortune is responsible for the stigma that followed.

anchor_text: public means which public manners breeds
summary: 'Public means' is a livelihood earned before a paying public audience — almost certainly a reference to acting. Elizabethan actors were socially suspect: they were legally classified near vagabonds unless they had a noble patron, and the stage was attacked as a school of immorality. The line says that earning a living this way inevitably shapes — 'breeds' — a coarser, more public set of habits and values.

A player's 'name receives a brand' in the next line: 'brand' had specific force as the mark burned into convicted criminals and vagrants. That the poet connects the stigma to his livelihood rather than to personal vice is the sonnet's pointed self-defense: Fortune, not character, made him a public man. The same self-consciousness about the player's social position runs through Sonnet 110 ('I have gone here and there, / And made myself a motley to the view').

anchor_text: my name receives a brand
summary: A 'brand' is a mark burned into the skin of criminals and escaped servants in early modern England as a permanent sign of disgrace. Livestock were branded; convicted rogues and those whipped for vagrancy could be branded on the shoulder or cheek. The poet says his public livelihood has stamped him with this kind of indelible stigma — not on his body, but on his name and reputation.

The word 'brand' carries both the hot iron and the resulting mark, giving it force as something both violent and permanent. In this context the 'brand' is metaphorical — a social stigma attached to his name because of his trade — but the physical violence of the image is part of the point: it is not a mild embarrassment but a lasting, public mark of dishonor.

anchor_text: my nature is subdu'd / To what it works in, like the dyer's hand
summary: A dyer — someone who colors cloth in vats of pigment — cannot wash the dye out of his hands; the color becomes permanent. The simile makes the point that the poet's character ('nature') has been stained by long immersion in his public trade the same way: the work has entered him and cannot be scrubbed out. 'Subdu'd' means overcome, brought under the power of something else.
detail: The dyer's-hand image is the sonnet's controlling conceit and its most precisely observed metaphor. 'Subdu'd to what it works in' picks up the language of subjection and craft simultaneously: workers were said to be mastered by their trade. The image is morally neutral — a dyer's stained hands are not a fault, they are simply the unavoidable mark of the work — which mirrors the poet's defensive posture: he is not vicious, he is marked. Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie (1589) discusses simile as a device that illuminates an abstract quality through a concrete familiar thing; here the familiar thing (a craftsman's hands) makes palpable something invisible (the corruption of character).

The core reading of the dyer simile — craft-immersion staining character as dye stains hands, 'subdu'd' as overcome/subjugated — is sound; the claim that the image is 'morally neutral' is a defensible interpretive shade held by major editors.

anchor_text: Potions of eisel 'gainst my strong infection
summary: 'Eisel' is an archaic word for vinegar — specifically the strong, bitter vinegar used as a medicine and as a liquid of penance. The image is of the poet agreeing to dose himself with the harshest available remedy, accepting the bitterness without complaint. Vinegar was used in early modern medicine to treat fevers and purge infection, and the word carried a secondary resonance from the vinegar offered to Christ on the cross.
detail: The word derives from Old French 'aisil,' ultimately from Latin 'acetum' (vinegar). The OED cites it in English verse from at least the 13th century; it appears in Wycliffite biblical translation for the vinegar given to Christ at the Crucifixion (John 19:29-30). In this sonnet 'eisel' against a 'strong infection' casts the speaker's penance in medical terms — he is diseased by his public trade and will self-administer bitter cure — while the Passion resonance (vinegar at the cross) adds a note of voluntary suffering willingly embraced. Hamlet uses the same word ('drink up eisel') when protesting the intensity of his grief for Ophelia (5.1), confirming that Shakespeare's audience would have recognized both its taste and its penitential overtone.

The medical-vinegar reading with a secondary Passion resonance (John 19:29, confirmed by the Hamlet 5.1 parallel) is well-attested and not an overreach.

anchor_text: vulgar scandal stamp'd upon my brow
summary: 'Vulgar' here means 'common' or 'belonging to the common people,' not obscene as in modern usage. 'Scandal stamp'd upon my brow' continues the conceit of line 1: public censure is a mark pressed into him like a seal into wax, and the beloved's love now fills that impression.

'vulgar,' adj. sense A.1.a). 'Stamp'd' picks up 'impression' from line 1: the opening conceit is that public scandal has made a seal-impression in the speaker, and the beloved's love and pity fill the dent. The exact nature of the poet's disrepute is left unspecified in the sequence; editors have proposed theatrical scandal, social condemnation, or sexual misconduct, but none is confirmed by external record.

anchor_text: o'er-green my bad, my good allow
summary: 'O'er-green' means to cover over with fresh green growth, the way grass or moss reclaims a scar in the earth. 'Allow' here is stronger than modern 'permit': it means 'approve' or 'sanction.' The poet says that as long as the beloved covers his faults and endorses his good qualities, no other judge matters.

It images the beloved's approval as a natural restorative, like vegetation reclaiming wounded ground. 'Allow' carries its older sense of 'approve, commend, sanction as right' (OED s.v. 'allow,' v., sense 5), standard in 16th and 17th century English. Together the two actions -- 'o'er-green my bad' and 'my good allow' -- cast the beloved as a complete moral accountant who both excuses the speaker's faults and ratifies his merits.

anchor_text: None else to me, nor I to none alive, / That my steel'd sense or changes right or wrong
summary: 'Steel'd sense' means a judgment or perception hardened like steel -- made firm and impervious. 'Or...or' is an archaic correlative meaning 'either...or.' The poet declares that no other living person can shift his sense of what is right or wrong: that power belongs to the beloved alone.

'Or...or' as a correlative pair meaning 'either...or' was common in 16th-century English before 'either' standardized the construction; it is not an error (Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'or'). The full logical claim of lines 10-11 is: no other person either changes what I call right or changes what I call wrong. This is the emotional core of the sonnet: the speaker has ceded his entire moral and aesthetic judgment to the beloved, making the relationship a complete replacement for social consensus.

'Or...or' as a correlative ('either...or') is correct Elizabethan usage, 'steel'd sense' as hardened/impervious judgment is standard, and while 'a complete replacement for social consensus' is a slightly strong formulation, it accurately captures the sonnet's logic that the beloved is the speaker's sole moral tribunal; the reading does not overreach.

anchor_text: my adder's sense / To critic and to flatterer stopped are
summary: The adder was believed to make itself deaf by pressing one ear to the ground and stopping the other with its tail, so no snake-charmer could reach it. The image comes from Psalm 58. The poet says he has made himself equally deaf to both critics and flatterers -- neither hostile nor flattering external judgment can penetrate him, because only the beloved's voice counts.

The adder's willful deafness to a charmer was proverbial in Elizabethan England, and readers familiar with the Psalter would have recognized the allusion immediately. The pairing of 'critic' and 'flatterer' is pointed: the poet blocks out not just insult but all external evaluation, whether hostile or complimentary -- both are equally irrelevant before the single private tribunal of the beloved. The inverted syntax 'stopped are' (object-complement-verb) is normal Elizabethan word order for emphasis.

The Psalm 58:4-5 adder-deafness allusion is the standard identification (endorsed by Booth, Vendler, and the OED's illustrative citations), the detail about the tail-stopping mechanism is traditional natural-history lore circulating in Elizabethan bestiaries, and the reading that both critics and flatterers are equally shut out while the beloved alone has access is the mainstream interpretation of the couplet.

anchor_text: mine eye is in my mind
summary: The poet states the sonnet's controlling conceit: his eye has migrated into his mind. The physical organ of sight still operates, but it has stopped delivering images to the heart; instead, the mind commandeers every image and reshapes it into the absent beloved's face. The eye 'seems seeing, but effectually is out' — it looks without truly seeing.
detail: The conceit engages Renaissance faculty psychology, which divided the soul into vegetative, sensitive, and rational powers. In normal perception the sensitive soul (including the five senses and the faculty of imagination) receives sense-data and passes it upward to the rational soul. Here the rational soul ('mind') has colonized the first stage, intercepting images before they can register as real sensation. Sidney in 'The Defence of Poesy' (1595) argues that the poet's imagination fashions a 'golden world' beyond nature; Shakespeare literalizes that creative overwriting as a symptom of love. The disruption of the normal hierarchy of inner faculties prepares the paradox the couplet will clinch: perfect mental fidelity produces a faithless eye. Sonnet 114 continues the argument directly, asking whether this distortion of sight is 'flattery' or 'infection of the eye.'

The faculty-psychology reading (sensitive soul colonized by rational soul) is mainstream Renaissance cognitive theory, Sidney's 'golden world' parallel is apt, and the link to Sonnet 114 is textually accurate.

anchor_text: no form delivers to the heart
summary: 'Delivers' here means transmits or conveys — the eye does not pass along to the heart the form (shape, image) of what it sees. In Elizabethan anatomy and philosophy the heart was the seat of feeling and judgment, not merely the pump that circulates blood; to deliver an impression to the heart was to make it emotionally real. Because the mind intercepts every image, nothing real ever reaches that inner seat.

anchor_text: shape which it doth latch
summary: 'Latch' means to catch or seize — the eye grabs at each passing object (bird, flower, shape) but cannot hold it, because the mind immediately replaces the real image with the beloved's face. The word also carried the physical sense of latching shut a door: the eye snaps shut to the world the moment it perceives anything.

anchor_text: rud'st or gentlest sight
summary: 'Rud'st' is a contracted superlative of 'rude,' meaning roughest or most shapeless — the ugliest possible thing the eye could encounter. The sonnet pairs extremes in a series of antitheses (rud'st / gentlest, deformed'st / most sweet, mountain / sea, day / night, crow / dove) to make the argument universal: no object, however coarse or lovely, can stop the mind from converting it into the beloved's face.
detail: The elided superlative 'rud'st' (for 'rudest') and 'deformed'st' two lines later are standard verse contractions that preserve the iambic pentameter. 'Rude' in sixteenth-century English covered: rough, harsh, coarse, unrefined, and ugly (OED s.v. 'rude' adj., senses 3, 5, and 7). The accumulation of paired contraries across four lines is the rhetorical figure antitheton (Puttenham, 'The Arte of English Poesie,' Book III, ch. 19, 'Of the Quarreller'), which in classical oratory proved a universal claim by covering both ends of a spectrum. Shakespeare uses the same device in the plays to assert absolutes: 'I am constant as the northern star' (Julius Caesar 3.1). The crow-and-dove pair is especially charged in the Fair Youth sequence, where the youth's fairness is a recurring term of praise: even the blackest bird is transformed into his image.

anchor_text: Incapable of more, replete with you
summary: The couplet closes with the sonnet's paradox: the mind is so full of the beloved ('replete with you,' unable to hold any more) that it cannot receive any other image ('incapable of more'). This total fidelity — the mind that is 'most true' — is exactly what makes the eye 'untrue': devoted to the beloved's image, it cannot faithfully report what it actually sees. Perfect inner loyalty produces an inaccurate outer eye.

Shakespeare's couplet puns on both: the 'most true mind' is supremely loyal to the beloved, but that loyalty makes the eye 'untrue' in the second sense, inaccurate and reporting falsely. The same double sense of true/untrue runs through Sonnet 138 ('When my love swears that she is made of truth, / I do believe her, though I know she lies'). 'Replete' (filled to saturation, OED s.v. 'replete' adj., sense 1) figures the mind as a vessel so gorged on one image it cannot receive another. The volta, conventionally at line 9 in the Shakespearean sonnet, is deferred here to the final couplet, which resolves three quatrains of catalogue into a single logical inversion. Puttenham's 'Arte of English Poesie' (1589) describes the couplet as the place where the lyric argument is 'closed up and concluded'; here Shakespeare closes by opening a new question Sonnet 114 will pursue.

anchor_text: monarch's plague, this flattery
summary: Flattery was understood as the occupational disease of kings: courtiers who tell a ruler only what pleases him distort his judgment. The poet's mind, 'crowned' with love for the youth, suffers the same corrupting disease a monarch suffers when surrounded by yes-men.
detail: The idea that flattery is uniquely dangerous to rulers was a Renaissance commonplace, elaborated in mirror-for-princes literature from Erasmus's 'The Education of a Christian Prince' (1516) onward. A king insulated by flattery cannot see reality; the poet fears that love has put him in exactly that insulated position, seeing only what he wishes. The word 'plague' reinforces the medical framing — flattery is not a vice but a contagion. Onions (Shakespeare Glossary) records 'flattery' as meaning specifically the distortion of judgment by excessive praise.

anchor_text: Such cherubins as your sweet self resemble
summary: Cherubins (cherubs) are the second-highest order of angels in Christian tradition, associated with divine radiance and beauty. By saying his eye transforms monsters into cherubs 'resembling' the youth, the poet places the beloved at the very top of the scale of created beauty — the closest earthly thing to an angel.

The form 'cherubins' (treating the Hebrew plural -im as singular and adding an English -s) was common in Shakespeare's day — he uses 'cherubins' similarly in Othello 4.2 and The Merchant of Venice 5.1. The claim that the youth resembles a cherub belongs to the Fair Youth sequence's sustained argument that the young man embodies an angelic or quasi-divine beauty.

anchor_text: what with his gust is 'greeing, And to his palate doth prepare the cup
summary: 'Gust' here means taste or appetite — the eye knows what the mind's palate craves and prepares a cup to match. The passage develops an extended metaphor: the mind is a drinker, its desire is its 'gust' or relish, and the eye acts as the cupbearer who selects only what the master will enjoy.

The eye 'agrees with' — suits, satisfies — what the mind already wants, rather than reporting what is really there. anchor_text: reckoning Time, whose million'd accidents
summary: 'Reckoning' here means taking full account of, measuring honestly — as in a financial reckoning or settlement. 'Million'd accidents' means the countless, unforeseeable events that time produces; 'million'd' is a coinage stretching the number into something vast and unmanageable. The four actions in lines 1603-1605 — creeping between vows, changing kings' decrees, tanning beauty, blunting intents — are themselves a rhetorical list (gradatio) that moves from the intimate (vows) to the political (kings) to the physical (beauty) to the psychological (intents).

anchor_text: Tan sacred beauty, blunt the sharp'st intents
summary: 'Tan' means to discolor or darken — as sunlight and weather tan leather or human skin. Time tans 'sacred beauty' in the way weather ruins fine material: what is precious and set apart ('sacred') is nonetheless worn down by exposure. 'Blunt' means to dull the edge of something sharp; 'intents' are purposes or intentions. The line pairs two verbs of steady, slow damage: tanning does not destroy outright but discolors and toughens; blunting does not shatter but gradually robs a blade of its edge.

anchor_text: When I was certain o'er incertainty, Crowning the present, doubting of the rest
summary: 'Incertainty' is an early modern spelling of uncertainty — not knowing what will come. 'Certain o'er incertainty' is an oxymoron: the speaker was confident precisely because he acknowledged he could not be confident. 'Crowning the present' means treating the present moment as supreme, like a coronation, while 'doubting of the rest' means staying unsure about everything beyond it. The logic: he claimed 'now I love you best' only because he knew the future was unknowable, so 'best' referred only to the present.

The rhetorical structure of lines 1606-1609 is a retrospective justification, a kind of apologia: knowing time's tyranny, was it not reasonable to declare love's peak only provisionally, with 'crowning' as a gesture of current sufficiency rather than absolute finality?

anchor_text: marriage of true minds / Admit impediments
summary: The opening lines quote and then refuse the legal formula from the Church of England marriage service, which required any witness who knew 'cause or just impediment' why a couple should not marry to say so. The poet applies the ceremony to the joining of two minds and insists no such bar can apply.

The formula was legally binding: a declared impediment could void the marriage. Shakespeare's speaker mimics the priest's demand in the first person ('Let me not... Admit impediments') and immediately answers it: no impediment will be admitted. The move is precise — it transforms a civil-religious ceremony into a philosophical axiom, claiming for the union of minds the same indissolubility the marriage rite claimed for the union of bodies. anchor_text: alters when it alteration finds, / Or bends with the remover to remove
summary: These two lines give the negative definition — what love is not — before the poet states what it is. Repeating a root word in changed grammatical form ('alters'/'alteration', 'remover'/'remove') was a recognised figure called polyptoton, and it makes the argument feel ironclad: love that changes with change, or departs with the one who departs, is by its own logic not love.
detail: Polyptoton — using the same root in different grammatical forms — was catalogued by George Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) under the name 'traductio' and treated as a figure of amplification and wit. Here it does argumentative work: 'alters when it alteration finds' means 'changes because circumstances have changed' (conditional love, dependent on external conditions remaining stable); 'bends with the remover to remove' means 'withdraws when the beloved withdraws.' 'Remover' (OED v. 7, 'to go away, depart') is active — the person walking away — not merely someone relocated. The couplet-like tightness of the two lines, the near-rhyme of 'alteration/alteration' and 'remover/remove,' enacts the figure.

anchor_text: ever-fixed mark, / That looks on tempests and is never shaken
summary: A 'mark' here is a fixed navigational landmark — a coastal headland, tower, or church spire that sailors steered by. Unlike a ship tossed in a storm, the mark stands unmoved. Love, the poet argues, is just such a fixed reference point: storms may rage around it, but it does not waver.

Before reliable charts, coastal navigation depended on permanent shore-marks visible from the water. The phrase 'ever-fixed' sets the mark against the 'wandering bark' of line 7 and the 'tempests' of this line: everything else moves; the mark does not. The shift at line 9 ('O, no!') — the sonnet's volta — has already been prepared by this image: the argument has been building toward something that cannot be shaken.

anchor_text: rosy lips and cheeks / Within his bending sickle's compass come
summary: Time was pictured as a figure carrying a sickle or scythe — the same curved blade a farmer uses to cut grain at harvest. 'Bending' is both the curve of the blade and the arc of its swing; 'compass' means the sweep or range of that arc. Rosy lips and cheeks — the standard blazon attributes of youth and beauty — fall within Time's harvest. Love, the poet insists, does not.
detail: The figure of Time as reaper derives from representations of Saturn (Greek Kronos) carrying a curved blade, fused in medieval iconography with the Grim Reaper as harvester of lives. By Shakespeare's day the image appeared in emblem books, woodcuts, and common speech. 'Compass' (OED n., sense 3a: 'the space enclosed within a circular movement; range, sweep of an arc') is precise: the sickle sweeps a circular compass that encompasses everything subject to time. 'Rosy lips and cheeks' are stock Petrarchan blazon attributes — the conventional currency of beauty — so the poet is saying: even the loveliest things the sonneteer praises are time's harvest. Ovid, 'Metamorphoses' 15.234-236 (Golding 1567), supplies the classical source for Time as the devourer ('tempus edax rerum') that consumes all things.

anchor_text: even to the edge of doom
summary: 'Doom' here means the Last Judgment — God's final sentence at the end of the world, not mere ruin or disaster. 'The edge of doom' is the very last moment of created time, the boundary before eternity begins. Love endures not just for a lifetime but to that ultimate instant.

'Edge' (OED n., sense 5: 'the extreme limit or brink') makes the image spatial: love persists right to the outermost limit of time. anchor_text: Book both my wilfulness and errors down,
summary: The poet invites the youth to draw up a full legal charge: enter ('book') every proven fault in the record, then pile unproven conjecture ('surmise') on top. The move is prolepsis — pre-emptively conceding every accusation before answering it — a classical oratorical tactic.
detail: Prolepsis (Latin 'praesumptio') is the rhetorical figure of anticipating and restating an opponent's objection before refuting it; Quintilian describes it as disarming the adversary by voicing the charge oneself (Institutio Oratoria 9.2.16-17). 'Book down' means to enter in an account-book or legal register: OED s.v. 'book' (v.), sense 1a, 'to enter in a book or written record.' 'Surmise' is an Elizabethan legal term for conjecture offered as evidence without sufficient proof: OED s.v. 'surmise' (n.), sense 2, 'a charge or allegation of a formal or legal nature.' 'Accumulate' (accent on the second syllable in Elizabethan pronunciation) means to heap up, pile one item upon another. The compound instruction — record what is proven, then add what is merely guessed — is perversely generous, and its generosity is the poet's strategy: by conceding everything, he controls the ground on which the couplet will turn.

anchor_text: to prevent our maladies unseen, We sicken to shun sickness when we purge
summary: To 'purge' is to take a strong laxative or emetic to cleanse the body of harmful excess. Galenic medicine held that disease arose from an imbalance of the four bodily humours (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile); a purge forced out the dangerous surplus before symptoms appeared, making the patient temporarily ill to prevent a worse illness. The speaker compares seeking out unpleasant company to this prophylactic medicine.
detail: Galen (129-216 CE), whose theories dominated European medicine through the sixteenth century, maintained that health required equilibrium of the four humours. When a humour threatened to overflow — recognizable by its smell, color, or the patient's lassitude — the physician prescribed a 'purge' (from Latin purgare, to cleanse) to evacuate the excess, usually by inducing diarrhea or vomiting. The patient was made briefly sick in order to be made better. Thomas Elyot's 'The Castel of Helth' (1539) and Andrew Boorde's 'Breviary of Healthe' (1547) both recommend pre-emptive purging before the body reaches crisis, exactly the logic the poet invokes. The conceit allows him to argue that infidelity was rational self-care — an argument the couplet demolishes.

sources.name: Galen

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1642

The Galenic prophylactic-purge reading is accurate: humoral medicine did prescribe pre-emptive evacuation to forestall imbalance, and the logic that one 'sickens to shun sickness' maps cleanly onto the poem's argument.

anchor_text: sick of welfare, found a kind of meetness To be diseas'd
summary: 'Meetness' means fitness or appropriateness. 'Sick of welfare' means sickened or surfeited by well-being — not ill, but so saturated with contentment that it became its own discomfort. The speaker reasoned it was fitting ('meetness') to court suffering before he actually needed to, because excess pleasure had dulled him.

anchor_text: potions have I drunk of Siren tears

anchor_text: Distill'd from limbecks foul as hell within
summary: A limbeck (also spelled alembic) is a vessel used in alchemy and early chemistry to distil liquids: the substance is heated in one flask, the vapor rises through a bent tube, and the purified or concentrated liquid drips out the other end. anchor_text: mine eyes out of their spheres been fitted
summary: In the astronomy accepted in Shakespeare England, every celestial body moved through the heavens inside its own hollow crystalline sphere, a rotating transparent globe centered on the earth. The eyes were compared to small planets moving inside their own rounded sockets. To have eyes out of their spheres means to be so overwhelmed by shock or madness that the eyes seem to have been shaken from their proper orbits, an image of total psychological dislocation.
detail: The Ptolemaic model, transmitted to Renaissance Europe chiefly through Ptolemy Almagest (c. 150 CE) and Aristotelian natural philosophy, placed the earth at the center of nested crystalline spheres, each carrying its planet. The image of eyes as small spheres within their sockets was a common anatomical metaphor; out of their spheres appears in similar contexts in Twelfth Night 3.1. The word fitted here carries the sense of dislodged or displaced, as if the orbs of the eyes have been forced from their proper setting. Distraction in the adjacent line reinforces the medical sense: the word literally means a pulling-apart (from Latin distrahere), the mind torn from its settled position.

anchor_text: distraction of this madding fever
summary: Madding is an adjective meaning causing madness or maddening, not mad itself. A madding fever is a fever that drives a person out of their mind, a feverish frenzy that is the cause of the distraction rather than its result. The speaker treats his infatuation not as a deliberate choice but as a disease, something that happened to him and robbed him of his senses.

The speaker self-diagnosis as a patient in the grip of a madding fever frames the whole octave as a period of clinical derangement, which prepares the volta (O benefit of ill!) where lucidity finally returns.

anchor_text: gain by ill thrice more than I have spent
summary: The couplet closes the sonnet in the language of commercial accounting. Spent means money or emotional capital paid out; gain means profit returned; thrice more is a three-fold return on investment. The speaker counts himself richer for having strayed: the infatuation cost him something, but the renewed and fortified love he has come back to is worth three times what he lost. Content means the state of being satisfied or at peace with what one has. Rebukd means rebuked or chastened; he returns corrected by experience, not triumphant.

To spend in Shakespeare regularly means to use up, expend, or waste (OED s.v. spend v., sense 3); gain is its commercial antonym. The ratio of thrice more is deliberately extravagant, not precise accounting but a claim of overwhelming surplus. The word content frames the speaker prior state as one he is returning to, not discovering for the first time; the infatuation was a digression from something already valued.

anchor_text: your trespass now becomes a fee; / Mine ransoms yours, and yours must ransom me
summary: The couplet resolves the poem's mutual accounting with a legal-financial conceit. A 'trespass' in English common law was a wrongful act causing harm — the same word used in the Lord's Prayer ('forgive us our trespasses,' Matthew 6:12). A 'fee' here means a payment that settles a debt. A 'ransom' was the sum paid to release a captive or cancel a penalty. The verbal wit is that guilt and pardon are perfectly exchangeable: your wrong against me is the ransom I use to pay my debt to you, and vice versa — a circular settlement that cancels all outstanding claims. anchor_text: my sportive blood

By calling it 'sportive' rather than 'lustful,' the speaker reframes his nature as playful rather than vicious. anchor_text: I am that I am
summary: This phrase echoes God's self-declaration to Moses: 'I AM THAT I AM' (Exodus 3:14, Geneva 1599). Whether readers hear this as spiritual confidence or alarming presumption is part of the poem's calculated provocation. The inversion of the formula — 'I am not what I am' — is Iago's self-description in Othello 1.1, which sets the same words in a context of radical self-concealment; the contrast sharpens both uses.

anchor_text: thy tables, are within my brain
summary: 'Tables' are writing tablets — small boards coated in wax or chalk on which people jotted notes, then smoothed over and reused. They were common personal possessions and a conventional gift of remembrance in the Elizabethan period. The speaker has apparently given away (or discarded) a set the youth had given him, and must now justify that act.

anchor_text: need I tallies thy dear love to score
summary: 'Tallies' were notched wooden sticks used to record numerical transactions before widespread literacy. A stick was split lengthwise after the notches were cut, and each party kept half as proof; the halves could be matched ('scored') to verify a debt or payment. The speaker says love is too deep to be kept in such crude ledger marks.
detail: The tally-stick system was England's main form of financial record-keeping well into the early modern period; the Exchequer used tally sticks until 1826 (the burning of a vast stock of them in a furnace under the Houses of Parliament accidentally set fire to the building in 1834). 'Score' retains its original meaning of a cut or notch — to score a tally — giving the couplet a financial register: love is not a debt to be counted in notches. The dismissal of tallies alongside the dismissal of wax tablets extends the poem's anti-writing-instrument argument.

anchor_text: To keep an adjunct to remember thee / Were to import forgetfulness in me
summary: The poem's closing paradox: to keep an external memory aid ('adjunct') would itself be an act of forgetfulness — it would imply the speaker's natural memory has already failed. The paradox is sharp: the very act of using a mnemonic device would be evidence of forgetting. 'Adjunct' (OED s.v. anchor_text: Thy pyramids built up with newer might / To me are nothing novel, nothing strange
summary: In Elizabethan English 'pyramids' covered any tall, tapering monument — obelisks, columns, triumphal arches, or spectacular new buildings designed to look ancient — not only the Egyptian structures. The speaker dismisses Time's grandest productions as mere repackagings of older things, not genuine novelties.

The plural 'pyramids' suggests categories of wonder rather than specific Egyptian structures; the Elizabethan era saw renewed European interest in ancient obelisks — Sixtus V had four Roman obelisks re-erected in Rome between 1586 and 1590, events widely reported across Europe as impressive monuments 'built up with newer might' from ancient originals. Either way the speaker's point is consistent: what Time presents as staggering novelty is only an old form rebuilt.

anchor_text: Thy registers and thee I both defy, / Not wondering at the present nor the past, / For thy records and what we see doth lie

anchor_text: child of state, It might for Fortune's bastard be unfather'd
summary: A 'child of state' is something born of outward circumstance — political favour, wealth, or power — rather than of any inner quality. The poem's argument opens on a legal and social pun: if love were merely a product of 'state' (meaning both political standing and personal condition), Fortune could disown it the way a bastard child can be legally stripped of parentage and left with no claim on anything.
detail: OED records 'state' in Shakespeare's period with two active meanings that the line holds simultaneously: (1) political condition or position of power, and (2) personal estate or fortune. A 'bastard' in English law had no right of inheritance and could be 'unfather'd' — denied legal paternity — at any time. Fortune (the classical goddess of chance, conventionally fickle and blind) could therefore repudiate a love built on her gifts the moment the external conditions changed. The poem's whole argument depends on denying this contingency: the poet's love was not built on such foundations and therefore cannot be disowned. The pairing of 'child' and 'bastard' also moves the love-relationship into the language of parentage and legitimacy, giving the poem an unusual juridical authority.

anchor_text: suffers not in smiling pomp, nor falls Under the blow of thralled discontent
summary: 'Thralled discontent' means grievance held in bondage — resentment that has become a kind of captivity. 'Thrall' in Elizabethan English meant a slave or serf, so 'thralled' is 'enslaved.' The poet pairs two external dangers that his love resists: 'smiling pomp' (the treacherous goodwill of the powerful when times are good) and 'thralled discontent' (the violent reaction of the oppressed when times are bad). Love that endures must be indifferent to both.

'Thralled discontent' thus names the resentment that builds when people are enslaved or oppressed — precisely the social unrest that might topple a political regime. 'Pomp' here is not merely ceremonial display but the full power and splendour of worldly authority at its height. The structural pairing — rising ('smiling pomp') against falling ('thralled discontent') — covers the full arc of political fortune: love is vulnerable neither to the seductions of prosperity nor to the violence of rebellion.

anchor_text: witness call the fools of time, Which die for goodness, who have lived for crime
summary: The couplet summons 'the fools of time' as witnesses — those who 'die for goodness' having 'lived for crime.' The most widely supported reading: people who repent on their deathbed, having spent their lives in vice or political scheming, then died confessing and seeking grace, performing 'goodness' only at the last moment. They are 'fools of time' because time duped them — they thought a deathbed conversion could undo a life of corruption. Even such dubious witnesses confirm love's independence from earthly calculation.
detail: The phrase 'fools of time' is deliberately ambiguous. OED records 'fool' both as one who lacks sense and as one who is made a dupe or victim (s.v. 'fool' n., sense 4). 'Fools of time' therefore admits two readings: those who are foolish about time (failing to reckon with its passing), and those who are time's fools — its dupes, subject to its reversals. The image of the last-minute religious convert dying 'for goodness' after 'living for crime' was a recognizable Elizabethan type: in a period of religious change many powerful figures made conspicuous deathbed recantations. Some commentators connect the phrase to specific political figures who conformed to the Elizabethan settlement after serving under a Catholic regime, though no single identification commands agreement. That the poet calls even these compromised witnesses to support his claim amplifies the sonnet's forensic confidence: love's independence from worldly policy needs no better testimony than those who trusted in policy and found it fail them at the last.

anchor_text: bore the canopy, With my extern the outward honouring
summary: To 'bear the canopy' was to hold one of the poles of the cloth-of-state carried on poles over a sovereign or great dignitary in formal procession — a recognized ceremonial honor in Tudor court and civic pageantry. 'Extern' is used as a noun meaning external bearing or outward show. The speaker dismisses both: even this conspicuous display of proximity to the beloved would mean nothing if it were only outward performance.
detail: Royal and noble entries, civic processions, and liturgical occasions all featured canopy-bearers; the role was assigned to household officers or honored guests and placed them visibly at the great person's side. Shakespeare's audience would have recognized it as the kind of service that earns public notice but not private trust. The OED records 'extern' as a rare substantive ('outward show, external appearance'), with this line among the earliest uses; Schmidt glosses it as 'the outward man, exterior.' The redundancy of 'extern ... outward honouring' is deliberate: the speaker accumulates synonyms to empty ceremonial service of any content. The opening question — 'Were't aught to me' — frames the whole sonnet's argument that outward honor is worthless without the inward 'mutual render' offered in the sestet.

anchor_text: paying too much rent For compound sweet; forgoing simple savour
summary: 'Compound sweet' means an elaborate, blended pleasure — a mixture of many ingredients, like a spiced confection — as opposed to 'simple savour,' the taste of a single unmixed thing. 'Rent' here means payment or price paid. The speaker says those who pursue elaborate, costly pleasures pay too high a price for them and lose the simpler, truer satisfactions. The metaphor sets artificial complexity against natural plainness.
detail: In Early Modern English 'simple' carried its primary sense of 'unmixed, single, pure' rather than merely 'easy'; a 'simple' in medicine was a single herb used alone, as opposed to a compound remedy. 'Compound sweet' echoes the Elizabethan perfumery and confectionery trade, where elaborate blended spices and sweets (compounds) commanded high prices and were associated with fashionable excess. The 'dwellers on form and favour' of line 1742 are those who live by outward show; their error, the speaker argues, is over-investing in compound pleasures — flattery, ceremony, rich display — while losing the 'simple savour' of genuine exchange. The commercial language of 'rent' (cost, price) connects this second quatrain to the 'seconds' (adulterated goods) of line 1748: the whole sestet replies to a marketplace of false values with the counter-offer of pure, unpurchased devotion.

anchor_text: obsequious in thy heart, And take thou my oblation, poor but free
summary: 'Obsequious' in Early Modern English meant devoutly attentive or dutifully devoted — it had not yet narrowed to the modern sense of cringing flattery. 'Oblation' is a religious term for a formal offering or sacrifice made to God. Together the two words cast the poet's inner devotion as a kind of sincere worship — the true alternative to canopy-bearing and monument-building. His offering is 'poor' (unadorned, without outward splendor) but 'free' (freely given, without hidden price).
detail: The OED records 'obsequious' sense 1 as 'prompt to serve, compliant, dutiful,' used especially of religious or memorial service — the word shares a root with 'obsequies,' funeral rites. The modern pejorative meaning is a later development. 'Oblation' (Latin oblatio, an offering) was the technical term in the Church of England liturgy for the presentation of the elements at the Eucharist, as well as for any votive offering to God; Schmidt glosses it as 'offering, sacrifice.' The volta of the sonnet arrives at line 9 with 'No; let me be' — a turn from the two-quatrain catalogue of hollow honors to this positive, inward statement. The religious register ('oblation,' 'obsequious') quietly elevates the speaker's plainly stated love to something more serious than a compliment.

anchor_text: not mix'd with seconds, knows no art
summary: 'Seconds' were the lower, coarser grades of flour or other goods mixed into a product to bulk it out cheaply — adulteration by inferior material. To say the offering is 'not mix'd with seconds' means it is pure and unadulterated, with no hidden self-interest blended in. 'Art' here means cunning or calculated contrivance, not skill; the offering contains neither adulterant nor artifice.
detail: The OED records 'seconds' in the sense of 'the second or inferior quality of a commodity, esp. flour; the coarser residue' (s.v. 'second' n., sense 7b). The metaphor extends the marketplace language of 'compound sweet' and 'simple savour' three lines above: the speaker's love, like unmixed grain, is less elaborate than a compound product but honest all the way through. 'Art' in the sense of cunning or stratagem is well attested in Shakespeare (OED s.v. 'art' n.1, sense 6: 'skill applied to bad purposes; cunning, craft, artifice'). The line thus rejects two kinds of adulteration — material (seconds) and moral (art) — before arriving at the bare simplicity of 'mutual render, only me for thee.'

anchor_text: suborned informer! a true soul When most impeach'd, stands least in thy control
summary: 'Suborned' means corruptly hired or bribed to make false accusations; a 'suborned informer' is a paid false witness. 'Impeach'd' means charged or accused. The couplet makes a sudden, combative turn: the speaker dismisses an unnamed accuser — possibly someone working against him with the youth — by declaring that a genuinely honest person, when most heavily accused, is least vulnerable to the charge. The accusation slides off because there is nothing in it to grip.
detail: Both terms are legal. To 'suborn' a witness was a specific criminal offense in Elizabethan law — inducing someone by payment or pressure to give false testimony (OED s.v. 'suborn' v., sense 1). 'Informer' often meant a professional accuser who laid charges for financial reward, a figure widely resented in Shakespeare's England. 'Impeach' (from Anglo-French empecher) is OED sense 2: 'to accuse, charge with a crime or misdemeanour; to call in question.' The identity of this 'suborned informer' is unknown; editors have variously connected the figure to the Rival Poet material of Sonnets 78-86, to a hostile court go-between, or to Time itself (since the preceding sonnet, 124, explicitly addresses Time as an enemy). The couplet's reversal — that being most accused proves most innocent — gives the poem a defiant, defensive close that sits in tense contrast with the quiet devotion of the sestet.
