anchor_text: Time's fickle glass, his fickle hour
summary: 'Glass' means mirror. 'Fickle' means changeable, unreliable. The lovely boy holds Time's own mirror, which reflects inconstant and shifting images — a face that seems to refuse ageing — and he also holds Time's unstable hour, controlling how the hour runs for him. The repetition of 'fickle' stresses that both the mirror and the time it measures are treacherous.
detail: In Elizabethan English a 'glass' is always a mirror, never a drinking vessel in this context. Time is commonly given attributes (scythe, hourglass) in the sonnet sequence; here the mirror doubles as a timepiece, because a glass both shows what age does to a face and measures the hour. The paradox is that the youth seems to hold this normally unstoppable instrument in his own power — hence the poem's warning that even this charmed relationship with time must end. OED s.v. 'glass', sense 4 (mirror, looking-glass), and s.v. 'fickle', sense 1 (inconstant, changeable).

anchor_text: by waning grown, and therein show'st
summary: 'Waning' means diminishing, as the moon wanes — decreasing in visible light. The paradox is that the youth has grown (become more beautiful or more himself) by waning: as time passes and those who love him visibly age and wither, he seems to become more, not less. The poem sets his apparent increase against his admirers' visible decline.
detail: The moon's waxing and waning was the standard Elizabethan image of cyclical change and natural diminishment. Shakespeare reverses the expected direction: in the ordinary course of things, to 'wane' is to diminish and fade toward nothing. Here the youth 'grows' by doing so — possibly in the sense that his beauty is defined and magnified against the aging of his lovers, or that the passage of time has distilled rather than eroded him. The figure sets up the poem's central irony: Nature herself seems to be resisting time on the youth's behalf, but she cannot do so forever. OED s.v. 'wane' (v.), sense 1b: 'to decrease gradually in power, prosperity, or importance; to decline.'

anchor_text: Nature, sovereign mistress over wrack
summary: 'Wrack' means ruin or destruction — the same word as 'wreck,' used broadly for decay and devastation. Nature is here personified as the supreme ruler ('sovereign mistress') even over ruin itself: she governs destruction, and therefore she alone decides when beauty decays. While she still favours the youth, she plucks him back from time's damage as he goes forward through life.
detail: In the sonnet sequence Nature is repeatedly figured as a creditor, a sovereign, or a craftsperson who fashions and then reclaims her creations. 'Wrack' (variant spelling of 'wreck') carried in Elizabethan English the senses of shipwreck, destruction, and general ruin (OED s.v. 'wrack', n., senses 3 and 4). The phrase 'sovereign mistress over wrack' positions Nature above even Time in the hierarchy of destructive powers: Time destroys, but Nature governs that destruction. The conditional logic of lines 7-8 is the poem's hinge: Nature's protection is purposeful — she keeps the youth alive so that her skill can disgrace Time and kill its minutes — but purpose implies limit, and the poem moves immediately to 'yet fear her.'

anchor_text: minion of her pleasure!
summary: A 'minion' is a favourite or darling — someone who enjoys the special favour of a powerful patron. The youth is Nature's beloved pet and plaything. But the word also implies dependency and powerlessness: a minion exists at the patron's pleasure, not his own, and 'she may detain, but not still keep' means Nature can hold him back from ageing for a while, but she cannot hold him forever — 'still' here means 'always' or 'permanently.'
detail: OED records 'minion' in the senses of a favoured person, a servant of low or servile condition kept for the master's pleasure, and a darling or spoiled favourite (OED s.v. 'minion', senses 2 and 3). The word could be affectionate or slightly diminishing: to call someone a 'minion' acknowledges their charm while stressing their subordination. 'Still' in Elizabethan English almost always means 'always' or 'continually,' not 'quietly' (OED s.v. 'still', adv., sense 6). The line's grammar therefore reads: 'She can delay [his ageing] but she cannot keep him always.' The turn from line 9 ('Yet fear her') marks the closest thing this poem has to a volta: the poet grants Nature's power but insists the youth must not be complacent.

anchor_text: Her audit (though delayed) answered must be,
summary: Both 'audit' and 'quietus' are legal and financial terms. An 'audit' is a formal examination of accounts — here Nature has kept the youth as a kind of loan, and that loan must eventually be settled ('answered'). A 'quietus' is a final discharge of debt, a receipt that closes the account entirely — by extension, death. The two words together figure Nature as a great creditor whose books must balance: the youth himself is the payment she will finally collect.
detail: In Elizabethan commercial and legal practice an 'audit' was the formal rendering and examination of financial accounts, and 'quietus est' (Latin: 'he is quit') was the formal written receipt given when a debt was settled and a debtor discharged. Shakespeare uses 'quietus' elsewhere in Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' soliloquy — 'When he himself might his quietus make / With a bare bodkin' (Hamlet 3.1) — where it means death as the final discharge of life's account. The same commercial vocabulary runs throughout the sequence (Sonnets 4, 6, 20) and returns here at its close: Nature, who made the youth and has been protecting him from time, will at last call in her debt. The word 'render' also belongs to the accounting register: to render an account is to hand it over for inspection; to render a person is to give them up. OED s.v. 'audit' (n.), sense 1 (formal examination of accounts); s.v. 'quietus' (n.), sense 1 (final settlement, discharge); s.v. 'render' (v.), sense 7 (to hand over, deliver up).

anchor_text: black beauty's successive heir, And beauty slander'd with a bastard shame
summary: 'Successive heir' means a legitimate heir who inherits by lawful right of succession. The poet casts dark coloring as beauty's true inheritor, then pairs it with 'bastard shame': the conventional pale ideal is illegitimate, like a bastard child — born outside lawful right. 'Slander'd' means both dishonored and falsely defamed. The legal pair (heir versus bastard) frames the argument as one about legitimacy, not merely preference.
detail: The dynastic vocabulary exploits strict Elizabethan law of inheritance: a successive heir is the one who stands next in the recognized line; a bastard is excluded from that succession and has no legal claim. Shakespeare applies both terms to beauty itself: natural dark beauty is the true heir; artificial fairness is the counterfeit usurper. 'Slander' in the period carried both the forensic sense (false accusation) and the social sense (disgrace or dishonor) — OED s.v. 'slander' v. sense 2b. Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'successive') glosses the adjective as 'constituting or forming a succession, hereditary.'

anchor_text: Fairing the foul with Art's false borrowed face
summary: Elizabethan cosmetics — chiefly ceruse (white-lead face paint) and vermilion for lips — let women artificially lighten their skin and add color. Shakespeare's verb 'fairing' (making fair) captures this: craft ('Art') creates a pale, rosy face that is 'false' because it counterfeits natural fairness, and 'borrowed' because the beauty belongs to someone else. The argument is that cosmetics have made natural and artificial beauty indistinguishable.
detail: Ceruse, made from white lead, was the dominant Elizabethan skin-lightener and was well known to be toxic; moralists attacked it on grounds of deception and danger. The verbal form 'fairing' — to make fair — is noted by Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'fair,' verb) as a deliberate coinage. 'Art' throughout the sonnets means skill or craft, not fine arts; the 'borrowed' face picks up the legal-property language of the heir/bastard couplet above: a borrowed thing is not yours and must eventually be returned, exposing the true face beneath. The phrase equates cosmetics with theatrical disguise — a mask worn over the real self.

anchor_text: Sweet beauty hath no name, no holy bower, But is profan'd
summary: A 'bower' is a sheltered private space — a lady's inner chamber or a shaded garden retreat — and by extension a sanctuary. 'Profaned' (from Latin pro fanum, 'outside the temple') means treated as common or impure: something sacred has been desecrated. The poet says that genuine beauty has no name anyone will honor and no protected space left; it has been cast out of the sacred enclosure into the degraded world of cosmetic imitation.
detail: OED records 'bower' in two senses current in 1609: a lady's private apartment or boudoir (n.1 sense 4) and a shaded garden arbor (sense 2). Both reinforce the poem's argument: beauty, which should be sheltered and reverenced, has nowhere left to dwell. The sacral language — 'holy bower,' 'profaned' — is characteristic of the sonnets' habit of treating authentic beauty and love in near-sacramental terms. 'Profane' retains its root force: what belongs inside the temple has been dragged out. Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'bower') glosses it as 'the inner apartment, the sanctuary of a lady.'

anchor_text: they mourn becoming of their woe, That every tongue says beauty should look so
summary: 'Becoming of their woe' is a compressed double meaning: (1) befitting, appropriate to their grief — they mourn in a graceful, fitting manner; and (2) graceful by means of their mourning — the act of grieving makes them beautiful. Both senses are active simultaneously. The couplet delivers the wry conclusion: those eyes mourn so becomingly that public opinion ('every tongue') has declared that beauty itself should look exactly as the mistress does — black-eyed.
detail: OED records 'becoming' as an adjective meaning 'that suits well; graceful, appropriate' (adj. sense 1, in use from the 1580s) and the verb 'become' in sense 5: 'to be becoming to, to grace.' Both collapse in the line. The epigrammatic reversal is the sonnet's final move: it opened by denying that black could be counted fair (line 1); it closes by having 'every tongue' declare that beauty should look exactly like the Dark Lady. The argument has been won without the poet ever admitting it was personal preference he was advancing. Sidney's Defence of Poesy (1595) discusses how the poet's feigning can reshape the reader's sense of what is real — the couplet enacts exactly that move.

anchor_text: blessed wood whose motion sounds
summary: 'Blessed wood' is the keyboard of a virginal — a small plucked-string keyboard instrument common in Elizabethan households, with a rectangular wooden case. When a key is pressed, an upright 'jack' (a small wooden tongue tipped with a quill) springs up and plucks the wire string; this mechanism is the 'motion' that 'sounds.' The virginals were the standard domestic keyboard instrument of the period and were strongly associated with women's music-making.
detail: The virginal (often used in the plural, 'a pair of virginals') was the most common household keyboard instrument in Elizabethan England — smaller than a harpsichord, its strings running parallel to the keyboard rather than perpendicular. The OED records 'virginal' in this sense from c. 1530. Its strings were of wire (hence 'wiry concord' at line 4), plucked by quill-tipped jacks that leap upward when a key is pressed, then fall back when released. Thomas Morley, 'A Plaine and Easie Introduction to Practicall Musicke' (London, 1597), describes the instrument's domestic place; Queen Elizabeth I was famously accomplished on the virginals, which reinforces the instrument's association with refined women. The 'motion' of line 2 refers technically to the action of the key mechanism, and 'sway'st' (line 3) describes the flowing wrist-motion of the player.

anchor_text: wiry concord that mine ear confounds
summary: 'Wiry concord' means the harmonious sound produced by the instrument's wire strings — 'concord' is the musical term for notes sounding pleasingly together (opposite of 'discord'), and 'wiry' points to the metal strings that make it. To 'confound' the ear here means to overwhelm or bewilder it with delight, not to damage it: the music so fills the speaker's senses that he cannot think of anything else.
detail: In the virginal, strings were of wire rather than gut, giving the instrument its bright, metallic timbre — making 'wiry' both a technical description and an evocative sound-word. 'Concord' as a music term for consonant sound was standard in Elizabethan usage; Shakespeare uses it in the same sense at Richard II 5.5.45 ('the concord of my state and time'). Schmidt, 'Shakespeare-Lexicon', s.v. 'confound': 'to overcome, to overpower, to perplex'; OED s.v. 'confound, v.' sense 3 records the meaning 'to bring into confusion; to bewilder, overwhelm' throughout the sixteenth century. The secondary sense of 'destroy' (OED sense 1) hovers lightly — the sound undoes the speaker's composure, which motivates the envy that follows.

anchor_text: those jacks that nimble leap, / To kiss the tender inward of thy hand
summary: In the virginal's mechanism, each 'jack' is a small upright piece of wood that springs upward to pluck its string when a key is pressed, then drops back when released — it literally leaps to touch the underside of the player's finger. But 'jack' in Elizabethan English also meant a low-born, presumptuous fellow (a 'cheap jack,' an 'every man jack'). Both meanings fire at once: the mechanical parts are also impertinent upstarts who dare touch the Dark Lady's palm when the poet's lips must stand at a distance.

'jack, n.1' sense 21: 'In a keyed instrument of the harpsichord class: an upright piece of wood fixed upon the back of each key-lever, bearing a tongue of leather or quill which twangs the string when the key is depressed.' OED s.v. 'jack, n.1' sense 1b: 'A low-bred or ill-mannered fellow; a knave, rogue.' Both senses were current and available; the word's double charge is confirmed and extended in the couplet's 'saucy jacks' (TLN 1790), where 'saucy' (impudent, forward) clinches the human-knave reading. 'The tender inward of thy hand' is the sensitive inner palm, the most intimate surface available — the contact made by a rising jack is imagined as a kiss. Onions, 'Shakespeare Glossary', s.v. 'jack': records both the instrument sense and the term of contempt.

anchor_text: To be so tickled, they would change their state / And situation with those dancing chips
summary: 'Tickled' carries an erotic suggestion alongside its plain sense of 'lightly touched': the lips wish to feel exactly the light, repeated finger-touch that the keyboard keys receive. 'Chips' dismisses the keys as mere splinters of dead wood — which makes the paradox sharper: a fragment of wood enjoys what living lips are denied. The word 'tickled' is the sonnet's most explicit erotic signal before the couplet's outright request for a kiss.
detail: OED s.v. 'tickle, v.' sense 3b records the pleasurable and sexually suggestive sense ('to affect with a pleasurable sensation') in the period; Schmidt, 'Shakespeare-Lexicon', s.v. 'tickle': 'to touch lightly so as to cause a titillating sensation.' The erotic reading is not concealed but is present simultaneously with the plain sense — the speaker acknowledges both openly, which suits the sonnet's tone of self-mocking wit. 'Chips' (OED s.v. 'chip, n.' sense 1: 'A small piece cut or broken off; a fragment, splinter') is contemptuous: the keys are reduced to their material and dismissed, heightening the irony that they are 'more bless'd than living lips' (line 12). The topos of the lover who envies an inanimate object its contact with the beloved is classical in origin — Ovid envies a ring he sends to his mistress at Amores 2.15.1-8 ('I would I were the ring thou dost put on') — but Shakespeare presses it through the instrumental pun into specifically Elizabethan wit.

anchor_text: expense of spirit in a waste of shame
summary: "Expense" means expenditure or spending, not cost in the modern sense. The opening line therefore enacts its diagnosis before the poem explains it: spending spirit in a waste of shame is simultaneously the act, the consequence, and the moral landscape it produces. anchor_text: A bliss in proof,-- and prov'd, a very woe; Before, a joy propos'd; behind a dream.
summary: "In proof" means while being experienced or tested — while the act is actually happening. "Prov'd" means once it is finished, once the experience is over and its result is known. The dash after "proof" enacts the moment of reversal: what was bliss in the doing becomes "a very woe" in the having-done. "Before" means before the act; "behind" means after — a joy imagined in advance collapses to a dream (something that felt real and turned out not to be).

The sequence "proposed joy" becoming "a dream" echoes the standard physiological account of post-coital depression (a recognized phenomenon in Galenic medicine: the body's vital spirits spent, the mind left cold and emptied). Schmidt notes that "before" and "behind" here function as temporal adverbs meaning prior to and subsequent to the act (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. "before" adv. 2; "behind" adv. 2).

anchor_text: I never saw a goddess go,-- / My mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground
summary: 'Go' here means 'walk' or 'move.' The poet grants he has never personally seen a goddess walk, then observes that his mistress, by contrast, demonstrably does touch the ground. The 'concession' is the anti-blazon's wittiest move: he cannot disprove what he has never seen, but he can report what he has.

The rhetorical figure here is praeteritio in reverse: the poet omits mentioning what he has not seen (a goddess), then substitutes what he has. The line also sets up the couplet's logical argument: having denied all the false comparisons, the poet can finally claim his love is grounded in something real.

anchor_text: my love as rare, / As any she belied with false compare
summary: This is the volta — the turn that reverses the whole poem's apparent direction. 'Belied' means both 'lied about' and 'misrepresented'; 'false compare' means inaccurate comparisons. The couplet argues that the women praised in conventional sonnets were also not actually like suns, coral, snow, and roses — their poets were simply lying. His mistress, honestly perceived, is as rare and worth loving as any woman falsely flattered into an impossible ideal. The anti-blazon turns out to be a love poem.

The volta — normally at line 9 in the Petrarchan sonnet, here compressed into the closing couplet — is the engine of the poem's argument. The couplet thus does not concede defeat; it accuses all other sonnet-writers of flattery. Philip Sidney's Defence of Poesy (1595) already raised the question of whether the poet 'lies' when he praises — 'he nothing affirmeth, and therefore never lieth.' Shakespeare answers: the bad sonneteer does lie, and the lie dishonors the real woman. The connection to the Fair Youth / Dark Lady sequence's running meditation on truth and falsehood is direct (compare Sonnets 127 and 138).

anchor_text: In nothing art thou black save in thy deeds, And thence this slander, as I think, proceeds
summary: The couplet turns on a double meaning of 'black.' The poet has been defending the Dark Lady's dark complexion, then suddenly uses 'black' in its moral sense — wickedness, evil behavior. He is saying: I have proved your physical darkness is beautiful; the only true darkness in you is in your conduct. That moral darkness, he speculates, is the real source of the slander against your looks — as if people, sensing your moral fault, project it onto your appearance.

The couplet thus enacts the sonnet's central irony: physical beauty is redeemed, moral beauty is not.

anchor_text: put on black and loving mourners be
summary: To 'put on black' is to dress in mourning clothes. In Elizabethan England, deep black garments were the required costume of formal grief after a death. The poet's conceit turns the Dark Lady's dark eyes into a pair of mourners who have voluntarily dressed themselves in black out of sympathy — as if the eyes are attending the funeral of his happiness.

Shakespeare uses the convention in Hamlet, where the prince's 'inky cloak' and 'suits of solemn black' are the outward badge of grief that the court has set aside. Here the conceit is that the Dark Lady's dark irises have 'put on' the black of mourning of their own accord — a gentler, more sympathetic act than the deliberate hardness of her heart. The pun on 'mourning / morning,' sustained through lines 1836 and 1838, doubles the visual logic: the eyes are in mourning (grief) and they resemble the morning sun beautifying the grey east.

anchor_text: full star that ushers in the even
summary: The 'full star that ushers in the even' is the evening star — the planet Venus, which appears bright in the western sky just after sunset. Venus was identified in classical astronomy with both the morning star (Phosphorus or Lucifer) and the evening star (Hesperus). The poet says the Dark Lady's eyes outshine even this star as an ornament of the sky — and since Venus is the goddess of love, the comparison quietly acknowledges what draws him to her.
detail: The identification of the evening star with Venus (Aphrodite) is ancient: Pliny the Elder notes in Natural History 2.36-37 that the same planet appears as the morning star before sunrise (called Lucifer, 'light-bearer') and as the evening star after sunset (called Vesper or Hesperus), and that it is sacred to Venus. Horace names it 'Hesperus' in Odes 2.9. The planet's brilliance made it the most conspicuous object in the western sky at dusk, so it was the natural comparison for any bright light that 'ushers in' — leads in, introduces — the evening. That Venus, the planet of love, should be the comparator for the Dark Lady's eyes is not accidental: the divine association deepens the erotic charge of the astronomical compliment.

anchor_text: let it then as well beseem thy heart
summary: Line 9 is the volta — the turn in the sonnet's argument. The first eight lines praise the Dark Lady's mourning eyes as more beautiful than the morning sun or the evening star. At 'O! let it then as well beseem thy heart' the poet pivots from compliment to plea: if mourning so becomes your face, let your heart mourn for me too. 'Beseem' means to suit or become, as in 'what becomes you.' The logic is almost a legal argument: the precedent set by the eyes should bind the heart.
detail: In the Shakespearean (English) sonnet form, the turn of thought — the volta — occurs at the opening of the third quatrain (line 9) or in the couplet. George Puttenham in The Arte of English Poesie (1589) describes the volta as the hinge on which the whole sonnet turns: the first eight lines establish a premise or description, and the final six drive to a conclusion. Here the pivot is logically elegant: the poet uses the beauty of the lady's mourning eyes as evidence that mourning itself is becoming, then argues it should extend inward to her heart. 'Beseem' is recorded by OED (s.v. 'beseem' v., sense 1) as 'to be becoming or suitable to; to suit, befit' — standard in Elizabethan usage and obsolete thereafter.

anchor_text: beauty herself is black, And all they foul that thy complexion lack
summary: The closing couplet inverts the conventional equation of beauty with fairness (pale skin, light colouring) that dominated Petrarchan love poetry. Here the couplet presses further — not merely that her darkness does not disqualify her, but that it defines beauty itself. 'Foul' (OED s.v. 'foul' adj. 1: 'offensive to the senses, ugly') is the standard antonym of 'fair' (OED s.v. 'fair' adj. 1: 'beautiful, attractive,' with specific connotations of light colouring), so the reversal is total. The sonnet's volta at line 9 set up the conditional: if she pities him, he will be her champion and redefine the entire standard of beauty in her favour. Puttenham in The Arte of English Poesie (1589) classifies this reversal of a stated value as 'antitheton,' the figure of counter-turn.

anchor_text: Beshrew that heart
summary: 'Beshrew' is a mild Elizabethan imprecation meaning 'a plague on' or 'shame upon.' The mildness is rhetorically pointed: the poet accuses without condemning, which mirrors his inability to sever himself from the woman he blames.

anchor_text: my next self thou harder hast engross'd
summary: 'My next self' is the Renaissance formula for a closest friend — a second self, another version of the same person. 'Engross'd' means seized entirely; it is also a legal term for writing out a deed in the large formal hand that makes a contract binding and final. The mistress has acquired the friend as absolutely as a signed instrument conveys property.

Florio, 1603) and into standard English Renaissance usage. The OED records 'engross' in the legal sense 'to write out a document in large formal characters, rendering it official and binding' from the fourteenth century, and in the commercial sense 'to buy up the whole supply of a commodity so as to monopolize it' from the fifteenth. Both senses are audible: the mistress has formalized her hold on the friend as a deed formalizes ownership, and has taken him wholesale. 'Harder' — more harshly, more firmly — means her grip on the friend is even tighter than on the poet, compounding the injury.

anchor_text: Prison my heart in thy steel bosom's ward
summary: Lines 1856-1859 build a sustained legal conceit using four interlocked prison-law terms: 'ward' (a prison cell; also legal custody), 'bail' (security that releases a prisoner pending trial), 'guard' (a jailer or keeper), and 'rigour' (strict enforcement of a penalty, without mercy). The poet proposes a formal deal — imprison his heart in the mistress's custody so it stands as surety for the friend's release.
detail: Each term carries precise legal weight in Elizabethan English. A 'ward' was both a division of a prison and a person held under legal guardianship; 'thy steel bosom's ward' makes the mistress's body itself a prison, and the poet a ward (dependent) within it. 'Bail' was the recognizance pledged by a third party (the bailor) guaranteeing a released prisoner's return for trial; forfeiture of the pledge followed if the prisoner absconded. 'Rigour' denoted untempered legal strictness — the antonym of equity or mercy, the quality the poet begs the mistress to withhold. The conceit is identified by Puttenham in 'The Arte of English Poesie' (1589) as 'allegoria': a sustained metaphor in which the whole argument is carried by a single vehicle. The couplet collapses the deal: 'pent in thee,' the poet is already her prisoner, and whatever he pledges as bail is hers to revoke.

anchor_text: mortgag'd to thy will
summary: A mortgage in Elizabethan law was a pledge of property as security for a debt: the borrower forfeited the pledged asset if the debt went unpaid. The poet says he has pledged himself as collateral to the Dark Lady. 'Will' simultaneously means desire, the legal term for a testamentary will, and — in the Dark Lady sonnets — the name Will, pointing to the poet himself. All three senses are active: he is bound to her desire, subject to her will as property, and literally named 'Will.'

A mortgage did not transfer ownership outright; the mortgagor retained possession while the debt ran, but forfeited the property on default. The poet figures himself as property in default — already forfeited. OED records 'will' in the senses of volition, testament, and carnal desire from the medieval period; the name-pun is clinched by sonnets 135-136 where 'Will' appears capitalized in the 1609 quarto.

anchor_text: surety-like to write for me, / Under that bond
summary: A surety (pronounced 'shoor-it-ee') was a person who formally guaranteed someone else's debt: if the original debtor could not pay, the surety was legally obligated to pay instead. The friend signed himself as the poet's guarantor — 'wrote for' him, meaning co-signed the bond — and is now as tightly bound by it as the poet ever was.

anchor_text: The statute of thy beauty thou wilt take
summary: A 'statute' (short for 'statute staple') was an Elizabethan legal instrument that gave a creditor immediate rights over a debtor's land and goods upon default, without further court proceedings. The poet says the Dark Lady will invoke the full legal force of her beauty to seize everything owed her. Her beauty is the instrument of debt, and she will enforce it to the last penny.

By Shakespeare's day 'take the statute' meant to enforce this right. The metaphor is precise: the Dark Lady's beauty created the bond (the poet and the friend were enslaved by it), and she now 'takes' it — calls in the full claim. The phrase also anticipates 'sue a friend' in the next line, extending the legal proceedings through two consecutive lines.

anchor_text: Thou usurer, that putt'st forth all to use
summary: A usurer was a moneylender who charged interest — condemned by the medieval Church and by Aristotle as morally corrupt, because money is 'barren' and should not breed more money. 'Putt'st forth all to use' means lends out everything at interest: the Dark Lady deploys every person and every asset for gain, withholding nothing for free. The word 'use' (= interest, profit from lending) is repeated from the financial conceit that runs through the whole sonnet.
detail: The English statute 13 Elizabeth I c. 8 (1571) permitted interest up to ten per cent while still condemning usury as sinful. The moral stigma meant that calling someone a usurer was a serious insult — it implied greed, exploitation, and the substitution of gain for human feeling. 'Putt'st forth all to use' echoes the economic meaning of 'use' throughout the sonnet sequence: in Sonnet 6 the poet urges the Fair Youth to put his beauty 'to usury' by having children. Here the direction is reversed — the Dark Lady extracts use from others rather than generating new life. Aristotle, Politics 1.10 (1258b) is the locus classicus for the 'money is barren' argument.

anchor_text: thou hast thy 'Will,' And 'Will' to boot
summary: 'Will' carries three meanings simultaneously throughout this sonnet: (1) the speaker's own name, William; (2) sexual desire or appetite; (3) a legal will or testament. anchor_text: will is large and spacious, Not once vouchsafe to hide my will in thine
summary: 'Vouchsafe' means to condescend to grant; to deign. The word signals that the speaker petitions from a position below the woman, asking a favor she has the power to refuse. anchor_text: Make but my name thy love, and love that still

anchor_text: anchor'd in the bay where all men ride
summary: 'Anchor'd in the bay' is a seafaring metaphor for a ship that has found its harbor and rides at anchor there — but 'bay where all men ride' simultaneously figures the Dark Lady as a woman sexually available to many. anchor_text: think that a several plot, Which my heart knows the wide world's common place
summary: A 'several plot' is a privately enclosed parcel of land belonging to one person (OED s.v. 'several' adj., sense 6a). 'Common place' means land open to all — a public common. The speaker's heart deludes itself that the Dark Lady is his exclusively (a private plot), while it knows she belongs to everyone (a public common). 'Common' also carried the sense of promiscuous or sexually accessible to many.

Shakespeare deploys it here to give the self-deception precise economic content: the heart is not just romantically confused but is claiming private property rights over something that is, legally and morally, a public thoroughfare. 'Commonplace' simultaneously alludes to the rhetorical term (locus communis — a universally known saying or fact), sharpening the irony: what the heart denies is a commonplace, something everyone else already knows.

anchor_text: this false plague are they now transferr'd
summary: 'Plague' was not a metaphor for mild misfortune in Elizabethan English — it named the bubonic plague that periodically swept London, closing theatres and sealing houses. Calling his infatuation a 'plague' invokes contagion, bodily corruption, and mortality. 'False plague' means both a disease of falsehood and a deceptive disease that disguises its own lethality.

'False' modifies 'plague' in two directions: the plague is false in that it generates false perceptions, and it is itself a deception (it does not look like a mortal danger but is one). OED records 'plague' in the figurative sense of a corrupting moral influence from the mid-16th century, but the literal epidemic sense is never fully eclipsed.

anchor_text: some untutor'd youth
summary: 'Untutor'd' means untaught or without formal schooling — someone who has not yet learned how the world works. The speaker pretends to be this naive young man so that his mistress will think she is getting away with her deception, a pose he knows is false on both sides.

The pretence is doubly ironic: the speaker is old enough to know exactly what he is doing, yet he performs youth and simplicity to flatter her vanity. anchor_text: vainly thinking that she thinks me young

anchor_text: Therefore I lie with her, and she with me, And in our faults by lies we flatter'd be
summary: The couplet turns on the verb 'lie': 'to lie' means both 'to tell a falsehood' and 'to recline with someone' — that is, to have sex. Both meanings operate simultaneously and cannot be separated. The entire arrangement — mutual flattery through mutual deception — is crystallized in a couplet where the word for sexual union is also the word for the dishonesty that makes it possible.

Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon) notes the sexual sense of 'lie with' as standard in Shakespeare and his contemporaries. The word 'faults' in the last line is also double: it means both the partners' moral failing (dishonesty) and, in Elizabethan English, sexual transgression. Onions glosses 'fault' with this secondary sense. The volta in this sonnet thus falls at the couplet: the preceding twelve lines build the reciprocal self-deception, and the couplet compresses it into the single pun that makes both lies — the spoken ones and the sexual one — inseparable.

anchor_text: o'erpress'd defence can bide
summary: 'O'erpress'd' means crushed or overwhelmed under weight — the speaker's capacity to resist has been pressed flat by the force of her power over him. 'Bide' means to endure or withstand. The military language of the octave ('wound,' 'might,' 'defence') treats the beloved's cruelty as a siege; the speaker's 'defence' is not a moral stance but a garrison already broken. The word cluster anticipates the couplet's concession: since he is 'near slain' already (line 1944), killing him outright is mercy.

anchor_text: pretty looks have been mine enemies; And therefore from my face she turns my foes, That they elsewhere might dart their injuries
summary: The speaker personifies the Dark Lady's 'looks' (glances) as a hostile army that wounds by darting — shooting — at him. He then imagines she redirects them elsewhere as an act of mercy, turning his 'enemies' (her glances) away from his face so they cannot wound him further. The conceit treats the roving eye as a weapon.

Shakespeare typically handles the conceit with some irony — here the 'dart' metaphor is turned by the speaker's desperate charity into an excuse for his mistress's infidelity. By calling her glances 'foes' and 'injuries,' the speaker maintains the militarized vocabulary of the octave while pretending to construct a defence of her. The argument collapses: if her looks wound whoever they land on, turning them on others merely redistributes the injury.

anchor_text: tongue-tied patience with too much disdain

summary: 'Pity-wanting' means lacking pity -- the pain receives no compassion from her. In Elizabethan English 'wanting' regularly means 'lacking' or 'without,' not 'desiring.' The line says sorrow may force him to put into words exactly what it feels like to suffer with no mercy shown.

anchor_text: my five wits nor my five senses can
summary: The 'five wits' are the five mental faculties recognized in Renaissance psychology: common wit (which processes sensory data), imagination, fantasy, estimation, and memory. Together with the five physical senses, they were the complete apparatus of human cognition. Listing both 'five wits' and 'five senses' means not one capacity of the mind or the body can talk the heart out of its attachment.
detail: The distinction between the five exterior senses (sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell) and the five interior wits derives from Aristotle's 'De Anima' and Galen, transmitted through medieval faculty psychology and widely disseminated in Renaissance England through encyclopedias and popular literature. The faculties were understood to process sensory input and pass it through reason to the will: senses report the world, the wits interpret it, reason deliberates, and the will decides. The sonnet describes a complete system failure: the senses have condemned the Dark Lady (quatrains 1-2), the mental faculties have presumably done the same, and yet the will — embodied in 'one foolish heart' — has gone rogue. This is structurally identical to the account of lust in Sonnet 129 ('Th'expense of spirit in a waste of shame'), where desire bypasses reason entirely. On stage the same language appears in King Lear (3.4), where Poor Tom names 'five wits' — 'Tom's a-cold, / Obey thy parents, keep thy word justly, swear not, commit not with man's sworn spouse; set not thy sweet heart on proud array. Tom's a-cold' — though there in a collapsed order.

anchor_text: likeness of a man, Thy proud heart's slave and vassal wretch to be
summary: A 'vassal' was a feudal dependent bound by oath to serve an overlord; the vassal owed obedience, labor, and loyalty in exchange for protection. Calling himself a 'vassal wretch' — the lowest grade of feudal serf — the speaker places himself at the absolute bottom of the hierarchy of service. 'Leaves unsway'd the likeness of a man' means the heart deserts the mere outward form of a human being, abandoning reason and autonomy.
detail: OED records 'vassal' (n., sense 1) as a feudal tenant bound in homage and fealty to a superior lord; by extension (sense 2), any person in a position of servitude or submission. 'Unsway'd' means 'ungoverned, not ruled by reason' (OED s.v. 'sway' v., sense 9, 'to control, govern'). The phrase 'likeness of a man' is precise: the speaker retains only the outward shape — the simulacrum — of a human being, since what distinguishes a human from an animal (rational self-governance) has been surrendered. The combination 'slave and vassal wretch' piles up the vocabulary of degraded service to produce the sonnet's lowest point before the couplet: the speaker is not merely a lover but a thing deprived of full human status. Compare Iago's 'I am your own forever' and the enslavement language of Sonnets 57-58.

anchor_text: my plague thus far I count my gain, That she that makes me sin awards me pain
summary: 'Plague' is simultaneously a medical term for a devastating infectious disease and a theological term for divine punishment of sin. The couplet's turn — calling this plague a 'gain' — is bitter: his only consolation is that the woman who causes his sin also inflicts his punishment. Sin and suffering are inseparable; she is both disease and medicine.

In Christian moral theology, punishment is intrinsic to sin: to continue in a sin is to accumulate its penalty. The couplet's 'logic' is grimly circular: the speaker cannot stop sinning (as the previous twelve lines have established), and the sin itself brings its punishment through the same woman. The word 'awards' (OED s.v. 'award' v., sense 3, 'to adjudge as a penalty') suggests a quasi-judicial transaction — she dispenses pain as a sentence. This closes the sonnet on a note of resigned self-indictment rather than resolution: the 'gain' is not freedom but the identification of his torturer with his judge. Compare Sonnet 147 ('My love is as a fever, longing still / For that which longer nurseth the disease') for the same fever-as-punishment conceit, and Sonnet 129 for lust as a trap that punishes the moment it is satisfied.

anchor_text: seal'd false bonds of love as oft as mine, Robb'd others' beds' revenues of their rents
summary: Both lines use legal and financial language for infidelity. To 'seal' a bond was to press a wax seal onto a contract to make it binding; 'false bonds' are fraudulent contracts — promises of love made without intent to keep them. 'Revenues of their rents' means income rightfully belonging to others: the faithfulness owed to a spouse or partner. By calling adultery 'robbery,' the speaker treats it as a property crime against a third party, framing both himself and the Dark Lady as serial defaulters on love's obligations.
detail: Bond-sealing was a prominent legal act in Elizabethan England; Thomas Wilson's 'Arte of Rhetorique' (1553) uses the bond metaphor to illustrate contract law, and the language of bonds, seals, forfeits, and revenues saturates the sonnet sequence (compare Sonnet 134: 'The statute of thy beauty thou wilt take, / Thou usurer that putt'st forth all to use'). 'Revenues' (three syllables, stress on the second: re-VEN-ues) is archaic in its stress pattern; OED s.v. 'revenue' n. notes the variant pronunciation current through the seventeenth century. 'Rents' here means income due to a rightful owner — not money for a room, but the return due from an estate. Shakespeare's Sonnets use the economic metaphor of conjugal 'debt' (conjugal rights legally owed to a spouse) to make adultery legible as theft.

anchor_text: Be it lawful I love thee, as thou lov'st those Whom thine eyes woo
summary: 'Be it lawful' is a subjunctive construction meaning 'let it be granted' or 'let it be considered permissible' — closer to 'grant that it is lawful for me to love you.' The legal idiom continues from the bonds-and-revenues metaphor of the preceding quatrain: the speaker frames his desire as a petition before a court. The argument of lines 9-10 is: you pursue others with your eyes just as my eyes importune you — so by your own standard, my love for you should be allowed.

'Importune' (to press urgently, to solicit persistently) is from Latin importunus and was common in Elizabethan petitionary language — OED s.v. 'importune' v., sense 2: 'To urge or press (a person) with requests or solicitations.' The parallelism 'as thou lov'st those... as mine importune thee' sets the Dark Lady's conduct as the template by which the speaker's own should be judged — the tu quoque logic of the whole poem reduced to a single syntactic balance.

summary: 'Careful' here means full of care — attentive, industrious — not merely worried (OED s.v. 'careful,' adj., sense 2: 'taking pains, diligent'). 'Housewife' names the mistress of a household, a woman responsible for the domestic economy. The word is neutral and competent, not demeaning: a careful housewife is one who does her job well, which is exactly what makes the irony land — this very diligence is what causes her to abandon the child.

Shakespeare's point is not that the woman is careless but that she is so conscientious about the escaped fowl that she neglects the child — a comic inversion in which the virtue of attention produces the failure of attention.

anchor_text: pray that thou mayst have thy 'Will,'
summary: The 1609 quarto sets 'Will' in italics and with a capital, signalling a triple pun elaborated at length in Sonnets 135-136: (1) 'will' as desire or lust (OED s.v. In 143 the quarto's italics (the conventional marker for a proper name in print) hold all three meanings open at once. OED documents 'will' as sexual appetite from the fourteenth century (sense 9a). The self-humiliation of the couplet is complete: the poet does not withhold himself as a rival but offers to serve as intercessor for his own displacement, provided he receives the maternal 'kiss' of line 13 first.

anchor_text: woman colour'd ill
summary: 'Colour'd ill' collapses two meanings into one phrase: dark-complexioned (having a dark or swarthy complexion, as opposed to the conventional fair-skinned Petrarchan mistress) and morally tainted or evil-natured. The Dark Lady is defined by her darkness simultaneously in the physical and moral senses, and the ambiguity is deliberate.

'Ill' equally spans 'dark' (as in 'ill-coloured,' of an ugly or dark hue — cf. OED s.v. 'ill', adj., sense 1a) and 'morally bad.' The sonnet sequence consistently conflates the Dark Lady's physical darkness with her moral darkness: Sonnet 131 ('Thou art as tyrannous... as those whose beauties proudly make them cruel, / In nothing art thou black save in thy deeds') and Sonnet 147 make the same collapse explicit. anchor_text: one angel in another's hell
summary: In addition to its theological meaning (the angel has fallen into the devil's realm), 'hell' carried a common Elizabethan slang sense for the female genitalia. The line therefore contains a second, explicit reading: the poet guesses that the Fair Youth is now sexually inside the Dark Lady. The pun is functional — it makes the suspicion concrete — rather than merely decorative.
detail: The sexual sense of 'hell' is documented in Elizabethan usage: Eric Partridge, Shakespeare's Bawdy (1947, 3rd ed. 1968), s.v. 'hell,' traces it through multiple plays (notably All's Well That Ends Well 2.3, where the Clown makes the same equation explicit). The same pun recurs in Sonnet 129 ('th' expense of spirit in a waste of shame') and Sonnet 147, and the sequence presses it again in the final two sonnets (153-154) on Cupid's brand. In Sonnet 144 the pun closes the couplet's only concrete image of what the poet fears: not abstract corruption but an act of intercourse between his two loves. The religious register (angel, fiend, hell) and the sexual register run together throughout the sestet, each requiring the other for the full meaning of the poem.

anchor_text: bad angel fire my good one out
summary: On the surface, 'fire out' means 'expel' or 'drive out by fire' — confirming whether the good angel has been corrupted. But the phrase also carries a secondary sense rooted in the period's understanding of syphilis ('fired' = infected with venereal disease, 'fired out' = expelled from the good angel by infecting him). 'fire,' notes the Elizabethan connection between fire, burning, and venereal infection; 'burning' as a symptom of syphilis or gonorrhoea is attested widely (cf. The 1609 quarto text reads 'fire my good one out,' and editors from Malone onward have recognized the venereal dimension as consistent with the sestet's language of corruption and the sequence's wider preoccupation with disease (Sonnets 118, 147). The ambiguity is structural: both readings — supernatural corruption and sexual infection — are active simultaneously, and the poet cannot know which has occurred, which is the explicit point of lines 2014-2015 ('Yet this shall I ne'er know, but live in doubt').

anchor_text: Those lips that Love's own hand did make
summary: Sonnet 145 is the only poem in the 1609 sequence written in iambic tetrameter — eight syllables per line, four stresses — rather than the standard iambic pentameter of ten syllables. The shorter measure gives it a lighter, more song-like pace that sets it apart from the sequence surrounding it.

Every other poem in 'Shake-speares Sonnets' (1609) uses the five-stress line. Most modern editors regard 145 as an early composition, possibly predating the main sequence by years, its brevity and lightness preserved as a curiosity. Andrew Gurr identified the probable early dating in 'Shakespeare's First Poem: Sonnet 145,' Essays in Criticism 21 (1971), pp. 221-226.

anchor_text: languish'd for her sake
summary: 'Languish'd' means to waste away from longing — to suffer the physical and emotional depletion of unrequited love. It is not mere sadness but a near-physical decline, as though desire itself were draining the body. The word was a standard term for the Petrarchan lover's condition.

The medical basis was Galenic: unrequited love was classed as a genuine illness, 'love-melancholy,' that could cause pallor, sleeplessness, and wasting. Petrarch's Canzoniere gave the European lyric tradition its image of the lover pining for a cold mistress; by the 1590s the word 'languish' carried that whole convention with it.

anchor_text: gentle day, Doth follow night, who like a fiend From heaven to hell is flown away
summary: Night is compared to a 'fiend' — a devil — cast from heaven down to hell. The image draws on the biblical tradition of Lucifer's fall: the rebel angel who was expelled from heaven at the dawn of creation. As day breaks and drives away the night, the movement mirrors Satan's expulsion — the fiend flees the light.
detail: Isaiah 14:12 (Geneva 1599) reads 'How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, sonne of the morning!' — the classic proof-text for the fall of Satan, read by Christian interpreters as the rebel angel cast out at the first dawn. Luke 10:18 (Geneva 1599) has Christ say 'I sawe Satan, like lightning, fall downe from heaven.' The Geneva Bible was the standard household Bible of Elizabethan England. The image of night-as-fallen-angel works precisely: night is the realm of the fiend (hence 'works of darkness'), and the coming of day is both a natural fact and a metaphor for the expulsion of evil. The comparison also prepares the couplet's drama — 'I hate' was the hellish word, and its cancellation is a kind of dawn. The same Lucifer-fall theology animates Wolsey's self-reproach in Henry VIII (3.2): 'By that sin fell the angels.'

anchor_text: 'I hate', from hate away she threw, And sav'd my life, saying 'not you'
summary: The couplet's doubled 'hate away,' spoken aloud, sounds like 'Hath-a-way' — the surname of Shakespeare's wife, Anne Hathaway, whom he married in 1582 at age eighteen. Most scholars read this as a deliberate embedded pun, and take it as evidence that the sonnet was composed early in Shakespeare's career, possibly during courtship.
detail: The pun rests on the phonetic identity of 'hate away' and 'Hathaway' in Elizabethan pronunciation. Andrew Gurr first argued the case in detail in 'Shakespeare's First Poem: Sonnet 145,' Essays in Criticism 21 (1971), pp. 221-226, noting that the tetrameter, the simple diction, and the embedded name all point to an early, occasional lyric. Katherine Duncan-Jones endorses the reading in her Arden Third Series edition (Shakespeare's Sonnets, Arden, 1997, note to 145.13-14). Anne Hathaway was eight years older than Shakespeare; their marriage was licensed 27 November 1582, when she was already pregnant. If the pun is deliberate, the couplet doubles as a private love-gesture: 'I hate, from Hathaway she threw' — hate was dismissed by the Hathaway herself. The name appears once in each line of the couplet: 'hate away' (2028) and the silent repetition in the closing resolution.

anchor_text: Poor soul, the centre of my sinful earth
summary: The speaker directly addresses his own soul. 'Sinful earth' is the body — the mortal, fallen flesh that the soul inhabits. The soul is called the 'centre' because Christian thought located it within the body as its ruling core, though the body continually rebels against it. The repetition of 'my sinful earth' that opens line 2 was almost certainly a compositor's mistake in the 1609 Quarto printing; every editor since has emended those words to something else ('Fool'd by those rebel powers that thee array,' 'Thrall to those,' etc.), though no reading is universally agreed.
detail: The body-soul address draws on a tradition reaching from Plato's Phaedo (the soul imprisoned in the body, freed by death) through Paul's letter to the Romans (7:23, 'I see another law in my members, rebelling against the law of my mind') and into devotional prose. The 1609 Quarto reads 'My sinful earth these rebel powers array,' repeating the last three words of the previous line at the start of this one — a clear printing error, since the repeated phrase produces a metrically broken line with no plausible sense. The emendation does not affect interpretation of the surrounding lines. Shakespeare's title for the sonnet sequence names no such spiritual turn: 146 stands as the one poem in the 154-sonnet collection that looks entirely away from human love and toward the soul's own transcendence.

anchor_text: rebel powers array
summary: 'Rebel powers' are the body's appetites — hunger, desire, the senses — which mutiny against the soul's authority. 'Array' here means to marshal or equip for battle, as an army is arrayed before a fight. The soul is besieged from within by the very body it inhabits.

Thomas Elyot's 'The Governour' (1531) and Richard Hooker's 'Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity' (1593) both use the language of inward rebellion for the appetites; Paul's Romans 7 is the biblical locus. The 'body as enemy garrison' image structures the whole sonnet's argument: if the soul's own house is occupied by mutineers, it is foolish to spend resources on the walls.

anchor_text: live thou upon thy servant's loss, And let that pine to aggravate thy store
summary: The soul is told to live at the body's expense, as a master would live on a servant's labour. 'Pine' means to waste away or starve — here the body should do the suffering and deprivation it has imposed on the soul. 'Aggravate' is an archaic usage meaning to make heavier or increase — not (as in modern usage) to irritate. 'Thy store' is the soul's stock or supply of spiritual wealth: the body's self-denial adds to it.

anchor_text: Buy terms divine in selling hours of dross
summary: 'Dross' is the waste matter — slag or impurities — skimmed off molten metal during smelting; by extension, anything worthless or cheap. 'Hours of dross' are the soul's wasted worldly hours spent on vanity. 'Terms divine' are stretches of sacred or eternal time — increments of immortal life purchased by renouncing earthly pleasures. The line frames the soul's choice as a trade: give up the cheap stuff, gain the priceless.
detail: The metallurgical sense of 'dross' (slag separated from metal by melting) was primary in Shakespeare's time; OED s.v. 'dross' n. 1 records 'the scum or refuse produced in the melting of metals,' which from the fourteenth century had extended to anything worthless in comparison with what is pure and valuable. The investment idiom of 'buy' and 'selling' runs through the sestet: the soul is counselled to conduct a profitable exchange — divine time bought at the cost of earthly vanity. 'Terms' carries its legal-commercial sense (a period of time stipulated in a contract or lease), extending the mansion-and-lease metaphor of the octave into the closing argument. This is the sonnet's volta, where the rebuking questions of lines 1-8 give way to positive instruction: live so that each surrendered worldly hour 'purchases' soul-time. The Jesus of Matthew 6:19-21 supplies the underlying theological logic: 'Lay not vp treasures for your selues vpon the earth... But lay vp treasures for your selues in heauen.'

anchor_text: feed on Death, that feeds on men, And Death once dead, there's no more dying then
summary: The couplet delivers the sonnet's central paradox: if the soul turns the body's mortality into spiritual nourishment, then Death — which normally feeds on human lives — will itself be consumed and die. Once Death is dead, dying ends. The argument draws on Paul's first letter to the Corinthians (15:26, 15:54-55), where the resurrection of Christ is said to swallow Death in victory, making it 'the last enemy' to be destroyed.
detail: Paul's language in 1 Corinthians 15 is exact: 'The last enemie that shalbe destroied, is death' (15:26); and at the resurrection 'Death is swallowed vp in victorie. O death where is thy sting? O graue where is thy victorie?' (15:54-55). Shakespeare turns the theological promise into a logical chain that the soul can enact by its own choices now: live on the body's loss, and you rob Death of its sting incrementally. The cannibalistic image — Death as an eater of men — has patristic precedent; Ephesians 5:14 ('rise from the dead, and Christ shall giue thee light') and the Revelation's promise that 'there shalbe no more death' (21:4) support the eschatological horizon. The paradox that Death can be killed belongs to the same anti-triumphalist tradition as John Donne's Holy Sonnet 10 ('Death, be not proud'); both writers draw on the same Pauline source, though Donne's sonnet is later. The compressed syntax 'Death once dead' — an absolute construction — means 'once Death is itself dead.'

anchor_text: My love is as a fever longing still, For that which longer nurseth the disease
summary: The first eight lines are built on an extended medical conceit: love is a fever, the beloved is the thing that sustains the illness, and Reason is the physician whose prescriptions the patient ignores. The speaker has fired his own doctor. 'Physic' (line 8) means medicine or medical treatment.
detail: Elizabethan medicine held that the body's health depended on the balance of four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile). A fever arose when one humor was in excess; obsessive love was classified as a genuine pathology — amor hereos, a form of melancholy — that physicians prescribed against with cold baths, travel, and music. By making Reason the physician who has abandoned the case, Shakespeare maps onto a recognized medical-philosophical framework: the Stoic principle that reason must govern the passions, and when it fails to govern them, disorder follows. That Reason 'left' — not that it was defeated, but that it walked away from a hopeless patient — is the crux of the speaker's self-diagnosis. 'Physic' (from Greek physis, nature) meant medicine or the medical art; 'prescriptions' are the physician's orders for diet and behavior. The word pair 'physic / prescriptions' carries the conceit throughout the octet. The term 'amor hereos' is attested in Robert Burton, Anatomy of Melancholy (1621), Part 3, Section 2, as a recognized medical category; the tradition goes back through medieval physicians to ancient sources.

anchor_text: give the lie to my true sight
summary: 'Give the lie' is an Elizabethan idiom for calling someone a liar to their face — the most serious public insult one person could offer another. The poet says the Dark Lady compels him to accuse his own eyes of lying: to 'swear that brightness doth not grace the day' means to deny something as plain as daylight.
detail: To 'give the lie' was a formal accusation; in aristocratic circles it could demand satisfaction by combat and is catalogued in dueling manuals of the period. Shakespeare places it at Touchstone's catalogue of the degrees of the lie in As You Like It 5.4. Here the poet turns the phrase inward: he gives the lie not to a rival but to his own sight, swearing against the plain evidence of his eyes. The hyperbole — denying that brightness graces the day — is the strongest possible illustration: to lie about daylight itself. Shakespeare uses a cognate conceit in Sonnet 148, the sonnet three before this one.

anchor_text: the very refuse of thy deeds There is such strength and warrantise of skill
summary: 'Refuse' (accent on the first syllable: REF-yooz) is a noun meaning cast-off waste, the worst leavings — not 'refusal.' 'Warrantise' is a legal term: a formal guarantee or warranty of quality. Together they say: even in the discarded dregs of her conduct, the poet finds something that seems to certify mastery.

'warrantise,' n., sense 1) is drawn from property law: a covenant by which a grantor warranted good title; extended here to mean a certified proof or assurance of skill. The legal register — refuse, warrantise — gives the quatrain a mock-judicial tone, as if the poet is weighing evidence and still reaching a verdict against reason.

anchor_text: Love is too young to know what conscience is
summary: Love here is personified as Cupid, the Roman god of desire, conventionally depicted as a young child — and therefore incapable of moral knowledge. The paradox in line 2 ('Yet who knows not conscience is born of love?') then immediately undercuts this excuse: the very faculty of moral feeling grows out of the experience of loving someone.
detail: Cupid (Greek Eros) was routinely represented in classical and Renaissance art as a small boy, often blindfolded, who shoots arrows at random. Ovid's Metamorphoses 1.452-474 and 5.365-384 establish the blind, boyish, irrational figure that Renaissance poets inherited. The argument 'Love is a child, so Love lacks conscience' was a recognized sophism in erotic verse; Shakespeare sets it up only to demolish it with the turn of line 2101. Puttenham's 'Arte of English Poesie' (1589) identifies the figure of 'antitheton' (placing opposite propositions side by side) as a device of argument; the two-line pivot here is a compressed example.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.452-474 (Cupid as the archer-boy who inflames Apollo with golden arrow; the classic image of his arbitrary, childish power).

sources.name: Ovid, Amores
sources.citation: Ovid, Amores 1.1 (the poet protests against the boy-god Cupid's authority: 'Arma gravi numero... puer saeve, quid obicis?'); the standard Latin school-text for the figure of Love as an irrational child.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2100

The Cupid-as-child reading is the plain sense of the line and the standard Renaissance trope; the Puttenham antitheton gloss is a reasonable bonus observation rather than overreach, and the two-line pivot is accurately described.

anchor_text: gentle cheater, urge not my amiss
summary: 'Gentle cheater' is a deliberate oxymoron: 'gentle' means well-born, tender, and loving; 'cheater' means one who deceives or defrauds. The speaker accuses the Dark Lady of treachery while addressing her with affection in the same breath. 'Urge not my amiss' means 'do not press me about my wrongdoing' — 'amiss' as a noun denoting fault or transgression.
detail: OED records 'gentle' in the senses of 'well-born,' 'kind,' and 'mild' (s.v. 'gentle' adj., senses I-III), all current in the period. 'Cheater' derives from 'escheat,' the legal forfeiture of property to the crown through fraud or failure of heirs; by Shakespeare's day it had extended to any deceiver. OED s.v. 'cheater' n., sense 2: 'one who cheats or defrauds; a swindler.' The oxymoron is a standard sonnet device for capturing the lover's contradictory relationship to the beloved — affection and accusation simultaneous. 'Amiss' as a noun (a fault, an offence) is recorded by Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'amiss' n.

'Gentle cheater' as affectionate-yet-accusatory oxymoron is well-supported by the immediate context (TLN 2103 confirms her guilt mirrors his), and 'amiss' as a noun denoting fault is documented Shakespearean usage.

anchor_text: I do betray My nobler part to my gross body's treason
summary: 'Nobler part' means the rational soul or faculty of reason, as opposed to the body and its appetites. Renaissance moral philosophy divided the human being into a higher, rational soul (capable of virtue and conscience) and a lower, bodily nature driven by appetite and sensation. The speaker confesses that the Dark Lady's betrayal of him has caused him to betray his own soul to the demands of his flesh.
detail: The soul-versus-body hierarchy is the central assumption of Neoplatonic moral philosophy as it reached Elizabethan England. The soul's 'nobility' derives from its proximity to divine reason; the body is 'gross' — material, heavy, earthbound. OED s.v. 'gross' adj., sense 3: 'coarse, thick; material as opposed to spiritual.' The word 'treason' applied to the body is pointed: the body is not merely weak but actively treasonous — it overthrows the legitimate sovereign (reason-as-soul). Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'part,' records the sense of a constituent element or faculty of a person.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2104

The soul/body hierarchy underlying 'nobler part' is the plain Neoplatonic framework the poem explicitly invokes (TLN 2104-2106 name 'soul' and 'body' directly), and 'gross' for corporeal/material is standard period usage.

anchor_text: flesh stays no farther reason, But rising at thy name doth point out thee
summary: 'Stays no farther reason' means 'waits for no further argument' — the body requires no more persuading. 'Rising at thy name' simultaneously means standing up at attention (as a soldier summoned) and sexual arousal. 'Point out' means to indicate, but 'point' was Elizabethan slang for the penis. The passage is deliberately explicit: the soul gives the body permission to act, and the body acts entirely in physical terms.
detail: OED s.v. 'stay' v., sense 10: 'to wait, pause, tarry; to await.' 'Stays no farther reason' = requires no further delay for reasoning. The sexual senses are confirmed by OED s.v. 'rise' v., sense 20b: 'of the male organ: to become erect' (examples from the period). 'Point' as a bawdy term is documented in Partridge, Shakespeare's Bawdy (3rd ed. 1968), s.v. 'point': 'the penis'; compare Sonnet 20's 'one thing to my purpose nothing' and the plays' widespread use of the pun (e.g. Love's Labour's Lost 4.1, Much Ado About Nothing 2.1). The lines carry the double register throughout: the language of rational deliberation (reason, soul's counsel, triumph) and the language of the body acting without deliberation.

anchor_text: To stand in thy affairs, fall by thy side
summary: 'Stand' and 'fall' operate on two levels simultaneously. In the literal sense the body-as-drudge stands ready in the mistress's service and falls beside her. In the sexual sense 'stand' means erection and 'fall' means detumescence or the act of coition. The couplet extends the same pun ('rise and fall,' line 2113), where 'rise' echoes the earlier 'rising at thy name' and 'fall' closes the bodily action. The poem ends not with moral resolution but with the body's physical rhythm.

'fall' v., sense 43: 'to have sexual intercourse; to fall (to sin)' — the moral and physical senses were blurred deliberately. Partridge, 'Shakespeare's Bawdy' (3rd ed., 1968), s.v. 'stand' and 'fall,' documents both terms as standard erotic vocabulary in the period. The volta of the couplet — 'No want of conscience hold it that I call / Her love' — appears to return to the moral register of line 2100 but immediately re-grounds 'love' in the same physical sense that has driven the last six lines: the speaker calls her 'love' precisely because she makes him rise and fall. The moral paradox (love without conscience is still called love) is left unresolved.

anchor_text: thou know'st I am forsworn
summary: 'Forsworn' means guilty of breaking a solemn oath. In Elizabethan England an oath was sworn before God, making its violation not just a social failing but a spiritual crime. The poet admits he is forsworn by loving the Dark Lady; she is 'twice forsworn' because she broke her marriage vow to be with him, and then swore new love while bearing new hate.
detail: The legal and theological weight is precise: perjury in a court of law was a punishable offence; perjury before God was a sin against the Third Commandment ('Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain,' Exodus 20:7, Geneva 1599). The OED records 'forsworn' meaning 'perjured, having violated one's oath' from Old English through the seventeenth century (OED s.v. 'forswear' v., sense 2). The sonnet opens by conceding the poet's own guilt before he can accuse anyone else — a rhetorical move that strips him of standing even as he levels the charge.

anchor_text: In act thy bed-vow broke
summary: 'Bed-vow' is the vow of fidelity sworn at marriage — specifically the promise of sexual faithfulness made in the context of the marriage bed. 'In act' means in deed, not merely in intention: the Dark Lady has broken this oath by sleeping with the poet. This makes her affair with him adultery, not just romantic disloyalty.
detail: The compound 'bed-vow' does not appear to be common before Shakespeare; the OED cites this line as the first recorded use (OED s.v. 'bed-vow' n.). The phrase 'in act' meaning 'in deed, actually, not merely in word or thought' is recorded from the late sixteenth century (OED s.v. 'act' n., sense 10). The line specifies the Dark Lady's double offence: breaking the marriage vow in deed and then swearing new love to the poet while secretly bearing him new hate. The tripling of her offences against his single one sets up his eventual reversal of the charge in the sestet.

'In act thy bed-vow broke' straightforwardly means adultery in deed, and the compound 'bed-vow' as marriage oath is defensible; the detail remains within what lines 2116-2117 actually say.

anchor_text: sworn thee fair; more perjur'd I, To swear against the truth so foul a lie
summary: 'Sworn thee fair' carries two meanings at once: to have sworn an oath that she is fair (beautiful), and to have sworn in an honest or fair manner. Both senses are simultaneously false. The Dark Lady is dark-complexioned, not conventionally fair; and to call her fair required perjuring the evidence of his own sight. The couplet collapses aesthetic and moral judgment: 'foul' is the direct antonym of 'fair' in both senses — ugly and dishonest.
detail: The fair/dark opposition is the structural axis of the Dark Lady sequence, established at Sonnet 127 ('In the old age black was not counted fair') and sustained through Sonnet 152. There the poet committed to calling her beautiful by redefinition; here he recants: the redefinition was always a sworn falsehood. OED s.v. 'fair' records the simultaneous senses: A.1.a, 'beautiful to the eye'; A.2, 'free from moral stain, just, honest'; and the now-archaic sense of light complexion (as opposed to dark). 'Foul' in the last line carries equal double force: morally wicked and physically ugly (OED s.v. 'foul' adj., senses 1 and 4). George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book 3, ch. 19, names the figure of double meaning 'amphibologia.' The Petrarchan blazon convention — cataloguing the lady as fair, blonde, lily-pale — is the tradition the Dark Lady sequence has been dismantling from Sonnet 127; the couplet admits that dismantling was built on a lie.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'fair' adj., sense A.1.a: 'beautiful to the eye'; sense A.2: 'free from moral stain; just, honest'; and the light-complexion sense contrasted with dark. OED s.v. 'foul' adj., senses 1 and 4: ugly and morally corrupt.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2126

The simultaneous fair/foul polysemy (beautiful/honest vs. ugly/dishonest) is textually present and central to the Dark Lady sequence; the Puttenham amphibologia citation is appropriate and the blazon reading is mainstream.

anchor_text: Cupid laid by his brand
summary: A 'brand' is a burning torch. Cupid, the Roman god of desire, was pictured in ancient poetry carrying a torch that set hearts alight — as well as his bow and arrows. Laying the brand aside to sleep is the premise on which the whole sonnet's myth turns.
detail: The torch-bearing Cupid appears throughout Ovid: in Metamorphoses 1.456-458 Cupid is described with 'burning torch' (faces accensas) alongside his arrows. Golding's 1567 English version was the standard school text. The detail that the brand is set down — temporarily unwatched — is what the nymph of Diana exploits, and the poem's epigram-logic requires a literal transferable heat: love's fire can be physically steeped in water, borrowed, and re-ignited.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.456-458 (Cupid's burning torch); Arthur Golding's English translation (1567). OED s.v. 'brand' n. sense 1b: 'a piece of burning wood; a torch.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2128

Torch-bearing Cupid is a mainstream classical identification; the premise that a set-down brand is physically transferable heat is the poem's explicit conceit, not an over-reading.

anchor_text: dateless lively heat, still to endure, And grew a seeting bath
summary: 'Dateless' means without end or expiration — perpetual ('dateless night,' Richard II 1.3). 'Lively' means life-giving or animating, not merely cheerful. 'Seeting' is an old spelling of 'seething,' meaning boiling or bubbling. The cold spring, charged with Cupid's eternal fire, is permanently transformed into a hot, actively bubbling therapeutic bath.
detail: OED records 'dateless' adj. in the sense 'having no fixed date of termination; endless' from the 16th century; Shakespeare uses it in Richard II 1.3 ('a dateless bargain to engrossing death') and elsewhere. 'Lively' in the sense 'life-giving, vital' is attested from the 16th century (OED s.v. 'lively' adj., sense 2). 'Seething' for an actively boiling or bubbling hot liquid is standard early modern usage. The concept of a spring whose therapeutic heat was divine in origin connects to well-known classical lore about sacred hot springs (Pliny, Natural History 2.103, on sulfur springs and their medicinal uses), and to the practical fame of the Roman baths at Bath (Aquae Sulis).

anchor_text: a sad distemper'd guest
summary: 'Distempered' means physically out of balance or disordered — sick in the humoral medical sense, where health depended on the correct proportion of the four bodily fluids. 'Sad' here means heavy or grave, not merely unhappy. The speaker goes to the bath as a clinically ill patient, casting love-sickness in the language of actual medicine.
detail: OED s.v. 'distempered' adj.: 'deranged in constitution or function; disordered; disturbed.' Elizabethan medicine, derived from Galen, held that fever was an excess of heat upsetting the balance of the humors; love was diagnosable as exactly such a fever. Shakespeare uses the same humoral vocabulary throughout the Dark Lady sonnets, most explicitly in Sonnet 147 ('My love is as a fever, longing still / For that which longer nurseth the disease... past cure I am'). The detail that the speaker is 'distempered' makes the therapeutic bath plot medically coherent — he is genuinely sick; the bath is a real remedy; and its failure is therefore a real disappointment, not just a conceit.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2139
