'Distempered' in the Galenic humoral sense and 'sad' as heavy/grave are both correct early modern usages, and the cross-reference to Sonnet 147's fever vocabulary is widely noted by editors as the Dark Lady sonnets' governing conceit.

anchor_text: the general of hot desire / Was, sleeping, by a virgin hand disarm'd
summary: Cupid is called 'the general of hot desire' — a military metaphor casting him as the commander-in-chief of erotic longing, his torch the weapon of his whole army. 'Disarm'd' extends the conceit: the god who sets the world ablaze is caught asleep and stripped of his weapon by a single unarmed girl. The humor turns on the bathos — the invincible commander undone by an unguarded nap.
detail: The military personification of Cupid as general (Latin imperator) was a recognized convention of Latin erotic elegy, where the lover was styled as a soldier of love (miles amoris) under Cupid's command. Ovid's Amores 1.9 develops this at length: 'Every lover is a soldier, and Cupid has his camp' ('Militat omnis amans, et habet sua castra Cupido'). Shakespeare condenses the whole militia-amoris tradition into a single ironic scene of the general asleep and disarmed. The phrase 'hot desire' identifies the brand (the warm torch) with the psychological state it produces, making Cupid literally the 'heat' of passion he metaphorically commands.

sources.name: Ovid, Amores
sources.citation: Ovid, Amores 1.9.1-2: 'Militat omnis amans, et habet sua castra Cupido' ('Every lover is a soldier, and Cupid has his own camp'); the militia amoris tradition.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2148
Amores 1.9.1-2 ('Militat omnis amans, et habet sua castra Cupido') is accurately quoted and the militia amoris tradition it represents is correctly characterised.

The militia amoris reading and the Amores 1.9 parallel are well-established; equating 'general' with Latin imperator is loose but the overall military-commander identification of Cupid is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: This brand she quenched in a cool well by, / Which from Love's fire took heat perpetual, / Growing a bath and healthful remedy
summary: When the votary quenches Cupid's torch in the well, it transforms the water into a perpetually hot therapeutic spring. This maps onto the Elizabethan fashion for medicinal thermal baths: spas at Bath (Aquae Sulis) and Buxton were popular resorts where wealthy patients 'took the waters' as cures for fever, gout, and other ailments. The speaker comes there as a patient — and finds the waters useless against the fever of love.
detail: Thermal springs were framed medically in Shakespeare's England: John Jones, Beneficiall Boke of the Natures and Properties of Baths (1572), and William Turner, A Booke of the Natures of Bathes (1562) both describe the waters of Bath and Buxton as sovereign remedies for heat-related illnesses, skin diseases, and 'corrupt humors.' The joke of the poem is that the bath, born of love's fire, is meant to cure 'men diseas'd' — and the speaker arrives as just such a patient — but the cure fails on the one condition for which the bath was made: love's own fever cannot be cooled by water that love itself heated. The companion sonnet (153) calls the same waters 'a healthful remedy' that fails the speaker for the same reason.

sources.name: William Turner, Baths
sources.citation: William Turner, A Booke of the Natures and Properties of the Baths of England (1562), on the medicinal thermal waters of Bath.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2150
William Turner's Booke of the Natures and Properties of the Baths of England (1562) is a real, extant publication and its description as a work on English thermal medicinal waters is accurate.

Connecting the mythological bath to Elizabethan spa culture is a recognized topical reading (supported by Duncan-Jones and Booth) rather than an overreach, since the period documents cited are real and the bathos-of-cure argument accurately follows the poem's logic.

anchor_text: I, my mistress' thrall
summary: 'Thrall' means a slave or bondsman — a person held entirely in servitude to another's will. To be a 'thrall' to one's mistress is the standard conceit of Petrarchan love poetry: the lover's will is so completely conquered by desire that he becomes her captive. The speaker calls himself this even as he admits the bath (Cupid's cure for the diseased) has not worked for him.
detail: OED records 'thrall' in the sense of slave or serf from Old English (OED s.v. 'thrall,' sense A.1); its figurative application to the enslaved lover was conventional in Elizabethan sonneteering, inherited from Petrarch's image of Amor binding the poet's hands. The word surfaces in the same Dark Lady group at Sonnet 133 ('thou art the better part of me') and 134, where the poet is a 'slave' and the youth a 'bond-slave.' Here it caps the poem's turn from myth to autobiography: having narrated the classical story of Cupid and the votary, the poet steps into it as a character — the sick man who came for cure and found none, enslaved still.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'thrall,' sense A.1: 'A person in bondage; a slave, serf.' Figurative use as a slave of love is common in 16th-c. verse.

anchor_text: Love's fire heats water, water cools not love
summary: The closing line is a chiasmus — a rhetorical figure that reverses the order of paired terms (fire/water then water/love) to make a paradox. Love can transform the world (it heats even cold water into a hot spring) but the world cannot transform love (water, however hot, cools not the lover). It is simultaneously the poem's logical conclusion and its joke: the cure built from love's own heat is the one thing that cannot cure love.
detail: Chiasmus (from Greek chi, the X-shaped letter) places corresponding terms in reverse order: A-B / B-A. Here: 'Love's fire [A] heats water [B], water [B] cools not love [A].' The effect is epigrammatic — a point clicked shut like a latch. Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie (1589), lists this as 'the counter-turne' or 'Antimetabole' and notes its use for aphorisms and conclusive statements. The couplet is also the volta of the whole sonnet (and of the whole sequence, since this is the final poem): it swings from narrative back to universal principle, ending not in the speaker's recovery but in an irrefutable demonstration of love's power. The same paradox runs through the Dark Lady group, notably Sonnet 147, which opens 'My love is as a fever, longing still / For that which longer nurseth the disease.'

sources.name: Puttenham, Arte of English Poesie
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book 3, ch. 19 ('Antimetabole, or the Counterchange'), on the rhetorical figure of reversed terms.

Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie (1589) Book 3 does discuss antimetabole under the heading 'Counterchange' (Antimetauole); the chapter-19 assignment cannot be confirmed precisely but falls within the known figures section (chs. 10-20) and the substance of the citation is accurate.

The antimetabole identification and Puttenham citation are accurate; calling this line 'the volta of the whole sequence' is an interpretive stretch but not a harmful one, and the Sonnet 147 fever parallel is apt and widely noted.
